Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025): covers information and communication needs relating to disability, impairment or sensory loss, through six stages: identify, record, flag, share, meet and review.

n.0: Language needs without a disability are met through interpreting services, not the AIS.
n.1: Receiving copies is an access right, not an AIS communication need.
n.3: A general preference unrelated to disability or sensory loss is outside the AIS.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Tanaka, 82, has severe hearing loss and lip-reads. The nurse needs to explain his discharge plan. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Stand beside him and speak loudly into his better ear
Face him in good light and speak clearly at a normal pace
Give the information to his daughter to pass on later
Speak very slowly with exaggerated mouth movements
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 2.3: recognise and accommodate sensory impairments. Code 7.2-7.3: meet people's communication needs using a range of methods.

n.0: He lip-reads, so he needs to see the speaker's face; shouting distorts lip patterns.
n.2: This excludes him from his own care when he can communicate with adjustments.
n.3: Exaggeration distorts lip shapes and makes lip-reading harder.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mrs Lowe, 88, who has dementia, seems not to respond during the nurse's admission assessment. Her daughter mentions she normally wears hearing aids, which are in her bag. What should the nurse do first?
o: Complete the assessment by asking her daughter the questions
Refer her to audiology for a review of her hearing
Record that she is unable to answer the assessment questions
Check the hearing aids are working and help her put them in
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 2.4: support and manage the use of personal communication aids. Code 7.2: take reasonable steps to meet people's communication needs.

n.0: Her daughter can contribute, but Mrs Lowe should first be helped to take part herself.
n.1: A referral may be useful later, but her own aids should be fitted now.
n.2: Recording her as unable to communicate before fitting her aids would be inaccurate.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Evans, 69, has expressive aphasia after a stroke. He understands speech but struggles to find words. Which approach best supports communication?
o: Finish his sentences for him to reduce his frustration
Use closed questions, picture boards and extra time
Ask his wife to answer all questions on his behalf
Speak more loudly and repeat each sentence twice
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 2.5: identify the need for and manage alternative communication techniques. Code 7.3: use a range of verbal and non-verbal methods.

n.0: Finishing sentences may misrepresent what he means and reduces his control.
n.2: He can understand and should be supported to communicate for himself.
n.3: His difficulty is expressing words, not hearing; volume does not help.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Jamie, 30, has a learning disability and becomes very anxious in busy clinics. He is booked for a blood test. Which is the most appropriate reasonable adjustment?
o: Book a standard appointment and ask him to wait outside
Offer the first appointment of the day with extra time
Postpone the test until he feels less anxious about clinics
Ask his carer to attend in his place and take the sample later
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Proficiency P3.7: apply principles and processes for making reasonable adjustments; Equality Act 2010 s20. Annexe A 2.2 reasonable adjustments in communication.

n.0: Waiting outside does not reduce the time pressure or anxiety.
n.2: Delaying may harm his health; adjustments should make the test accessible now.
n.3: A carer cannot give the blood sample; Jamie needs an adjusted appointment.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Dunn, 66, is going home on a new medicine. He says he 'doesn't get on with reading' and has left his leaflet unopened. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Explain in plain words with pictures, then use teach-back
Explain it once in full medical terms to be accurate
Ask the pharmacist to post a copy of the leaflet to him
Give him a second copy of the leaflet in larger print
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Proficiency P2.10: provide information in accessible ways; Annexe A 2.2 clear language and appropriate materials; Annexe A 2.6 repetition and positive reinforcement; Code 7.4 check understanding.

n.1: Medical terms reduce understanding; Code 7.1 requires terms people can understand.
n.2: Posting the same written information will not help him understand it.
n.3: Larger print does not address difficulty with reading.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mrs Harper, 58, is choosing between two treatment options for her knee. She asks the nurse what she would do. What is the nurse's most appropriate response?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to decide by tomorrow morning
Tell her which of the two options the nurse would personally choose
Advise her to follow whatever the consultant recommends
Explore what matters to her and each option's risks and benefits
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire [2015] UKSC 11: patients must be made aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. Code 2.3: encourage and empower people to share decisions; P4.2 shared decision making.

n.0: Written information alone, with a deadline, does not support shared decision making.
n.1: Personal preference replaces her own values and undermines shared decision making.
n.2: This removes her from the decision instead of supporting an informed choice.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Lin, 72, needs a urinary catheter. Before starting, what information is most important for the nurse to give him?
o: The infection statistics for catheters in the trust
The size of catheter and type of lubricant being used
How long the nurse has been carrying out catheterisation
Why it is needed, what it involves and what he will feel
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Proficiency P4.3: provide accurate information before, during and after interventions. Code 4.2: gain properly informed consent before any action.

n.0: Statistics alone do not explain the procedure or support consent.
n.1: Technical details matter less than understanding the reason and experience.
n.2: The nurse's experience does not inform him about the procedure itself.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: After removing Mrs Fox's urinary catheter, the nurse wants to provide appropriate information. Which information is most important to give at this stage?
o: How the catheter was inserted on admission
The cost to the NHS of treating catheter-related infections
When to expect to pass urine and what to report if not
Which brand of catheter was used during her stay
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Proficiency P4.3: provide accurate information after interventions. Annexe A 2.8: provide information and respond to questions about treatment and care.

n.0: Past insertion details do not help her manage the next few hours.
n.1: Cost information does not support her recovery or safety.
n.3: Product details are not needed for her to recognise problems.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Adeyemi, 52, has type 2 diabetes and feels he 'always gets it wrong'. Which statement by the nurse best reflects a strengths-based approach?
o: "Your HbA1c is still too high, so we need to fix your diet."
"Most people find diabetes hard. Keep trying your best."
"Let's list all the things that went wrong this month."
"You've walked every day this month. How could we build on that?"
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Proficiency P2.9: use communication skills and strength-based approaches to support people to make informed choices. Code 2.2 recognise the contribution people make to their own health.

n.0: This focuses on deficits rather than his strengths.
n.1: This is generic and does not identify or use his strengths.
n.2: Focusing on failures reinforces his belief that he gets it wrong.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mrs Brennan, 66, has heart failure and wants to stay well at home. Which nursing action best supports her self-management?
o: Agree a written plan with her, including when to seek help
Tell her to rest and avoid activity until her next review
Arrange for a carer to manage her medicines at home
Ask her to phone the ward whenever she feels unwell
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Proficiency P4.2: work in partnership to encourage shared decision making and support people to manage their own care. Code 2.1-2.3.

n.1: This is not person-centred and may not reflect her condition or goals.
n.2: Taking over her medicines reduces self-management without a reason to do so.
n.3: This keeps her dependent and does not build her own management skills.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Rowe, 74, is recovering from a hip fracture. The nurse and Mr Rowe are agreeing a mobility goal. Which goal is most appropriate?
o: Improve his mobility as much as possible before discharge
Walk to the day room with his frame by Friday, as he chose
Follow the physiotherapy plan written for all hip patients
Walk 200 metres unaided by tomorrow, as set by the team
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Proficiency P3.4: apply a person-centred approach to shared assessment, planning, decision making and goal setting. Code 2.1 work in partnership.

n.0: This is vague and not measurable or time-bound.
n.2: A standard plan is not a personal, shared goal.
n.3: This is set for him, not with him, and may be unrealistic.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Daly, 80, has capacity. When the nurse begins to explain his scan results, he says, "I don't want the details. Just tell my daughter." What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain the results fully, as he has a legal right to know them all
Respect his wish, check what he wants to know and his consent to share
Tell his daughter everything and give him no information himself
Delay the conversation until he is ready for all the details
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Code 2.4: respect the level to which people want to be involved in decisions about their care. Code 5.5: share information with families as far as the law allows, with consent.

n.0: Code 2.4 requires respect for the level of involvement he wants.
n.2: He should be asked what he does want to know, and his consent confirmed first.
n.3: He has stated his wish now; delaying ignores it.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mrs Taylor cares for her husband, 79, who has capacity and is being discharged after a stroke. She says nobody has involved her in his care planning. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer her to the GP to discuss her husband's care plan
Ask if he wants her involved, then involve her and offer a carer's assessment
Involve her fully, as she will be the one providing his care at home
Explain that his care plan is confidential and cannot be shared with her
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Code 5.5: share information with families as far as the law allows; Code 2.1 partnership. Care Act 2014 s10: carers have a right to a carer's assessment. Proficiency P1.13 relationships with carers.

n.0: Passing her elsewhere does not involve her in his discharge planning.
n.2: His consent is needed before sharing his information and involving her.
n.3: If he agrees, she can be involved; refusing outright ignores her role.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Nurse Holly has been asked to support a doctor who will tell Mr Pearce, 61, that his biopsy shows cancer. Which preparation is most appropriate?
o: Tell Mr Pearce the result first so the doctor can focus on treatment
Arrange a private room and hand her bleep to a colleague
Ask a relative to break the news before the doctor arrives
Use the bay with curtains drawn to save time
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 2.9: engage in difficult conversations including breaking bad news. Code 1.1 dignity, 5.1 privacy and 2.6 respond compassionately to distress.

n.0: Delivering the diagnosis outside the planned conversation risks giving it without support.
n.2: Results should be given by the clinical team, with the patient's consent to involve others.
n.3: Curtains do not give privacy; a private room protects dignity and confidentiality.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Before giving Mrs Okoro, 54, the results of her scan, the doctor and nurse want to check what she already understands. Which opening question is most appropriate?
o: "Have you prepared yourself for some bad news today?"
"What have you been told so far about the scan?"
"Do you know what a malignant tumour is?"
"Shall I go straight to the results for you?"
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations; Code 7.4 check understanding; Code 7.1 use terms people understand.

n.0: This alarms her without finding out what she knows.
n.2: This uses jargon and jumps ahead before her understanding is known.
n.3: Going straight to results skips checking her understanding first.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: After hearing his cancer has spread, Mr Ward, 70, falls silent and starts to cry. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Step out of the room and return once he is calmer
Reassure him that many people live for years with this
Stay with him, allow silence and acknowledge his feelings
Explain the treatment options to him while he takes it in
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 2.9 convey compassion during difficult conversations; Code 2.6 respond compassionately to distress; P1.12 support people who are emotionally vulnerable.

n.0: Leaving may feel like abandonment at a vulnerable moment.
n.1: This may be inaccurate and closes down his emotions.
n.3: Giving more information while he is distressed is unlikely to be absorbed.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mrs Bishop is angry at the nurses' station because her father's call bell went unanswered for 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her to put her complaint in writing to the manager
Explain that the ward is short-staffed with two nurses off sick
Listen, acknowledge her concern and apologise to her
Call security as she is raising her voice at staff
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations with compassion; Code 2.6 respond compassionately and politely to distress; Code 14.2 apologise when things go wrong.

n.0: Formal routes may follow, but she first needs to be heard.
n.1: Giving reasons first can sound defensive and does not acknowledge her concern.
n.3: Raised voices about a genuine concern do not warrant security as a first step.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Hale has made a formal complaint about Nurse Ivy's attitude. He is still on her ward and allocated to her care today. What does the Code require of Ivy?
o: Discuss the complaint with him to resolve it today
Continue to give him the same standard of care
Avoid speaking to him beyond essential care tasks
Ask to be moved from his care until the complaint is closed
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Code 24.1: never allow someone's complaint to affect the care that is provided to them. Code 24.2: use complaints as feedback for reflection and learning.

n.0: Handling the complaint is for the complaints process; her duty is to keep caring for him fairly.
n.2: Limiting communication lets the complaint affect his care.
n.3: Moving may be considered locally, but the Code requirement is that the complaint must not affect his care.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Burke, 64, has capacity and is waiting for biopsy results. His wife asks the nurse to make sure he is not told if it is cancer, as 'it would destroy him'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer the decision to the consultant to settle with his wife
Tell her that her request is unlawful and end the conversation there
Explore her worries and explain he will be asked what he wants to know
Agree, and record her request on the front of the notes
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Code 2.4 respect the level of involvement a person wants; Code 5.5 share with the person the information they want or need to know. Annexe A 2.9 difficult conversations.

n.0: The decision about what he is told rests with him, not with his wife and the consultant.
n.1: This dismisses her distress; her worries need exploring with compassion.
n.3: He has capacity; withholding his diagnosis at another's request breaches his right to information.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: A doctor needs to tell Mrs Ibrahim, 70, who speaks Somali and limited English, that her husband has died in intensive care. Her adult niece is with her. What is the most appropriate way to communicate?
o: Wait until her son arrives to translate later that day
Use a professional Somali interpreter for the conversation
Give the news in simple English and check she understands
Ask the niece to interpret, as she is family and will support her
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: NHS England interpreting guidance (2018): always offer a registered interpreter; reliance on family is strongly discouraged. Code 7.2 meet language needs; Annexe A 2.9.

n.0: Delaying the news without reason causes distress; an interpreter can be arranged now.
n.2: Simple English risks misunderstanding when news is this serious.
n.3: Relying on family is discouraged; the niece is also grieving and may filter the news.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: At 03:00 Mr Fry, 58, recently diagnosed with motor neurone disease, is awake and tearful and says, "What's the point of carrying on?" What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reassure him that things will look brighter in the morning light
Offer him a sleeping tablet so that he can rest
Tell him the doctor will talk it through with him on the ward round
Sit with him, explore his meaning and ask about self-harm thoughts
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Proficiency P1.12: support people who are emotionally vulnerable; Code 2.6 respond compassionately to distress; Code 17.1 protect people at risk. NICE NG225: assess and support with a safety plan, not risk tools.

n.0: False reassurance dismisses possible suicidal thoughts that need exploring.
n.1: Sedation does not address his distress or assess his safety.
n.2: Delaying leaves a possibly at-risk person unsupported now.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Kerry, 35, smokes 20 cigarettes a day. She says, "I know I should stop, but it's the only thing that calms me." Which response reflects motivational interviewing?
o: "Here is a leaflet listing all the risks of smoking."
"You must stop smoking now for the sake of your long-term health."
"What are the good and less good things about smoking for you?"
"Let's agree a date this week when you will stop."
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 3.1: motivational interview techniques. MI explores ambivalence through open questions and reflection rather than persuasion.

n.0: Giving information without exploring her views is not MI.
n.1: Direct persuasion tends to increase resistance; MI explores ambivalence.
n.3: Setting a date before exploring her ambivalence skips the MI process.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: A community mental health nurse asks Leon, 27, "Think of a day recently when things were a little better. What was different about that day?" Which approach is the nurse using?
o: Cognitive behavioural therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Motivational interviewing
Reminiscence therapy
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 3.2: solution-focused therapies. Asking about exceptions, when the problem was less present, builds on existing strengths.

n.0: CBT works on links between thoughts, feelings and behaviour.
n.2: MI explores ambivalence about change.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories to support wellbeing, mainly in older adults.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: On a ward for older people, a nurse uses old photographs, wartime songs and conversation about his working life with Mr Black, 89, who has dementia. Which therapeutic intervention is this?
o: Positive behaviour support
Distraction and diversion
Reminiscence therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 3.3: reminiscence therapies use memories, photographs and music to support wellbeing and identity.

n.0: PBS is a framework for understanding behaviour that challenges.
n.1: Distraction redirects attention from a stressor; this is planned recall of life history.
n.3: Solution-focused work looks for exceptions and future goals.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: On an acute ward, Mr Stone, 40, is pacing and shouting that he wants to leave. He has not harmed anyone. What is the nurse's most appropriate first approach?
o: Tell him firmly to sit down and stop shouting
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and listen to him
Call security to restrain him before he leaves
Stand in the doorway to block his exit from the ward
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 3.5: de-escalation strategies and techniques. Code 13.4 personal safety; calm voice, open posture and listening come before restrictive interventions.

n.0: Commands can escalate agitation; de-escalation uses calm listening.
n.2: Restraint is a last resort; de-escalation should be tried first.
n.3: Blocking his exit increases risk and may escalate the situation.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Tara, 22, tells the nurse, "I always fail at everything." The nurse asks her to list examples that support and contradict this thought. Which technique is this?
o: A cognitive behavioural therapy method
A motivational interviewing technique
A distraction and diversion technique
A reminiscence therapy based technique
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 3.6: cognitive behavioural therapy techniques. Examining evidence for and against an unhelpful thought is cognitive restructuring.

n.1: MI explores ambivalence about change, not evidence for thoughts.
n.2: Distraction moves attention away; this examines the thought directly.
n.3: Reminiscence uses past memories for wellbeing, not testing thoughts.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Ellie, 5, is having a cannula inserted tomorrow. Today the play specialist uses a doll with a cannula to show Ellie what will happen and let her practise on it. Which approach is this?
o: Distraction and diversion
Cognitive behavioural therapy
Solution-focused therapy
Therapeutic play
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 3.7: play therapy. Therapeutic play prepares children for procedures and helps them express feelings.

n.0: Distraction is used during the procedure; this prepares her beforehand.
n.1: CBT addresses thoughts and behaviour; this uses play to prepare.
n.2: Solution-focused work looks for exceptions and goals.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Omar, 7, is anxious during a blood test. Which intervention is most appropriate during the procedure itself?
o: Distract him with bubbles, a game or a story
Delay the test until he is no longer anxious
Explain each step of the procedure in technical detail
Ask his parent to leave the room to reduce fuss
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 3.8: distraction and diversion strategies. Distraction reduces procedural distress; Annexe A 3.7 play supports children.

n.1: Waiting for anxiety to resolve may delay needed care.
n.2: Detailed explanation during the procedure may increase anxiety.
n.3: Parental presence usually comforts children during procedures.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Sam, 26, has a learning disability and often hits out in the noisy dining room at mealtimes. The team wants to use positive behaviour support. What should they do first?
o: Assess what triggers the behaviour and what it achieves
Increase his sedation before every mealtime
Use restraint whenever he begins to hit out
Withdraw meals in the dining room as a planned consequence
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 3.9: positive behaviour support approaches. PBS uses functional assessment to understand behaviour and changes the environment proactively.

n.1: Medication as first response is not PBS and may cause harm.
n.2: Restraint is reactive; PBS starts with understanding the function of behaviour.
n.3: Punishment is not part of PBS and may breach his rights.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Nurse Ali phones a doctor about Mr Cole using SBAR. He says, "I think he may be developing sepsis." Which part of SBAR is this?
o: Assessment
Situation
Background
Recommendation
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: NHS England SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation): Assessment is the nurse's evaluation of the problem.

n.1: Situation states the immediate problem, for example 'his NEWS2 is 6'.
n.2: Background gives history and context.
n.3: Recommendation states what the nurse wants done.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Using SBAR, Nurse Mai tells the doctor, "She is 74, had a bowel resection two days ago and has COPD." Which SBAR element is this?
o: Recommendation
Assessment
Background
Situation
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: NHS England SBAR tool: Background gives the relevant history and context, such as age, admission reason and past medical history.

n.0: Recommendation is what she wants the doctor to do and by when.
n.1: Assessment is her judgement of what the problem is, for example 'I think she is dehydrated'.
n.3: Situation is the opening statement of the current problem, for example her NEWS2.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: At the end of a shift, which item is most important for Nurse Ben to include when handing over Mrs Webb, 77?
o: Her IV antibiotic is due at 18:00; her NEWS2 rose to 4
She was admitted four days ago from her own home
She enjoyed her lunch and watched television all afternoon
Her daughter visited during the afternoon
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.11: provide clear information when handing over care. Code 10.2 identify risks and problems; Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed.

n.1: Admission date is less urgent than outstanding care and deterioration.
n.2: Social details matter less than risks and time-critical care.
n.3: Visitor details are not the priority for safe handover.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Nurse Rose delegates afternoon observations on Mrs Lee, 81, to a healthcare assistant. Which instruction is clearest?
o: "Do her observations at 14:00; tell me at once if systolic is under 100."
"Keep an eye on Mrs Lee this afternoon and let me know of any concerns."
"Do Mrs Lee's obs whenever you have a moment this afternoon."
"Do Mrs Lee's observations and write them on the chart."
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Code 11.1: delegate only within competence and make sure instructions are fully understood. Annexe A 1.11: clear instructions when delegating.

n.1: This is vague and gives no time or reporting threshold.
n.2: No time is set and no reporting instructions are given.
n.3: There is no time or instruction on what to report.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: A laboratory scientist phones the ward with a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L for Mr Shaw. What is the most appropriate way for the nurse to take this result?
o: Ask the laboratory to email the result to the doctor directly
Remember it and tell the doctor at the next ward round
Write it on the handover sheet for the night team to act on
Write it down, read it back, then tell the doctor at once
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.9 and 1.11: share verbal information clearly. Writing a telephoned result down and reading it back confirms it was heard correctly, and a potassium of 6.8 mmol/L needs the doctor told at once (Code 13.2 timely referral).

n.0: Email may not be seen promptly; the nurse must act on it now.
n.1: Relying on memory risks error, and waiting delays urgent treatment.
n.2: A critical result needs immediate action, not handover.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Nurse Ella is discharging Mr Kerr, 70, with a leg wound to the district nursing team. Which referral content is most useful?
o: The wound plan, next dressing date, allergies and ward contact
A request for the team to phone the ward for details
A brief note saying that a leg wound needs regular care at home
A copy of the full nursing notes for the whole admission
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.9: share written reports clearly. Code 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care; Code 10.2 identify risks so colleagues have the information they need.

n.1: This delays care and relies on verbal handover.
n.2: This lacks the detail needed for safe continuity.
n.3: Bulk notes bury the key information the team needs.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: A practice nurse needs to send a patient's wound photographs and care plan to the community nursing team. Which method is most appropriate?
o: Send them by WhatsApp to the community nurse's phone
Print them and post them by second class mail
Email them from her personal account as it is faster
Send them through an approved, secure NHS system
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.10: analyse, record and share digital information safely. Code 10.5 keep records secure; Caldicott principles; UK GDPR integrity and confidentiality.

n.0: Personal messaging apps are not approved secure systems for clinical data.
n.1: Post is slower and less secure than approved electronic routes.
n.2: Personal email breaches data security (Code 10.5).

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Long's NEWS2 is 7. The nurse calls the junior doctor using SBAR, who says he will come 'when he can' in about two hours. What should the nurse do next?
o: Escalate now to a senior or the critical care outreach team
Record the call in the notes and hand it over to the next shift
Call the junior doctor again in one hour for an update
Wait for the junior doctor and repeat observations hourly
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): score 7 or more requires emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies and continuous monitoring. Code 16.1 escalate concerns; Annexe A 1.9.

n.1: Recording is needed, but the patient needs urgent senior review now.
n.2: Delaying further escalation for an hour is unsafe at this score.
n.3: A NEWS2 of 7 needs emergency assessment; waiting two hours is unsafe.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Nurse Leon is admitting Mrs Clarke, 63, after a bowel resection. He wants to encourage her to describe her recovery in her own words. Which question is most appropriate?
o: "Are you feeling better than yesterday?"
"Have you had any pain since your operation?"
"You're managing well with the pain now, aren't you?"
"How have you been feeling since your operation?"
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.4: make appropriate use of open and closed questioning. Open questions invite the person to describe their experience in their own words; Code 2.1 work in partnership.

n.0: This closed question limits her to a comparison and a short answer.
n.1: This is a closed question that invites a yes or no answer.
n.2: This is a leading question that suggests the answer she should give.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Mr Bell, 76, tells the nurse he is 'fine' after hip surgery, but he is grimacing, gripping the bed rail and avoiding eye contact. What is the most appropriate response?
o: "Many people say that after surgery. I'll check on you in an hour."
"You say you're fine, but you look uncomfortable. Can you tell me more?"
"Are you sure? Shall I fetch you some painkillers to be safe?"
"That's good to hear. Let me know if anything changes later on."
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.1: actively listen, recognise and respond to verbal and non-verbal cues. Code 2.6: recognise when people are anxious or in distress and respond compassionately.

n.0: This dismisses the cues and delays assessment of possible pain.
n.2: Offering analgesia without assessment skips exploring what he is experiencing.
n.3: This accepts the verbal message and misses the non-verbal cues of pain.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Nurse Ola is about to give intravenous co-amoxiclav to Mr Grant, 55, who is alert. Which question type is most appropriate immediately before giving the first dose?
o: An open question about how he feels about his treatment
A reflective question about his previous hospital stays
A closed question confirming any penicillin allergy
A leading question assuming that he has no allergies
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.4: make appropriate use of open and closed questions. Closed questions obtain specific facts, such as allergy status, quickly and clearly; Code 18 safe medicines practice.

n.0: Open questions are useful for exploring feelings but not for confirming a specific safety fact.
n.1: This does not establish the specific allergy information needed now.
n.3: Leading questions can produce a false answer to a safety-critical check.

Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.q: Nurse Jo has taught Mrs Akhtar, 70, how to use a new inhaler. Which approach best checks that Mrs Akhtar has understood?
o: Give her a leaflet and ask her to read it tonight
Ask her whether she understands how to use the inhaler
Ask her to show how she will use the inhaler at home
Repeat the explanation slowly a second time
Communication & Therapeutic Relationship.w: Annexe A 1.6: check understanding and use clarification techniques. Code 7.4: check people's understanding from time to time to keep misunderstanding or mistakes to a minimum.

n.0: A leaflet supports learning but does not check understanding now.
n.1: A yes or no answer does not show whether she can use it correctly.
n.3: Repetition may help, but it does not check what she has understood.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Ellis, 81, has advanced heart failure and full capacity. A doctor completes a DNACPR form overnight and asks the nurse not to mention it to her because 'it will only upset her'. Mrs Ellis has said she wants to be involved in all decisions. Which statement best reflects the legal position?
o: She should be consulted unless this is likely to cause her physical or psychological harm
She should be told once the decision has been reviewed by a second consultant
She need not be told because a DNACPR decision is a clinical decision for the doctor
Her husband should be told instead, as the decision affects the whole family
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: In R (Tracey) v Cambridge University Hospitals [2014] EWCA Civ 822, the Court of Appeal held that Article 8 is engaged by DNACPR decisions and that there is a presumption in favour of consulting the patient unless there is a convincing reason not to, such as consultation causing physical or psychological harm. Possible upset is not enough.

n.1: A second opinion does not replace the duty to consult her before the notice is placed; delaying her involvement is not lawful on these facts.
n.2: Tracey held that although CPR is a clinical decision, the patient must be involved and consulted; the clinical nature of the decision does not remove that duty.
n.3: Mrs Ellis has capacity, so the duty to consult is owed to her; informing her husband in her place breaches her Article 8 rights and confidentiality.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Grace has worked as a registered nurse in Manchester and is moving to a post in Glasgow. She asks her manager which statute governs decisions for adults who lack capacity once she is practising in Scotland, as Code 4.3 requires her to follow the law where she practises. Which statute should the manager name?
o: Mental Health (Care and Treatment) (Scotland) Act 2003
Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000
Mental Capacity Act 2005
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Capacity law is devolved. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies in England and Wales; in Scotland decisions for adults lacking capacity fall under the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000. Code 4.3 requires registrants to keep to the mental capacity law of the country in which they practise.

n.0: The 2003 Scottish Act concerns compulsory care and treatment for mental disorder, not general decisions for adults lacking capacity.
n.1: The 2019 Act amends the MCA 2005 in England and Wales to create the Liberty Protection Safeguards, which are not in force.
n.3: The MCA 2005 covers England and Wales, so it would not govern Grace's practice in Glasgow.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Siobhan, a registered nurse, is charged by the police with a drink-driving offence on a day off. She has not yet been to court and her line manager is unaware. According to the Code, what should Siobhan do?
o: Declare the charge at her next revalidation application
Tell the NMC and her employer as soon as she can
Tell her employer, who will then notify the NMC for her
Tell the NMC if the court convicts her of the offence
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and your employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, or if you have received a conditional discharge or been found guilty of a criminal offence (other than a protected caution or conviction). A charge is reportable before any conviction.

n.0: Revalidation is every 3 years and includes a health and character declaration, but Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as possible, not at the next renewal.
n.2: The duty is personal to the registrant and covers both the NMC and the employer; passing it to the employer does not meet it.
n.3: Code 23.2 applies at the point of charge; waiting for a conviction delays a report that is already due.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: During a teaching session, a practice educator lists four sources a nurse might rely on when explaining informed consent: the Mental Capacity Act 2005, the Care Act 2014, the NMC Code and Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015]. A student asks which of these is case law made by the courts. Which source should the educator identify?
o: The Mental Capacity Act 2005
The NMC Code, professional standards of practice
Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015]
The Care Act 2014
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11 is a Supreme Court judgment, so it is common (case) law. The two Acts are statutes made by Parliament and the Code is a set of professional standards set by the regulator.

n.0: The MCA 2005 is primary legislation (statute) passed by Parliament, not case law.
n.1: The Code is the NMC's professional standards; it is a regulatory document, not a court decision.
n.3: The Care Act 2014 is statute; its safeguarding duties come from Parliament, not a court judgment.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Lewis, 64, is on a medical ward. The nurse explains that she needs to take a blood sample to check his kidney function and asks if that is all right. Mr Lewis nods, rolls up his sleeve and holds out his arm. Which type of consent has Mr Lewis given?
o: Expressed consent recorded in writing
Deemed consent through admission to hospital
Implied consent shown by his actions
Presumed consent under the Mental Capacity Act
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Consent can be given verbally, in writing or implied by conduct. Having been told what is proposed and why, Mr Lewis shows agreement by rolling up his sleeve and offering his arm: implied consent. It remains valid because it is voluntary and informed, from a person with capacity (Code 4.2).

n.0: Nothing has been written down; expressed consent is stated verbally or in writing, not shown by gesture.
n.1: Being admitted to hospital does not amount to consent to each intervention; consent is specific to each procedure.
n.3: The MCA 2005 does not create 'presumed consent'; it presumes capacity, which is different.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Adeyemi, 72, has capacity and a leg ulcer. When the nurse arrives to change the dressing she says firmly that she does not want it done today because she is tired. The dressing is not urgent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Change the dressing gently because it is in her best interests
Respect her decision, explore her reasons and record the refusal
Ask her daughter to persuade her to accept the dressing change
Assess her capacity because she is refusing recommended care
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to accept or refuse care and treatment. Mrs Adeyemi has capacity, so her refusal is valid. The nurse should explore why, explain any consequences, offer another time and document the refusal.

n.0: Best interests decisions apply to people who lack capacity (MCA s4); treating a capacitous person against her refusal is unlawful.
n.2: Using a relative to pressure her undermines the voluntariness of any later consent.
n.3: Refusing care is not evidence of incapacity; MCA s1(4) says an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity, and capacity is presumed.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Ms Novak, 45, is a professional violinist due to have a hand operation. She asks whether there is any risk to the feeling in her fingers. The surgeon says the risk is low, so it is not usually mentioned. Under Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015], which risks must be disclosed?
o: Risks the patient specifically asks about during the consent discussion
Risks a responsible body of hand surgeons would usually choose to mention to patients
Risks that occur in more than one in a hundred operations of this type
Risks she, or a reasonable person in her position, would see as significant
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11 requires reasonable care to make the patient aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would attach significance to it, or the clinician knows or should know this patient would. A violinist would attach significance to altered sensation.

n.0: Disclosure of material risks is the clinician's duty; it does not depend on the patient knowing what to ask.
n.1: This is the older professional-practice (Bolam) approach that Montgomery replaced for risk disclosure.
n.2: Montgomery rejected a fixed percentage threshold; materiality depends on the person, not a statistic.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Bello, 30, gave verbal consent for a urinary catheter to be inserted. Partway through, he becomes distressed and says, 'Stop, I don't want this any more.' The nurse is concerned that his bladder is still full. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Stop the procedure, then discuss his concerns and the options
Finish quickly because stopping now would cause more discomfort
Continue, because consent was obtained before the procedure began
Pause, then restart once a colleague is present to reassure him
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Consent is ongoing and a person with capacity may withdraw it at any point (Code 2.5 and 4.2). The nurse should stop, explore his worries, explain the risks of not proceeding and agree a plan with him, then document the discussion.

n.1: Completing a procedure after consent is withdrawn is treatment without consent, however brief.
n.2: Earlier consent does not continue once it has been withdrawn by a person with capacity.
n.3: Restarting without fresh consent overrides his refusal; a colleague's presence does not supply consent.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A surgical registrar asks Priya, a registered nurse, to obtain Mrs Kaur's signature on a consent form for a laparoscopic procedure tomorrow. Priya has never seen this operation and does not know its specific risks or alternatives. What should Priya do?
o: Read the consent form aloud and witness Mrs Kaur's signature
Decline and ask the registrar to take consent from Mrs Kaur
Ask Mrs Kaur whether she has any questions before she signs
Obtain the signature and ask the registrar to explain risks later
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Valid consent needs the person to be informed of material risks and reasonable alternatives (Montgomery 2015). Code 13 requires nurses to work within the limits of their competence, asking a suitably qualified professional for anything beyond it (13.3). Priya cannot give that information, so the clinician who can should seek consent.

n.0: Reading the form does not allow Priya to answer questions about risks and alternatives she does not know.
n.2: Priya could not answer Mrs Kaur's questions about this operation's risks, so her consent would not be properly informed.
n.3: A signature obtained before the risks are explained does not show informed consent; the form is evidence, not consent itself.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Oyelaran, 79, is being discharged to a care home. Her son repeatedly tells staff in front of her that she 'has to go' and answers questions for her. When asked, Mrs Oyelaran looks at her son and says, 'I suppose so.' What should the nurse do first?
o: Refer her for an assessment of her mental capacity
Ask her son to sign the agreement on his mother's behalf
Record that she has agreed to the move to the care home
Speak with Mrs Oyelaran alone to explore her own wishes
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Valid consent must be given voluntarily, free from pressure by others. The nurse should first speak with Mrs Oyelaran privately to establish her own view. Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)), so concern about influence is not a reason to question capacity.

n.0: There is nothing to suggest an impairment of mind or brain; pressure from a relative raises a question of voluntariness, not capacity.
n.1: A son has no authority to consent for an adult unless he holds a relevant LPA or deputyship; nothing suggests this.
n.2: Her hesitant answer under pressure may not be voluntary; recording it as agreement could be invalid.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Tran, 52, speaks little English and is due to have a chest drain inserted later today. His consultant has asked the nurse to make sure he understands the procedure and its risks before he agrees. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Rely on his nodding to show that he understands
Use pictures and gestures to explain the main steps of the procedure
Arrange a professional interpreter for the consent discussion
Give him an English information leaflet to read first
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Consent must be informed: the person needs to understand the procedure, material risks and alternatives (Montgomery 2015). Code 7.2 requires reasonable steps to meet people's language and communication needs, so a professional interpreter should be used for the discussion.

n.0: Nodding may reflect politeness rather than understanding, so it is not evidence of informed consent.
n.1: Pictures and gestures may support communication but cannot convey material risks and alternatives reliably for a chest drain.
n.3: A leaflet in a language he cannot read well does not inform him and does not meet Code 7.2.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Ms Clarke, 38, agrees to have a wound swab taken after the nurse explains why it is needed and what it involves. The swab is taken without problems. According to Code 4.2, what should the nurse also make sure of?
o: That the consent is confirmed again by the doctor
That Ms Clarke signs a consent form for the swab
That the consent obtained is documented in her record
That a second nurse witnesses Ms Clarke's agreement
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Code 4.2: make sure that you get properly informed consent and document it before carrying out any action. Verbal consent is valid for a wound swab; the record should show it was obtained.

n.0: The nurse taking the swab obtains the consent; the doctor does not need to confirm it.
n.1: Written consent is not required for a routine swab; verbal consent is valid if documented.
n.3: There is no requirement for a witness to verbal consent for a routine procedure.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Dawson, 84, has a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease and is on a ward in England. She tells the nurse she wants to go home today rather than wait for physiotherapy. A junior doctor says, 'She has dementia, so she can't make that decision.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
o: She can go home, because a person with dementia keeps all their rights
A best interests meeting should be arranged before any assessment
Her capacity for this decision must be assessed, not assumed from diagnosis
Her daughter should be asked to decide, as she is her next of kin
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it. s2(3): lack of capacity cannot be established merely by reference to a person's condition. Capacity must be assessed for this decision at this time.

n.0: Whether she can safely go home depends on whether she has capacity for this decision; that has not yet been assessed.
n.1: Best interests decisions (s4) follow a finding that the person lacks capacity; the assessment comes first.
n.3: Next of kin has no legal power to make decisions for an adult unless they hold a relevant LPA or deputyship.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Pearce, 67, has capacity and peripheral vascular disease. After a full explanation of the risks, he declines a recommended below-knee amputation, saying he would rather take his chances. The team thinks this is an unwise choice. Which principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies most directly?
o: Making an unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity
Any act done for a person must be in their best interests
The less restrictive option must be considered first
All practicable steps must be taken to help the person decide
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Mr Pearce has capacity, so his refusal must be respected (Code 2.5).

n.1: Best interests (s1(5)) applies to acts for people who lack capacity; Mr Pearce has capacity.
n.2: The less restrictive principle (s1(6)) applies when acting for someone who lacks capacity.
n.3: Supporting decision-making (s1(3)) has already been met by the full explanation; the issue now is respecting an unwise choice.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Ali, 76, has delirium from a urinary infection. She can repeat back what the nurse has told her about a proposed blood transfusion, but she cannot relate the risks and benefits to her own situation when making a choice. Which part of the functional test of capacity is she unable to meet?
o: Communicating her decision to staff
Retaining the information
Understanding the information
Using or weighing the information
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s3(1): a person is unable to make a decision if unable to understand, retain, use or weigh the information, or communicate the decision. Mrs Ali understands and retains it but cannot use or weigh it in reaching a decision.

n.0: She can speak and express choices; the difficulty is in weighing the information.
n.1: She can recall the information when asked, so retention is not the problem described.
n.2: She can repeat back what she was told, which suggests she understands the information.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Nowak, 70, has expressive aphasia after a stroke and cannot speak clearly. A decision is needed about moving him to a rehabilitation unit. Before anyone concludes he lacks capacity, what should the nurse do?
o: Wait for his speech to recover fully before discussing the move
Record that he lacks capacity because he cannot speak clearly
Ask his wife to make the decision as she knows his wishes best
Arrange communication aids or speech and language therapy input
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s1(3): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. s3(1)(d) allows communication by any means, so aids and specialist input should be tried.

n.0: Delaying indefinitely is not required; the duty is to take practicable steps to support his decision now.
n.1: Inability to speak does not mean inability to communicate a decision; s3(1)(d) covers any means.
n.2: His wife cannot decide for him unless she holds a relevant LPA; the first step is to support him to decide.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Osei, 80, has mild cognitive impairment. The nurse explains the options for his discharge. He understands, weighs the options and chooses home with carers, but 20 minutes later he cannot recall the details of the conversation. What should the nurse conclude?
o: He lacks capacity, because his cognitive impairment is lifelong
His capacity must be reassessed by a psychiatrist before discharge
He lacks capacity, because he could not recall the information
He can still make the decision, as retaining it briefly is enough
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s3(3): the fact that a person can retain information for a short period only does not prevent him from being regarded as able to make the decision. Mr Osei retained it long enough to make his choice.

n.0: A condition cannot establish incapacity (s2(3)); the test is functional and decision-specific.
n.1: Any suitably skilled decision maker can assess capacity; a psychiatrist is not required when the s3 test is already met.
n.2: s3(3) states that short-term retention is sufficient; later forgetting does not mean he lacked capacity.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Ms Ruiz, 59, has hepatic encephalopathy. She is drowsy and confused in the evenings but alert and orientated most mornings. A non-urgent decision is needed about whether she wants to join a clinical trial. When is it most appropriate to assess her capacity for this decision?
o: In the evening, so the assessment reflects her worst state
In the morning, when she is usually at her most alert
After discharge, once her condition has fully resolved
At any time, since capacity is a fixed state
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific (MCA 2005 s2(1), 'at the material time'), and s1(3) requires all practicable steps to help the person decide. Choosing the time when she is most alert supports her to make the decision herself.

n.0: Assessing at her worst ignores the duty to take practicable steps to help her decide.
n.2: Delaying until full recovery is unnecessary when she has lucid periods now in which she may be able to decide.
n.3: Capacity can fluctuate; s2(2) recognises that an impairment may be temporary.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Brennan, 74, was assessed last month as lacking capacity to manage his complex investments. Today he tells the nurse he would like fish rather than chicken for lunch and wants to wear his own clothes. Which statement is correct?
o: His financial attorney should make these choices on his behalf
He lacks capacity for all decisions until a new assessment is completed
He can choose his lunch but not his clothing without an assessment
He may be able to make these decisions, as capacity is decision-specific
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s2(1): lack of capacity relates to a specific matter at the material time. Being unable to manage complex investments says nothing about everyday choices, which he is presumed able to make (s1(2)).

n.0: A property and financial affairs attorney has no authority over personal welfare choices such as food or clothing.
n.1: Incapacity is not global; a finding about one decision does not transfer to others.
n.2: There is no basis for treating clothing differently from food; both are everyday choices he is presumed able to make.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: On a children's ward in England, the nurse is caring for Lily, 15, who needs a decision about a minor procedure. A student nurse asks whether the Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs this decision. Which statement is correct?
o: It applies to children of any age if parents agree
Its powers generally apply to people aged 16 and over
Its powers apply to people aged 18 and over
It applies to anyone over 12 who is in hospital
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s2(5): the powers under the Act do not generally apply to a person under 16 (subject to s18(3), which concerns property). Decisions for Lily follow the law on children's consent and parental responsibility.

n.0: Parental agreement does not bring a child under 16 within the MCA.
n.2: The MCA starts at 16, not 18; it covers 16 and 17 year olds.
n.3: There is no age-12 threshold in the MCA; s2(5) sets 16.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Price, 88, has advanced dementia and has been assessed as lacking capacity to decide about a feeding tube. The team is making a best interests decision. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 s4 checklist, which should the decision maker take into account?
o: Her past wishes, beliefs and values, as reported by those close to her
Her son's own preference, because he is recorded as next of kin
The option that places the least demand on the ward's nursing time
Her age and diagnosis, as the main guide to her likely outcome
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s4(6) requires consideration of the person's past and present wishes and feelings, beliefs and values; s4(7) requires consulting carers and others interested in her welfare about what she would want. s4(1) prohibits basing the decision on age or condition alone.

n.1: Relatives are consulted about what the person would want; their own preference does not decide the matter.
n.2: Staff convenience is not part of the s4 checklist; the focus is the person's best interests.
n.3: s4(1) states a best interests determination must not be made merely on the basis of age or condition.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Shah, 69, has motor neurone disease. He shows the nurse a document he wrote and signed refusing mechanical ventilation. It was witnessed but contains no statement that it applies even if his life is at risk. He now lacks capacity and is in respiratory failure. What is the status of the document?
o: It is not valid because it was not drafted by a solicitor
It is not valid as a refusal of this life-sustaining treatment
It is valid because it is written, signed and witnessed
It is valid because his family confirm these were his wishes
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s25(5)-(6): an advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment must be in writing, signed, witnessed and include a statement by the person that it is to apply even if life is at risk. Without that statement it does not apply to ventilation, although it must still inform the best interests decision.

n.0: There is no requirement for a solicitor to draft an advance decision.
n.2: Writing, signature and witness are necessary but not sufficient; the life-at-risk statement is missing.
n.3: Family confirmation cannot supply a missing statutory formality.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Ms Douglas, 55, has capacity. Last year she made a valid advance decision refusing antibiotics for pneumonia. Today she tells the nurse she has changed her mind and would want antibiotics if she became unwell. She does not want to put this in writing. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep following the advance decision until it is replaced
Ask her to sign a written withdrawal before it can apply
Accept the withdrawal and document it in her records
Ask two witnesses to confirm her change of mind
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s24(3)-(4): a person may withdraw an advance decision at any time when they have capacity, and a withdrawal need not be in writing. The nurse should record it clearly and tell the team.

n.0: Her withdrawal takes effect now; the old decision does not continue until replaced.
n.1: Withdrawal does not need to be in writing, so a signature is not required.
n.3: There is no witness requirement for withdrawing an advance decision.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Fox, 82, lacks capacity to consent to a hip operation. His nephew produces a registered lasting power of attorney for property and financial affairs and says he will give consent. What should the nurse explain?
o: The nephew can consent because the LPA is registered
The nephew can consent if the surgeon agrees
The LPA covers treatment once two doctors sign it
This LPA does not cover decisions about medical treatment
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s9(1) distinguishes an LPA for personal welfare (health and welfare, which can cover medical treatment) from one for property and affairs. A property and financial affairs attorney has no authority over health decisions, so the surgeon must decide in Mr Fox's best interests (s4), consulting the nephew.

n.0: Registration does not change the scope of the power; this LPA covers finances, not health.
n.1: A surgeon's agreement cannot widen the authority given by the LPA.
n.2: There is no provision for doctors to extend a financial LPA to cover treatment.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Kowalski, 79, lacks capacity to decide about a proposed move to long-term residential care. She has no family, friends or unpaid carers who could be consulted about her wishes. Who should be involved to represent her in the decision?
o: Her GP, as the person who knows her best
The ward manager, acting as her advocate
An independent mental capacity advocate
A Court of Protection deputy appointed by the trust
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s35 establishes independent mental capacity advocates to represent people who lack capacity and have nobody appropriate to consult. An IMCA supports and represents Mrs Kowalski in the best interests decision.

n.0: The GP is a professional involved in her care, not an independent representative of her wishes.
n.1: Ward staff involved in her care cannot act as her independent advocate.
n.3: Deputies are appointed by the Court of Protection, not by a trust, and none is needed here.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A healthcare assistant in a care home in England is found to have left Mr Garner, who lacks capacity, in a soiled bed without food for a whole day on purpose. The manager asks the nurse what legal status this conduct has. What should the nurse say?
o: It is an offence under the Care Act 2014 safeguarding section
It may be a criminal offence of wilful neglect under MCA s44
It is a regulatory matter for the CQC with no criminal liability
It is a disciplinary matter for the employer to deal with
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s44 makes it an offence for a person who has the care of someone who lacks capacity to ill-treat or wilfully neglect them; on indictment the maximum is 5 years' imprisonment. It should also be raised as a safeguarding concern.

n.0: Care Act s42 places a duty on the local authority to make enquiries; it does not create this offence.
n.2: CQC regulates the provider, but s44 creates individual criminal liability.
n.3: Employer discipline may follow, but deliberate neglect of a person lacking capacity is also a potential criminal offence.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Okonjo, 74, now lacks capacity after a cardiac arrest. He has a valid and applicable advance decision refusing CPR, written and signed, witnessed and stating it applies even if his life is at risk. His daughter is distressed and demands that CPR be given if he arrests again. What should the nurse do?
o: Seek a best interests decision from the medical team
Follow the advance decision and support his daughter
Give CPR because the daughter is the next of kin
Ask the daughter to sign a form overriding the refusal
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: A valid and applicable advance decision has the same effect as a contemporaneous refusal (MCA 2005 s26(1)), and the s25 formalities for life-sustaining treatment are met. Relatives cannot override it. The nurse should explain this sensitively and support the daughter.

n.0: A best interests decision is not made where a valid and applicable advance decision already refuses the treatment.
n.2: Next of kin has no power to override a valid advance decision.
n.3: A relative cannot sign away a valid advance decision made by the person.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Ibrahim, 86, has delirium after surgery and currently lacks capacity to decide whether to move into a nursing home. The team expects her delirium to settle within a week. The current placement is safe. What is the most appropriate approach to the decision?
o: Delay the decision until she may have regained capacity
Arrange the move and review it once the delirium settles
Ask her husband to decide as he will be most affected
Make a best interests decision now to avoid delay
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s4(3) requires the decision maker to consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and, if so, when. Where the decision can wait, it should, so Mrs Ibrahim can make it herself.

n.1: Moving her first and reviewing later pre-empts a decision she may soon be able to make herself.
n.2: Her husband has no legal authority to decide unless he holds a relevant LPA.
n.3: A best interests decision now ignores s4(3) when she is likely to regain capacity soon and there is no urgency.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A ward manager in an English hospital is updating staff training on people who lack capacity and whose care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. A nurse asks which legal scheme is currently in force to authorise such arrangements in hospitals and care homes. What should the manager say?
o: The nurse's holding power under the Mental Health Act 1983
The Liberty Protection Safeguards under the 2019 Amendment Act
The community treatment order scheme under the Mental Health Act
The Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards under the MCA 2005
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: DoLS (MCA 2005 Schedules A1 and 1A) remain the scheme in force in England and Wales for hospitals and care homes. The Liberty Protection Safeguards in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 have not been implemented.

n.0: The nurse's holding power under MHA s5(4) briefly detains an informal inpatient with mental disorder; it does not authorise care arrangements under the MCA.
n.1: The LPS have not been brought into force; DoLS remain the live scheme.
n.2: Community treatment orders apply to certain detained patients leaving hospital, not to people lacking capacity in hospitals or care homes.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Gill, 87, has delirium and lacks capacity to understand her risk of falling. At night she repeatedly tries to climb out of bed and is unsteady. A healthcare assistant suggests putting the bed rails up. Which action best follows the least restrictive principle?
o: Request a sedative to help her stay in bed at night
Raise both bed rails while she is asleep at night
Tuck the sheets in tightly so she cannot get out
Use a low bed with a crash mat and closer observation
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: MCA 2005 s1(6): before acting, consider whether the purpose can be achieved as effectively in a way less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom of action. A low bed, crash mat and closer observation reduce injury risk without confining her; rails may increase harm if she climbs over them.

n.0: Sedation to keep her in bed is chemical restraint and may worsen delirium and falls risk.
n.1: Bed rails restrict her movement and may increase the height and severity of a fall if she climbs over them.
n.2: Tucking sheets to prevent her leaving bed is a form of restraint and risks entrapment.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A nursing student asks when it is lawful to restrain an adult who lacks capacity, for example by holding his hand to stop him pulling out a cannula during essential IV treatment. Which statement best describes the legal position under the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
o: It is lawful once the person has been assessed as lacking capacity
It needs a DoLS authorisation in place before any restraint
It must be necessary to prevent harm and proportionate to that harm
It is lawful once a close relative has agreed to the restraint
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Under MCA 2005 s6, restraint in connection with care or treatment is permitted if the person doing it reasonably believes it is necessary to prevent harm to the person lacking capacity, and it is a proportionate response to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm. It must also be in best interests (s1(5)) and the least restrictive option (s1(6)).

n.0: Lacking capacity is a precondition, but restraint also needs necessity and proportionality.
n.1: Brief proportionate restraint under s6 does not itself need a DoLS authorisation; DoLS concerns deprivation of liberty.
n.3: A relative's agreement does not make restraint lawful; they cannot consent for an adult without a relevant LPA.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Lowe, 90, lives in a care home in England and lacks capacity to decide where to live. The manager has concluded that her care arrangements amount to a deprivation of liberty. What is needed to make these arrangements lawful?
o: A best interests note in her care plan by the manager
An authorisation under the Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards
Her daughter's signed consent to the locked doors
An authorisation under the Liberty Protection Safeguards
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Where a person who lacks capacity is deprived of liberty in a care home or hospital, the arrangements need authorisation under DoLS (MCA 2005 Sch A1). Article 5 of the Human Rights Act 1998 protects liberty, and DoLS supply the required safeguards.

n.0: Recording that the arrangements are in her best interests does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
n.2: A relative cannot consent to a deprivation of liberty for an adult.
n.3: The LPS are not in force, so no LPS authorisation can be given.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Daniel, 24, has a learning disability and becomes agitated in a busy emergency department. He is shouting and pacing but has not hurt anyone. His support worker says loud noise upsets him. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the doctor to prescribe rapid tranquillisation
Tell him he must sit down or he will be removed
Move him somewhere quieter and use calm de-escalation
Call security to hold him until he is calmer
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Restraint and restrictive interventions are a last resort. The first response to distress is to identify and reduce triggers and use de-escalation, applying the least restrictive option (MCA s1(6)) and person-centred information from those who know him.

n.0: Rapid tranquillisation is a restrictive intervention considered after other measures have been tried.
n.1: Threats are likely to escalate distress and are not person-centred de-escalation.
n.3: Physical holding is a last resort when there is risk of harm and de-escalation has failed; he has not harmed anyone.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: On a dementia ward, Mr Payne, 81, lacks capacity and needed to be briefly held by two trained staff to stop him hitting another patient. He is now calm. Besides checking him for injury, what should the nurse record about the incident?
o: The details in the incident system, rather than his care record
A brief note that restraint was needed, to avoid labelling him
The reasons for the hold, technique used, duration and his response
That he was held in his best interests, with the names of staff
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Code 10.1-10.4 requires accurate, timely records that attribute, date and time entries. Any restraint must be justified as necessary and proportionate (MCA s6), so the record should show why it was used, how, for how long and its effect, supporting review and learning.

n.0: Incident reporting is appropriate, but the care record must also document what happened to him.
n.1: A minimal note fails Code 10 and prevents review of whether the restraint was justified.
n.3: Stating 'best interests' without reasons, technique and duration does not show the hold was necessary and proportionate.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: At a training session on restrictive practice, a nurse asks which Article of the Human Rights Act 1998 Schedule 1 is engaged when a person who lacks capacity is deprived of their liberty in a care home. Which Article should the trainer name?
o: Article 14, the prohibition of discrimination
Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Article 5 (HRA 1998 Sch 1) protects the right to liberty and security and requires lawful procedures for any deprivation of liberty. DoLS exist to provide those safeguards for people lacking capacity.

n.0: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of other rights; it is not the liberty right itself.
n.1: Article 3 concerns torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, not lawful authority for deprivation of liberty.
n.3: Article 8 may be relevant to care arrangements, but deprivation of liberty engages Article 5.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Hart, 83, has dementia and lacks capacity. For three nights she has called out repeatedly, disturbing other patients. A colleague suggests asking for regular night-time lorazepam 'so everyone gets some sleep'. She has not been reviewed for pain or constipation. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Move her to a side room and close the door at night
Assess for pain, constipation and delirium before considering medication
Request regular lorazepam, as other patients on the bay also need sleep
Give PRN lorazepam tonight and review tomorrow whether it helped her
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Using sedation to control behaviour for others' convenience is chemical restraint and must be in her best interests and the least restrictive option (MCA s1(5)-(6)). NICE NG97 rec 1.7.1: before any treatment for distress in dementia, assess for and address causes such as pain, delirium or inappropriate care, so she should be assessed first.

n.0: Isolating her behind a closed door is restrictive and does not address the cause of her distress.
n.2: Medication for the benefit of others is not in her best interests and is a restrictive practice.
n.3: Giving sedation before assessing for treatable causes skips the least restrictive approach.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Evans, 77, is being discharged home with a new leg ulcer that will need daily dressings from the district nursing team. The ward nurse hesitates to send details of his wound and medicines, worried about breaching confidentiality. Which Caldicott principle best guides her?
o: Inform patients and service users about how their information is used
Sharing for individual care matters as much as protecting confidentiality
Use the minimum necessary personal confidential data for each purpose
Access to personal confidential data should be on a strict need-to-know basis
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Caldicott principle 7 (National Data Guardian, 2020): the duty to share information for individual care is as important as the duty to protect patient confidentiality. Sharing with the district nurses supports his direct care.

n.0: Informing patients (principle 8) is good practice but does not resolve her concern about sharing for direct care.
n.2: Minimum necessary data (principle 3) shapes how much is shared, but the nurse's hesitation is about whether to share at all.
n.3: Need-to-know access (principle 4) limits who sees data; the district nurses clearly need to know.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Ruth, a staff nurse, is writing a referral to a dietitian for Mrs Smith, 63, who has lost weight after bowel surgery. The electronic record includes her full medical history, including a termination of pregnancy 30 years ago. What should Ruth include in the referral?
o: The information relevant to the dietetic assessment
Everything except the termination of pregnancy
Her full medical history so the dietitian has the whole picture
A summary written after asking her family
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Caldicott principle 3: use the minimum necessary personal confidential data. UK GDPR data minimisation also requires data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary. Only information relevant to nutrition should be shared.

n.1: Removing one sensitive item still shares other irrelevant data; relevance, not sensitivity, decides what is sent.
n.2: Sending the full history exceeds what the dietitian needs and breaches the minimum necessary principle.
n.3: Families are not a source for a clinical referral, and involving them without consent breaches confidentiality.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Carter died on the ward last week. A local journalist phones, saying she is writing a tribute, and asks the nurse what illness he died from. His family have not given any permission. How should the nurse respond?
o: Confirm the details if the journalist knew him personally
Share general details but not the diagnosis itself
Share the cause of death, as he can no longer be harmed
Decline to share, as confidentiality continues after death
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Code 5.3: make sure that people's confidentiality is respected after they have died. There is no lawful basis to disclose his health information to a journalist.

n.0: Knowing the patient personally gives no right to confidential information.
n.1: Any health details about Mr Carter remain confidential; partial disclosure is still a breach.
n.2: Confidentiality does not end at death (Code 5.3).

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Thomas, 35, is an inpatient. He tells the nurse that he intends to stab his ex-partner, names her and says he knows where she lives. He asks the nurse to keep this to herself. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell him this cannot be kept confidential and escalate urgently
Keep it confidential, as he has asked and has capacity
Ask him to promise not to act and then respect his wishes
Note it in his record and discuss it at the next ward round
