n.0: His wife may add useful information, but he can speak for himself and should be asked first.
n.1: Setting goals for him rather than with him is not shared goal setting.
n.3: Completing a checklist first and then informing him is not shared assessment or decision-making.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Fisher, 89, is frail and lives in a care home. Staff report she has become drowsy and less able to feed herself since yesterday. Her temperature is 36.4°C and her urine is cloudy. A colleague says infection is unlikely because she has no fever. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that frail older people may have infection without fever
Ask the care home to collect a urine sample at the next GP visit
Agree, and look for a non-infective cause of her new drowsiness
Agree, and plan to recheck her temperature again in 4 hours
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.4.1: do not rely on fever or hypothermia alone to rule sepsis in or out; rec 1.4.2 notes older or very frail people may not develop a raised temperature, and rec 1.4.9 that cognitive change may present as acute change in function. She needs full assessment and NEWS2.

n.1: Deferring a sample delays assessment of an acute change in an older, frail person.
n.2: Excluding infection on the basis of a normal temperature contradicts NG253 rec 1.4.1.
n.3: Waiting 4 hours for a temperature ignores signs of possible sepsis that need assessment now.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Kim, 71, takes bisoprolol for heart failure. He has pneumonia and his respiratory rate is 24, but his heart rate is 74 bpm. A student nurse says his normal pulse shows he is not seriously unwell. Which explanation should the nurse give?
o: His normal pulse means a sepsis screen is not needed today
Heart rate is the most reliable sign of infection in older adults
Bisoprolol tends to raise the pulse, so 74 bpm is a low reading
Beta-blockers can blunt the heart rate rise with infection
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.4: interpret heart rate in context; older people may not develop an increased heart rate, and the response may be affected by medicines such as beta-blockers. His raised respiratory rate still needs scoring and escalation as appropriate.

n.0: A pulse in the normal range does not exclude sepsis in someone taking a beta-blocker.
n.1: NG253 warns that older people may not show a rise in heart rate, so it is not the most reliable sign.
n.2: Bisoprolol is a beta-blocker that slows the heart rate; it does not raise it.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Holt, 80, has advanced dementia and limited speech. During a wash she grimaces, guards her left hip and pulls away when touched there. She cannot say whether she is in pain. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
o: As refusal of care, so the wash should be abandoned
As non-verbal signs of physical distress that need assessment
As features of her dementia that need no further action from staff
As agitation that should be treated with a sedative
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Annexe B 1.2.2 requires nurses to recognise symptoms and signs of physical distress. In people who cannot report pain, behaviours such as grimacing, guarding and withdrawal may indicate pain, so the hip should be assessed further (for example injury from a fall) using an appropriate observational tool.

n.0: Stopping the wash does not address the possible cause of her distress.
n.2: Attributing new behaviour to dementia risks missing a treatable cause such as a fracture.
n.3: Sedation masks the signs and does not treat the underlying cause; assessment comes first.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ravi, 55, is a day after a hernia repair. He is anxious and says he 'cannot catch his breath'. RR 26, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 128/80, alert, temperature 37.2°C. You have called for help. Which action best reflects the ABCDE approach?
o: Start oxygen, then continue to C and D while reassessing his breathing
Complete C, D and E fully before deciding whether he needs oxygen
Reassure him that anxiety is common after surgery and observe hourly
Wait for the doctor to examine him before giving any treatment
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: ABCDE treats each life-threatening problem as it is found and then reassesses. Hypoxaemia (93% with RR 26) is a B problem: start oxygen to a target of 94-98% (BTS; NG253 rec 1.10.1), then continue through C, D and E, re-evaluating after each intervention.

n.1: Completing the rest of the assessment first delays treatment of a breathing problem already identified.
n.2: Attributing tachypnoea and low saturation to anxiety risks missing a pulmonary embolism or other serious cause.
n.3: Nurses start initial treatment within competence while help arrives; waiting delays care (Code 15).

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Hannah, 24, has type 1 diabetes and is on an orthopaedic ward. You are called because she is sweaty and confused. Airway is clear, RR 18, SpO2 97%, pulse 98, BP 118/72. She responds to voice. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give her 300 mg aspirin to chew while awaiting review
Complete a 4AT delirium screen before any other test
Request an urgent CT head scan to exclude a stroke
Check her capillary blood glucose straight away
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: With A, B and C stable, D includes a capillary blood glucose. In someone with diabetes who is sweaty and confused, hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L, RCUK first aid 2025) is the most likely reversible cause and must be excluded quickly.

n.0: Aspirin is for cardiac-sounding chest pain and is not indicated for confusion.
n.1: Delirium screening is relevant later; a reversible metabolic cause should be excluded first.
n.2: Imaging is not a nursing first step and would delay checking for a common reversible cause.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Maya, 61, is two hours after a hip replacement. Her observations are: RR 22, SpO2 95% on 2 L/min oxygen, pulse 118, BP 94/58, alert, temperature 36.4°C. Her A and B are managed. During C and E you find the dressing soaked with fresh blood. What is the priority?
o: Change the soiled dressing using aseptic technique and continue observing
Increase her oxygen and recheck her observations in 30 minutes
Apply firm pressure to the wound and escalate urgently as a medical emergency
Complete a fluid balance chart before informing the surgical team
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Tachycardia, hypotension and visible fresh bleeding indicate haemorrhage. Control external bleeding with direct pressure (RCUK first aid 2025) and escalate urgently; her NEWS2 is 7 or more (RR 2, SpO2 1, oxygen 2, HR 2, BP 2 = 9), which requires an emergency response (RCP 2017).

n.0: Changing the dressing treats the appearance of the wound, not the bleeding or shock.
n.1: Oxygen does not address the circulatory cause, and 30 minutes is too long with a NEWS2 of 9.
n.3: Charting delays urgent escalation of probable haemorrhage.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Kofi, 72, has a NEWS2 of 6. You have completed an ABCDE assessment, given oxygen and called the doctor using SBAR. The doctor will arrive in 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate next action?
o: Hand over to the next shift that he has been reviewed
Leave him to rest and record observations again in 4 hours
Repeat the ABCDE assessment to check his response to interventions
Start the oral antibiotics left on his drug chart from yesterday
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: ABCDE is cyclical: after each intervention reassess from A. A NEWS2 of 5 or more requires at least hourly monitoring, and any deterioration should trigger re-escalation (RCP 2017 chart 4).

n.0: He has not yet been reviewed, so this handover would be inaccurate and unsafe.
n.1: A NEWS2 of 5-6 requires at least hourly observations, not 4-hourly.
n.3: Oral antibiotics from yesterday are not a response to an acute deterioration and need medical review.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Daniel, 52, is on a surgical ward breathing room air. His observations are: RR 18, SpO2 97%, BP 124/78, pulse 86, alert, temperature 37.4°C. His NEWS2 is 0. What is the minimum frequency of his observations under NEWS2?
o: Hourly
12-hourly
Every 30 minutes
4-6 hourly
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCP NEWS2 (2017) chart 4: an aggregate score of 0 requires a minimum of 12-hourly monitoring.

n.0: Hourly is the minimum for a single parameter scoring 3 or a total of 5 or more.
n.2: Every 30 minutes is not a NEWS2 chart 4 frequency; it is the NG253 recalculation interval for high sepsis risk.
n.3: 4-6 hourly is the minimum for a total score of 1-4.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Lucy, 40, is on air. Observations: RR 22, SpO2 95%, BP 116/70, pulse 96, alert, temperature 38.3°C. What is her NEWS2 score?
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): RR 21-24 = 2; SpO2 94-95% = 1; air = 0; systolic 111-219 = 0; pulse 91-110 = 1; alert = 0; temperature 38.1-39.0 = 1. Total 2+1+1+1 = 5, which is the key threshold for an urgent response.

n.1: 6 overscores; temperature 38.3°C scores 1, not 2 (2 starts at 39.1°C).
n.2: 3 omits two parameters, for example SpO2 95% and pulse 96, which each score 1.
n.3: 4 omits one of the scoring parameters (RR 2, SpO2 1, pulse 1, temperature 1).

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Edward, 66, scores 3 for a respiratory rate of 26 but 0 for every other parameter, giving a NEWS2 of 3. According to NEWS2, what is the appropriate response?
o: Observe at least hourly and ask the medical team to review him
Continue 4-6 hourly observations and review at the next drug round
Observe 12-hourly and reassess if he reports feeling unwell
Call the critical care outreach team for an emergency assessment
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCP NEWS2 (2017): a score of 3 in any single parameter is a low-medium clinical risk needing an urgent ward-based response, with a minimum of hourly monitoring and the registered nurse informing the medical team.

n.1: A red score of 3 in one parameter overrides the 1-4 aggregate band and needs hourly monitoring.
n.2: 12-hourly is for a score of 0 and would leave a respiratory rate of 26 unmonitored.
n.3: An emergency critical care assessment is the response to a total of 7 or more.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Which communication tool is widely used in UK healthcare to structure an urgent telephone escalation to a doctor about a deteriorating person?
o: SOAP: subjective, objective, assessment, plan
PDSA: plan, do, study, act
SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, timed
SBAR: situation, background, assessment, recommendation
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: SBAR is the standard structured tool used across the NHS for escalation, giving the listener the situation, relevant background, the nurse's assessment and a clear recommendation or request (Annexe A 4.2.6.2 appropriate escalation).

n.0: SOAP is a format for documenting a clinical encounter, not for escalation calls.
n.1: PDSA is the Model for Improvement cycle used in quality improvement.
n.2: SMART describes how to write goals or objectives.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Bernard, 74, has COPD with a prescribed target saturation of 88-92%, and his chart uses SpO2 Scale 2. He is on 2 L/min oxygen with SpO2 91%. RR 20, BP 132/84, pulse 88, alert, temperature 37.0°C. What is his NEWS2?
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: On Scale 2, SpO2 88-92% scores 0. Supplemental oxygen scores 2. RR 12-20, systolic 111-219, pulse 51-90, alert and temperature 36.1-38.0 all score 0. Total = 2 (RCP NEWS2 2017).

n.0: 0 omits the 2 points for supplemental oxygen.
n.1: 3 adds a point for SpO2, but 88-92% scores 0 on Scale 2.
n.2: 5 applies Scale 1 (91% = 3) to a patient with a prescribed 88-92% target.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Siobhan, 58, two days after a laparotomy, has a NEWS2 of 9: RR 25, SpO2 93% on air, pulse 112, BP 102/64, alert, temperature 38.4°C. Which response does NEWS2 require?
o: Request a ward doctor review within 4 hours and repeat the observations hourly
Recheck the observations in 30 minutes before escalating
Inform the medical team immediately and request a critical care assessment
Increase observations to 4-hourly and inform the nurse in charge
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: A NEWS2 of 7 or more is high clinical risk: continuous monitoring, the registered nurse immediately informs the medical team (at least specialist registrar level) and requests emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies (RCP NEWS2 2017 chart 4). Her score: RR 3, SpO2 2, pulse 2, BP 1, temperature 1 = 9.

n.0: A 4-hour review is far too slow for a high-risk score.
n.1: Delaying escalation to recheck wastes time; the score already meets the emergency threshold.
n.3: 4-hourly observations apply to a total of 1-4.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ellen, 81, has a NEWS2 of 1. Her son tells you she is 'not right' and much quieter than usual. You find she is newly confused but otherwise unchanged. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Rescore NEWS2 with 3 for new confusion and escalate to a doctor
Wait for her next scheduled observations before deciding
Explain that confusion is common in older people in hospital
Document her son's concern and continue 4-6 hourly observations
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: New confusion scores 3 in the consciousness parameter (ACVPU 'C', RCP NEWS2 2017). Her score becomes 4 with a single red parameter, which needs at least hourly monitoring and medical review. Family concerns are a valid trigger under Martha's Rule.

n.1: Waiting delays recognition of a new red-score parameter.
n.2: New confusion is a marker of deterioration, such as sepsis or delirium, and must not be normalised.
n.3: Documenting without rescoring misses a single-parameter 3, which needs hourly observations and medical review.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Isaac, 47, has been in hospital for a week. His wife says his breathing has worsened and she raised this with the ward team twice today without response. She asks how she can get a different team to review him. Under Martha's Rule, what should you tell her?
o: She should ask his consultant to arrange a formal second opinion
She can request a transfer to another hospital through the GP
She can request an urgent review by a different clinical team herself
She needs to submit a written complaint to the Patient Advice and Liaison Service
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Martha's Rule (NHS England) lets patients, families and carers request an urgent review from a different team, usually critical care outreach, if they are worried about deterioration and feel they are not being heard. It is a rapid review, not a second opinion.

n.0: Martha's Rule escalation is distinct from a formal second opinion by another consultant.
n.1: Transfer through the GP is not the route for an urgent inpatient review.
n.3: PALS and complaints are not designed for urgent clinical deterioration and would delay review.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Tom, 34, attends an acute medical unit with a urinary tract infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and sepsis is suspected. Under NICE NG253 (2025), within what time should broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics be given?
o: Within 3 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 6 hours of calculating the NEWS2 score
Within 4 hours of arrival in the department
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.8.3: for people at high risk (NEWS2 7 or more), give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour of calculating the NEWS2 score.

n.0: Up to 3 hours is the deferral window a clinician may use for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6).
n.2: Up to 6 hours is the deferral window for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.3: A 4-hour arrival target is not a sepsis treatment standard.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Joan, 70, has suspected sepsis and a NEWS2 of 7. The doctor prescribes an initial intravenous fluid bolus. Under NICE NG253 (2025), what is the recommended initial bolus?
o: 20 mL/kg of 5% glucose over 30 minutes
250 mL isotonic crystalloid over 10-15 minutes
500 mL isotonic crystalloid over 10-15 minutes
1,000 mL isotonic crystalloid over 1 hour
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.8.5-1.8.9: give an initial bolus of 250 mL isotonic crystalloid ideally over 10-15 minutes, reassess after each bolus, and repeat up to 1,000 mL in total.

n.0: 5% glucose is not an isotonic resuscitation fluid and 20 mL/kg is not the adult sepsis bolus.
n.2: 500 mL in under 15 minutes is the general CG174 resuscitation bolus, not the NG253 sepsis bolus.
n.3: 1,000 mL is the cumulative ceiling before seeking senior advice, not the first bolus.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Malik, 50, has suspected sepsis with a NEWS2 of 5. How often should his NEWS2 be recalculated under NICE NG253 (2025)?
o: Hourly
Every 4-6 hours
Every 12 hours
Every 30 minutes
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.6.5: recalculate NEWS2 every 30 minutes for high risk, hourly for medium risk (NEWS2 5-6), every 4-6 hours for low risk.

n.1: 4-6 hourly is for low risk (NEWS2 1-4).
n.2: 12-hourly is the general NEWS2 minimum for a score of 0, not for suspected sepsis at 5.
n.3: Every 30 minutes is for high risk (NEWS2 7 or more).

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Which finding should make a nurse consider that a person with suspected sepsis is at higher risk than their NEWS2 score suggests (NICE NG253, 2025)?
o: A pulse of 88 beats per minute
A temperature of 37.9°C
A respiratory rate of 19 per minute
A non-blanching petechial rash
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider higher risk than NEWS2 indicates if the person has mottled or ashen skin, a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash, or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue.

n.0: A pulse of 88 is within the NEWS2 0 band (51-90).
n.1: 37.9°C scores 0 on NEWS2 and is not a higher-risk feature in NG253.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 19 is within the NEWS2 0 band (12-20).

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ruth, 63, has cellulitis and suspected sepsis. Her NEWS2 is 6, made up of RR 3 and three single points, and her worsening is thought to be due to the infection. Under NICE NG253 (2025), how should she be managed?
o: As high risk, with IV antibiotics within 1 hour
As very low risk, with standard observation frequency
As medium risk, with antibiotics deferred up to 3 hours
As low risk, with review by a registered practitioner in 1 hour
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NG253: for a NEWS2 of 5-6 that includes a single parameter scoring 3, if this is likely to be due to the infection, manage as high risk. High risk means IV antibiotics within 1 hour of the NEWS2 score.

n.1: Very low risk applies to a NEWS2 of 0.
n.2: Medium-risk deferral does not apply where a single 3 is likely caused by the infection.
n.3: Low-risk management applies to NEWS2 1-4, not 6.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Callum, 29, has suspected sepsis and is high risk. He has received a 250 mL bolus. Ten minutes later his BP is still 86/50 mmHg and his chest is clear. What is the most appropriate next step under NICE NG253 (2025)?
o: Wait an hour for the first bolus to take effect before reassessing
Give a 1,000 mL bolus over 15 minutes to restore his blood pressure
Stop fluids and start oxygen at 15 L/min via a reservoir mask
Reassess him and give a further 250 mL bolus as prescribed
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NG253 rec 1.8.5-1.8.9: reassess after each 250 mL bolus and, if still hypotensive without signs of overload, give further 250 mL boluses up to 1,000 mL in total, seeking senior advice if no improvement after 1,000 mL.

n.0: NG253 requires reassessment after each bolus, not a fixed wait of an hour.
n.1: NG253 uses incremental 250 mL boluses rather than a single 1,000 mL bolus.
n.2: Stopping fluids leaves hypotension untreated, and oxygen is titrated to a target of 94-98%.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Nadia, 44, is seen by a district nurse at home. She has a chest infection, says she has not passed urine for 20 hours, and her systolic BP is 88 mmHg. Under NICE NG253 (2025) community criteria, what should the nurse do?
o: Advise her to increase oral fluids and recheck tomorrow
Take a urine sample and await the culture result
Ask the GP to review her within the next 24 hours
Arrange emergency transfer to hospital by 999 ambulance
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NG253 table 1 (community): not passing urine for 18 hours and systolic BP 90 mmHg or less are each high-risk criteria. High risk outside hospital needs emergency transfer, usually by 999 ambulance.

n.0: Oral fluids and next-day review leave a high-risk person at home.
n.1: Waiting for culture results delays emergency assessment.
n.2: A routine GP review in 24 hours is far too slow for high-risk sepsis criteria.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Agnes, 86, lives in a care home and has a NEWS2 of 2 with a suspected chest infection. The staff say she 'cannot have sepsis because she has no fever'. Which statement by the nurse is best?
o: Fever or hypothermia does not rule sepsis in or out
Older people with no fever are unlikely to have sepsis
Sepsis is ruled out while her NEWS2 remains below 5
A temperature above 38°C is needed before sepsis is considered
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.1: do not rely on fever or hypothermia alone to rule sepsis in or out. Older people may not mount a fever; NEWS2 supports, but does not replace, clinical judgement.

n.1: Older people frequently do not develop a fever, so its absence does not lower risk.
n.2: A NEWS2 below 5 means low risk, not that sepsis is excluded.
n.3: No temperature threshold is required before considering sepsis.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Fatima, 57, is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She has no history of lung disease and her SpO2 is 90% on air. What target oxygen saturation range should be prescribed?
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: BTS oxygen guideline and NICE NG253 (2025) rec 1.10.1: the target for most acutely ill adults is 94-98%.

n.0: 88-92% is for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some people with COPD.
n.2: 92-96% is not the standard BTS adult target range.
n.3: Aiming for 98-100% risks hyperoxaemia; BTS notes higher saturations are associated with harm.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: George, 71, has known COPD with previous hypercapnic respiratory failure. He arrives breathless with SpO2 84% on air. Blood gas results are awaited. What target saturation range is appropriate?
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: BTS guideline: for people with known COPD or other risk factors for hypercapnic respiratory failure, aim for 88-92% pending blood gas results; NEWS2 Scale 2 is then used if this target is prescribed (RCP 2017).

n.0: 85-88% leaves him below the recommended lower limit of 88%.
n.1: 92-95% overshoots the 88-92% target for people at risk of hypercapnia.
n.2: 94-98% risks worsening hypercapnia in someone with previous hypercapnic failure.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Which factor is most likely to give a falsely reassuring pulse oximetry reading?
o: A fever of 38.2°C on admission
Mild iron-deficiency anaemia
Carbon monoxide poisoning
Mild dehydration after vomiting
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Standard pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so carbon monoxide poisoning can show normal or high SpO2 despite severe hypoxia. Other pitfalls include poor perfusion, nail varnish, movement and reduced accuracy in people with darker skin tones.

n.0: Fever does not directly cause oximeters to over-read.
n.1: Mild anaemia does not by itself produce a falsely high SpO2.
n.3: Mild dehydration is not a recognised cause of falsely high oximeter readings.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Leah, 19, has asthma. You are recording her peak expiratory flow. Which instruction is correct?
o: Record a single attempt after a practice blow
Record the best of three attempts
Record the average of three attempts
Record the lowest of three attempts
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Peak flow technique: stand or sit upright, take a full breath, seal lips and blow as hard and fast as possible; repeat three times and record the highest reading, compared with the person's best or predicted value.

n.0: A single recorded blow is unreliable; three attempts are taken and the best recorded.
n.2: The average underestimates the true peak and is not how PEF is recorded.
n.3: The lowest reading reflects poor technique rather than true peak flow.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Harold, 76, has COPD with a prescribed target of 88-92%. He is on 28% oxygen via a Venturi mask with SpO2 95%. He is alert and comfortable. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remove the mask and recheck his saturation in 4 hours
Reduce the oxygen concentration and recheck his saturation
Continue the current oxygen, as 95% is a reassuring level
Increase the oxygen to 35% to prevent a fall in saturation
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: BTS guideline: titrate oxygen to keep saturation within the prescribed target. Above 92% in someone at risk of hypercapnia risks CO2 retention, so step down (for example to 24%) and monitor closely. On Scale 2, 95% on oxygen also scores 2 points (RCP 2017).

n.0: Stopping oxygen abruptly without close monitoring risks rebound hypoxaemia.
n.2: 95% is above his prescribed range and risks hypercapnia.
n.3: Increasing oxygen pushes his saturation further above target.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Winston, 69, has COPD with hypercapnia and is prescribed a salbutamol nebuliser. His target saturation is 88-92%. How should the nebuliser be driven?
o: By oxygen at 6-8 L/min for the whole nebulisation
By compressed air, with oxygen by nasal cannulae if needed
By oxygen at 2 L/min to reduce the risk of hypercapnia
By oxygen at 15 L/min through a reservoir mask
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: BTS oxygen guideline: in people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, nebulisers should be air-driven, with supplemental oxygen given by nasal cannulae to keep saturation at 88-92%.

n.0: Prolonged oxygen-driven nebulisation risks hypercapnia in this group.
n.2: 2 L/min is too low to nebulise the drug effectively.
n.3: A reservoir mask delivers high-concentration oxygen and is not a nebuliser driver.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Bethany, 38, has a tracheostomy and needs suctioning for audible secretions. Her SpO2 is 95% before the procedure. Which practice is correct?
o: Set the suction pressure to about -300 mmHg for better clearance
Limit each suction pass to about 10 seconds and monitor saturation
Instil 5 mL sodium chloride 0.9% before each pass
Apply suction while advancing the catheter to clear secretions
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: National Tracheostomy Safety Project (Suctioning guidance): suctioning can cause hypoxia, trauma and vagal stimulation. Do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; apply it on withdrawal, keep each period of suction to no more than 10 seconds, use a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg, and observe the patient (saturation, heart rate, colour) throughout, reattaching oxygen promptly.

n.0: The National Tracheostomy Safety Project advises a pressure no greater than -150 mmHg (-20 kPa) for most patients; higher pressure traumatises the mucosa and worsens hypoxia.
n.2: NTSP does not advise routine saline instillation; tenacious secretions are managed with better humidification, and saline is reserved for specific situations.
n.3: NTSP: do not apply suction while introducing the catheter; suction on insertion causes mucosal damage and hypoxia.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Margaret, 64, is breathless and anxious. Her SpO2 is 82% on air and she is drowsy with RR 30. She has no history of lung disease. Help has been called. What oxygen should be given first?
o: 28% oxygen via a Venturi mask with humidification
4 L/min via a simple face mask and reassess
15 L/min via a non-rebreathe reservoir mask
2 L/min via nasal cannulae and titrate up
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: BTS guideline: in critical illness or severe hypoxaemia start high-concentration oxygen via a reservoir mask at 15 L/min, then titrate down to a target of 94-98% once stable (NG253 rec 1.10.1).

n.0: 28% Venturi is a controlled low-concentration device for people at risk of hypercapnia.
n.1: A simple face mask at 4 L/min risks CO2 rebreathing and is inadequate here.
n.3: 2 L/min nasal cannulae delivers far too little oxygen for severe hypoxaemia.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: You are performing chest compressions on Alan, 60, who has collapsed in a hospital car park. According to RCUK 2025, what compression depth and rate are correct for an adult?
o: 5-6 cm at 100-120 per minute
6-7 cm at 80-100 per minute
4-5 cm at 100-120 per minute
5-6 cm at 120-140 per minute
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: compress on the lower half of the sternum to a depth of at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, at 100-120 per minute, allowing full recoil.

n.1: 6-7 cm is too deep and 80-100 per minute is too slow.
n.2: 4-5 cm is too shallow for an adult.
n.3: 120-140 per minute is faster than the recommended maximum of 120.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: You find Brenda, 72, unresponsive in a day room. She is not breathing normally and is making occasional gasping sounds. What does this indicate?
o: Sleep apnoea, so open her airway and observe
Cardiac arrest, so start CPR
A seizure, so protect her head
A faint, so raise her legs
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025: if a person is unresponsive with absent or abnormal breathing, assume cardiac arrest and start CPR. Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest, and brief seizure-like activity may occur at onset.

n.0: Observing an unresponsive person with abnormal breathing delays CPR.
n.2: Treating gasping as a seizure delays CPR in someone in cardiac arrest.
n.3: A faint does not cause unresponsiveness with agonal breathing.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: A trained healthcare worker is giving CPR to an adult with a pocket mask. What ratio of compressions to rescue breaths should be used?
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: trained rescuers give 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths, each breath just enough to make the chest start to rise.

n.1: 15:2 is the ratio used in paediatric life support by healthcare rescuers.
n.2: 5:1 is an obsolete ratio not used in current guidance.
n.3: 30:1 gives too few breaths for adult BLS.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: What is the standard UK in-hospital telephone number for calling the cardiac arrest team?
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 in-hospital resuscitation: 2222 is the standard UK internal number for cardiac arrest and medical emergency calls.

n.0: 3333 is not the standardised UK cardiac arrest number.
n.1: 999 is the external emergency number, used out of hospital.
n.3: 111 is the NHS non-emergency advice line.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Peter, 81, is found in cardiac arrest in a hospital bed with a pressure-relieving mattress. CPR is needed. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start CPR on the bed, compressing deeper if needed
Wait for the arrest team to bring a backboard
Move him to the floor before starting compressions
Start rescue breaths until the mattress is deflated
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025: do not move a person from a bed to the floor to do CPR; start compressions on the bed and compress deeper if needed to compensate for the mattress, deploying CPR mode on the mattress where available.

n.1: Waiting delays the start of compressions.
n.2: Moving him to the floor delays compressions and risks injury to staff.
n.3: Compressions take priority; breaths before compressions delay circulation.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: You are alone on a quiet community visit when Sandra, 55, collapses. She is unresponsive and you have a mobile phone. According to RCUK 2025, what should you do next?
o: Give 2 minutes of CPR before calling 999
Call 999 on speaker, then assess breathing
Leave her to find a defibrillator first
Assess her breathing for one minute before calling
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 adult BLS: if alone with a phone, call 999 on speakerphone as soon as unresponsiveness is identified, before assessing breathing, so the call handler can guide CPR and locate an AED.

n.0: Delaying the call delays emergency help and AED location.
n.2: Leaving her delays both the call and CPR; the call handler can direct others to an AED.
n.3: Breathing is assessed for no more than 10 seconds, and the 2025 guideline calls 999 first if alone.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: On a ward, an AED is attached to Kevin, 63, during CPR. The AED announces it is analysing the rhythm. What should the team do?
o: Stop compressions and ensure nobody touches him
Continue compressions during the rhythm analysis
Check his carotid pulse while it analyses
Give two rescue breaths while it analyses
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025: follow AED prompts; nobody should touch the person during rhythm analysis, as movement interferes with analysis. Resume compressions immediately after the shock or no-shock prompt.

n.1: Compressions during analysis cause artefact and can delay or prevent a shock.
n.2: Pulse checks involve touching him and delay the AED's decision.
n.3: Breaths involve touching him and interfere with analysis.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: During an in-hospital arrest, Joyce, 70, is in a non-shockable rhythm. The ALS team has IV access. When should adrenaline 1 mg IV be given according to RCUK 2025?
o: As soon as possible, then every 3-5 minutes
After 30 minutes, if no output has returned
After 10 minutes of CPR, then every 5 minutes
After the third shock, then every 3-5 minutes
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 ALS: in non-shockable rhythms give adrenaline 1 mg IV as soon as possible; for shockable rhythms give it after the third shock. Repeat every 3-5 minutes.

n.1: Adrenaline is not reserved until 30 minutes into the arrest.
n.2: Waiting 10 minutes delays adrenaline in a non-shockable rhythm.
n.3: After the third shock is the timing for shockable rhythms.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Grace, 34, develops a widespread rash, lip swelling and wheeze minutes after starting an IV antibiotic infusion. Her BP is 82/50 mmHg. What is the first action after calling for help?
o: Stop the infusion and give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg as the first drug
Give oral cetirizine and recheck her in 15 minutes
Slow the infusion rate and continue to observe her
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline (2021, current): remove the trigger (stop the infusion) and give IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Adults and children over 12: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL) into the anterolateral thigh.

n.1: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.
n.2: Antihistamines are third-line and do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
n.3: Continuing the infusion, even slowed, keeps exposing her to the trigger.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Wendy, 60, develops stridor, facial swelling and a blotchy rash after a wasp sting in the hospital garden. A colleague has called for help and brought the emergency box with adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Where should you inject the intramuscular adrenaline?
o: Deltoid muscle of the non-dominant arm
Anterolateral middle third of the thigh
Subcutaneous tissue of the abdomen
Upper outer quadrant of the buttock
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline: IM adrenaline is given into the anterolateral aspect of the middle third of the thigh, which gives reliable absorption.

n.0: The deltoid is not the recommended site for anaphylaxis.
n.2: Subcutaneous injection gives slower, less reliable absorption.
n.3: The buttock is not recommended and risks injection into fat or the sciatic area.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Simon, 38, has anaphylaxis after an iodinated contrast injection in the radiology department. The nurse opens the emergency drug box, which contains several adrenaline preparations. Which preparation should be drawn up for his intramuscular injection?
o: 5 mg/mL (1 in 200)
10 micrograms/mL (1 in 100,000)
100 micrograms/mL (1 in 10,000)
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK: IM adrenaline in anaphylaxis uses the 1 mg/mL (1 in 1,000) preparation, for example 0.5 mL = 500 micrograms in an adult.

n.0: 5 mg/mL is not a standard adrenaline preparation for anaphylaxis.
n.1: 1 in 100,000 is a dilution used by specialists for IV infusion, not IM.
n.2: 1 in 10,000 is the IV preparation used in cardiac arrest, not for IM anaphylaxis treatment.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Tariq, 8, has anaphylaxis after eating peanuts at a hospital clinic. What dose of IM adrenaline should be given?
o: 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL of 1 mg/mL)
500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL)
100 micrograms (0.1 mL of 1 mg/mL)
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK anaphylaxis doses (1 mg/mL): over 12 years 500 micrograms; 6-12 years 300 micrograms; 6 months to 6 years 150 micrograms; under 6 months 100-150 micrograms.

n.0: 150 micrograms is the dose for 6 months to 6 years.
n.2: 500 micrograms is for adults and children over 12.
n.3: 100 micrograms is within the range for infants under 6 months.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Deborah, 46, received IM adrenaline 500 micrograms for anaphylaxis 5 minutes ago. She remains wheezy with BP 84/52 mmHg. What should happen next?
o: Wait a further 15 minutes before repeating adrenaline
Give chlorphenamine IV and wait for it to take effect
Sit her upright with her legs lowered to ease breathing
Give a second IM adrenaline dose and an IV crystalloid bolus
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if there is no improvement and give an IV crystalloid bolus (adults 500-1,000 mL) for circulatory problems, with high-flow oxygen and monitoring.

n.0: RCUK advises a repeat dose after 5 minutes, not 15.
n.1: Antihistamines are not used to treat ABC problems in anaphylaxis.
n.2: With hypotension she should lie flat with or without legs raised; sitting with legs down worsens circulation.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ali, 52, has had anaphylaxis. Despite two appropriate doses of IM adrenaline, his breathing and circulation have not improved. How is this situation described in RCUK guidance?
o: Refractory anaphylaxis
Biphasic anaphylaxis
Recurrent anaphylaxis
Delayed anaphylaxis
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK (2021): refractory anaphylaxis is no improvement in respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms despite two appropriate doses of IM adrenaline; it needs expert help and a low-dose adrenaline infusion.

n.1: Biphasic anaphylaxis is a recurrence of symptoms after initial resolution.
n.2: Recurrent describes repeated episodes over time, not treatment failure.
n.3: Delayed anaphylaxis describes reactions starting some time after exposure, not failure to respond.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ellen, 29, had wheeze, hypotension and urticaria after eating a prawn curry on the ward. She improved after one dose of IM adrenaline and is now stable. The doctor plans her period of observation and later allergy referral. Which blood test should be taken to support the diagnosis?
o: Two sets of blood cultures
Mast cell tryptase level
Serum troponin level
Full blood count and film
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK guidance: take mast cell tryptase samples to help confirm anaphylaxis and support specialist allergy follow-up. Observation is risk-stratified, with a minimum of 6 hours in most people and 12 hours in higher-risk groups, or fast-track after 2 hours in selected cases.

n.0: Blood cultures are taken for suspected infection, not allergy.
n.2: Troponin assesses myocardial injury and does not confirm anaphylaxis.
n.3: FBC does not confirm anaphylaxis.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Olu, 41, has anaphylaxis with severe breathlessness. She is 30 weeks pregnant. While IM adrenaline is prepared, how should she be positioned?
o: Flat on her back with legs raised
Standing, supported by two members of staff
On her left side
Prone with her head turned
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK anaphylaxis guideline (2021, section 4.4): avoid sudden changes in posture; lie flat, with or without legs raised, or semi-recumbent if that eases breathing; pregnant patients should lie on their left side to prevent aortocaval compression.

n.0: Supine in late pregnancy causes aortocaval compression and worsens hypotension.
n.1: RCUK (2021) warns that standing, walking or sitting up suddenly can cause fatal cardiovascular collapse in anaphylaxis; patients must not stand during an acute reaction.
n.3: Prone positioning is unsafe and impedes assessment and treatment.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Martin, 66, is eating lunch in a ward day room when he clutches his throat. He is coughing forcefully, red in the face and can speak a few words. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give up to 5 back blows between his shoulder blades
Encourage him to keep coughing and monitor him closely
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts from behind him
Lie him on the floor and start chest compressions
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): with an effective cough (mild obstruction), encourage coughing and monitor for deterioration to an ineffective cough or until the obstruction is relieved.

n.0: Back blows are for an ineffective cough in a conscious person.
n.2: Abdominal thrusts follow back blows when the cough is ineffective.
n.3: CPR is started if the person becomes unconscious.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Valerie, 58, is choking in a hospital café. She cannot cough, speak or breathe but remains conscious. Help has been called. What should you do first?
o: Perform a blind finger sweep
Give up to 5 back blows
Start chest compressions
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK adult choking algorithm (2025): for severe obstruction in a conscious person, give 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, and repeat until relieved.

n.0: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further in and are not part of the algorithm.
n.2: Chest compressions start once she becomes unconscious.
n.3: Abdominal thrusts come after 5 back blows.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Colin, 49, is found on a hospital corridor floor. He is breathing normally but responds to pain only. There is no suggestion of injury. Help is on its way. How should he be positioned?
o: Sitting upright against the wall
In the lateral recovery position
Flat on his back with legs raised
Prone with his head to one side
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK first aid 2025: place a person with decreased responsiveness who does not meet the criteria for CPR in a lateral (side-lying) recovery position. Do not use it if breathing is agonal or there is trauma.

n.0: Sitting a person with reduced responsiveness upright risks airway compromise and falls.
n.2: Supine positioning risks airway obstruction from the tongue or vomit.
n.3: Prone positioning impedes airway assessment and breathing.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Pauline, 62, a visitor, develops central crushing chest pain while in the ward waiting area. She has no known allergies and is alert. 999 has been called. What first aid should be offered?
o: Give her 400 mg ibuprofen orally
Help her chew 300 mg aspirin
Give her 75 mg aspirin to swallow
Walk her to the emergency department
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK first aid 2025: encourage and assist a person with cardiac-sounding chest pain to self-administer 300 mg aspirin (ideally chewable or dissolvable) as soon as possible while awaiting help, unless allergic.

n.0: Ibuprofen is not an antiplatelet treatment for suspected heart attack.
n.2: 75 mg is the long-term antiplatelet dose, not the acute first aid dose.
n.3: Exertion increases cardiac workload; she should rest and await help.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ian, 35, has type 1 diabetes and is shaky and sweaty at a community clinic. He is alert and able to swallow. His capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. After giving 15-20 g of glucose tablets, his symptoms are no better at 15 minutes. What should you do?
o: Give a further 15-20 g of oral glucose
Call 999 and place him in the recovery position
Give him a meal containing complex carbohydrate
Recheck his blood glucose again in 30 minutes
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK first aid 2025: treat hypoglycaemia (below 4.0 mmol/L) in a person who can swallow with 15-20 g glucose; repeat if symptoms persist after 15 minutes; give a snack once recovered.

n.1: He is alert and swallowing, so oral treatment is repeated before an emergency call.
n.2: A snack follows recovery; complex carbohydrate alone is too slow while still hypoglycaemic.
n.3: Waiting another 30 minutes leaves hypoglycaemia untreated.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Lee, 27, is found unresponsive in a hospital toilet with pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing. A used needle is nearby. You are trained and the emergency box contains naloxone. Help has been called. What is the priority?
o: Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
Leave him to sleep it off in the recovery position
Give him sips of water and sit him upright
Search his belongings to identify the drug taken
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK first aid 2025: in suspected opioid overdose, support airway and breathing and administer naloxone if trained, following the instructions on repeat dosing; start CPR if breathing becomes absent or abnormal.

n.1: Respiratory depression needs active treatment, not observation alone.
n.2: Oral fluids are unsafe in an unresponsive person.
n.3: Searching belongings delays airway support and naloxone.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Jasmine, 22, has a tonic-clonic seizure in a clinic waiting area. She is on the floor near a chair. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Restrain her limbs to prevent injury during the jerking
Give her sips of water as the jerking slows down
Place a padded object between her teeth to protect her tongue
Move objects away, cushion her head and time the seizure
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Seizure first aid: keep the person safe by moving hazards, cushion the head, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, and place in the recovery position when the jerking stops. Seek emergency help for a prolonged seizure (RCUK special circumstances: treat with benzodiazepines).

n.0: Restraining limbs can cause injury to the person and the helper.
n.1: Oral fluids risk aspiration while consciousness is impaired.
n.2: Objects in the mouth can break teeth or obstruct the airway.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Dennis, 70, has a deep laceration to his forearm from a fall on the ward. Blood is spurting and soaking through the dressing despite firm direct pressure. You have called for help. What should be done next?
o: Elevate the arm and wait for the bleeding to stop
Apply an ice pack directly to the wound site
Apply a tourniquet 5-7 cm above the wound
Remove the soaked dressing and press on a new one
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: RCUK first aid 2025: use direct pressure and a haemostatic dressing; apply a tourniquet as soon as possible for life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by direct pressure, 5-7 cm above the injury and not over a joint, recording the time applied.

n.0: Elevation is not part of the RCUK 2025 escalating approach (pressure, haemostatic dressing, tourniquet) and waiting delays control.
n.1: Ice does not control arterial bleeding.
n.3: Removing the dressing disturbs clot formation; pressure is maintained and escalated.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Shona, 31, is on a medical ward awaiting results. She tells you quietly that she has been thinking about ending her life. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask her directly about her suicidal thoughts and any plans
Advise her to speak to her GP once she is discharged home
Tell her she has so much to live for and should stay positive
Change the subject to avoid putting ideas into her head
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Mental health first aid: asking directly and calmly about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and allows the nurse to understand the immediacy of the risk, listen non-judgementally and arrange urgent help (Annexe B 2.14; NICE NG225 focuses on a person-centred assessment and safety planning).

n.1: Deferring to a future GP appointment leaves current risk unmanaged.
n.2: Reassurance that dismisses her feelings blocks disclosure and is not a risk response.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves risk unassessed; asking does not plant the idea.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Kieran, 45, is shouting in a corridor after being told his discharge is delayed. He is pacing and red-faced but has not threatened anyone. Which approach is the best first step?
o: Call security to remove him from the ward straight away
Stand close and tell him firmly to lower his voice immediately
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and acknowledge his frustration
Walk away and leave him until he has calmed himself down
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: De-escalation (Annexe A 3.5; NICE NG10) is the first-line response to agitation: a calm, non-threatening stance at a safe distance, active listening and acknowledging feelings, offering choices and reducing stimulation. Restrictive options are a last resort.

n.0: Removal by security is restrictive and premature when de-escalation has not been tried.
n.1: Standing close and issuing commands can feel threatening and escalate the situation.
n.3: Leaving an agitated person unsupported misses the chance to de-escalate and to keep others safe.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Under NICE guidance on violence and aggression (NG10), when may manual restraint be used in a health setting?
o: As the first response whenever a person raises their voice
As a last resort when de-escalation fails and harm is likely
As a routine measure to give medicines a person has refused
As a punishment for breaking ward rules on two occasions
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG10 and Annexe B 2.17: restrictive interventions are used as a last resort, after de-escalation and other strategies fail, when there is a real risk of harm, and must be proportionate and for the shortest time possible.

n.0: Raised voices call for de-escalation, not restraint.
n.2: Restraint is not a routine method of giving refused medicines; covert or compulsory treatment has its own legal safeguards.
n.3: Restraint is never punitive; this would breach human rights and the Code.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ahmed, 28, is distressed and tearful after hearing bad news. Which skill is the cornerstone of mental health first aid in this situation?
o: Offering a sedative medicine
Distracting him with other topics
Listening non-judgementally
Giving clear advice on solutions
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Mental health first aid centres on approaching the person, listening non-judgementally, giving support and information, and encouraging appropriate professional help (Annexe B 2.14).

n.0: Medication is not a first aid response to normal distress.
n.1: Distraction can invalidate his feelings and block disclosure.
n.3: Jumping to advice can feel dismissive before the person feels heard.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ruby, 19, is restrained by trained staff after assaulting a nurse. She is taken to the floor face down. Which action is most important for the nurse coordinating the restraint?
o: Monitor her airway and breathing and move her off her front quickly
Hold her in the face-down position until rapid tranquillisation works
Apply weight across her back to keep her still until she is calm
Leave the room so that the restraining staff can work without distraction
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG10: avoid taking a person to the floor; if prone restraint is needed, use it for as short a time as possible, avoid pressure on the chest, neck or abdomen, and have one staff member monitor airway, breathing and physical condition throughout.

n.1: Prolonged prone restraint increases the risk of positional asphyxia.
n.2: Pressure on the back or chest restricts breathing and has caused deaths in restraint.
n.3: A staff member must stay to monitor her airway and wellbeing throughout.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Stephen, 52, received intramuscular rapid tranquillisation on a mental health ward 10 minutes ago. He is now drowsy. Under NICE NG10, how often should his vital signs be monitored initially?
o: Once, an hour after the injection was given
Every 2 hours until he is fully awake again
Every 4 hours for the first 24 hours after the dose
At least every 15 minutes until there are no further concerns
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG10 1.4.45: after rapid tranquillisation monitor side effects and vital signs at least every hour, increasing to at least every 15 minutes if the person appears asleep or sedated (as Stephen is), has had more than the BNF maximum, has used drugs or alcohol, has a physical health problem or was harmed during restraint; continue until there are no further concerns.

n.0: A single check an hour later misses the period of greatest risk.
n.1: 2-hourly observations are too infrequent after rapid tranquillisation.
n.2: 4-hourly observations miss early respiratory depression and hypotension.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Ivy, 84, has dementia and becomes agitated each evening, trying to leave the ward and hitting out during personal care. Her pain has not been assessed. Which action best responds to her behaviour?
o: Ask her family to stay overnight so that staff can step back
Assess for pain and unmet needs and adapt her care around them
Keep her in a chair with a lap belt to stop her leaving
Request a prescription for regular antipsychotic medicine
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Behaviour that challenges often communicates unmet need, such as pain, constipation, infection or fear. Assess pain with a behavioural observation tool where self-report is difficult (the 2018 UK guideline recommends PAINAD or Doloplus-2; Abbey is widely used) (UK guidance on pain assessment in older people, Age and Ageing 2018) and adapt care, using positive behaviour support before any restrictive or pharmacological option (Annexe A 3.5, P4.4).

n.0: Family involvement is helpful, but staff remain responsible for assessing and meeting her needs.
n.2: A lap belt is a restrictive practice and a potential deprivation of liberty, not a first response.
n.3: Antipsychotics carry significant risks in dementia and do not address the cause.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Noah, 23, is seen after self-harm. A colleague suggests using a risk scale to decide whether he can be discharged. Under NICE NG225, what should happen instead?
o: A person-centred psychosocial assessment and an agreed safety plan
A higher-risk score threshold before he is allowed to go home
Discharge if his risk is rated as low on the global scale
A repeat of the same scale after 24 hours of observation
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: NICE NG225 (2022): do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict suicide or repetition of self-harm or to decide who is discharged, and do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification. Develop a safety plan with, and agreed by, the person.

n.1: Adjusting a scale threshold still relies on a risk tool to make the decision.
n.2: Global low, medium or high stratification is specifically advised against.
n.3: Repeating the scale does not make it a valid basis for decisions.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Peter, 68, is two days after bowel surgery. A healthcare support worker reports that he is 'not himself'. You find him drowsy, with snoring respirations and his tongue falling back. Using the ABCDE approach, what is your first action?
o: Open his airway with a head tilt and chin lift and call for help
Check his capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia
Review his fluid balance chart and wound drain output
Record a full set of observations and calculate his NEWS2 score
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: The ABCDE approach (RCUK) deals with problems in order and treats each one as it is found. Snoring with a falling tongue is partial airway obstruction, which kills fastest, so open the airway with simple manoeuvres and call for help before moving on. Code 15 and P4.10 require a prompt response to deterioration.

n.1: Glucose is checked under D (disability); airway obstruction comes first in the sequence.
n.2: Fluid balance belongs to C (circulation) and does not address the immediate airway threat.
n.3: A full set of observations is useful but delays treating an obstructed airway, which must be dealt with first.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Amira, 45, has pneumonia. On assessment her airway is clear. Her respiratory rate is 28 breaths per minute and SpO2 is 89% on air. She has no history of lung disease. According to the ABCDE approach, what should you do next?
o: Give oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 88-92% and summon help
Move straight on to assess her pulse, blood pressure and capillary refill
Give oxygen to achieve a target saturation of 94-98% and summon help
Ask her to take deep breaths and recheck her saturation in an hour
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Problems found under B are treated before moving to C. For acutely ill adults not at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure the target is 94-98% (BTS; NICE NG253 rec 1.10.1), so start oxygen and get help early.

n.0: 88-92% is the target for people at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, which Amira is not.
n.1: ABCDE requires treating the breathing problem found at B before assessing circulation.
n.3: An hour's delay with SpO2 89% and RR 28 leaves hypoxaemia untreated.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: During an ABCDE assessment of Jordan, 30, who was admitted with a gastrointestinal bleed, you note a pulse of 124 beats per minute, BP 92/60 mmHg, cool peripheries and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Which assessment step are these findings part of?
o: Breathing
Circulation
Exposure
Disability
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: Pulse, blood pressure, peripheral temperature and capillary refill time are all assessed under C (circulation). These findings suggest hypovolaemia and need urgent escalation (NICE CG174 lists HR over 90, systolic under 100 and CRT over 2 seconds as indicators for urgent fluid resuscitation).

n.0: Breathing covers respiratory rate, effort, oxygen saturation and chest sounds, not perfusion.
n.2: Exposure covers full skin examination, temperature, wounds, drains and bleeding sites.
n.3: Disability covers level of consciousness, pupils and blood glucose.

Deterioration & Emergencies.q: Grace, 79, is found by her daughter on the ward to be confused and difficult to rouse. You have assessed and managed her airway, breathing and circulation. Under D (disability), which assessment should you complete?
o: Level of consciousness using ACVPU, pupils and capillary blood glucose
Respiratory rate, chest expansion and oxygen saturation
Pulse, blood pressure and urine output over the last hour
Skin inspection for rashes, pressure damage, wound leakage and drains
Deterioration & Emergencies.w: D in the ABCDE approach assesses neurological status: level of consciousness (ACVPU, which NEWS2 uses), pupils and a capillary blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia as a reversible cause of reduced consciousness.

n.1: Respiratory rate, expansion and saturation belong to B (breathing).
n.2: Pulse, BP and urine output belong to C (circulation).
n.3: Skin, rashes and wounds are examined under E (exposure).

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ada, 88, has been sleeping poorly. She dozes most of the afternoon, is woken for observations at 02:00 and 06:00, and has a NEWS2 of 0. She says she is tired all day. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Review her observation times with the team to protect her sleep
Ask the doctor to prescribe a sedative for her to take at night
Wake her more often in the afternoon so that she sleeps at night
Leave her plan unchanged, as observations have to be done at night
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: With a NEWS2 of 0 the minimum frequency is 12-hourly (RCP 2017), so night-time waking may be avoidable. Reviewing the care plan to cluster care and protect sleep supports rest (Annexe B 3.1, 3.6).

n.1: Sedatives are not first line and increase falls risk in older people.
n.2: Repeatedly waking her during the day adds fatigue rather than addressing the night-time disturbance.
n.3: Observation timing is a clinical decision and can be reviewed when the score is 0.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Krishna, 64, is a Hindu man on an acute ward. During his assessment he asks for a female nurse not to wash him and to wash with running water rather than a bowl. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Record his preferences in the care plan and arrange care to meet them
Ask his family to come in and do all his washing during visiting time
Tell him staffing makes it difficult and he will be washed by whoever is free
Explain that a bowl wash is the standard ward practice for every patient
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Code 1.1, 4.1 and Annexe B 3.4: treat people as individuals and respect their cultural and religious preferences in personal care, documenting them so that care can be arranged to meet them where possible.

n.1: Families may help if they wish, but care remains the nurse's responsibility.
n.2: Dismissing his preference fails to respect his dignity and beliefs.
n.3: Standard practice should adapt to individual needs where reasonably possible.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Rose, 79, rings her bell repeatedly at night. When you answer she says she is uncomfortable, cold and needs the toilet. Her pain score is 1 out of 10. What is the best approach to help her rest?
o: Meet her comfort and toileting needs and plan regular night checks
Explain that the bell is for emergencies and move it out of her reach
Give her a sedative to help her sleep without disturbing others
Close the door to her side room so that she is not disturbed
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 3.1 and 3.6: assess and meet comfort needs such as warmth, toileting and positioning, which are common barriers to sleep. Intentional rounding at intervals can reduce unmet need and calls.

n.1: Removing the call bell is unsafe and a breach of dignity and safety.
n.2: Sedation does not address her unmet needs and increases falls risk.
n.3: Closing the door does not meet her needs and reduces observation.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Olivia, 23, has a learning disability and is anxious about her admission. During a ward round several staff discuss her care at the bedside using medical terms, talking over her. Which action best role-models person-centred care?
o: Continue the round and explain the plan to her carer afterwards
Speak to her directly in plain language and include her in the discussion
Give her a leaflet about her condition after the ward round finishes
Ask the team to discuss her care at the nurses' station instead
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: P4.1 asks nurses to role-model person-centred care. Code 2.1-2.3 and 7.1-7.3: work in partnership, encourage people to be involved in decisions, and use terms people can understand, making reasonable adjustments (Equality Act 2010 s20).

n.0: Talking to her carer instead excludes her from decisions about her own care.
n.2: A leaflet afterwards does not involve her in the discussion and may not be accessible.
n.3: Moving the discussion away removes her from decisions that concern her.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Bill, 85, has advanced dementia and cannot describe his pain. After a fall he grimaces, groans and guards his left hip when moved. Which assessment is most appropriate?
o: A visual analogue scale explained slowly to him
A behavioural pain tool such as the Abbey pain scale
A 0-10 numerical rating scale completed by Bill himself
His daughter's estimate of his pain on a 0-10 scale
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Where a person cannot reliably self-report, for example because of dementia or a learning disability, use a validated behavioural or observational pain assessment tool such as the Abbey pain scale or PAINAD (NICE NG31 principle; Annexe B 3.1).

n.0: A visual analogue scale still needs him to self-report, which he cannot reliably do.
n.2: Numerical self-report relies on abilities Bill no longer has.
n.3: Family insight is valuable, but a proxy number is not a validated assessment.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Sarah, 41, is two hours after an appendicectomy. She rates her pain at 8 out of 10 and was given prescribed oral morphine 30 minutes ago. What should the nurse do next?
o: Give a second dose of morphine because her pain is still 8
Reassess her pain and document the effect of the morphine
Encourage her to walk around the ward to ease the pain
Wait until the next scheduled observations in four hours
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Pain management is a cycle of assessment, intervention and reassessment. Reassess at the expected time of peak effect (around 30-60 minutes after oral analgesia), document the response, and escalate if relief is inadequate (Annexe B 3.5, P4.8).

n.0: Repeating the dose without reassessment or a prescription for a further dose risks opioid toxicity.
n.2: Mobilising with severe uncontrolled pain is inappropriate and distressing.
n.3: Four hours is too long to leave severe pain without reassessing the response.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Joan, 74, has lower back pain after a fall at home and is being cared for on a frailty unit. Her care plan lists several pain-relieving interventions. Which of these is a non-pharmacological intervention?
o: A rectal paracetamol suppository
A topical lidocaine plaster
Patient-controlled analgesia pump
Repositioning using pillows
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Non-pharmacological measures include repositioning, heat or cold where appropriate, distraction, relaxation, reassurance and explanation. NICE NG31 gives repositioning as an example (Annexe B 3.5).

n.0: A suppository is a route for giving a drug.
n.1: A lidocaine plaster delivers a drug and is pharmacological.
n.2: PCA delivers opioid medicine and is pharmacological.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Mohammed, 58, has been taking regular codeine for back pain for a week. Which side effect should the nurse ask about and plan to prevent?
o: Constipation
Diarrhoea
Hypertension
Insomnia
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Opioids, including codeine, commonly cause constipation, so bowel habit should be assessed and a laxative considered with regular opioid use (P4.5, P4.15). Other effects include nausea, drowsiness and respiratory depression.

n.1: Opioids slow gut motility rather than causing diarrhoea.
n.2: Opioids do not typically raise blood pressure.
n.3: Opioids more commonly cause drowsiness than insomnia.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Nina, 33, has sickle cell disease and arrives with severe pain. A colleague says she is 'drug seeking' because she asks for morphine by name and her pain score is 9 while she is using her phone. What is the most appropriate nursing response?
o: Accept her report of pain and give prescribed analgesia promptly
Delay analgesia until her behaviour matches her pain score
Offer paracetamol until the doctor has assessed her pain
Ask her to stop using her phone before reassessing her pain
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Pain is what the person says it is; self-report is the most reliable measure. People with long-term painful conditions often know which analgesia works and may cope with distraction. Prompt analgesia is essential, and judgement based on stereotypes breaches Code 20.2 and 1.1.

n.1: Behaviour is a poor guide to pain in people with recurrent pain, and delay causes harm.
n.2: Withholding effective prescribed analgesia leaves severe pain undertreated.
n.3: Distraction is a coping strategy and does not invalidate her pain score.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Peggy, 90, has a hip fracture and is receiving regular analgesia. At 02:00 she is restless and calling out, her pain score using PAINAD is 7, and her bladder is distended with no urine output for 8 hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Assess for urinary retention and escalate to the medical team
Reorient her to time and place and recheck in the morning
Give a prescribed sedative to settle her for the night
Increase her analgesia without informing the medical team
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Agitation and pain can result from unmet needs such as urinary retention (NICE NG31 notes a full bladder as a reversible cause of pain and agitation). Assess the cause, for example with a bladder scan, and escalate: treat the cause, not just the symptom (P4.8, Annexe B 3.1).

n.1: Reorientation does not address her pain or retention, and waiting until morning is unsafe.
n.2: Sedation masks the cause and increases falls and delirium risk.
n.3: Changing analgesia outside the prescription is not within nursing scope and misses the cause.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ted, 67, has a PCA pump after bowel surgery. He is very drowsy, difficult to rouse, with RR 8 per minute and pinpoint pupils. His wife says he has been pressing the button for him while he slept. What is the priority?
o: Stop the PCA, support his breathing and call for urgent help
Explain to his wife that Ted must press the PCA button himself
Encourage him to take deep breaths and press the button less
Reduce the PCA bolus dose and recheck his observations in 1 hour
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: RR 8 scores 3 on NEWS2 and drowsiness scores 3: this is opioid toxicity. Stop the infusion, open and support the airway, give oxygen and get urgent help so that naloxone can be given as prescribed (P4.15). The PCA safety principle is that the person alone presses the button; this is addressed after the emergency.

n.1: Education is needed, but only after treating life-threatening respiratory depression.
n.2: He cannot respond reliably and needs emergency treatment, not encouragement.
n.3: Altering the dose and waiting an hour leaves respiratory depression untreated.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Grace, 52, has chronic osteoarthritis pain. She asks how she can manage flare-ups at home alongside her prescribed paracetamol. Which advice is most appropriate to support self-management?
o: Take her husband's leftover codeine tablets for bad days
Double her paracetamol dose on days when the pain is worse
Rest in bed until the pain fully settles after each flare-up
Pace activities and use local heat alongside regular analgesia
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Self-management of long-term pain combines pacing, gentle activity and non-drug measures such as heat with analgesia taken as prescribed (P4.5, P4.8). Medicine doses must not exceed the prescription or licensed maximum.

n.0: Taking medicines prescribed for someone else is unsafe and unlawful for prescription-only medicines.
n.1: Doubling paracetamol risks exceeding the maximum daily dose and liver toxicity.
n.2: Prolonged bed rest worsens stiffness and deconditioning in osteoarthritis.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Edna, 80, is admitted to a medical ward from home after a fall. She has limited mobility and a previous sacral pressure ulcer. Under NICE CG179, when should her pressure ulcer risk be assessed and documented?
o: When a skin change is first noticed
Within 72 hours of admission
At the first weekly skin review
On admission to the ward
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG179 (2014): assess and document pressure ulcer risk for adults on admission to secondary care or care homes, and reassess if clinical status changes.

n.0: Waiting for skin change means prevention starts after damage has begun.
n.1: 72 hours delays prevention in someone at risk, contrary to CG179.
n.2: A weekly review would leave her unassessed during the high-risk early period.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Lionel, 79, has had a stroke and cannot reposition himself. He is incontinent and his assessment shows he is at high risk of developing a pressure ulcer. His skin is currently intact. Under NICE CG179, what is the minimum frequency at which he should be helped to change position?
o: At least every 8 hours
At least every 6 hours
At least every 12 hours
At least every 4 hours
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG179: reposition adults at risk at least every 6 hours, and adults at high risk at least every 4 hours.

n.0: Every 8 hours is longer than any CG179 interval.
n.1: Every 6 hours is the minimum for adults at risk, not high risk.
n.2: Every 12 hours is far longer than CG179 recommends.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Winston, 73, has a red area over his sacrum. You want to check whether it is blanching. Which method is recommended by NICE CG179?
o: Applying a barrier cream and checking in a week
Measuring the area's temperature with a probe
Rubbing the area firmly to restore circulation
Finger palpation or diascopy with a clear disc
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG179: use finger palpation or diascopy (pressing a transparent disc onto the skin) to test whether erythema blanches. Non-blanching erythema can present as colour change or discolouration in darker skin tones.

n.0: Barrier cream does not assess blanching and a week's delay misses early damage.
n.1: Temperature probes are not the CG179 method for testing blanching.
n.2: Skin massage or rubbing is advised against in CG179 and can cause damage.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Sunita, 59, is admitted to a surgical ward for elective knee surgery. She is mobile, has no history of pressure damage and her skin is intact. The ward has several types of support surface available. According to NICE CG179, which mattress should she be given?
o: High-specification foam mattress
Sheepskin mattress topper
Water-filled mattress overlay
Standard hospital foam mattress
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG179: use a high-specification foam mattress for all adults admitted to secondary care, and consider a dynamic support surface if one is not sufficient for those at high risk.

n.1: Sheepskins are not the recommended pressure-redistributing surface for adults.
n.2: Water-filled overlays are not the CG179 standard support surface.
n.3: A standard foam mattress does not meet the CG179 recommendation.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ama, 68, has dark brown skin and is cared for in bed after a stroke. Over her heel you find an area that feels warmer and firmer than the surrounding skin, with a slightly purplish tone. It does not blanch with diascopy. What should you do?
o: Apply a dressing and recheck the area at the weekly skin review
Massage the area to stimulate blood flow and recheck it at the next shift
Record it as normal skin pigmentation and continue the current care plan
Start prevention and recheck her skin at least every 2 hours
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG179: in darker skin tones non-blanching erythema may appear as colour change or discolouration, and warmth and firmness are additional signs. If non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention (including heel offloading) and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until it resolves.

n.0: Weekly review is far too infrequent; CG179 sets at least 2-hourly checks until resolved.
n.1: Massage or rubbing is advised against in CG179.
n.2: Dismissing changes as pigmentation misses early pressure damage in darker skin.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Hazel, 77, is incontinent of urine. On her buttocks you find diffuse, shiny red areas with superficial skin loss, not over a bony prominence, with no evidence of pressure. How should this be classified?
o: As a category 1 pressure ulcer
As moisture-associated skin damage
As a category 2 pressure ulcer
As an unstageable pressure ulcer
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NHS Improvement (2018): damage caused by moisture alone is a moisture lesion (moisture-associated skin damage), not a pressure ulcer. Where pressure and moisture combine, it is classed as a pressure ulcer. CG179 advises barrier preparations for moisture lesions.

n.0: A category 1 ulcer is non-blanching erythema of intact skin caused by pressure.
n.2: A category 2 ulcer needs pressure or shear as a cause; here there is moisture alone.
n.3: Unstageable is the international label for full-thickness loss hidden by slough or eschar (recorded as Category 3 under the NWCSP 2024 tool in England); Hazel's damage is superficial and caused by moisture.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ruth, 85, has a sacral wound with full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible but no bone, tendon or muscle is exposed. Using the international NPIAP-EPUAP classification, which category is this?
o: Category 2
Suspected deep tissue injury
Category 3
Category 4
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NPIAP-EPUAP classification (used per NICE CG179): category 3 is full-thickness skin loss with subcutaneous fat visible but bone, tendon or muscle not exposed. Category 4 exposes bone, tendon or muscle; category 2 is partial-thickness loss.

n.0: Category 2 is partial-thickness loss of dermis, such as a shallow open wound or blister.
n.1: Suspected deep tissue injury is an area of purple or maroon intact skin or a blood-filled blister.
n.3: Category 4 involves exposed bone, tendon or muscle.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Jim, 70, has a well-nourished diet and is at high risk of pressure ulcers. His wife asks whether he should take a nutritional supplement drink to prevent ulcers, and whether a nurse could massage his heels. According to NICE CG179, what is the best response?
o: Both are recommended to protect his skin and should be started
A supplement is recommended, but heel massage is not advised
Neither is recommended; focus on repositioning and heel offloading
Heel massage is recommended, but a supplement is not advised
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG179: do not offer nutritional supplements specifically to prevent pressure ulcers in people whose intake is adequate, and do not offer skin massage or rubbing. Prevention relies on repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces and heel offloading for those at high risk.

n.0: CG179 advises against both measures in this situation.
n.1: Supplements are not recommended for prevention when intake is adequate.
n.3: Skin massage and rubbing are advised against in CG179.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Vera, 81, is recovering from pneumonia and is keen to return home. She can wash her face and upper body slowly but tires easily. A healthcare support worker suggests giving her a full bed bath to save time. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Postpone her wash until she can manage it without help
Set her up to wash what she can and help with the rest
Give her a full bed bath so that she can rest afterwards
Ask her daughter to wash her during the afternoon visit
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 4.3: assist with washing and dressing in a way that promotes independence. Encouraging Vera to do what she can, with help for the rest, maintains her abilities and dignity and supports her goal of going home (Code 1.2, 2.1).

n.0: Postponing hygiene leaves her needs unmet and risks skin problems.
n.2: A full bed bath removes the independence she needs to regain.
n.3: Hygiene is a fundamental of care that the nursing team is responsible for providing.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Bernard, 77, is unconscious and nil by mouth. When you give mouth care, you see white patches on his tongue that can be wiped off to leave a red base. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Brush the patches off firmly with a toothbrush at each mouth care
Rinse his mouth with a large volume of water to clear the patches
Report the probable oral thrush so that treatment can be prescribed
Apply petroleum jelly inside his mouth to soothe the area
