n.0: Temporary registration is for people staying in an area for a short time; having no fixed address does not restrict her to it, and she is entitled to full registration.
n.2: Directing routine care to the emergency department is inappropriate and deepens inequality of access.
n.3: Lack of proof of address is not a reason to refuse registration.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Jamie, 24, has a learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. He brings a hospital passport describing how he communicates. On the ward round, staff talk to his mother and ignore Jamie. What should his nurse do?
o: Ask his mother to explain the ward round decisions to Jamie later
Allow the conversation to continue, as his mother knows him best
Share the passport details and invite staff to speak directly to Jamie
Ask the learning disability liaison nurse to attend the next ward round
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Nurses advocate for people who are vulnerable or disabled and make reasonable adjustments (P7.9; Code 3.4; Equality Act 2010 s20). Using the hospital passport and speaking directly to Jamie in his preferred way respects his rights, involves him in decisions and supports any capacity assessment (MCA 2005 s1(3)).

n.0: Passing information on later excludes Jamie from the conversation about his own care.
n.1: His mother's knowledge is valuable, but Jamie must be involved directly in decisions about his care.
n.3: Liaison nurses offer valuable support, but the nurse should advocate for Jamie now rather than wait.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Leo, 19, is autistic and attends a busy emergency department with a wrist injury. He is covering his ears, rocking and becoming more distressed in the noisy waiting room. His triage category means he may wait two hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Suggest he returns tomorrow when the department is likely to be quieter
Move him up the triage queue ahead of patients with more urgent needs
Ask him to wait outside the department until a cubicle becomes free
Offer a quieter space to wait and explain clearly what will happen next
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Reasonable adjustments remove disadvantage arising from disability without compromising others' safety: a quieter waiting space and clear, predictable information reduce sensory overload while clinical priority is maintained (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7; P7.9). Two steps: recognise sensory distress, then select a proportionate adjustment.

n.0: Delaying treatment of an injury is not a reasonable adjustment and may worsen the outcome.
n.1: Triage order is based on clinical urgency; changing it could harm patients with more urgent needs.
n.2: Sending him outside removes him from observation and is not an adjustment that maintains his care.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Edna Fox, 83, is medically fit for discharge after a urinary tract infection. Before admission she managed alone at home. She will now go home with a new package of carers visiting twice a day for personal care. Which discharge pathway applies?
o: Pathway 1
Pathway 2
Pathway 3
Pathway 0
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Hospital discharge and community support guidance (DHSC/NHS England, updated January 2024): pathway 1 is discharge home or to the usual place of residence with new or additional health and/or social care needs (P4.18; P7.10).

n.1: Pathway 2 is a community bed-based setting with recovery support, not home.
n.2: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new or additional care needs; Mrs Fox needs a new care package.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Gordon Bailey, 79, is recovering from a hip fracture repair. He is not yet safe at home but the team expects he will be able to return home after a few weeks of rehabilitation in a community hospital bed. Which discharge pathway is this?
o: Pathway 3
Pathway 2
Pathway 1
Pathway 0
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Pathway 2 is discharge to a community bed-based setting with dedicated recovery support, where short-term care helps the person recover before living independently or receiving longer-term care (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.2: Pathway 1 is discharge home with new support; Mr Bailey is not yet ready to go home.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new needs.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Rita Holmes, 87, lived alone before a fall and is now medically fit for discharge but still slow and unsteady. At the board round, a doctor suggests arranging a permanent nursing home place directly from the ward. What does current discharge guidance in England advise?
o: Discharge her home with no support and review her needs if she falls
Arrange the permanent place now, as hospital is the best place to assess needs
Discharge her for a period of recovery, then assess her long-term needs
Keep Mrs Holmes in hospital until she has fully recovered her mobility
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under discharge to assess, long-term needs are assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery, not in hospital. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home placement for the first time without an opportunity to recover first (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P4.18). Two steps: recognise she is medically fit, then apply discharge to assess.

n.0: She has clear new needs; discharge without support is unsafe.
n.1: Assessing long-term needs in hospital, before recovery, tends to overestimate need; the guidance advises against it.
n.3: Staying in hospital once medically fit risks deconditioning and delays recovery.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Claire Bennett, 42, who has multiple sclerosis, is due for discharge after a relapse. During discharge planning, Sunil, her nurse, learns that her 14-year-old son provides much of her care at home. What should Sunil do?
o: Ask Claire to arrange more help from other family members before discharge
Plan the discharge around the son's school hours, as he already provides her care
Leave the son out of discussions, as he is under 18 and cannot be a carer
Involve the son appropriately and notify the local authority so it can assess him
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NHS trusts must involve unpaid carers, including young carers, in discharge planning as soon as feasible (Care Act 2014 s74 as amended by the Health and Care Act 2022). Where a young carer is identified, the local authority should be notified so it can carry out a young carer's needs assessment, including whether caring is appropriate or excessive (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Other support may help, but the young carer still needs to be identified and referred for assessment.
n.1: Relying on a child's care without assessment may place excessive responsibility on him and ignores safeguarding considerations.
n.2: Young carers are recognised in law and must be identified and involved appropriately, not excluded.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Leonard Ross, 74, is going home after a stroke. His wife, Margaret, will help him with washing and dressing. She tells the nurse she is already exhausted and worried about coping. What should the nurse tell her?
o: She should wait to see how she copes for the first few weeks at home
She can apply for a carer's assessment once he has been home a month
She has a right to a carer's assessment from the local authority
She can ask the GP to prescribe something to help her sleep better
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under section 10 of the Care Act 2014, where a carer appears to have needs for support, the local authority must carry out a carer's assessment. For a new caring role this should ideally happen before caring begins, organised so as not to delay discharge (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Waiting risks carer breakdown; carers' needs should be assessed early.
n.1: There is no one-month waiting period; the local authority's duty arises when it appears she may have needs.
n.3: Sleep problems may need attention, but this does not address her support needs as a carer.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Kwabena Asante, 66, is to be discharged on a newly started oral anticoagulant after a pulmonary embolism. Which final check before he leaves best supports a safe discharge?
o: He has been told to read the patient leaflet supplied with his tablets
He understands his medicine, has a supply, and follow-up is arranged
His observations are within normal limits on the morning of discharge
He has a copy of the discharge letter to hand in to his GP practice
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Safe discharge on a high-risk medicine requires the person to understand the medicine and its risks, have an adequate supply, and have follow-up arranged with information shared with primary care (P4.18 coordinate safe discharge; NICE NG5 medicines-related communication at transfer; Code 7 and 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care).

n.0: A leaflet does not confirm understanding of a high-risk new medicine.
n.2: Stable observations are needed but do not address the medicines and follow-up risks of anticoagulation.
n.3: Relying on the patient to carry the letter delays information reaching the GP; discharge information should be sent directly.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Joan Pike, 90, has social care needs and has been in hospital for a week with heart failure. Several professionals are involved and her daughter is confused about who to contact about discharge plans. According to NICE NG27, what should be in place?
o: A weekly letter to the daughter from the consultant in charge
A named discharge coordinator as the central point of contact
A rule that her daughter contacts the ward sister each morning
A referral to the hospital complaints team to manage contact
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NICE NG27 (2015) recommends a hospital-based multidisciplinary team and a named discharge coordinator who is the central point of contact for the person and their family during discharge planning (P7.10; P4.18).

n.0: A weekly letter is too infrequent and does not provide a single coordinating contact.
n.2: This places responsibility on the family rather than giving them a coordinator.
n.3: Her daughter's confusion is a coordination problem, not a complaint to be managed.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward wants to evaluate how well it plans discharges for people with complex care needs who go home with new support. Which approach would best capture the quality of their experience?
o: Count the number of discharges completed before midday each week
Review the ward's length-of-stay figures against other medical wards
Phone people and carers after discharge to ask about their experience
Audit how many discharge letters reached GPs within 24 hours
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The quality of people's experience of complex care is best evaluated by asking them and their carers directly about the discharge and transition, including whether support started as planned (P7.7 monitor and evaluate the quality of people's experience of complex care; P6.9).

n.0: Discharge timing is a process measure that says little about the person's experience.
n.1: Length of stay measures efficiency, not experience.
n.3: Letter timeliness is an important process measure but does not capture the experience of people and carers.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: During a team meeting, Ellie, a nurse three months after registration, says that leadership is something for ward managers and that her job is to look after her own patients. How does the NMC Code describe leadership for registrants?
o: All registrants have opportunities to show leadership whatever their role
Leadership is required where a nurse is formally in charge of a shift
Leadership is expected once a nurse is appointed to a band 6 role or above
Leadership is expected after completing a recognised leadership course
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Code standard 25 (provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences) applies to every registrant; the NMC states that all registrants have opportunities to show leadership regardless of formal position (P5.6 exhibit leadership potential).

n.1: Being in charge adds responsibilities (Code 25.1), but leadership is expected of all registrants at all times.
n.2: The Code links leadership to professional practice, not to pay band or grade.
n.3: Courses can develop leadership skills, but the Code's expectation does not depend on them.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward is moving from paper charts to electronic observations next month. Several experienced nurses tell Raj, the ward manager, that the system will slow them down and they do not want it. Which approach is most likely to support the change?
o: Ask the nurses who object to work on other wards during the changeover
Involve staff early, explain the reasons, act on concerns and pilot it
Delay the change until every member of the team agrees to it
Set a firm start date and tell staff the system is mandatory from that day
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Effective change management involves the people affected: explaining why the change is needed, listening to and addressing concerns, and testing the change on a small scale so staff can shape it (P5.1 principles of leadership and organisational culture; AnnexA.4.2.1 strengths-based approaches to managing change).

n.0: Removing staff who raise concerns loses their expertise and damages trust in the team.
n.2: Waiting for unanimous agreement can block necessary safety improvements indefinitely.
n.3: Imposing change without engagement tends to increase resistance and workarounds.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: At her appraisal, Joy, a healthcare assistant, is praised by families for her skill in calming people living with dementia who are distressed. Her line manager, Paul, wants to use a strengths-based approach to developing the team. What should Paul do?
o: Concentrate the appraisal on the areas where Joy needs to improve
Move Joy to the dementia unit so that her skills are used there
Ask Joy to spend less time with families so she can do other tasks
Agree a plan for Joy to share her approach and support colleagues
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Strengths-based team development recognises what people do well and builds on it, for example by enabling a team member to share skills and act as a resource, which improves care and motivation (AnnexA.4.2.1; P5.2 strength-based approaches in teams).

n.0: Development needs matter, but a strengths-based approach starts from what the person does well.
n.1: Moving her removes the skill from the team rather than building on it within the team.
n.2: Reducing the activity she excels at undermines a strength that benefits patients and families.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: On a leadership study day, students are asked to distinguish leadership from management. Which activity is best described as leadership rather than management?
o: Preparing the ward's off-duty rota for the next four weeks
Setting a shared vision for care and motivating the team
Recording and reviewing staff sickness absence each month
Monitoring the ward's monthly spending against its budget
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Management is concerned with planning, organising and controlling resources (rotas, budgets, absence); leadership is concerned with direction, vision and influencing and motivating people. Nurses need both (P5.1 principles of effective leadership and management).

n.0: Rota planning organises resources, a management task.
n.2: Absence monitoring is a management process.
n.3: Budget monitoring is a management control activity.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: At a ward meeting, a healthcare assistant says that safeguarding children is the job of social services and that hospital staff only treat injuries. The children's nurse wants to correct this using the relevant statute. Which statement is accurate?
o: NHS trusts must refer every child who attends with any injury to children's social care under s17
NHS trusts must carry out child protection investigations themselves under section 47 of the Children Act 1989
NHS trusts lead local safeguarding arrangements in place of the police under the Children Act 2004
NHS trusts must arrange their functions to safeguard and promote children's welfare (Children Act 2004 s11)
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 11 of the Children Act 2004 requires named bodies, including NHS trusts and ICBs, to make arrangements to ensure their functions are discharged having regard to the need to safeguard and promote the welfare of children.

n.0: Section 17 concerns services for children in need; there is no duty to refer every injured child, only those where there are concerns.
n.1: Section 47 enquiries are the local authority's duty; health staff contribute information but do not lead them.
n.2: The three statutory safeguarding partners are the local authority, the ICB and the chief officer of police; trusts are not partners and do not replace the police.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Leo, 11, has been in hospital for several weeks and is subject to care proceedings. He tells his nurse he wants to live with his grandmother and asks whether the judge will listen to him. Under the Children Act 1989 welfare checklist, how will the court treat Leo's wishes?
o: His wishes bind the court once he reaches the age of 10
His wishes are put to the court through his parents' evidence
His wishes are considered in light of his age and understanding
His wishes are set aside until he is assessed as Gillick competent
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 1(3)(a) of the Children Act 1989 lists the ascertainable wishes and feelings of the child, considered in the light of age and understanding, as the first item of the welfare checklist. They inform, but do not dictate, the decision. In care proceedings a children's guardian represents the child's views.

n.0: No age makes a child's wishes binding; the court weighs them with the other checklist factors and decides on welfare.
n.1: The child's own views are put to the court, usually through the children's guardian, because they may differ from the parents'.
n.3: Gillick competence concerns consent to treatment; the welfare checklist considers every child's wishes according to age and understanding.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: At 02:00 police bring Mia, 2, to the emergency department after finding her alone at home while both parents were heavily intoxicated. The officer says Mia has been taken into police protection under the Children Act 1989. For how long can police protection last?
o: Up to 72 hours
Up to 24 hours
Up to 8 days
Up to 28 days
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Under s46 of the Children Act 1989 no child may be kept in police protection for more than 72 hours. If longer protection is needed, the local authority must apply to court, for example for an emergency protection order under s44.

n.1: 24 hours is the basic detention limit for an adult arrested under PACE, not the police protection limit.
n.2: Eight days is the maximum initial duration of an emergency protection order under s45, not police protection.
n.3: 28 days is not a Children Act time limit for emergency protection of a child.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: During a multidisciplinary meeting about Ellie, 5, who is ready for discharge, a manager suggests postponing a decision about where she should live for several months to 'see how things settle'. The children's nurse wants to challenge this using the Children Act 1989. Which principle is most relevant?
o: A court should make an order when it is better than making none
Delay in deciding is likely to prejudice the child's welfare
Local authorities must work in partnership with parents
Parental responsibility is shared between both parents
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 1(2) of the Children Act 1989 sets the 'no delay' principle: any delay in determining a question about a child's upbringing is likely to prejudice the child's welfare. Open-ended postponement directly conflicts with it.

n.0: The no-order principle (s1(5)) stops unnecessary orders; it does not address postponing a decision.
n.2: Partnership with parents is good practice but does not answer the risk caused by delay.
n.3: Shared parental responsibility concerns who can make decisions, not the timing of decisions.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Noah, 7, needs a general anaesthetic for dental extractions in England. His father, who was never married to Noah's mother, attends alone. Noah was born in 2019 and his father is named on the birth certificate. Can the father give consent for Noah's treatment?
o: No, he needs a parental responsibility agreement signed by the mother
Yes, every biological father holds parental responsibility from birth
No, an unmarried father needs a court order to hold parental responsibility
Yes, being registered on the birth certificate gave him parental responsibility
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Under s4(1)(a) of the Children Act 1989 an unmarried father acquires parental responsibility by being registered as the father on the birth register; this applies to births registered in England and Wales from 1 December 2003. One person with PR can usually give valid consent.

n.0: A PR agreement is an alternative route, not needed when the father is already registered.
n.1: Biological fatherhood alone does not confer PR; an unmarried father needs registration, an agreement or an order.
n.2: A court order is one route to PR, but registration on the birth certificate is sufficient for births registered from 1 December 2003.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Sofia, 9, is listed for an elective grommet insertion. She arrives with her grandmother, who has looked after her most days for years while her mother works. The mother is at work and contactable by phone. The grandmother offers to sign the consent form. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the surgeon to proceed in Sofia's best interests as a planned case
Contact the mother, as the grandmother does not hold parental responsibility
Accept the grandmother's consent as Sofia's closest available relative
Accept the grandmother's consent as Sofia's main day-to-day carer
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Grandparents do not have parental responsibility automatically (Children Act 1989 ss2-4). For a planned, non-urgent procedure consent should come from a person with PR (or from Sofia if she were competent), so the nurse should contact the mother, who is available.

n.0: Acting in best interests without consent is for emergencies when no one with authority is available; this is an elective case and the mother can be reached.
n.2: Being a close relative does not confer PR or the authority to consent.
n.3: Providing day-to-day care does not give PR; consent for elective surgery should come from a PR holder.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Amir, 8, is subject to a full care order and lives with foster carers. He needs a minor surgical procedure. His mother visits and asks who now holds parental responsibility for him. Which answer is correct under the Children Act 1989?
o: The mother, as a care order leaves parental responsibility unchanged
The local authority, as the care order ended the mother's responsibility
The foster carers, as they now provide Amir's day-to-day care
The mother and the local authority, which shares it under the order
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Under s33 of the Children Act 1989 a care order gives the local authority parental responsibility, which it shares with the parents; the local authority may limit how far a parent exercises theirs. The mother keeps PR.

n.0: The care order does change the position: the local authority acquires PR alongside the parents.
n.1: A care order does not remove the mother's PR; it is shared, although the local authority may restrict its exercise.
n.2: Foster carers do not acquire PR through a placement; they act under delegated authority from the local authority.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Chloe, 12, has been accommodated by the local authority under section 20 of the Children Act 1989 with her parents' agreement while her mother receives inpatient treatment. She now lives with a foster carer and needs a minor procedure. Who holds parental responsibility for Chloe?
o: The foster carer, who acquires it for the length of the placement
The local authority and her parents jointly, as under a care order
The local authority, which acquired it when Chloe was accommodated
Her parents, who keep parental responsibility during accommodation
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 20 accommodation is voluntary. The local authority does not acquire parental responsibility; the parents keep it and can remove the child (Children Act 1989 s20). Consent should come from a parent with PR, or from Chloe if competent for the decision.

n.0: Foster carers do not acquire PR through a placement.
n.1: Shared PR with the local authority is the effect of a care order, which Chloe is not subject to.
n.2: The local authority gains PR under a care order (s33), not under voluntary s20 accommodation.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Ethan, 10, attends a day surgery unit with his stepfather, who has been married to Ethan's mother for four years and lives with them. There is no court order or formal agreement in place. The stepfather asks to sign the consent form for an elective hernia repair. What is the correct position?
o: He would first need to adopt Ethan to hold parental responsibility
He holds parental responsibility after living with Ethan for three years
He lacks parental responsibility without a section 4A agreement or court order
He holds parental responsibility because he is married to Ethan's mother
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Under s4A of the Children Act 1989 a step-parent married to (or the civil partner of) a parent with PR can acquire parental responsibility by agreement with the parents who have PR or by court order. Marriage alone does not confer it.

n.0: Adoption would give PR, but it is not needed: a s4A agreement or order is sufficient.
n.1: A period of living together does not confer PR; an agreement or order is required.
n.3: Marriage to the mother does not give a step-parent PR automatically.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Zara, 3, needs urgent but not life-threatening surgery. Her two mothers were civil partners when Zara was conceived through licensed fertility clinic treatment. The birth mother is abroad and cannot be reached; Zara's other mother, who is named on the birth certificate, is present. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Treat Zara under the emergency necessity principle without anyone's consent
Apply to court for an order, as the non-birth mother has no automatic parental responsibility
Obtain consent from the other mother, who is a legal parent with parental responsibility
Delay surgery until the birth mother can be reached to give consent
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Under the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 2008, a woman in a civil partnership with the birth mother at the time of licensed treatment is the child's second female parent, and she has parental responsibility (Children Act 1989 s2(1A)). Her consent is valid.

n.0: Necessity applies when no one with authority to consent is available; a parent with PR is present.
n.1: No court order is needed: the second female parent holds PR automatically in these circumstances.
n.3: Both legal parents hold PR here, so waiting for the birth mother would cause unnecessary delay to urgent surgery.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Harry, 6, is brought to the emergency department by a neighbour. He is drowsy with a non-blanching rash, a heart rate of 160 bpm and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. His parents are on a flight and cannot be contacted. The doctor prescribes immediate IV antibiotics. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the neighbour to sign the consent form as the responsible adult present
Withhold antibiotics until a parent can be reached, documenting the delay
Give treatment without delay in Harry's best interests while contact attempts continue
Ask the hospital legal team to obtain a court order before starting antibiotics
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Harry shows signs of possible meningococcal sepsis, a life-threatening emergency. When no one with parental responsibility is available and treatment cannot wait, clinicians may give necessary treatment in the child's best interests under the doctrine of necessity, while continuing to contact the parents and documenting the reasons.

n.0: A neighbour has no parental responsibility and cannot give valid consent.
n.1: Delaying antibiotics in suspected meningococcal sepsis risks death; necessity justifies immediate treatment.
n.3: Courts are used for disputes or non-urgent refusals; seeking an order here would dangerously delay emergency treatment.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Liam, 4, attends a children's outpatient clinic with his father, who never married Liam's mother and is not named on the birth certificate. The father has had regular contact for two years and asks how he could gain the legal right to consent to Liam's treatment. Which statement is accurate?
o: He gains parental responsibility by paying regular child maintenance
He can gain parental responsibility by an agreement with the mother
He gains parental responsibility once a DNA test confirms paternity
He gains parental responsibility after two years of regular contact
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Under s4(1) of the Children Act 1989 an unmarried father acquires parental responsibility by being registered on the birth certificate (including re-registration), by a parental responsibility agreement with the mother, or by court order.

n.0: Paying maintenance is a separate legal duty and does not confer PR.
n.2: Proof of paternity does not itself confer PR; he needs registration, an agreement or an order.
n.3: Contact, however regular, does not confer PR.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Priya, 14, is admitted with a fractured wrist that needs manipulation under anaesthetic. Her parents are on their way. A student nurse asks what must be shown for Priya to give valid consent herself. Which statement describes the Gillick test?
o: She can retain the information for at least 24 hours
She has passed the four-stage test of the Mental Capacity Act
She has enough maturity and understanding of what is proposed
She is 14 or older and her parents have no objection
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA [1986] held that a child under 16 can consent if they have sufficient maturity and understanding to fully understand what is proposed, including the risks, consequences and alternatives.

n.0: There is no 24-hour retention requirement; retention for long enough to decide is part of the MCA test for people 16 and over.
n.1: The MCA 2005 capacity test applies from 16; under-16s are assessed for Gillick competence.
n.3: There is no fixed age threshold for Gillick competence and parental agreement is not part of the test.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Ellie, 15, attends a sexual health clinic and asks a nurse for the contraceptive pill. She does not want her parents to know. The nurse wants to use the framework that applies specifically to giving contraceptive advice and treatment to under-16s without parental knowledge. Which framework applies?
o: The Bolam test for a responsible body of opinion
The Mental Capacity Act 2005 test of capacity
Section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969
The Fraser guidelines
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Lord Fraser's guidelines in Gillick set the conditions under which a practitioner may give contraceptive advice or treatment to an under-16 without parental knowledge; since Axon (2006) they are also applied to STI treatment and termination.

n.0: Bolam concerns the standard of care in negligence, not consent for a minor.
n.1: The MCA 2005 applies from age 16; Ellie is 15.
n.2: FLRA 1969 s8 gives 16 and 17-year-olds the right to consent, so it does not apply to Ellie.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Ben, 13, was assessed as Gillick competent to consent to a plaster cast for a minor fracture last month. He is now being considered for spinal surgery with significant risks and a long recovery. His father asks whether the earlier assessment means Ben can consent to the spinal surgery. What should the nurse explain?
o: Competence for surgery is assessed by the father, who holds parental responsibility
The earlier assessment applies to all treatment until he turns 16
Competence for major surgery is presumed from the age of 13
Competence is decision-specific, so it must be assessed for this decision
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Gillick competence is decision-specific: a child may be competent for a simple decision but not for a complex, higher-risk one. Ben's understanding of the spinal surgery, its risks, alternatives and consequences must be assessed afresh.

n.0: Competence is assessed by the clinician seeking consent, not by a parent.
n.1: A previous assessment for a simpler decision does not carry over to a more complex one.
n.2: There is no presumption of competence under 16; it must be demonstrated for each decision.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Ava, 12, attends a walk-in centre asking for emergency contraception. She tells the nurse she has been having sex with her 15-year-old boyfriend and does not want anyone told. What is the most appropriate action, in addition to arranging her clinical care?
o: Assess her against the Fraser guidelines and keep the matter confidential
Advise her to tell her parents and review her again in one week
Keep the matter confidential because her boyfriend is also under 16
Make a child protection referral following local safeguarding procedures
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: A child under 13 cannot consent to sexual activity in law (Sexual Offences Act 2003), and NSPCC guidance states that sexual activity with a child under 13 should always result in a child protection referral. Ava's clinical needs are met at the same time.

n.0: Fraser can guide the contraceptive decision, but sexual activity at 12 is a child protection concern that must be referred.
n.1: Delaying and relying on parental disclosure leaves a child protection concern unreported.
n.2: The boyfriend's age does not remove the safeguarding concern about a 12-year-old.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Grace, 15, asks the school nurse for contraception. She understands the advice, says she will continue having sex with her boyfriend of the same age, and the nurse believes her health would suffer without contraception. Which further finding means the Fraser guidelines are NOT yet met?
o: She says she will have sex whether or not she receives contraception
She can explain how the method works and its possible side effects
She agrees she could tell her mother and asks for help to do so
Her emotional health is likely to suffer if she is refused contraception
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: One Fraser condition is that the young person cannot be persuaded to inform their parents or allow the practitioner to do so. If Grace is willing to tell her mother, that condition is not met and the nurse should support her to involve her parent, which is always encouraged.

n.0: Being likely to begin or continue sex with or without contraception is itself a Fraser condition, so this supports provision.
n.1: Understanding the advice is a Fraser condition, so this supports provision.
n.3: Physical or mental health likely to suffer without contraception is a Fraser condition, so this supports provision.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Jade, 14, has a suspected appendix abscess and needs IV antibiotics and a drain. The surgeon assesses her as Gillick competent and she consents. Her mother, who has parental responsibility, objects because she wants a second opinion first. What is the legal position?
o: The mother's objection overrides Jade's consent while Jade is under 16
Treatment needs the agreement of both Jade and her mother
Treatment must wait for a court order because the two disagree
Jade's consent is valid and treatment can proceed
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: When a child under 16 is Gillick competent and consents, that consent is valid and treatment can proceed even if a parent disagrees (Gillick 1986; NSPCC Learning). Staff should still try to involve and support the mother.

n.0: A parent cannot veto the valid consent of a Gillick competent child to treatment in her interests.
n.1: The competent child's consent is sufficient; joint agreement is good practice, not a legal requirement.
n.2: A court is needed for refusals of life-sustaining treatment or genuine disputes over a child lacking competence, not to confirm a competent child's consent.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Daniel, 8, needs a blood test after a febrile illness. The nurse assesses that he does not understand the reasons, risks or alternatives. He says he does not want 'the needle'. His mother, who has parental responsibility, is present. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: His mother can consent, with Daniel involved as far as he understands
The test should wait until Daniel himself is able to give consent
Daniel's refusal must be followed because he has expressed a clear wish
His mother's consent is needed in writing before the test can go ahead
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: A child who is not competent for the decision cannot give or refuse consent; a person with parental responsibility consents. The child's views should still be sought and respected as far as possible (UNCRC Article 12), with preparation and distraction.

n.1: Delaying a needed test until an 8-year-old becomes competent is not in his interests.
n.2: A child who lacks competence for the decision cannot give a legally decisive refusal; his views are considered, not binding.
n.3: Written consent is not a legal requirement for a blood test; verbal consent from his mother is valid.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Mia, 15, attends a sexual health clinic asking for contraception. A 22-year-old man accompanies her, answers questions for her and says she 'definitely wants the implant'. Mia avoids eye contact. What should the nurse do first?
o: Speak to Mia alone to assess her understanding and possible coercion
Assess Fraser criteria with the man present to support Mia
Fit the implant, as Mia has nodded in agreement with the request
Refuse contraception and ask the man to bring Mia's mother
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Valid consent must be voluntary, and Gillick and Fraser assessments require the young person's own understanding. Seeing Mia alone allows the nurse to assess competence and explore signs of child sexual exploitation (age gap, controlling adult), which would need safeguarding action.

n.1: Assessing in the presence of a possibly coercive adult cannot establish voluntariness.
n.2: A nod under possible pressure is not evidence of voluntary, informed consent.
n.3: Refusing care without assessment may leave Mia unprotected; she needs to be seen alone first.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Kieran, 16, attends the day surgery unit alone for an elective knee arthroscopy. He has capacity and signs the consent form after a full discussion. His mother phones to say she has not been asked and wants to give consent herself. What is the legal position?
o: His consent needs countersigning by a second clinician
His mother's consent is also needed because he is under 18
His own consent is valid and parental consent is not needed
The surgery must wait until his mother can attend in person
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 8(1) of the Family Law Reform Act 1969 makes the consent of a 16 or 17-year-old to surgical, medical or dental treatment as effective as an adult's, and states that consent from a parent or guardian is then not necessary.

n.0: No countersignature is required for a capacitous 16-year-old's consent.
n.1: FLRA 1969 s8 removes the need for parental consent once a 16-year-old has effectively consented.
n.3: Parental attendance is not a legal requirement for a 16-year-old's valid consent.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Freya, 17, is admitted after a road traffic collision with a head injury. She is confused, cannot retain information about her injuries and needs a CT scan and a central line. Her parents cannot be reached. On what legal basis should the team act?
o: The Mental Capacity Act 2005, in her best interests
Section 8 of the Family Law Reform Act 1969 (her consent)
The Gillick test, as she is under 18 years old
The Mental Health Act 1983, as she is confused
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies from age 16. If a 16 or 17-year-old lacks capacity for a decision, treatment can be given in their best interests under ss4-5 of the MCA, involving family where possible.

n.1: FLRA s8 gives effect to a 16 or 17-year-old's own consent; Freya cannot currently consent.
n.2: Gillick competence applies to children under 16.
n.3: The MHA 1983 authorises treatment for mental disorder, not treatment of a physical head injury.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Aisha, 17, has capacity and refuses a blood transfusion that the team believes is needed to save her life after a major haemorrhage. She has discussed the risks clearly and understands she may die. What is the most appropriate course of action for the team?
o: Detain her under the Mental Health Act 1983 to give the transfusion
Treat under MCA best interests because the refusal shows she lacks capacity
Accept the refusal as final because she has capacity at 17
Seek urgent legal advice so that the High Court can decide
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: A capacitous 16 or 17-year-old's refusal of life-sustaining treatment can be overridden by the High Court under its inherent jurisdiction (Re W [1992]). The team should seek urgent legal advice and an application to court, giving emergency treatment needed to keep her alive in the meantime.

n.0: The MHA 1983 authorises treatment for mental disorder; a transfusion for haemorrhage is not that.
n.1: An unwise or life-threatening refusal does not itself show lack of capacity (MCA s1(4)).
n.2: Unlike an adult's, the refusal of a 16 or 17-year-old can be overridden by the court where life is at risk.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Lucy, 16, needs an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy under sedation to investigate weight loss. She has capacity and consents. A student nurse asks whether her consent covers a diagnostic test and the sedation, because the Family Law Reform Act refers to 'treatment'. What should the nurse explain?
o: Section 8 covers the test, but sedation needs separate parental consent
Section 8 covers the endoscopy once she has been assessed as Gillick competent
Section 8 covers treatment, so her mother must consent to diagnostic tests
Section 8 includes diagnostic procedures and anaesthesia ancillary to them
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: FLRA 1969 s8(2) states that 'surgical, medical or dental treatment' includes any procedure undertaken for the purposes of diagnosis, and that the section applies to procedures such as anaesthetic which are ancillary to treatment.

n.0: Anaesthesia and similar ancillary procedures are expressly covered by s8(2).
n.1: Gillick applies under 16; at 16 Lucy's consent is effective under s8 and she is presumed to have capacity.
n.2: Diagnostic procedures are expressly included in s8(2), so parental consent is not needed.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Callum, 17, has Down syndrome and needs a decision about a planned dental extraction. His parents tell the nurse that they always make his health decisions and will sign the form. Callum has not yet been asked. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask a doctor to complete a best interests decision for the extraction
Assess Callum's capacity for this decision, presuming he has capacity
Refer the decision to the Court of Protection because he is under 18
Accept his parents' consent, as he has a learning disability
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: The MCA 2005 applies from 16 and its first principle is that a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it (s1(2)). A diagnosis alone does not establish lack of capacity (s2(3)). Callum's capacity for this decision must be assessed, with support to decide.

n.0: A best interests decision is only reached after capacity has been assessed and found lacking.
n.2: The Court of Protection can deal with 16 and 17-year-olds, but there is no dispute requiring it before capacity is even assessed.
n.3: A learning disability does not in itself mean Callum lacks capacity, and parents cannot override a capacitous 17-year-old's own consent.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Jordan, 16, is brought to the emergency department heavily intoxicated with a 3 cm scalp laceration. He is not bleeding actively and is otherwise stable, but cannot currently weigh up information about suturing. He is expected to sober up within a few hours. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Wait until he regains capacity, as the wound can safely be closed later
Contact his parents for consent and suture once they agree
Suture now, as a 16-year-old's consent is presumed under FLRA s8
Suture now in his best interests, as he lacks capacity at present
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Under the MCA 2005 s4(3), a best interests decision must consider whether the person is likely to regain capacity and whether the decision can wait until then. A stable laceration can be closed safely within hours, so waiting respects Jordan's own decision.

n.1: Seeking parental consent bypasses Jordan's right to decide when he will shortly be able to.
n.2: FLRA s8 makes a 16-year-old's actual consent effective; it does not presume consent when he cannot give it.
n.3: Lack of capacity now does not justify acting if the decision can safely wait for him to regain it.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Megan, 17, has advanced cystic fibrosis and capacity. She tells her nurse she wants to make a legally binding advance decision refusing invasive ventilation in the future. What should the nurse explain?
o: She can make a binding advance decision now, as the MCA applies from 16
Advance decisions start at 18, so her wishes go in a care plan
An advance decision requires her parents' signature as she is a minor
An advance decision is valid if witnessed by two registered professionals
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 24 of the MCA 2005 allows a person aged 18 or over to make an advance decision to refuse treatment. Megan's wishes should be recorded in an advance care plan and will strongly inform best interests decisions; NICE NG61 supports advance care planning for young people.

n.0: Most of the MCA applies from 16, but advance decisions (and lasting powers of attorney) require the person to be 18.
n.2: Parental signatures cannot make a binding advance decision for a minor.
n.3: Witnessing is a formality for life-sustaining refusals by adults; it does not make a 17-year-old's decision valid.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: A student nurse on an adolescent ward plans to carry out a Gillick competence assessment before asking Hannah, 16, to consent to a lumbar puncture. Hannah has no known cognitive impairment. Which response by the registered nurse is best?
o: Gillick is correct, but her parent must also countersign the form
At 16 the MCA presumption of capacity applies, not Gillick
Gillick is correct, as it applies to every patient under 18
At 16 she needs a formal MCA assessment before every procedure
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Gillick competence is the test for under-16s. From 16 the MCA 2005 presumption of capacity applies and FLRA 1969 s8 makes her consent effective; capacity is assessed only if there is reason to doubt it.

n.0: Parental countersignature is not required for a 16-year-old's effective consent.
n.2: Gillick applies to children under 16, not to all under-18s.
n.3: The presumption of capacity means a formal assessment is needed only where there is doubt.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Oscar, 9, needs a cannula for IV antibiotics. The nurse asks which hand he writes with, explains the options and lets him choose the site and whether to watch. A student asks which article of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child this reflects most directly. Which article is it?
o: Article 24, the right to health and health services
Article 3, the best interests of the child
Article 31, the right to play and leisure
Article 12, the right to express views and be heard
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: UNCRC Article 12 gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting them, with due weight given according to age and maturity. Involving Oscar in choices about his procedure applies it directly.

n.0: Article 24 concerns access to health care, not the child's voice in decisions about it.
n.1: Article 3 makes the child's best interests a primary consideration; the action described is about hearing Oscar's views.
n.2: Article 31 concerns play, rest and leisure, not participation in decisions.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: To create space for an extra bed bay, a ward manager proposes closing the playroom on a busy children's surgical ward. The play specialist objects, citing the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Which article most directly supports her objection?
o: Article 12, the right to be heard in decisions
Article 31, the right to rest, leisure and play
Article 19, protection from violence and abuse
Article 24, the right to health and health services
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: UNCRC Article 31 recognises the child's right to rest, leisure and play appropriate to their age. Play in hospital also supports coping and procedural preparation.

n.0: Article 12 concerns children's views; children could be consulted, but the right to play is Article 31.
n.2: Article 19 concerns protection from abuse and neglect.
n.3: Article 24 concerns access to health care; play is specifically protected by Article 31.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: A children's ward in England introduces a rule limiting parents to two hours of visiting a day to reduce noise. The parents of Lola, 2, who is distressed when they leave, complain that this breaches their human rights. Which article of the Human Rights Act 1998 is most directly engaged?
o: Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 2, the right to life
Article 8, respect for private and family life
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Article 8 (Schedule 1, Human Rights Act 1998) protects respect for private and family life. A blanket restriction separating a young child from her parents engages it; as a qualified right, any interference must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.

n.0: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, which the visiting rule does not involve.
n.1: Article 3 is engaged by serious ill-treatment; a visiting rule is better analysed as an interference with family life.
n.2: Article 2 concerns the protection of life, not family contact.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: A newly qualified nurse asks why the Human Rights Act 1998 matters to everyday practice on an NHS children's ward. Which statement is accurate?
o: It applies to adults, while the UNCRC governs NHS care of children
It applies to disputes between private individuals rather than to the NHS
It applies once a case has reached the European Court of Human Rights
It requires NHS bodies to act compatibly with Convention rights
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 makes it unlawful for a public authority, including NHS bodies and staff acting for them, to act incompatibly with Convention rights. Rights such as Articles 2, 3, 8 and 14 apply to children as well as adults.

n.0: Convention rights apply to everyone, including children; the UNCRC is not directly enforceable in English courts.
n.1: The Act's main duty is on public authorities, which include NHS trusts.
n.2: The Act lets rights be enforced in UK courts without going to Strasbourg first.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: During a teaching session, a student nurse says that a family in England could take an NHS trust to court for breaching the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Which statement best describes the UNCRC's status in England?
o: It was made part of English law by the Children Act 1989 in full
The UK has ratified it, but English courts cannot enforce it directly
It binds NHS bodies in England from the age of 12 upwards
It is enforced in English courts through the Human Rights Act 1998
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: The UK ratified the UNCRC (in force in the UK from 1992), so the government is bound in international law and it guides policy and practice, but it has not been incorporated into English law and cannot be directly enforced in English courts. Scotland and Wales have their own incorporation measures.

n.0: The Children Act 1989 shares principles with the UNCRC but did not incorporate it.
n.2: The UNCRC covers everyone under 18 and its status does not depend on age.
n.3: The HRA 1998 gives effect to the European Convention on Human Rights, not the UNCRC.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: On a children's ward, a nurse notices that the family of Marius, 6, who are Roma, are repeatedly asked to leave at night while other parents are allowed to stay at the bedside. No clinical reason is recorded. The nurse raises a concern. Which article of the Human Rights Act 1998 is engaged together with Article 8?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair hearing in court
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 14, prohibition of discrimination
Article 5, the right to liberty and security of person
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of the other Convention rights. Treating one family differently because of ethnicity, in relation to family life (Article 8), engages Articles 14 and 8 together. The nurse should also challenge discrimination under the Code and the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings in legal proceedings.
n.1: Article 9 concerns belief and religion; the issue is unequal treatment based on ethnicity.
n.3: Article 5 concerns deprivation of liberty, which is not described.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Daria, 10, recently arrived in England as an asylum seeker and is not registered with a GP. Her school nurse advocates for her to be registered and seen, citing the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Which article most directly supports this?
o: Article 24, the right to health and health care
Article 31, the right to rest, leisure and play
Article 19, protection from all forms of violence
Article 12, the right to be heard in decisions
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: UNCRC Article 24 recognises the child's right to the highest attainable standard of health and to facilities for treatment, so no child should be deprived of access to health care services.

n.1: Article 31 concerns play and leisure.
n.2: Article 19 concerns protection from abuse and neglect.
n.3: Article 12 concerns participation in decisions, not access to services.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Tobi, 5, attends an urgent care centre in England with a bruise shaped like a handprint on his upper arm. His father says he smacked him for misbehaving and that this is legal discipline. What is the most appropriate response by the nurse?
o: Follow safeguarding procedures, as injury from punishment is not lawful
Tell the father that any smack is a criminal offence in England
Record the injury and review it at Tobi's next routine appointment
Accept the explanation, as smacking a child is lawful in England
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: In England the 'reasonable punishment' defence (Children Act 2004 s58) cannot justify assault causing actual bodily harm, such as bruising. UNCRC Article 19 requires protection from all forms of physical violence. A visible injury from punishment is a safeguarding concern requiring referral under local procedures.

n.1: A full ban on physical punishment applies in Scotland (2020) and Wales (2022), not England, so this statement is inaccurate.
n.2: Delaying action until a routine review leaves a safeguarding concern unaddressed.
n.3: Reasonable punishment does not cover an injury such as a handprint bruise.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Isla, 14, sees the school nurse about severe acne and asks for advice about a GP appointment. The nurse judges her competent to make this decision. Isla asks that her parents are not told, as she is embarrassed. There are no safeguarding concerns. How should the nurse respond?
o: Respect her wishes, as she is owed the same duty of confidence as an adult
Tell her that the matter will be shared with her parents by her GP
Agree to tell her parents unless she arranges the appointment herself
Inform her parents, because she is under 16 and they hold parental responsibility
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Young people are owed the same duty of confidentiality as adults. With no risk of serious harm, a competent 14-year-old's wish for privacy should be respected, while encouraging her to involve her parents if she wishes (Code 5).

n.1: The GP owes Isla the same duty of confidence; there is no automatic sharing with parents.
n.2: Making disclosure conditional on her behaviour is coercive and has no basis when there is no risk of harm.
n.3: Parental responsibility does not entitle parents to a competent child's confidential information.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: A nurse in a young people's clinic is about to take a psychosocial history from Ruby, 15, about home, education, activities, drugs, sexuality and mood. What should the nurse say about confidentiality before starting?
o: Explain that her parents will receive a summary as she is under 16
Leave confidentiality until she raises the subject herself
Explain what stays private and when sharing may be needed for her safety
Promise that what she says will stay between the two of them
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Explaining the limits of confidentiality at the start builds trust and avoids false promises: what she says is private unless there is a risk of serious harm to her or others, when information may need to be shared with the right people, and she would normally be told first.

n.0: Routine sharing with parents breaches the confidence owed to a young person.
n.1: Waiting for her to ask leaves her unaware of the limits before she discloses.
n.3: Absolute promises cannot be kept if a safeguarding concern arises and would damage trust later.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Nadia, 16, tells a ward nurse that her stepfather has been sexually abusing her 11-year-old sister at home. She begs the nurse not to tell anyone because she fears her family will break up. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell Nadia's mother so that the family can decide what to do
Share the concern with children's social care, explaining this to Nadia
Encourage Nadia to report it herself and review in a week
Keep the disclosure confidential, as Nadia is 16 and has capacity
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: A risk of serious harm to a child overrides confidentiality. Under the s16LA Children Act 2004 information sharing duty (from 30 September 2026) consent is not required and disclosure to a relevant agency does not breach confidence. The nurse should be honest with Nadia about what will be shared, why and with whom, and support her.

n.0: Telling the mother first could alert the alleged abuser and put both girls at risk; the referral goes to children's social care.
n.2: Delaying leaves the sister at continuing risk of sexual abuse.
n.3: Capacity does not oblige the nurse to keep secret a disclosure of abuse of another child.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Sam, 15, is assessed as competent and is receiving treatment for an eating disorder. His father asks the nurse for a copy of Sam's clinical notes. Sam has said he does not want his parents to read them, although he is happy for his care plan to be discussed with them. What should the nurse do?
o: Release the notes once the father submits a written request
Refuse to discuss any aspect of Sam's care with his father
Ask for Sam's views, as a competent young person decides on access
Release the notes, as his father holds parental responsibility
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: A competent young person's confidential information is generally disclosed only with their agreement. Sam's views on access to his records should be sought and respected, while sharing what he agrees to (his care plan) to support family involvement, a key part of eating disorder care.

n.0: A written request does not change whose consent is needed.
n.1: Sam agrees to his care plan being discussed; refusing all contact would undermine family-based treatment.
n.3: Parental responsibility does not override a competent young person's confidentiality.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Tara, 16, attends the emergency department after taking 20 paracetamol tablets. Once medically fit she tells the nurse she still intends to end her life and has a plan for tonight. She has capacity and asks that nobody, including her parents, is told. What should the nurse do?
o: Share with her parents, leaving the mental health team uninformed
Share with those needed to keep her safe, explaining why to her
Ask her to sign a no-suicide contract and keep her confidence
Respect her wishes, as she has capacity and is 16
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Confidentiality can be breached where there is a risk of death or serious harm. The nurse should share relevant information with the mental health team and those who need to know to keep Tara safe, telling her what is being shared and why (Code 5.4; NICE NG225).

n.0: The mental health team must be involved for assessment; informing parents without specialist assessment is incomplete.
n.2: NICE NG225 advises against no-harm contracts; they do not reduce risk.
n.3: Capacity does not oblige silence when there is an imminent risk to life.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: While a nurse changes his dressing, Kai, 10, says, 'I'll tell you something about my uncle, but you have to promise not to tell anyone.' What is the best response?
o: 'Please wait while I fetch the safeguarding lead to hear it with me.'
'You should tell your mum about this rather than tell me.'
'I promise, you can tell me anything and it will stay between us.'
'I can't promise that, but I'll share it with people who can help.'
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Practitioners must not promise secrecy to a child, but should keep the child talking and explain honestly that information may be shared with people who can help, then listen, record in the child's words and follow safeguarding procedures.

n.0: Pausing to fetch someone may shut down the disclosure; the nurse should listen now and escalate afterwards.
n.1: Redirecting him may stop a disclosure; the uncle may be someone the mother cannot protect him from.
n.2: A promise of secrecy cannot be kept if Kai discloses harm and would break his trust.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Zoe, 16, is admitted with an ectopic pregnancy and has capacity. She asks staff not to tell her mother the reason for admission. Her mother phones the ward asking why Zoe is in hospital. What should the nurse say?
o: 'I can't share details without Zoe's agreement, but I'll pass on a message.'
'As she is under 18, I can share her diagnosis with you as her parent.'
'Please come in and the doctor will explain her diagnosis to you.'
'She is having treatment for a pregnancy complication and is stable.'
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: A 16-year-old with capacity is owed the same duty of confidence as an adult. Without her consent and with no safeguarding need, the nurse should not disclose the reason for admission, but can offer to pass on a message and encourage Zoe to involve her mother.

n.1: Parental responsibility does not give a right to a capacitous 16-year-old's confidential information.
n.2: Arranging for the doctor to explain her diagnosis still discloses it without her consent.
n.3: This discloses confidential health information without Zoe's consent.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Ryan, 17, is on a children's ward after a fight. He tells the nurse calmly and in detail that when discharged he will stab a named boy from his estate who 'disrespected' him, and says he has a knife hidden at home. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Keep the confidence, as Ryan is a minor and owed extra protection
Share with the police and safeguarding team to prevent serious harm
Inform his parents and ask them to remove the knife from home
Wait for Ryan's agreement before sharing his statement with anyone
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Disclosure without consent is justified in the public interest to prevent serious harm to others (Code 5.4). A specific threat with a weapon to a named person needs urgent sharing with the police and the safeguarding team, recorded with the rationale. The named boy may also need protection.

n.0: Being under 18 does not create extra confidentiality that outweighs a risk of serious violence.
n.2: Parents cannot be relied on to manage a credible threat to life; the police must be informed.
n.3: Consent is not required where disclosure is needed to prevent serious harm to others.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Tomasz, 17, is admitted to a children's ward in England after a fall from scaffolding at work. A student nurse suggests that, because he is employed full time and lives with his partner, the Children Act 1989 no longer applies to him. How should the nurse respond?
o: The Act applies, because it defines a child as a person under 18
The Act does not apply, because it defines a child as a person under 16
The Act applies, because it covers young people up to their 21st birthday
The Act does not apply, because full-time work ends his status as a child
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 105 of the Children Act 1989 defines a child as a person under the age of 18. Working Together 2026 adds that a 16 or 17-year-old living independently, working or in hospital keeps the same status and entitlement to protection.

n.1: 16 is the age for consent under FLRA 1969 s8 and for most of the MCA 2005, not the Children Act definition of a child.
n.2: Some leaving-care duties extend into the early twenties, but the Act's definition of a child stops at 18.
n.3: Employment or independent living does not change a young person's status as a child under s105.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: A family court in England is deciding where Ruby, 6, should live after her parents separate. The children's nurse who has cared for Ruby during a long admission is asked to provide a statement and wants to understand the principle the court must apply. Which principle governs the court's decision?
o: The rights of each parent are weighed equally with Ruby's welfare
The wishes of the parent who has day-to-day care decide the outcome
Ruby's best interests are a primary consideration among several
Ruby's welfare is the court's paramount consideration
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: The Children Act 1989 s1(1) states that when a court determines any question about a child's upbringing, the child's welfare shall be the court's paramount consideration (the paramountcy principle).

n.0: Parental rights are not balanced equally against the child's welfare; welfare is paramount under s1(1).
n.1: The resident parent's wishes are one factor the court may consider, not the deciding test.
n.2: 'A primary consideration' is the UNCRC Article 3 wording; the domestic court test under s1(1) is stronger, making welfare paramount.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: Jamal, 4, has cerebral palsy and complex feeding needs. His parents tell the community children's nurse they are exhausted and ask whether the local authority can assess the family for short breaks and practical support. How is Jamal best described under the Children Act 1989?
o: A looked-after child accommodated under section 20
A child in need under section 17 because he is disabled
A child subject to a supervision order under section 31
A child at risk of significant harm under section 47
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 17(10) of the Children Act 1989 defines a child in need as one unlikely to achieve a reasonable standard of health or development without services, whose health or development is likely to be significantly impaired without services, or who is disabled. The local authority has a duty to safeguard and promote the welfare of children in need.

n.0: Section 20 accommodation means the child is looked after away from home; Jamal lives with his parents.
n.2: A supervision order under s31 is made by a court when the significant harm threshold is met, which is not the situation described.
n.3: Section 47 enquiries need reasonable cause to suspect significant harm; nothing here suggests harm, only unmet need.

Children's Law, Rights and Consent.q: A children's nurse refers Kayla, 3, to children's social care after she attends with linear burns on her back that her mother cannot explain. The social worker says enquiries will begin under section 47 of the Children Act 1989. Which test triggers the local authority's duty to make these enquiries?
o: Parental agreement that an assessment of the family is needed
Proof on the balance of probabilities that harm has occurred
Reasonable cause to suspect significant harm, actual or likely
A police decision that a criminal offence has been committed
Children's Law, Rights and Consent.w: Section 47 of the Children Act 1989 requires the local authority to make enquiries where it has reasonable cause to suspect that a child is suffering, or is likely to suffer, significant harm. Unexplained burns in a 3-year-old meet that test.

n.0: Section 47 enquiries are a statutory duty and do not depend on parental agreement, unlike a voluntary s17 assessment.
n.1: Proof on the balance of probabilities is the standard a court applies to facts in care proceedings, not the trigger for s47 enquiries.
n.3: Police may investigate in parallel, but s47 enquiries do not wait for a decision that a crime has occurred.

Safeguarding Children.q: A nurse in an NHS trust's children's emergency department is unsure whether a toddler's injuries warrant a referral and wants expert safeguarding advice from within the trust. Under Working Together 2026, whose role is it to provide this advice in a provider organisation?
o: The trust's Caldicott Guardian for patient data
The Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO)
The trust's named nurse for safeguarding children
The designated nurse for safeguarding children at the ICB
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 says NHS trusts should identify a named doctor and a named nurse (named professionals) who promote good practice, give advice and expertise to colleagues and support safeguarding within the provider. Designated professionals work at strategic level across the ICB area.

n.0: The Caldicott Guardian oversees use of confidential information, not clinical safeguarding decisions.
n.1: The LADO manages allegations against people who work with children.
n.3: Designated professionals provide strategic leadership across the health system in the area, not routine case advice within one trust.

Safeguarding Children.q: Children's social care starts a Family Help assessment for Ollie, 6, after a nurse's referral about neglect. His father asks the nurse how long the assessment can take. Under Working Together 2026, what is the maximum time from referral to a decision on the assessment?
o: 35 working days from the point of referral
45 working days from the point of referral
10 working days from the point of referral
15 working days from the point of referral
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 states that the time from referral to the decision at the end of the assessment should be no longer than 45 working days; if it exceeds this, the lead practitioner should record the reasons.

n.0: 35 working days is not a Working Together timescale.
n.2: Ten working days is the core group timescale after an initial child protection conference.
n.3: Fifteen working days is the timescale for an initial child protection conference after the strategy discussion.

Safeguarding Children.q: A community children's nurse referred Ivy, 3, to children's social care for neglect: she is losing weight, has untreated scabies and is often left with a 10-year-old sibling. Social care decide on no further action. The nurse believes Ivy remains at risk. What should the nurse do?
o: Accept the decision, as social care are responsible for the threshold
Discuss with the safeguarding lead and use the local escalation procedure
Refer Ivy directly to the police as an alternative route
Re-refer the family every week until a different decision is made
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 expects mutual challenge between practitioners and agencies, and local safeguarding arrangements must tell relevant agencies how to escalate concerns and how disputes are resolved (para 79). The nurse should seek support from the named or safeguarding lead, use the local escalation procedure and record the reasons.

n.0: Practitioners keep a responsibility to challenge and escalate if they believe a child remains at risk.
n.2: The police may be contacted where a crime or emergency is suspected, but disagreement with social care is resolved through the escalation procedure.
n.3: Repeated referrals without new information do not resolve the disagreement and bypass the escalation process.

Safeguarding Children.q: Ava, 7, became the subject of a child protection plan at an initial conference last week. Her school nurse is part of the core group and asks when the first child protection review conference should be held. What does Working Together 2026 state?
o: Within six months of the initial conference
Within three months of the initial conference
Within 45 working days of the initial conference
Within 10 working days of the initial conference
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 states the first review should be held within three months of the initial child protection conference, and further reviews at intervals of no more than six months while the plan continues. The core group first meets within 10 working days.

n.0: Six months is the maximum interval between later reviews, not the first one.
n.2: 45 working days is the assessment timescale.
n.3: Ten working days is when the core group first meets, not the review conference.

Safeguarding Children.q: Finn, 6, is admitted with asthma. He tells the nurse he hides under his bed when his dad shouts at his mum and hits her, and he has started wetting the bed again. Finn has no injuries. How is Finn best described for safeguarding purposes?
o: He is a victim of domestic abuse in his own right
He is at risk of neglect, as his mother is unable to protect him
He is not a victim, as he has not himself been physically harmed
He is a child in need, as he has a long-term health condition
Safeguarding Children.w: Section 3 of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 recognises a child who sees or hears, or experiences the effects of, domestic abuse and is related to either party as a victim in their own right. Working Together 2026 includes seeing or hearing the ill-treatment of another within emotional abuse. A safeguarding referral is needed.

n.1: Labelling the non-abusing mother as neglectful misdirects the response; the harm arises from the father's abuse.
n.2: Physical injury is not required; witnessing domestic abuse is harm in itself.
n.3: Asthma may make him a child in need, but the safeguarding issue here is domestic abuse.

Safeguarding Children.q: A health visitor reviews Kacper, 3. He has extensive untreated dental decay, has missed his last four hospital appointments, is often seen in dirty clothes in winter without a coat, and his weight has fallen from the 25th to below the 2nd centile. Which category of abuse does Working Together 2026 use for this pattern?
o: Physical abuse
Neglect
Fabricated or induced illness
Emotional abuse
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 defines neglect as the persistent failure to meet a child's basic physical and/or psychological needs, likely to result in serious impairment of health or development, including failing to provide adequate food and clothing or to ensure access to appropriate medical care.

n.0: There is no inflicted injury described.
n.2: FII involves a carer fabricating or inducing illness; here care is being omitted.
n.3: Emotional abuse is persistent emotional maltreatment; this pattern is failure to meet physical and health needs.

Safeguarding Children.q: Ruby, 2, attends the emergency department with scalds to both feet. Her father says she climbed into a hot bath by herself. Which pattern of injury would most strongly suggest a non-accidental immersion scald?
o: An irregular scald on one foot with scattered splash marks
Symmetrical scalds to both feet with a sharp upper line
A scald of varying depth on the top of one foot and the shin
A small blister on one toe with redness spreading towards the ankle
Safeguarding Children.w: Forced immersion typically produces symmetrical 'stocking' or 'glove' scalds with a sharp upper tide-mark and no splash marks, because the child is held still. A child stepping into hot water accidentally usually shows asymmetry, splash marks and irregular depth. NICE CG89 lists scalds in a pattern suggesting immersion as a reason to suspect maltreatment.

n.0: Asymmetry and splash marks are more typical of a child moving in or withdrawing from hot water accidentally.
n.2: Irregular depth on one limb fits an accidental spill or step.
n.3: A small, localised blister with spreading redness suggests a minor burn or infection rather than forced immersion.

Safeguarding Children.q: On a children's ward, staff hear a mother repeatedly call her 7-year-old son 'disgusting' and 'a baby' in front of other families because he wets the bed, and tell him he will be sent away if it happens again. Which category of abuse does this most closely fit?
o: Emotional abuse
Child criminal exploitation
Neglect
Physical abuse
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 describes emotional abuse as persistent emotional maltreatment causing severe effects on emotional development, including making a child feel worthless or unloved, imposing developmentally inappropriate expectations, and threats. A pattern of humiliation and threats of abandonment fits.
