n.1: Criminal exploitation is coercing a child into crime, which is not described.
n.2: Neglect is failure to meet basic needs; this is active emotional maltreatment.
n.3: No physical harm is described.

Safeguarding Children.q: During a clinic appointment for her 4-year-old's eczema, Mrs Begum quietly says her husband checks her phone, controls her money, and last week pushed her down the stairs while the children watched. He is in the waiting room. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask her husband to join them so that both views can be heard
Document the disclosure and review it at the child's next appointment
Advise her to contact a domestic abuse helpline when she is ready
See her alone, assess risk and refer the children to social care
Safeguarding Children.w: Seeing the victim alone allows safe disclosure and a risk assessment (for example the DASH checklist, with MARAC referral if high risk). Because the children witnessed the abuse they are victims in their own right (Domestic Abuse Act 2021 s3), so a children's safeguarding referral is needed under local procedures.

n.0: Involving the alleged perpetrator could escalate risk to Mrs Begum and the children.
n.1: Delaying action leaves the children exposed to ongoing harm.
n.2: Signposting alone leaves the children's safeguarding concern unaddressed.

Safeguarding Children.q: Lily, 5, is seen in the children's emergency department with a vaginal discharge. Swabs confirm gonorrhoea. Her mother is shocked and says Lily must have caught it from a towel. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Treat the infection and test the mother before any further action
Treat the infection and refer urgently under child protection procedures
Treat the infection and reassure the mother that towel transmission occurs
Treat the infection and ask the GP to follow up the family in a month
Safeguarding Children.w: Gonorrhoea in a prepubertal child (outside the neonatal period) is a strong indicator of sexual abuse; NICE CG89 advises suspecting sexual abuse when a child has gonorrhoea unless there is clear evidence of perinatal transmission. An urgent child protection referral is required alongside treatment.

n.0: Testing the mother does not replace an immediate child protection referral.
n.2: Non-sexual transmission of gonorrhoea via towels is not an acceptable explanation, so reassurance would leave Lily unprotected.
n.3: A delayed GP review is not an adequate response to a strong indicator of sexual abuse.

Safeguarding Children.q: Ella, 9, tells a nurse that her 14-year-old cousin makes her touch him when he babysits. A colleague says that because both are children this is 'experimenting' and not abuse. Which response reflects Working Together 2026?
o: Treat it as experimentation and advise the parents to supervise
Wait for a second disclosure before deciding whether it is abuse
Refer it as child sexual abuse; both children may need help
Refer the 14-year-old to the police and take no action for Ella
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 recognises that child sexual abuse can be perpetrated by other children. A 14-year-old coercing a 9-year-old is harmful sexual behaviour and child sexual abuse; Ella needs protection and the older child also needs a safeguarding assessment.

n.0: The age and power gap and coercion make this abuse, not developmentally normal experimentation.
n.1: A single disclosure is enough to act; waiting leaves Ella at risk.
n.3: Ella is the victim and needs a safeguarding response; the police may be involved, but referral to children's social care is required.

Safeguarding Children.q: A neonatal nurse cares for a baby with neonatal abstinence syndrome. The mother used heroin throughout pregnancy and missed antenatal care. A pre-birth assessment was not done. Under Working Together 2026, which category of harm can occur during pregnancy through maternal substance misuse?
o: Neglect
Child sexual exploitation
Emotional abuse
Physical abuse
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 states that neglect may occur during pregnancy, for example as a result of maternal substance abuse. Parts of the guidance apply to unborn children, which is why pre-birth assessments are made.

n.1: CSE involves exploiting a child for sexual activity and is unrelated.
n.2: Emotional abuse is not the category the guidance links to substance misuse in pregnancy.
n.3: Physical abuse involves inflicted harm such as hitting or poisoning a child; the guidance places substance misuse in pregnancy under neglect.

Safeguarding Children.q: Alfie, 4 months, is brought to the GP practice for his routine immunisations. The practice nurse notices a 1 cm bruise on his cheek. His mother says his 3-year-old sister probably hit him with a toy. Alfie is otherwise well and cannot yet roll over. What should the nurse do?
o: Follow the local bruising protocol for urgent paediatric assessment and referral
Give the immunisations and ask the health visitor to check the bruise at home
Record the bruise and the explanation, then review it at the next immunisations
Reassure the mother, as the explanation offered is consistent with the bruise
Safeguarding Children.w: Bruising in a child who is not independently mobile is rare accidentally and is a recognised indicator of physical abuse (NICE CG89: suspect maltreatment). Local safeguarding partnership protocols require urgent paediatric assessment and a children's social care referral, whatever explanation is given.

n.1: Delegating a later home check delays the assessment the protocol requires.
n.2: Waiting weeks for a review leaves a possibly abused infant unprotected.
n.3: A plausible explanation does not remove the need for assessment in a non-mobile infant.

Safeguarding Children.q: A student nurse asks which infants count as 'not independently mobile' for the purpose of bruising protocols. Maya, 7 months, can roll from front to back but cannot crawl, cruise or bottom shuffle. How should Maya be classified?
o: Independently mobile, as she can roll over without help
Independently mobile, as she is older than 6 months
Not independently mobile, as she cannot crawl or shuffle
Not independently mobile until she is able to walk unaided
Safeguarding Children.w: NICE CG89 (child maltreatment, last updated December 2025) defines a child as independently mobile if they can crawl, bottom shuffle, pull themself up to stand, stand unaided, cruise, walk with a push-along walker or walk, and says age alone should not decide. Rolling is not on the list, so Maya is not independently mobile and a bruise on her would need assessment under the protocol.

n.0: Rolling is not independent mobility for this purpose.
n.1: Mobility is defined by ability, not by age.
n.3: A child who crawls, cruises or bottom shuffles is mobile even before walking.

Safeguarding Children.q: A health visitor sees Noor, 3 months, at home and notices a small bruise on her thigh. Her mother, who is attentive and has no previous concerns, says it happened when she fastened the car seat buckle. Under the local bruising protocol, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise the mother to take Noor to the GP if more bruises appear
Refer Noor for urgent paediatric assessment under the protocol
Ask the mother to photograph the bruise daily for one week
Accept the explanation, as the mother is caring and it is plausible
Safeguarding Children.w: Bruising protocols for non-mobile infants apply to any bruise however small, and irrespective of the explanation or how caring the parent appears. The infant needs paediatric assessment and children's social care involvement to exclude abuse and medical causes such as a bleeding disorder.

n.0: Waiting for further bruising risks further harm.
n.2: Monitoring photographs delays the urgent assessment the protocol requires.
n.3: Judging the parent's character is not a safe basis for not referring a non-mobile infant with a bruise.

Safeguarding Children.q: Toby, 6, has had extensive investigations for reported daily vomiting and 'collapses'. Staff on the ward have not observed any vomiting or collapse during a 10-day admission, although his mother reports them each night. Which feature is a recognised alert for fabricated or induced illness?
o: Toby has had a previous admission with a viral illness
Toby is anxious about blood tests and cries during cannulation
Symptoms are reported by the parent but not seen by staff
Toby's mother asks detailed questions about his diagnosis
Safeguarding Children.w: NICE CG89 and RCPCH guidance list reported symptoms and signs that are observed only in the presence of the parent or carer, and a lack of corroboration by independent observers, as alerting features for fabricated or induced illness.

n.0: A single previous viral admission is common in childhood.
n.1: Procedural anxiety is common and not an alerting feature.
n.3: Asking questions about a child's diagnosis is normal parental behaviour.

Safeguarding Children.q: Grace, 8, is admitted for the fourth time with 'seizures' described by her mother. No episode has been witnessed by staff, video EEG is normal and her mother is requesting a further brain scan. The nurse is increasingly concerned. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange the brain scan the mother is requesting to reassure the family
Tell the mother the seizures are probably not real and observe her reaction
Record observations factually and inform the named safeguarding nurse
Ask the mother to keep a seizure diary for the next three months
Safeguarding Children.w: In suspected FII, staff should keep factual, contemporaneous records of what is observed and reported, and share concerns promptly with the named safeguarding professional and the responsible consultant. Confronting the parent before a multi-agency plan may increase risk to the child.

n.0: Further unnecessary investigation exposes Grace to harm, which is a feature of FII itself.
n.1: Confronting the parent may increase risk to the child and compromise the safeguarding response.
n.3: A parental diary relies on the source of the concern and delays action.

Safeguarding Children.q: Jacob, 2, is admitted with recurrent unexplained hypoglycaemia. During an episode, his blood glucose is 1.8 mmol/L with a high insulin level and a very low C-peptide level. He has no diabetes. What does this result most strongly suggest?
o: Injected insulin, raising concern of induced illness
Adrenal insufficiency causing fasting hypoglycaemia
Congenital hyperinsulinism causing excess insulin secretion
An insulin-secreting tumour of the pancreas (insulinoma)
Safeguarding Children.w: Endogenous insulin is secreted with C-peptide in equal amounts, whereas injected insulin contains no C-peptide. High insulin with suppressed C-peptide indicates insulin from outside the body; in a child without diabetes this raises concern of induced illness and needs an urgent safeguarding response.

n.1: Adrenal insufficiency causes hypoglycaemia with appropriately low insulin.
n.2: Congenital hyperinsulinism produces high insulin with high C-peptide because the insulin is made by the pancreas.
n.3: An insulinoma secretes insulin with C-peptide, so C-peptide would be raised.

Safeguarding Children.q: A nurse caring for Ivy, 10 months, who has unexplained faltering growth, walks into the cubicle and sees Ivy's mother withdrawing fluid from Ivy's nasogastric tube into a syringe and squirting it into a nappy. What should the nurse do first?
o: Ask the mother to explain what she is doing and record her answer
Ensure Ivy's immediate safety, keep the evidence and escalate at once
Discuss the event with colleagues at the next ward handover
Replace the feed, recalculate Ivy's intake and continue the care plan
Safeguarding Children.w: Interference with feeding in a child with faltering growth suggests induced illness. The priority is the child's safety: stay with Ivy, preserve the evidence (syringe and nappy), inform the nurse in charge, the consultant and the safeguarding team immediately and record exactly what was seen.

n.0: Questioning the mother first may lead to evidence being lost and could increase risk; escalation comes first.
n.2: Waiting until handover delays protection.
n.3: Carrying on with care ignores a serious safeguarding concern.

Safeguarding Children.q: Leo, 3, attends the emergency department with several bruises. His father says he is 'always falling over'. Which distribution of bruising is most suggestive of non-accidental injury in a mobile toddler?
o: A bruise on the centre of the forehead
Grazes and bruising on the palms and elbows
Bruises over both shins and knees
Bruises on both ears and the side of the neck
Safeguarding Children.w: Accidental bruises in mobile children typically occur over bony prominences at the front of the body (shins, knees, forehead). NICE CG89 lists bruising on non-bony parts of the body or face, including the ears, neck, cheeks and buttocks, as a reason to suspect maltreatment.

n.0: Forehead bruises over bone are common from falls in toddlers.
n.1: Palm and elbow injuries are typical of falls onto outstretched hands.
n.2: Shin and knee bruises are typical accidental injuries in mobile toddlers.

Safeguarding Children.q: Deshawn, 15, attends the emergency department with a cut to his hand. He has two mobile phones, £300 in cash and was found by police in a town 80 miles from home. His mother says he has gone missing four times this month. Which form of harm do these features most strongly suggest?
o: Neglect by his parents at home
Child criminal exploitation
Child sexual exploitation online
Radicalisation towards extremism
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 defines child criminal exploitation as coercing, controlling, manipulating or deceiving a child into criminal activity, with county lines as an example. Multiple phones, unexplained cash, repeated missing episodes and being found far from home are classic indicators.

n.0: His mother is reporting the missing episodes; the indicators point to harm from outside the family.
n.2: Nothing described suggests sexual activity in exchange for something.
n.3: There is no indication of extremist ideology.

Safeguarding Children.q: Kayla, 15, tells the school nurse that her 24-year-old 'boyfriend' buys her phones, vodka and takes her to parties where she sleeps with his friends. She says she loves him and it is her choice. How should the nurse interpret this?
o: As child sexual exploitation, even though she says she consents
As a consensual relationship, as Kayla is near the age of consent
As a matter for Kayla's parents to resolve with her at home
As a police matter requiring a formal complaint by Kayla first
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 defines child sexual exploitation as an imbalance of power used to coerce, manipulate or deceive a child under 18 into sexual activity in exchange for something they need or want; it may appear consensual. A safeguarding referral is needed.

n.1: A 15-year-old is under the age of consent, and CSE can appear consensual.
n.2: CSE is extra-familial harm needing a multi-agency safeguarding response, not a family matter.
n.3: Safeguarding action does not depend on Kayla making a complaint; she is a child at risk of exploitation.

Safeguarding Children.q: A children's nurse is completing a psychosocial assessment for Jordan, 14, who has frequent minor injuries. Which finding would most strongly raise concern about county lines exploitation?
o: Repeated missing episodes and trips to another city
A new group of older friends from his football club
Spending long evenings playing online games at home
Falling grades during his exam year at school
Safeguarding Children.w: Repeated missing episodes and unexplained travel to other areas are key county lines indicators, as children are used to move drugs and money between areas (Working Together 2026, child criminal exploitation).

n.1: New friends through an organised club are not in themselves an exploitation indicator.
n.2: Online gaming alone is not an indicator of criminal exploitation.
n.3: Falling grades are non-specific and common in adolescence.

Safeguarding Children.q: Hana, 14, tells the school nurse that she sent a nude photo to a boy who has now shared it in a group chat. She is distraught and wants it taken down. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask her to show the image so the nurse can describe it in the record
Tell her that sending the image was illegal and she must report herself
Advise her to delete social media accounts and wait for it to pass
Support her to use Report Remove and follow safeguarding procedures
Safeguarding Children.w: Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation's Report Remove tool lets under-18s report nude images of themselves for removal. The nurse should reassure her, not view or copy the image, and follow safeguarding procedures because a child's image is being shared.

n.0: Practitioners should not view, copy or forward indecent images of children.
n.1: Blaming the child is harmful; she is the victim and the focus is protection and removal.
n.2: Deleting accounts does not remove the image or address the safeguarding concern.

Safeguarding Children.q: Tyler, 15, is treated in the emergency department for a stab wound. He tells the nurse that older men make him carry drugs and have threatened to hurt his younger sister if he stops. Police officers arrive and say he will be arrested for possession. What should the nurse do?
o: Leave the response to the police, as an offence has been committed
Advise Tyler to tell the police about the threats when interviewed
Treat his account as unreliable until the police have investigated
Treat Tyler as a victim of exploitation and make a safeguarding referral
Safeguarding Children.w: Children involved in county lines are victims of child criminal exploitation even when they commit offences (Working Together 2026). The nurse should make a safeguarding referral to children's social care, share the threat to his sister, and ensure he is treated as a child at risk alongside any police action.

n.0: An offence by the child does not remove the need for a safeguarding response to his exploitation.
n.1: Relying on Tyler to disclose to police leaves him and his sister unprotected.
n.2: Disclosures of exploitation should be acted on, not dismissed pending investigation.

Safeguarding Children.q: Amira, 12, is in hospital after an appendicectomy. She shows the nurse messages from someone she met in an online game who says he is 14, asks her to keep their chats secret, move to a private app and send photos in her pyjamas. What should the nurse do?
o: Advise Amira to block the contact and reassure her parents
Tell Amira to stop using online games while in hospital
Recognise possible grooming and follow safeguarding procedures
Ask the contact directly through the app to confirm his age
Safeguarding Children.w: Requests for secrecy, moving to a private platform and requests for images are signs of online grooming, which Working Together 2026 includes within child sexual abuse. The nurse should follow safeguarding procedures, preserve the messages and involve police (for example via a CEOP report) as advised.

n.0: Blocking the contact loses evidence and does not address possible abuse of Amira or others.
n.1: Restricting game use does not protect her or address the grooming.
n.3: Contacting the suspect could alert him and is not a nurse's role.

Safeguarding Children.q: Zainab, 14, is being exploited by a gang who meet her outside school and at a shopping centre. Her parents have reported her missing each time and are desperate to protect her. How does Working Together 2026 describe this type of harm and the parents' role?
o: Peer-on-peer bullying, managed by the school
Extra-familial harm, with parents as partners in protecting her
Intra-familial harm, with parents as the focus of enquiries
Neglect, as her parents are unable to keep her safe
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 describes extra-familial harm as harm occurring outside the home, for example in peer groups, schools, shopping centres and online. Parents are often not the source of risk and should be worked with as partners in protecting the child.

n.0: Gang exploitation is exploitation, not bullying.
n.2: The risk comes from outside the family; parents are not the source of harm.
n.3: Her parents are actively trying to protect her, so neglect does not fit.

Safeguarding Children.q: A nurse caring for Ellie, 16, notices she is collected each night by different older men in cars and has new jewellery and a phone she cannot explain. A colleague says Ellie cannot be sexually exploited because she is over the age of consent. Which statement is correct?
o: CSE can affect any child under 18, including those aged 16 and 17
CSE applies at 16 and 17 if the adults involved are over 25
CSE applies to Ellie if she agrees to an assessment
CSE applies to under-16s, so this is a matter for adult safeguarding
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 defines CSE as affecting any child under 18. A 16 or 17-year-old can be sexually exploited even though over the age of consent; children's safeguarding procedures apply.

n.1: There is no age threshold for the adults involved in the definition.
n.2: Safeguarding action does not depend on her agreement to assessment.
n.3: Children's safeguarding applies to all under-18s, not adult safeguarding.

Safeguarding Children.q: Amina, 15, attends a sexual health clinic in England with painful periods. During the consultation she tells the nurse that she was 'cut' when she was 7 during a family visit abroad. What must the nurse do under the FGM mandatory reporting duty?
o: Seek Amina's consent before reporting, as she is 15 and competent
Report the case to the police personally, usually by calling 101
Inform the clinic's safeguarding lead, who will make the police report
Refer Amina to children's social care, who will decide whether to inform the police
Safeguarding Children.w: Section 5B of the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 requires regulated health and social care professionals and teachers in England and Wales to report to the police when a girl under 18 discloses that FGM has been carried out on her. Home Office procedural information recommends reporting by calling 101; the duty is personal and does not require consent.

n.0: The duty applies regardless of consent, and complying with it does not breach confidentiality.
n.2: The duty is personal to the professional who hears the disclosure and cannot be transferred to a safeguarding lead.
n.3: A social care referral is good practice alongside, but the legal duty is a report to the police.

Safeguarding Children.q: During her daughter's asthma review, Mrs Diallo tells the practice nurse that her 12-year-old daughter Fatou had FGM as a baby. Fatou is not present and the nurse has not examined her. What should the nurse do?
o: Follow local safeguarding procedures and refer to children's social care
Arrange to examine Fatou to confirm the FGM before acting
Record the disclosure and take no further action, as it happened years ago
Report to the police under the mandatory duty within one working day
Safeguarding Children.w: The mandatory reporting duty applies when the girl herself discloses FGM or the professional observes signs. A disclosure by a parent or other person falls outside the duty, so the nurse follows local safeguarding procedures, including a referral to children's social care (Home Office procedural information, 2016).

n.1: Professionals should not carry out a genital examination for the purpose of confirming FGM.
n.2: FGM is a serious crime and Fatou and any sisters may need protection and support, whatever the time elapsed.
n.3: The mandatory police report does not apply to third-party disclosures; normal safeguarding procedures apply.

Safeguarding Children.q: Sara, 19, attends a gynaecology clinic and discloses that she underwent FGM aged 8. She has a 6-year-old sister living at home. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Support Sara and assess her sister's risk under local procedures
Report Sara's case to the police under the mandatory duty
Take no action, as Sara is an adult and the duty does not apply
Report Sara's case to the police within one month of disclosure
Safeguarding Children.w: The mandatory duty applies only to girls under 18 at the time of disclosure, even if FGM was done in childhood. Sara should be supported, given information and signposted, and professionals must consider whether others in the family, such as her younger sister, are at risk, using local safeguarding procedures.

n.1: The mandatory duty does not apply because Sara is over 18 at the time of disclosure.
n.2: Although the duty does not apply, the possible risk to her younger sister must be considered.
n.3: The one-month limit relates to the mandatory duty, which does not apply to an adult.

Safeguarding Children.q: A school nurse in England becomes aware on Monday afternoon, through a disclosure by a 14-year-old girl, that she has had FGM. There are no immediate safety concerns. According to Home Office procedural information, when should the report to the police normally be made?
o: Within 72 hours of the disclosure
Within 7 days of the disclosure
By the close of the next working day
Within one month of the disclosure
Safeguarding Children.w: Best practice is to report by the close of the next working day. A maximum of one month from discovery is allowed for exceptional cases, for example where consultation is needed because reporting may create an immediate safeguarding risk.

n.0: 72 hours is not the timescale in the procedural information.
n.1: 7 days is not a timescale in the procedural information.
n.3: One month is the legal maximum for exceptional cases, not the normal expectation.

Safeguarding Children.q: A ward nurse tells the trust's safeguarding lead that a 13-year-old patient disclosed FGM to her during a dressing change. The safeguarding lead says she will phone the police herself so that the nurse can return to her busy shift. What is the correct position?
o: The safeguarding lead can report, as a regulated professional in the same trust
The safeguarding lead must report, as the nurse is not trained in FGM
The nurse must make the report herself, as the duty cannot be transferred
Either can report, as both are regulated professionals in the trust
Safeguarding Children.w: The mandatory reporting duty is a personal duty: the professional who receives the disclosure must make the report, and the responsibility cannot be transferred. The nurse should still involve the safeguarding lead for support and wider safeguarding action.

n.0: Working in the same trust does not allow the duty to be passed to another person.
n.1: Training level does not change who holds the duty.
n.3: Being regulated in the same trust does not allow the duty to be shared or passed on; it stays with the nurse who heard the disclosure.

Safeguarding Children.q: A health visitor learns that Halima, 6, is going on a 'long holiday' this summer to a country with a high prevalence of FGM. Her older sister underwent FGM. Halima has not had FGM. What should the health visitor do?
o: Advise the parents that FGM is illegal and document the advice given
Report to the police under the mandatory duty within one working day
Make a safeguarding referral under local procedures, as Halima is at risk
Wait to see Halima on her return and examine her for signs of FGM
Safeguarding Children.w: The mandatory duty applies to known cases, not to at-risk or suspected cases. Halima is at risk, so the health visitor follows local safeguarding procedures and makes a referral to children's social care; an FGM protection order can be sought. If there is immediate danger, the police should be contacted.

n.0: Advice alone does not protect Halima when there are clear risk factors.
n.1: The mandatory police report does not apply to girls at risk who have not had FGM.
n.3: Waiting until after the trip fails to prevent harm, and professionals should not examine to look for FGM.

Safeguarding Children.q: A children's nurse inserting a urinary catheter for Maryam, 9, after surgery notices genital appearances that she believes show FGM. She has not had specialist FGM training and is unsure of the type. What should she do?
o: Report to the police, as the duty applies once signs appear to show FGM
Report once a doctor's diagnosis of FGM is recorded in the notes
Ask a gynaecologist to examine Maryam and confirm the type of FGM first
Record the findings and ask the parents whether FGM has been carried out
Safeguarding Children.w: Under the procedural information, the duty applies at the point a professional sees physical signs that appear to show FGM in the course of their work. A full clinical diagnosis is not required, and no further examination should be carried out for the purpose of confirming it.

n.1: A medical diagnosis is not required before the duty applies.
n.2: An examination solely to confirm FGM should not be carried out; the duty applies on what was observed.
n.3: Asking the parents first may put Maryam at risk and does not discharge the duty.

Safeguarding Children.q: During a sexual health appointment, a nurse notices that Chloe, 16, has a genital piercing. Chloe says she had it done at a piercing studio. Under the Home Office FGM procedural information, what should the nurse do?
o: Make a report under the FGM mandatory duty
Take no action, as Chloe chose the piercing herself
Refer to trading standards as an unlicensed procedure
Advise Chloe about infection risk and record the finding
Safeguarding Children.w: The Home Office procedural information advises that a girl under 18 identified as having a genital piercing (a form of FGM under the WHO type 4 classification) should be reported; the professional does not need to be satisfied that a criminal offence has been committed.

n.1: Under-18s' genital piercings fall within the FGM duty regardless of the girl's agreement.
n.2: Trading standards is not the route required by the FGM duty.
n.3: Clinical advice is appropriate but does not discharge the reporting duty.

Safeguarding Children.q: Callum, 15, is an inpatient after a sports injury. Staff notice he repeatedly watches videos glorifying a recent terrorist attack, has drawn extremist symbols in his notebook and says people of a certain ethnicity 'deserve what is coming'. What is the most appropriate first action for the nurse?
o: Discuss the concern with the trust's Prevent or safeguarding lead
Confiscate his phone and notebook and inform his parents
Phone the counter-terrorism police hotline directly
Challenge his views and record the conversation in his notes
Safeguarding Children.w: Prevent duty guidance (2023) treats radicalisation as a safeguarding concern. Staff should follow the notice, check, share approach: share the concern with the organisation's Prevent lead or designated safeguarding lead, who helps decide whether a Prevent referral is needed.

n.1: Seizing belongings is not a nurse's role, and telling parents first may not be appropriate before advice.
n.2: Direct police contact is for an immediate risk; here the concern goes through the trust's Prevent or safeguarding route.
n.3: Recording is needed, but the concern must also be shared through the safeguarding route.

Safeguarding Children.q: A student nurse asks what the Prevent duty actually requires of an NHS trust. Which statement is accurate?
o: Trusts must have due regard to the need to prevent people being drawn into terrorism
Trusts must screen all patients aged over 12 for radicalisation on admission
Trusts must carry out counter-terrorism investigations into referred patients
Trusts must report every patient who expresses extreme political views to the police
Safeguarding Children.w: Section 26 of the Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015 requires specified authorities, including NHS trusts, to have due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism. The 2023 guidance explains due regard as giving this appropriate weight within their usual functions.

n.1: There is no requirement for routine radicalisation screening of patients.
n.2: Investigation is a police function; health staff identify and share concerns.
n.3: Holding extreme views is not in itself a reason to report a person to police; concerns go through a safeguarding route.

Safeguarding Children.q: A Prevent referral about Zak, 14, is accepted for discussion by the local Channel panel. His mother asks whether he will be forced to take part. What does the Prevent duty guidance say about Channel for a person under 18?
o: Channel is voluntary, and a child aged 14 or over consents for himself
Channel is voluntary; a parent, guardian or agency consents for him
Channel is compulsory if the local authority applies for a court order
Channel is compulsory once the panel accepts the referral of a child
Safeguarding Children.w: Prevent duty guidance (2023, para 20) states that Channel is a voluntary process and people must give consent before receiving support; where the person is under 18, consent is given by a parent, guardian or the agency responsible for their care.

n.0: For under-18s the guidance gives consent to a parent, guardian or responsible agency, not the child alone at 14.
n.2: Channel is not a court-ordered process.
n.3: Channel is voluntary; acceptance of a referral does not compel participation.

Safeguarding Children.q: During a night shift, Daniel, 16, tells a nurse that he has bought chemicals online and will 'make the school pay' tomorrow morning. He shows her a photograph of a device in his bedroom. What should the nurse do?
o: Discuss his comments with him again after he has rested
Inform the designated safeguarding lead at Daniel's school next day
Make a Prevent referral through the trust's Prevent lead in the morning
Contact the police immediately on 999, then inform the safeguarding team
Safeguarding Children.w: Prevent processes are for people at risk of being drawn into terrorism. Where there is an immediate risk to life, staff should contact the police on 999 without delay and then inform the organisation's safeguarding and Prevent leads.

n.0: Delay could cost lives; the threat is specific and imminent.
n.1: Waiting to inform the school delays action against an imminent threat.
n.2: A routine Prevent referral is too slow for an imminent threat to life.

Safeguarding Children.q: A community children's nurse is uneasy after Aisha, 13, repeats extremist slogans she has seen online, but the nurse is not sure whether this is a real concern or bravado. According to the Prevent duty guidance, which approach should the nurse use?
o: Discuss the concern with Aisha's parents to decide together
Wait for a second incident before taking action
Notice, check and share the concern through the Prevent lead
Refer straight to the Channel panel for assessment
Safeguarding Children.w: Prevent duty guidance (2023, paras 42-43) says the notice, check, share procedure should be applied: notice the concern, check it with the organisation's Prevent or designated safeguarding lead, and share it if a referral is needed.

n.0: Parents may be involved later, but the guidance route is to check with the Prevent or safeguarding lead.
n.1: Waiting for a further incident risks missing the chance to support Aisha early.
n.3: Channel receives referrals that have been through the Prevent process; practitioners do not refer straight to the panel.

Safeguarding Children.q: After a Prevent referral, the Channel panel offers mentoring to Liam, 15. His parents refuse consent. The panel still believes Liam is vulnerable to radicalisation. What happens next?
o: Channel cannot proceed; other safeguarding support is considered
The police apply for a court order to compel Channel support
Channel support goes ahead if Liam agrees, as he is over 13
Channel support goes ahead, as Liam's welfare is paramount
Safeguarding Children.w: Channel is voluntary, and for under-18s consent is given by a parent, guardian or responsible agency (Prevent duty guidance 2023, para 20). Without consent Channel support cannot proceed, but the case continues to be managed through other appropriate safeguarding and support routes.

n.1: Channel is not court-ordered.
n.2: For under-18s the guidance places consent with a parent, guardian or responsible agency.
n.3: Paramountcy governs court decisions under the Children Act; it does not make Channel compulsory.

Safeguarding Children.q: During safeguarding training, a colleague says that Prevent is about Islamist extremism and does not apply to Jack, 14, who is sharing far-right material online. Which response is correct?
o: Prevent covers Islamist extremism, so Jack's case is for the police
Prevent covers far-right views once violence has been committed
Prevent covers adults, so Jack's case goes to child protection
Prevent covers all forms of terrorism, including extreme right-wing
Safeguarding Children.w: The Prevent duty applies to all ideologies that can draw people into terrorism, including Islamist and extreme right-wing terrorism. Jack's case should be shared through the Prevent or safeguarding lead like any other.

n.0: Prevent is not limited to Islamist extremism.
n.1: Prevent works before violence occurs; it is about preventing people being drawn into terrorism.
n.2: Prevent applies to children as well as adults, alongside child safeguarding procedures.

Safeguarding Children.q: A newly qualified nurse on a children's ward has a concern that a 15-year-old patient may be being radicalised by an older relative. She is unsure who to contact within her NHS trust for specialist advice. Who is the most appropriate person?
o: The trust's Prevent lead
The counter-terrorism police unit
The Local Authority Designated Officer
The chair of the local Channel panel
Safeguarding Children.w: NHS trusts have a Prevent lead who advises staff and handles Prevent concerns alongside the safeguarding team, using the notice, check, share approach before any referral.

n.1: Police contact is for immediate risk; specialist advice in the trust comes from the Prevent lead.
n.2: The LADO handles allegations against people who work with children.
n.3: Channel panels consider referrals once made; they are not the first point of advice within a trust.

Safeguarding Children.q: In October 2026 a community children's nurse in England is worried that Noah, 7, is often hungry and tired at clinic. She plans to share this with his school's designated safeguarding lead so they can offer support. Noah's mother refuses consent. What is the correct position?
o: The nurse must wait until concerns reach the threshold for a referral
The nurse should share the information, as consent is not required under s16LA
The nurse needs the mother's consent before sharing, as there is no s47 enquiry
The nurse can share once a court has authorised disclosure to the school
Safeguarding Children.w: From 30 September 2026, s16LA of the Children Act 2004 requires relevant persons to share information that may help another relevant person safeguard or promote a child's welfare. Consent is not required and lack of consent is not a reason to withhold (statutory guidance, September 2026). The nurse should usually tell the mother what is being shared and why, unless that would put Noah at risk.

n.0: No statutory threshold has to be met before the duty applies; it covers early help and unmet needs.
n.2: Consent is not required under the duty, and sharing is not limited to s47 enquiries.
n.3: No court authorisation is needed; the duty itself requires sharing.

Safeguarding Children.q: A health visitor has low-level concerns about Kai, 18 months, whose mother has recently disclosed depression and is struggling with routines. The concerns do not meet the threshold for a child protection referral. Does the s16LA information sharing duty apply to sharing with the Family Help service?
o: No, as the duty applies once s47 enquiries have started
Yes, as no statutory threshold must be met before the duty applies
Yes, once the mother has given written agreement to share
No, as the duty applies to children on a child protection plan
Safeguarding Children.w: The statutory guidance (September 2026) states that no statutory or local threshold has to be met before information can be shared under the duty; it applies wherever sharing may help another relevant person assess need, provide support or safeguard and promote the child's welfare, including early help.

n.0: The duty is not limited to child protection enquiries.
n.2: Consent is not required under the duty; written agreement is not a condition.
n.3: The duty is not limited to children subject to a plan.

Safeguarding Children.q: A nurse is deciding whether to share information about Yasmin, 13, who is living in a refuge with her mother after fleeing domestic abuse. Under the s16LA statutory guidance, in which circumstance may the nurse decide not to share particular information?
o: When Yasmin's father, who has parental responsibility, objects
When the family has not given consent to the sharing
When sharing would be more detrimental to Yasmin than not sharing
When the nurse feels uncomfortable about the possible consequences
Safeguarding Children.w: The duty does not apply in extremely limited circumstances where sharing would be more detrimental to the child than not sharing, for example where disclosing a refuge address would place the child at immediate risk (statutory guidance, Limitation: detriment to the child). Other relevant information should still be shared and the decision recorded.

n.0: Parental objection is not a reason to withhold under the duty.
n.1: Lack of consent is expressly not a reason to withhold.
n.3: Practitioner discomfort is not a reason to withhold; the guidance says seek prompt advice instead.

Safeguarding Children.q: A practice nurse in England plans to share concerns about Leo, 5, with children's social care under the s16LA duty. She intends to share whether or not his father agrees. How should she approach the conversation with the father?
o: Leave him uninformed, as the duty does not require openness
Ask for his consent, then withhold if he refuses it
Ask for his consent, then share anyway if he refuses it
Explain openly what will be shared and why, not asking consent
Safeguarding Children.w: The statutory guidance says that where the lawful basis is public task or legal obligation, practitioners should avoid seeking consent if they intend to share anyway, and should not imply that the family's agreement decides the matter. Where safe, they should be open and transparent about what is shared and why.

n.0: Practitioners should be transparent with families where it is safe to do so.
n.1: Lack of consent is not a reason to withhold information under the duty.
n.2: Seeking consent that will then be overridden is misleading and is discouraged by the guidance.

Safeguarding Children.q: A ward nurse has concerns about Mia, 11, but is anxious because Mia's mother has said she will complain if any information is shared with the school. The nurse is unsure what to do. According to the s16LA statutory guidance, what is the best course of action?
o: Share once the mother's complaint has been resolved by the trust
Seek prompt advice from the safeguarding lead and share as needed
Ask Mia whether she wants the school to be informed
Withhold the information to avoid a complaint about the trust
Safeguarding Children.w: The statutory guidance states that information must still be shared where concerns relate only to a parent being unhappy, fear of complaint or a practitioner feeling unsure; in those cases practitioners should seek prompt advice from their manager, safeguarding lead or Caldicott Guardian.

n.0: Delaying until a complaint is resolved leaves Mia without timely support.
n.2: Mia's views matter, but her agreement is not what decides whether the duty applies.
n.3: Fear of complaint is expressly not a reason to withhold.

Safeguarding Children.q: A school nurse must share information about Oliver, 9, with children's social care. Some of the information includes old, unverified allegations about his mother's past and labels such as 'chaotic family'. How should the nurse share in line with the s16LA guidance?
o: Withhold everything until each allegation has been verified
Share all historical material so the full picture is passed on
Share what is relevant, avoiding labels and untested allegations
Share the allegations, but remove Oliver's name from the report
Safeguarding Children.w: The statutory guidance asks practitioners to consider relevance and to mitigate harm by limiting information, avoiding stigmatising language, identity labels, historical narrative and untested allegations unless strictly relevant to safeguarding the child.

n.0: Relevant safeguarding information should not be withheld pending verification.
n.1: Irrelevant historical material is not required and may cause harm.
n.3: Removing the child's name would stop the recipient acting to safeguard him.

Safeguarding Children.q: After sharing safeguarding information about Ruby, 3, with her health visitor and children's social care, what should the children's nurse record, according to the s16LA statutory guidance?
o: A note of the decision when information is withheld, not when shared
The mother's response, as this decides whether further sharing is lawful
What was shared, with whom, when and the reason for sharing
That the information was shared, without detail to protect privacy
Safeguarding Children.w: The guidance requires a clear record of the decision to share or not share: what information was shared, with whom, when and why. Decisions not to share must also be recorded with reasons.

n.0: Decisions to share must be recorded as well as decisions not to share.
n.1: The parent's response does not decide whether sharing under the duty is lawful.
n.3: A record without detail does not show what was shared or why.

Safeguarding Children.q: A GP practice nurse in England identifies that a parent's alcohol use may be affecting her 6-year-old patient's care. The nurse wonders whether the s16LA information sharing duty applies to primary care. Which statement is correct?
o: It applies to health staff on a child protection plan
It applies to local authorities and the police, not health
It applies to NHS trusts, but not to GP practices
It applies to providers including GPs and dentists
Safeguarding Children.w: The statutory guidance states the duty applies to section 11 organisations (including ICBs, NHS trusts and the police), designated education and childcare agencies, and providers delivering services for them, which includes GPs, dentists and other primary care providers.

n.0: The duty is not limited to children with a child protection plan.
n.1: Health bodies such as ICBs and NHS trusts are relevant persons under the duty.
n.2: GPs and other primary care providers are expressly included.

Safeguarding Children.q: A student nurse on a paediatric intensive care unit asks which organisations in England are responsible for making sure that every child death in the local area is reviewed. Under Working Together 2026, who are the child death review partners?
o: The ICB and the NHS trust where the child died
The local authority, the ICB and the police
The coroner and the NHS trust where the child died
The local authority and any ICB operating in its area
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 defines child death review partners, for a local authority area in England, as the local authority and any integrated care boards operating in that area. They must arrange reviews of all deaths of children normally resident there, through a Child Death Overview Panel.

n.0: NHS trusts take part in reviews but the statutory partners are the local authority and ICBs.
n.1: These three are the safeguarding partners; the police are not child death review partners.
n.2: Coroners investigate and share information but are not child death review partners.

Safeguarding Children.q: Ellie, 9, has a life-limiting neuromuscular condition and dies peacefully at a children's hospice, as planned in her advance care plan. A new nurse asks whether a child death notification is needed, as the death was expected. What is the correct answer?
o: No, the GP's death certificate completes the process
Yes, the death of every child is notified for review
No, deaths in hospices are reviewed by the hospice
No, notification is for sudden or unexpected deaths
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 states that practitioners in all agencies should notify the child death review partners, via the local CDOP administrator, of the death of any child, using the child death notification form. All child deaths, expected or not, are reviewed.

n.0: Certification does not replace notification to the child death review process.
n.2: Hospice deaths are reviewed through the same statutory process.
n.3: All child deaths are notified and reviewed, not only unexpected ones.

Safeguarding Children.q: Which of the following child deaths requires a joint agency response under Working Together 2026?
o: A 4-month-old found dead in his cot with no immediately apparent cause
A 10-year-old who dies on a ward from known end-stage cancer
A 2-year-old with a known cardiac condition who dies after planned surgery
A 15-year-old with cystic fibrosis who dies in hospital as anticipated
Safeguarding Children.w: A joint agency response is required where a child's death is or could be due to external causes; is sudden with no immediately apparent cause (including sudden unexpected death in infancy); occurs in custody or under the Mental Health Act; raises suspicion of not being natural; or is a stillbirth with no health professional present (Working Together 2026, para 449).

n.1: An expected death from a known condition does not meet the joint agency response criteria.
n.2: A death following planned treatment for a known condition is reviewed through the usual process, unless other concerns arise.
n.3: An anticipated death from a known condition does not meet the criteria.

Safeguarding Children.q: Paramedics attend a 6-month-old who is found unresponsive at home and cannot be resuscitated. There are no obvious signs of injury. Unless the police decide otherwise, where should the baby normally be taken?
o: To the local mortuary for post-mortem examination
To the nearest children's hospice
To the GP surgery for the death to be certified
To a hospital emergency department
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 (para 450) states that if there is an unexplained death of a child at home or in the community, the child should normally be taken to a hospital emergency department rather than a mortuary, unless the police decide the body should not be moved, for example for forensic examination.

n.0: The guidance directs the child to an emergency department rather than a mortuary in the first instance.
n.1: Hospices care for expected deaths, not unexplained deaths needing a joint agency response.
n.2: GP surgeries are not the place for an unexplained child death response.

Safeguarding Children.q: After the death of Josh, 3, from sepsis on a children's ward, a multi-agency meeting is arranged before the CDOP review. The ward nurse who cared for Josh is invited. What is this meeting, and who should attend?
o: A rapid review, attended by the three safeguarding partners
A strategy discussion, attended by police, health and social care
A CDOP meeting, attended by staff who were not involved in his care
A child death review meeting, attended by staff involved in his care
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 (para 453) describes the child death review meeting as the multi-agency meeting before the CDOP review, attended by professionals directly involved in the child's care in life and in the investigation of the death, not limited to medical staff. A draft analysis form is then sent to CDOP.

n.0: A rapid review follows a serious incident notification about abuse or neglect, not every child death.
n.1: A strategy discussion plans action where significant harm is suspected in a living child.
n.2: CDOP is the later independent scrutiny by professionals who had no responsibility for the child.

Safeguarding Children.q: A CDOP reviews the deaths of three infants in its area that involved co-sleeping after parental alcohol use. The panel recommends a local safer sleep campaign. What is the main purpose of the CDOP review, as described in Working Together 2026?
o: Independent scrutiny to find modifiable factors and prevent deaths
Determination of the medical cause of death in place of the coroner
Investigation of the deaths to decide whether criminal charges should follow
Disciplinary review of practitioners involved in each child's care
Safeguarding Children.w: The CDOP review is the final, independent scrutiny of a child's death by professionals with no responsibility for the child during life. It aims to identify modifiable factors that could be altered to prevent future deaths and to share learning, including with the National Child Mortality Database.

n.1: The coroner retains responsibility for inquests into the cause of death.
n.2: Criminal investigation is the responsibility of the police and CPS.
n.3: CDOP reviews are for learning, not for disciplining individuals.

Safeguarding Children.q: A 2-year-old dies following severe physical abuse. The local authority, on behalf of the safeguarding partners, notifies the Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel. Under Working Together 2026, within what time should the rapid review be submitted to the Panel?
o: Within 45 working days of the notification
Within 6 months of the notification
Within 15 working days of the notification
Within 5 working days of the notification
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 requires serious incident notification within five working days of the safeguarding partners becoming aware, and the rapid review to be submitted to the Panel within 15 working days of the notification.

n.0: 45 working days is the maximum assessment timescale for children's social care.
n.1: Six months relates to completing a local child safeguarding practice review, not the rapid review.
n.3: Five working days is the timescale for the notification itself.

Safeguarding Children.q: A nurse involved in a child death review asks where the information from all child death reviews in England is analysed nationally to identify trends and inform prevention. Which body is this?
o: The Healthcare Safety Investigation Branch
The National Child Mortality Database
The Child Safeguarding Practice Review Panel
The Care Quality Commission
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 states that child death review partners must arrange for information from all deaths reviewed to be analysed by the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD), which identifies trends and similarities to inform local and national prevention.

n.0: HSIB (now HSSIB) investigates selected patient safety incidents, not all child deaths.
n.2: The Panel oversees serious safeguarding case reviews, not all child deaths.
n.3: The CQC regulates providers and does not analyse all child death reviews.

Safeguarding Children.q: On Monday morning a children's nurse in England telephones and then confirms in writing a referral to children's social care about Leah, 4, who has unexplained bruising. Leah's mother asks how soon she will hear what happens next. Under Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026, when should social care decide on next steps?
o: Within one working day of receiving the referral
Within 3 working days of the referral
Within 24 hours of the written confirmation arriving
Within 5 working days of receiving the referral
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 (para 167) states that within one working day of a referral being received, local authority children's social care should decide on next steps, such as no further action, Family Help or s47 enquiries, and inform the referrer.

n.1: Three working days is not the Working Together decision timescale.
n.2: The timescale is expressed in working days from receipt of the referral, not hours from written confirmation.
n.3: Five working days is the timescale for notifying a serious incident to the national panel, not for a referral decision.

Safeguarding Children.q: Following a referral about Josh, 8, who disclosed that his father burned him with a cigarette, the local authority holds a strategy discussion because there is reasonable cause to suspect significant harm. Under Working Together 2026, which agencies must, as a minimum, be involved?
o: Police, health and the Local Authority Designated Officer
Children's social care, health and the child's parents
Local authority children's social care, the school and the GP
Local authority children's social care, police and health
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 states that a strategy discussion involving local authority children's social care, the police and health (and other bodies as appropriate, such as the referring agency and education) should take place whenever there is reasonable cause to suspect significant harm.

n.0: The LADO manages allegations against people who work with children; children's social care must be involved here.
n.1: Parents are not participants in a professionals' strategy discussion, and the police are required.
n.2: Schools and GPs may contribute, but the police must be involved as a minimum.

Safeguarding Children.q: Section 47 enquiries are started at a strategy discussion about Mason, 2, who has a femoral fracture with no explanation. The health visitor asks when an initial child protection conference should take place if concerns are substantiated. What timescale does Working Together 2026 set?
o: Within 10 working days of the strategy discussion
Within 5 working days of the strategy discussion
Within 45 working days of the original referral
Within 15 working days of the strategy discussion
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 sets the initial child protection conference within 15 working days of the strategy discussion, or of the last strategy discussion if more than one was held, at which s47 enquiries were initiated.

n.0: Ten working days is the timescale for the first core group meeting after the initial conference.
n.1: Five working days is too short and is not the conference timescale.
n.2: 45 working days is the maximum for completing an assessment, not for convening the conference.

Safeguarding Children.q: A mother tells a nurse on a children's ward that she saw a healthcare assistant roughly grab her son's arm and swear at him during the night. The healthcare assistant is still on shift. Under Working Together 2026, what should happen to this allegation?
o: It is recorded in the incident system and reviewed at the next team meeting
Report it to a senior manager now; the LADO is told within one working day
The nurse discusses it with the healthcare assistant before deciding to report
It is reported to the NMC, which will decide whether the LADO needs to be involved
Safeguarding Children.w: Working Together 2026 (para 264) says any allegation against a person who works with children should be reported immediately to a senior manager, and the Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO) should be informed within one working day. Immediate action to protect the child, such as removing the staff member from contact, is also needed.

n.0: Waiting for a team meeting delays protection and the required report to the LADO.
n.2: Discussing the allegation with the person concerned first may compromise any investigation and leaves the child at risk.
n.3: The NMC does not regulate healthcare assistants, and the LADO advises on regulator referrals, not the other way round.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Lucas, aged 2 years 3 months, is seen for a review. His mother says he used to say about 20 words and wave goodbye, but over the last 3 months he has stopped talking and no longer responds to his name. He is walking and climbing well. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer him promptly for specialist developmental assessment
Review his speech again at the 3-year contact before deciding
Arrange a hearing test and await the result before any other referral
Reassure her that speech often plateaus while children focus on motor skills
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Loss of previously acquired skills (regression) at any age is a developmental red flag. NICE CG128 rec 1.3.1 says to refer children younger than 3 years to the autism team if there is regression in language or social skills, so Lucas needs prompt specialist assessment. A hearing test is part of the work-up but should not delay referral.

n.1: Waiting nearly a year delays assessment and support for a child with a red flag.
n.2: Hearing should be checked, but loss of social skills such as waving shows the problem is not hearing alone, so referral should not wait.
n.3: A plateau is different from losing skills; regression is a recognised warning sign and should not be explained away.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Isla, aged 10 months, is admitted with bronchiolitis. While playing, the nurse notices Isla reaches for every toy with her right hand and keeps her left hand fisted. Her mother says she has always done this. Isla sits and babbles normally. What is the best interpretation?
o: This is a red flag that suggests a possible motor problem and needs review
Fisting usually reflects tiredness from her current respiratory illness
A clear hand preference is expected by 10 months and needs no action
Hand preference is linked to speech, so a speech referral is needed
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Hand preference normally develops in the second year or later. NICE NG62 rec 1.3.5 lists early asymmetry of hand function (hand preference) before 1 year, corrected for gestational age, as a common delayed motor milestone in cerebral palsy, and rec 1.3.6 advises referring children with delayed motor milestones to a child development service. A fixed preference with a persistently fisted other hand can reflect weakness of that side (for example hemiplegic cerebral palsy), so Isla needs medical review.

n.1: Her mother reports this has always happened, so it predates the acute illness.
n.2: Early, fixed hand preference in infancy is not expected and is a sign of asymmetry.
n.3: The concern is a motor asymmetry, not speech; Isla's babbling is normal.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ruby, 19 months, moves around by bottom shuffling and does not yet walk. She can pull to stand briefly. Her father also bottom shuffled and walked at 22 months. Ruby's other development is normal. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Advise a baby walker to encourage her to bear weight and step
Note the family history and arrange a review for when she reaches 3 years
Reassure and recheck at the 2-year review because shufflers often walk late
Refer for assessment because she is not walking at 18 months
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Not walking by 18 months (corrected for gestational age) is one of the delayed motor milestones listed in NICE NG62 rec 1.3.5, and rec 1.3.6 advises referring all children with delayed motor milestones to a child development service for further assessment. Bottom shufflers and children with a family history often walk later, but assessment confirms the normal variant and excludes causes such as cerebral palsy or a muscle disorder, rather than assuming one.

n.0: Baby walkers do not help children learn to walk and carry a risk of injury, so they are not advised.
n.1: Waiting until 3 years would delay assessment of a red flag by well over a year.
n.2: Bottom shuffling makes late walking more likely but does not remove the need to assess a child not walking at 18 months; waiting another 5 months delays diagnosis if there is a cause.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: A nurse on a children's surgical ward is planning activities for Maya, aged 9 months, who is staying for several days. Her parents must leave briefly each day. Which behaviour should the nurse expect and plan for at this age?
o: Indifference to her parents leaving because attachment forms after 2 years
Wariness of strangers and distress when separated from her parents
Cooperative play with other children in the ward playroom
Comfort from any adult who picks her up, including new staff
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Stranger wariness and separation distress typically emerge around 8 to 9 months as attachment to main carers strengthens (CDC 2022: shy, clingy or fearful around strangers at 9 months). The nurse should plan consistent named carers, comfort objects and family-centred visiting to reduce distress.

n.0: Attachment to main carers is well established in the first year, so separation distress is expected rather than indifference.
n.2: Cooperative play with other children develops around 3 years or later; infants play alone or alongside others.
n.3: At this age infants often become wary of unfamiliar adults, so comfort from a stranger is less likely.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Amara, a breastfed baby, weighed 3.4 kg at birth. On day 5 she weighs 3.02 kg. She is alert and feeding every 2 to 3 hours, and her mother is anxious. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure her mother that losing up to 15% of birth weight is normal in the first week
Weigh Amara twice daily to track the trend closely
Advise formula top-ups after every breastfeed until birth weight is regained
Assess Amara clinically and take a detailed feeding history, including observing a feed
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Amara has lost 0.38 kg, about 11% of her birth weight (0.38 / 3.4 x 100). NICE NG75 rec 1.1.2: if an infant loses more than 10% of birth weight, perform a clinical assessment for dehydration or illness, take a detailed feeding history and consider direct observation of feeding by someone with appropriate expertise.

n.0: More than 10% loss is the NICE threshold for assessment; 15% is not a normal figure.
n.1: NG75 rec 1.1.5 advises weighing no more often than daily; twice-daily weights add anxiety without useful information.
n.2: Routine formula top-ups can end breastfeeding (NG75 rec 1.1.6); assessment and feeding support come first.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: A health visitor explains early weight change to a new father. Which statement about weight in the first weeks of life is accurate?
o: Most babies have regained their birth weight by 3 weeks of age
Most babies regain their birth weight by 6 weeks of age
Weight loss usually continues for about 2 weeks before gain begins
Babies should not lose any weight if feeding is going well
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.1.1: it is common for infants to lose some weight in the early days, this usually stops after about 3 or 4 days, and most have returned to birth weight by 3 weeks. Not regaining birth weight by 3 weeks is a trigger for assessment (rec 1.1.4).

n.1: Six weeks is too late; regaining birth weight is expected by 3 weeks.
n.2: Early weight loss usually stops after 3 or 4 days, not 2 weeks.
n.3: Some early weight loss is common and expected even when feeding goes well.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Finley, aged 18 months, is admitted with faltering growth. The nurse needs to measure him for plotting on a UK-WHO growth chart. Which measurement should be taken?
o: Head circumference, which replaces length after 12 months
Mid-upper arm circumference, because he is under 5
Standing height, because he can walk independently
Supine length, because he is under 2 years old
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.2: weigh the child and measure length from birth to 2 years old, or height if aged over 2 years, then plot current and previous measurements on the UK-WHO growth charts (AnnexB.2.6: measuring weight and height).

n.0: Head circumference is a separate measure and does not replace length.
n.1: Mid-upper arm circumference is a nutritional screening tool, not the measurement used to assess linear growth on UK-WHO charts.
n.2: Standing height is used over 2 years; walking ability does not change the method below that age.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Harvey, aged 4 months, is being monitored at home for faltering growth. His mother asks the community children's nurse how often he should be weighed. He is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Usually no more often than weekly at his age
Usually no more often than daily until he gains weight
Usually no more often than fortnightly at his age
Usually no more often than monthly at his age
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.27: when there is concern about faltering growth, weigh usually no more often than daily if under 1 month, weekly between 1 and 6 months, fortnightly between 6 and 12 months and monthly from 1 year. Weighing too often adds parental anxiety (rec 1.2.28).

n.1: Daily weighing is the limit for babies under 1 month; at 4 months it adds anxiety without benefit.
n.2: Fortnightly is the guide for 6 to 12 months, not 4 months.
n.3: Monthly is the guide from 1 year of age.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Poppy, aged 10 months, had a birth weight on the 50th centile. Her weight is now just below the 9th centile, a fall across 2 centile spaces on the UK-WHO chart. She is well, active and developing normally. Which interpretation is correct?
o: This needs urgent admission for investigation of an underlying cause
This meets the threshold if her length has also dropped by 2 centile spaces
This meets the threshold for concern and needs clinical and feeding assessment
This needs no action because her current weight is above the 2nd centile
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.1: a fall across 2 or more weight centile spaces when birthweight was between the 9th and 91st centiles is a threshold for concern about faltering growth. Rec 1.2.6 then advises a clinical, developmental and social assessment with a detailed feeding history.

n.0: NG75 rec 1.2.32 advises against admission unless the child is acutely unwell or there is a specific indication such as starting tube feeding.
n.1: The NG75 weight threshold stands on its own; a parallel fall in length is not required.
n.3: Below the 2nd centile is one threshold, but a fall across 2 centile spaces from a middle birthweight is a separate trigger.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Leo, aged 14 months, has faltering growth confirmed on his growth chart. He is well, and a detailed feeding history shows small, grazing meals. He eats bread and pasta. Which investigations does NICE advise considering at this stage?
o: Full blood count, ferritin and stool culture
Skeletal survey and a full clotting screen
Urine test for infection and coeliac screening
Sweat test and thyroid function tests
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.6: when there is concern about faltering growth, consider investigating for urinary tract infection and for coeliac disease if the diet has included gluten; further tests only if the clinical assessment indicates them (rec 1.2.13: other investigations are unlikely to reveal a cause in a well child).

n.0: These are not the routine tests NICE recommends for a well child with faltering growth.
n.1: A skeletal survey is a safeguarding investigation for suspected physical abuse, which nothing in this history suggests.
n.3: A sweat test and thyroid tests are not routine; they are done only if the clinical assessment points to cystic fibrosis or thyroid disease.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ella, aged 6, is reviewed for poor growth. Her BMI is calculated and plotted on the BMI centile chart; it lies below the 0.4th centile. Her parents are both of average height. What does this finding suggest, and what is needed?
o: A small build that needs no intervention given average parental height
Probable undernutrition that needs assessment and intervention
A primary growth disorder that needs growth hormone treatment
Normal variation that should be rechecked in 12 months
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.4: in a child over 2 years, a BMI below the 2nd centile may reflect undernutrition or a small build, but a BMI below the 0.4th centile suggests probable undernutrition that needs assessment and intervention.

n.0: A small build can explain a BMI below the 2nd centile, but below the 0.4th centile NICE says undernutrition is probable.
n.2: A low BMI points to undernutrition; growth disorders are suggested by low height compared with mid-parental height, and treatment would follow specialist diagnosis.
n.3: A BMI below the 0.4th centile needs action now, not a recheck in a year.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Jasmine, 7 weeks, is breastfed and has faltering growth. After assessment, the team recommends supplementing with infant formula. Her mother wants to keep breastfeeding. What advice best supports this?
o: Offer any breast milk first, then formula, and express to build supply
Give the formula first at each feed so Jasmine takes the full volume
Stop breastfeeding for a week to measure formula intake accurately
Alternate breastfeeds with formula feeds and stop expressing
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: NICE NG75 rec 1.2.18: if formula supplementation is given to a breastfed infant because of faltering growth after the early days, support the mother to continue breastfeeding, advise expressing to promote milk supply, and feed any available breast milk before giving formula. Rec 1.2.17 warns that supplementation often leads to stopping breastfeeding.

n.1: Giving formula first fills the baby and reduces breast milk demand and supply.
n.2: A break from breastfeeding risks losing supply and is not advised.
n.3: Stopping expressing reduces milk supply and makes it harder to continue breastfeeding.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Kayla, 15, is admitted to an adolescent ward with abdominal pain. The nurse plans a HEEADSSS psychosocial assessment and has seen Kayla alone after explaining confidentiality. With which area should the nurse begin?
o: Suicide and mood, because risk is the priority
Drugs and alcohol, to identify risks early
Sexual activity, because it may explain the abdominal pain
Home life, such as who she lives with
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: HEEADSSS (Home, Education/employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/depression, Safety) is designed to move from the least threatening topics to the most personal and sensitive ones, which builds rapport before sensitive questions (Doukrou and Segal, Arch Dis Child Educ Pract 2018).

n.0: Mood and suicide are covered later in the sequence once trust is established, unless she raises them first.
n.1: Drugs are asked about after rapport has been built through less sensitive topics.
n.2: Sexual health is relevant, but opening with it is likely to close down the conversation.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ethan, 14, attends a clinic with his mother. The nurse wants to complete a psychosocial assessment. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask Ethan to fill in a questionnaire and pass it to his mother to check
See Ethan alone for part of the visit and explain confidentiality limits
See Ethan with his mother throughout so she can add any missing detail
Ask his mother to answer the questions because Ethan is still under 16
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Good adolescent practice is to see the young person on their own for part of the consultation and to explain at the start what will stay confidential and when information may need to be shared to keep them or others safe (NICE NG204 rec 1.5.2 offer young people time on their own; Doukrou and Segal 2018, HEEADSSS). This respects developing autonomy (P2.6, P3.1).

n.0: Passing his answers to his mother breaches the confidence he would expect and discourages honest answers.
n.2: Young people are less likely to disclose risks such as substance use or self-harm in front of a parent.
n.3: Young people under 16 can give their own history, and a parent may not know about many psychosocial risks.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Chloe, 10, has started to develop breast buds. Her father asks the school nurse whether this is too early and what will happen next. Which response is accurate?
o: Breast development is usually the first sign and is normal from 8 to 13
Periods usually come first, so breast buds at 10 need investigation
Periods usually start about 6 months after breast buds appear
Breast development before 12 is early and should be referred
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: In girls, the first sign of puberty is often the start of breast growth, and it is normal for puberty to begin between 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys (NHS 111 Wales, Puberty). Periods usually start about 2 years after breast development begins (NHS, Starting your periods).

n.1: Periods come later in puberty, not first.
n.2: Periods typically start around 2 years after breast development, not 6 months.
n.3: Puberty starting at 10 is within the normal range; early puberty is when signs appear before 8.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Jamal, 12, tells the school nurse he is worried because his voice has not broken and he is shorter than his friends. On talking, he says his testicles have recently got bigger. What is the best explanation?
o: Testicular enlargement is usually the first sign, so puberty has started
Voice breaking is the first sign, so puberty has not yet begun
Boys normally finish their growth spurt before any genital changes
Puberty is delayed because boys usually start by the age of 10
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: In boys the first sign of puberty is often enlargement of the testicles with thinning and reddening of the scrotal skin; the voice breaks and the growth spurt come later. Puberty normally starts between 9 and 14 in boys, average 12 (NHS 111 Wales, Puberty).

n.1: Voice change happens later in male puberty, not first.
n.2: The growth spurt in boys comes later in puberty, after genital changes begin.
n.3: The normal range for boys is 9 to 14 years, so starting at 12 is not delayed.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Sophie, aged 6, is seen in clinic. Her mother reports breast development and some pubic hair over the last few months, and Sophie has grown quickly. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange a routine recheck at the next school nurse contact
Reassure her mother that puberty can start from age 6 in girls
Advise reducing dietary fat to slow the changes
Refer to a paediatrician for assessment of early puberty
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Signs of puberty starting before the age of 8 are classed as early (precocious) puberty and need assessment by a paediatrician, as there can be an underlying cause and treatment may be needed (NHS, Early or delayed puberty). A rapid growth spurt adds to the concern.

n.0: A routine recheck would delay assessment of early puberty.
n.1: Puberty normally starts from 8 in girls, so changes at 6 are early.
n.2: Dietary change is not the management of early puberty and would delay assessment.
