Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Callum, 15, has type 1 diabetes and has been admitted twice with DKA this year. His parents say he used to manage well but now skips insulin when out with friends. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask his parents to take over all his insulin injections until he is 18
Warn Callum firmly that further admissions will lead to a safeguarding referral
Arrange for him to move to the adult diabetes service now to promote independence
Speak with Callum alone, explore what gets in the way, and plan goals with him
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Adolescence brings a drive for autonomy, peer influence and risk taking, and adherence often falls. A non-judgemental conversation alone with the young person, exploring barriers (for example embarrassment in front of friends) and agreeing realistic goals, supports self-management and health behaviour change (P2.6, P3.1).

n.0: Removing all responsibility undermines developing independence and is unlikely to be accepted by a 15-year-old.
n.1: Threats are not a therapeutic approach and may further reduce engagement.
n.2: Transition is planned gradually (NICE NG43), not used as a response to poor adherence.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: During a HEEADSSS assessment, Mia, 14, tells the nurse she has a boyfriend aged 20 who buys her alcohol and that they are having sex. She asks the nurse not to tell anyone. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep it confidential because Mia is Gillick competent and has asked
Tell Mia this must be shared to keep her safe, then inform the safeguarding lead
Advise Mia to end the relationship and record the advice in her notes
Contact Mia's boyfriend to discuss the risks of the relationship with him
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: A 14-year-old in a sexual relationship with a 20-year-old who supplies alcohol raises serious concern about sexual exploitation and is an offence. Safeguarding overrides confidentiality: the nurse should tell Mia honestly that information will be shared and why, then act through the safeguarding lead (Working Together 2026; s16LA Children Act 2004 duty to share). Two steps: recognise the risk, then share it.

n.0: Gillick competence relates to consent to treatment and does not allow risk of harm to be kept confidential.
n.2: Advice alone leaves a child at risk of exploitation without any safeguarding action.
n.3: Contacting the alleged abuser could increase risk to Mia and compromise any investigation.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ryan, 16, is admitted after a cycling accident. During a psychosocial assessment, he says that lately he feels nothing is worth it and he sometimes wishes he would not wake up. What is the nurse's most appropriate next response?
o: Move on to the safety questions and come back to his mood later
Tell Ryan you will refer him to his GP once he is discharged
Reassure Ryan that these feelings are a normal part of adolescence
Ask Ryan directly about thoughts of ending his life and any plans
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: The suicide/depression part of HEEADSSS requires a direct, sensitive question about suicidal thoughts, intent and plans when a young person expresses hopelessness; asking does not increase risk. The answer then guides urgent mental health assessment before discharge (NICE NG225 self-harm; P2.6, P3.1). Two steps: explore risk, then act.

n.0: Moving on misses a possible disclosure of suicidal thoughts.
n.1: A GP referral after discharge delays assessment of possible current risk.
n.2: Hopelessness and wishing not to wake up are warning signs and should not be normalised.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Oscar, aged 3, needs a blood test this afternoon. His mother asks when she should tell him about it so that he is least frightened. What is the best advice?
o: Tell him once he is in the treatment room so he does not worry first
Tell him a week before and read a hospital story book each night
Tell him the day before so that he has time to get used to the idea
Tell him shortly before in simple words, showing him with play
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Toddlers and young preschool children have a limited sense of time, so preparing them a long time ahead increases anxiety. Brief, honest preparation shortly before, in simple concrete language with play (for example on a teddy), suits this developmental stage (AnnexA.3.7 play; P4.3).

n.0: Waiting until he is already in the treatment room gives him no chance to prepare and leaves him frightened by the unexpected.
n.1: A week is suited to older school-age children, not a 3-year-old.
n.2: A day's notice is too long for a 3-year-old and gives time for worry to build.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Lily, aged 4, is admitted for an operation. She tells the nurse she must have been naughty because she has to stay in hospital. What is the best response?
o: Say she has done nothing wrong and the operation will help her body
Agree that she should be good so that she can go home sooner
Tell her the doctors will explain everything after the operation
Tell her hospital is where children come when they need a good rest
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Preschool children often think magically and may see illness or hospital as a punishment. The nurse should correct this directly, in simple terms, and explain the reason for the operation at her level, using play if helpful (P4.3; T2 play therapy).

n.1: Linking good behaviour to going home reinforces the idea that hospital is a punishment.
n.2: Delaying any explanation until after the operation leaves her anxious beforehand.
n.3: A vague answer leaves her belief that she is being punished unaddressed.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Aiden, aged 2, needs a nasogastric tube passed. A health play specialist is not available. Which distraction is most suited to his age?
o: Blowing and popping bubbles or watching a light-up toy
Counting backwards from 100 in his head
Guided imagery about his favourite holiday
Explaining the anatomy of the nose using a diagram
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Distraction should match developmental stage: toddlers respond to simple, sensory, attention-grabbing activities such as bubbles, light-up or musical toys and songs (AnnexA.3.8 distraction and diversion strategies).

n.1: Counting backwards from 100 is beyond a 2-year-old's ability.
n.2: Guided imagery needs abstract thinking suited to older children and adolescents.
n.3: A diagram is a preparation tool for older school-age children, not a distraction for a toddler.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Sienna, aged 5, needs a cannula. Her bed is in a four-bed bay and the treatment room is free. Where should the procedure be done, and why?
o: In the treatment room, so her bed and the playroom stay safe spaces
In the playroom, so toys are close for distraction
At her bed, so she stays in surroundings she knows
At her bed with the curtains closed, so other children are not upset
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Painful or frightening procedures are carried out in a treatment room where possible so that the child's bed and the playroom remain places where nothing painful happens. This reduces anxiety during the rest of the stay (P4.3; health play practice).

n.1: The playroom should remain free of procedures so it stays a safe place.
n.2: Doing it at her bed links her bed space with pain, which can increase fear for the rest of her stay.
n.3: Curtains do not stop her bed space becoming linked with the procedure.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Noah, aged 7, needs a cannula in about 60 minutes. He is anxious about needles. The health play specialist is on the ward. What should the nurse do first?
o: Apply a topical anaesthetic cream now and ask the play specialist to prepare him
Ask his parents to hold him firmly so the cannula can be inserted quickly
Wait until the doctor arrives and then apply a topical anaesthetic cream
Tell Noah he will not feel anything so that he stays calm
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Two steps: plan pain relief, then preparation. Topical anaesthetic (for example lidocaine-prilocaine cream, which needs about an hour) must be applied in advance to work, and preparation by the health play specialist using age-appropriate explanation and medical play reduces anxiety (P4.3; AnnexA.3.7).

n.1: Holding is a last resort, not a first-line plan for an anxious child who can be prepared.
n.2: Waiting until the doctor arrives leaves too little time for the cream to work.
n.3: Saying he will feel nothing is untrue and damages trust if he feels the procedure.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Freya, aged 6, asks the nurse whether her blood test will hurt. Which reply is most appropriate?
o: "Big girls like you don't cry, so you will be fine."
"You might feel a quick sharp pinch; squeeze my hand."
"It won't hurt if you are brave and keep nice and still."
"Don't worry about that; let's talk about something nice."
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Honest, age-appropriate language about what will be felt, with a coping strategy such as squeezing a hand, maintains trust and helps the child cope. False reassurance or shaming undermines trust and future cooperation (AnnexA.3.7; P4.3).

n.0: Shaming her for possible tears increases distress and is not therapeutic.
n.2: Promising no pain is untrue and links pain with not being brave.
n.3: Avoiding the question leaves her worried and does not help her cope.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Daniel, 13, is to have planned spinal surgery next month. Which approach to preparation best suits his stage of development?
o: Give detailed information, invite his questions and involve him in decisions
Speak mainly with his parents and let them decide how much to tell him
Prepare him on the morning of surgery to avoid weeks of worry
Use doll play to act out the operation with him and his younger sister
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Adolescents can think abstractly and want detailed, honest information, privacy and a say in decisions about their care. Preparation well ahead, with time for questions (and a pre-admission visit if available), supports autonomy and reduces anxiety (P4.3; T2 play therapy and preparation).

n.1: Excluding a 13-year-old from information about his own surgery ignores his developing autonomy.
n.2: A last-minute explanation suits toddlers, not an adolescent facing major planned surgery.
n.3: Doll play suits younger children and may feel patronising to an adolescent.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ruby, aged 4, is very distressed and fighting as the nurse prepares to take a routine blood sample for a non-urgent test. Her father is upset. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Take the sample later while she is asleep so she is not aware of it
Stop, let her calm, then re-prepare with play and plan with her father
Ask two colleagues to hold her still so the sample is taken quickly
Carry on, because stopping teaches her that crying gets results
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: For a non-urgent procedure, the child's distress is a reason to pause and re-plan: calm her, prepare again with play or a play specialist, use distraction and agree a plan with the parent. Clinical holding should be a planned last resort for necessary procedures, not a response to distress (RCN guidance on clinical holding; P4.3).

n.0: Doing it while she is asleep without her knowledge breaks trust and is not good practice for a planned test.
n.2: Restraining a child for a non-urgent test is not justified and can cause lasting fear of procedures.
n.3: Continuing against distress for a non-urgent test causes harm and damages trust.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Mila, aged 2, has been admitted for nasogastric feeding. Her mother, Joanna, says she would like to give the feeds herself while she is resident. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that feeds are a nursing task and parents cannot give them on the ward
Let Joanna give the feeds from now on, since she is Mila's mother
Agree, teach and check Joanna's skills, and record what she has agreed to do
Agree, with a nurse giving each feed alongside her for the whole of her stay
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Family-centred care is based on partnership and negotiation: parents choose how far they take part, and the nurse supports this by teaching, checking competence and agreeing and documenting each person's role (negotiated care). The nurse stays accountable for the care plan (P3.4, P4.2).

n.0: Excluding a willing parent from care she could safely learn goes against partnership with families.
n.1: Agreeing without teaching or checking competence risks harm, such as giving a feed through a misplaced tube.
n.3: Requiring a nurse at every feed regardless of competence is not negotiated care and does not build her confidence for home.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Aaron, aged 5, has been in hospital for a week. His father has stayed every night and tells the nurse he feels he has to do all Aaron's care or the nurses will think he is a bad parent. What is the best response?
o: Reassure him he can choose how much care he gives and nurses will share it
Advise him to go home each night so that he is less tired in the day
Tell him that resident parents are expected to give all the basic care
Suggest he cuts down his visits so Aaron learns to settle with the staff
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: In family-centred care, parents' participation is negotiated and voluntary; they should not feel pressured to take on care. Acknowledging his feelings and agreeing what he wants to do, with nurses sharing care and offering breaks, supports both parent and child (P3.4, P4.2).

n.1: Telling him to go home removes his choice and may increase Aaron's distress.
n.2: There is no expectation that resident parents do all care; this adds pressure and is incorrect.
n.3: Reducing parental presence is not the aim and can increase a young child's separation distress.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Bilal, aged 3, is admitted with pneumonia. His mother speaks little English. His 11-year-old sister offers to interpret while the nurse takes a history. What should the nurse do?
o: Use simple English and gestures to complete the history
Ask a bilingual cleaner from the ward to interpret
Accept the sister's offer, because she knows the family best
Thank the sister and arrange a professional interpreter
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Children should not be used to interpret: it places an inappropriate burden on them and risks inaccurate or filtered information. A professional interpreter (face to face, telephone or video) ensures accurate, confidential communication with the family (P3.4; NHS England guidance on interpreting).

n.0: Simple English and gestures are not enough for an accurate clinical history.
n.1: An untrained member of staff may interpret inaccurately and the family's confidentiality is not protected.
n.2: Using a child as an interpreter is inappropriate and risks errors and distress for the child.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Evie, aged 7, has been diagnosed with leukaemia. Her parents tell the nurse that her brother Sam, 5, has started wetting the bed and asking whether he will get ill too. Which nursing response best reflects family-centred care?
o: Include Sam, with honest age-appropriate information and play support
Advise the parents to keep Sam away from the ward to protect him from worry
Suggest the parents wait until Sam is older before talking about Evie's illness
Refer Sam to his GP for investigation of the new bed wetting
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Family-centred care recognises that a child's illness affects the whole family, including siblings, who may feel anxious, jealous or responsible. Honest, age-appropriate information, involvement in visits and play specialist support help siblings cope (P3.4, P4.2).

n.1: Excluding Sam is likely to increase his anxiety and fantasies about the illness.
n.2: Delaying explanation leaves a worried child without support at a time of change.
n.3: New bed wetting here is a likely response to family stress; a medical referral alone misses his emotional needs.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Amina, 14, is admitted for investigations. Her parents ask that, where possible, only female staff carry out intimate examinations, for religious and cultural reasons. Amina agrees. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask Amina's parents to bring a female relative to be present instead
Record the preference and plan female staff where possible, explaining limits
Agree, and record that the request stands even if Amina later disagrees
Explain that staff are allocated by skill mix so requests cannot be met
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Respecting family cultures and beliefs is part of family-centred, person-centred care (P3.4; T2 family cultures). Reasonable requests for same-gender care should be recorded and met where possible, explaining honestly when it cannot be guaranteed (for example in an emergency), and checking the young person's own wishes.

n.0: A relative being present does not meet the request for female clinical staff and shifts responsibility to the family.
n.2: The young person's own wishes must be checked and respected; recording that her later view will not count overrides a 14-year-old's voice.
n.3: Refusing outright fails to respect the family's beliefs when the request can often be met.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Jack, aged 4, is admitted with two adults who introduce themselves as his mums. The admission form has fields for 'mother' and 'father'. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask which of them is the biological mother before continuing
Record the second adult as a family friend until legal papers are seen
Ask them how they would like to be named and record both as parents
Record one adult as mother and leave the father field blank
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Family-centred care respects the diversity of family structures and avoids assumptions. The nurse should ask how the family describes itself and record both parents, using their preferred terms, while confirming parental responsibility through the usual process if consent issues arise (P3.4; T2 family cultures).

n.0: Asking about biology is intrusive and not needed to care for Jack.
n.1: Labelling a parent as a friend is disrespectful and inaccurate.
n.3: Leaving one parent off the record is inaccurate and excludes her from her child's care.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Leah, aged 9, with complex epilepsy, is ready for discharge after a long admission. Her parents care for her and two younger children at home. Which discharge plan best reflects family-centred care?
o: Arrange for community nurses to do all of Leah's care so the parents can rest
Discharge once Leah's seizures are controlled and review her in clinic
Plan early with the parents, teach skills, and consider home, siblings, school
Give the parents a written medicine list and leaflets on the day of discharge
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Family-centred discharge planning starts early in partnership with the family, builds parents' skills and confidence, and takes account of the whole family's circumstances, including siblings, home routines and school (P4.2, P3.4).

n.0: Taking over all care is not what the family has asked for and does not support them to care for Leah.
n.1: Discharge based on seizure control alone misses the family's wider needs and readiness.
n.3: A list on the day gives no time to build skills or address family circumstances.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Zara, aged 6, is admitted for a week. Her parents work shifts and say they cannot stay overnight. A nurse comments that 'good parents stay with their child'. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse in charge?
o: Agree, and ask the parents to arrange for a relative to stay instead
Report the parents to the safeguarding team for leaving Zara overnight
Support the parents' choice and agree how they will stay in contact with Zara
Ask the parents to sign a form saying they have declined to stay
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Family-centred care respects that families have different circumstances and pressures; parents should not be judged for being unable to stay. The nurse in charge should challenge the judgemental comment, support the parents' choice and agree a plan for contact and updates (P3.4, P4.2; Code 1 and 20).

n.0: Pressuring the family to find a relative to stay reinforces the judgement and ignores their choice.
n.1: Being unable to stay overnight in hospital is not, on these facts, a safeguarding concern.
n.3: A declination form implies wrongdoing and damages the partnership.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Priya is 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She asks the practice nurse when she will first meet a health visitor under the Healthy Child Programme in England. What is the correct answer?
o: At the new baby review about 10 to 14 days after the birth
At an antenatal review from 28 weeks of pregnancy
At the 6 to 8 week review, alongside the baby's physical examination
At the 12-month review, when development is first checked
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: The Healthy Child Programme in England has five mandated health visitor reviews: antenatal (from 28 weeks), new birth, 6 to 8 weeks, 12 months (9 to 15 months) and 2 to 2.5 years. Health visitors first make contact in pregnancy, around 28 weeks, through an antenatal review, ideally face to face at home (DHSC/OHID, Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme, Part 2, Feb 2026).

n.0: The new baby review is the second mandated contact, not the first.
n.2: The 6 to 8 week review comes later, after the antenatal and new birth reviews.
n.3: The 12-month review is the fourth mandated contact.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: A new father asks the health visitor what the 'red book' he has been given is for. Which explanation is correct?
o: A booklet of feeding advice for parents that professionals do not use
The hospital's copy of the birth notes, which is returned after 6 weeks
The parent-held child health record of growth, vaccines and development
The GP practice's record of the baby's illnesses and prescriptions
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: The red book is the personal child health record (PCHR), held by parents and used by health visitors, GPs and others to record growth, vaccinations and development; parents can add information and should take it to every appointment (NHS, baby reviews; NICE NG75 rec 1.2.5).

n.0: Professionals write in it at each review; it is more than an advice booklet.
n.1: It is not the hospital's maternity record and is not returned.
n.3: It is held by parents, not kept as the GP's clinical record.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Before Leo's 2 to 2.5 year review, the health visiting team sends his parents a questionnaire about his communication, motor, problem-solving and personal-social skills. What is this tool?
o: The Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3)
The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ)
The Schedule of Growing Skills (SGS II)
The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Parents are sent the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3) to complete before the 9 to 12 month and 2 to 2.5 year reviews (NHS, baby reviews; Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme 2026 also names ASQ for the 12-month and 2 to 2.5 year reviews).

n.1: The SDQ is a behavioural screening questionnaire for older children, not the standard tool at these reviews.
n.2: The SGS II is a professional-administered developmental assessment, not the parent questionnaire sent before reviews.
n.3: The Edinburgh scale screens parents for postnatal depression, not child development.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: At Ella's 6 to 8 week check, her mother asks what the doctor will examine. Which answer is correct?
o: A heel prick blood test for rare inherited conditions
Hearing, which is screened for the first time at this check
Speech and language, using a structured questionnaire
Eyes, heart and hips, plus weight, length and head size
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: The 6 to 8 week physical examination (usually by a GP) checks the eyes, heart, hips and, in boys, testicles, and measures weight, length and head circumference; the parent is also asked about her own physical and emotional health (NHS, baby reviews).

n.0: The blood spot test is done at 5 to 8 days old, usually by the midwife on day 5.
n.1: The newborn hearing screen is done soon after birth, usually before this check.
n.2: Structured language questionnaires (ASQ-3) are used at the 1 and 2 year reviews, not at 6 to 8 weeks.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: A health visitor is planning the new birth review for baby Theo, born 5 days ago. Which approach best meets the Healthy Child Programme expectations?
o: A telephone call from the named health visitor within 6 weeks
A clinic appointment with any available team member at 4 weeks
A group session at the children's centre at 6 to 8 weeks
A home visit by the named health visitor within the first 2 weeks
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: The new birth review takes place in the first 2 weeks (usually 10 to 14 days). The antenatal, new birth and 6 to 8 week reviews should be delivered face to face in the home by a health visitor, and named health visitors should deliver the statutory reviews (Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme, Part 2, 2026; NHS, baby reviews).

n.0: A telephone call does not meet the face-to-face home expectation, and 6 weeks is too late for this review.
n.1: A clinic appointment at 4 weeks is outside the timing and setting for the new birth review.
n.2: A group session at 6 to 8 weeks is not the individual new birth review.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: At a 6 to 8 week review, Kezia's mother says she has felt low and tearful most days for the past month and no longer enjoys things. Her baby is feeding and growing well. What should the health visitor do?
o: Advise her to rest more and ask her partner to do night feeds
Focus the review on the baby and suggest she mentions it to her GP if it continues
Reassure her that 'baby blues' are common and usually settle by 6 months
Explore her mood further, assess risk and arrange prompt assessment
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Health visitors should routinely enquire about parents' physical and mental health at postnatal reviews (Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme 2026, using the NICE antenatal and postnatal mental health approach). Low mood and loss of interest for a month go beyond baby blues (which settle within about 2 weeks) and suggest possible postnatal depression, so further assessment, including risk, and prompt referral are needed (P2.6: early years and parental wellbeing).

n.0: Practical advice alone does not assess or treat possible depression.
n.1: Parental mental health is part of the review and affects the baby's development, so it should be addressed now.
n.2: Baby blues settle within the first couple of weeks; symptoms for a month need assessment, not reassurance.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: A school nurse explains the National Child Measurement Programme to parents at a primary school in England. Which statement is accurate?
o: Children's height and weight are measured in Reception and Year 6
Children who appear overweight are measured again in Year 3
Children are weighed every year from Reception to Year 6
Measurements are taken at the 2 to 2.5 year health visitor review
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: The National Child Measurement Programme measures the height and weight of children in Reception (age 4 to 5) and Year 6 (age 10 to 11) in state-maintained schools in England, to monitor trends in childhood weight and support families (school nursing, Healthy Child Programme 5 to 19; P2.1 health promotion).

n.1: All eligible children in Reception and Year 6 are offered measurement; there is no selective Year 3 measurement.
n.2: Children are not measured every year; it is done at two points.
n.3: The 2 to 2.5 year review is a health visiting contact, not part of the school programme.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: At Mason's 12-month review, his mother has not returned the ASQ-3 because she finds reading English difficult. She has missed the last review. Mason appears well. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the questionnaire as declined and close the 12-month review
Use an interpreter and go through the questionnaire with her at the review
Ask his mother to post the completed form back before next year's review
Assume normal development because Mason looks well and is walking
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Two steps: identify the barrier, then adapt. The review should be completed with the parent's help, using an interpreter where needed, as health visitors are expected to help parents complete the ASQ; missed contacts and barriers to engagement need follow-up to reduce health inequalities and safeguard the child (P2.5: reducing inequalities; NHS, baby reviews).

n.0: A language barrier is not a refusal, and closing the review leaves the child unassessed.
n.2: Waiting a year with no support repeats the barrier and misses development checks.
n.3: Looking well and walking does not assess communication, problem solving or social skills.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Sofia, aged 8 weeks, attends for her first routine immunisations in England in October 2026. Which vaccines should she be offered at this appointment?
o: 6-in-1, rotavirus and BCG
6-in-1, PCV and rotavirus
6-in-1, MenB and rotavirus
6-in-1, MenB and PCV
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: UKHSA routine schedule (from 1 September 2026): at 8 weeks, DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB (6-in-1) and MenB into the thigh, plus oral rotavirus vaccine. PCV is now given at 16 weeks and 1 year.

n.0: BCG is a selective vaccine for at-risk infants within 28 days of birth, not a routine 8-week vaccine.
n.1: PCV is not given at 8 weeks in the current schedule; the first dose is at 16 weeks.
n.3: PCV is given at 16 weeks, and rotavirus is due at 8 weeks.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ali, aged 16 weeks, attends for his third set of routine immunisations. His mother asks which injections he will have today. What is correct under the current UK schedule?
o: MenB and PCV
6-in-1 and PCV
6-in-1 and MenB
6-in-1, MenB and PCV
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: UKHSA routine schedule (from 1 September 2026): at 16 weeks, the third 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) and PCV (Prevenar 13). The second MenB dose is given at 12 weeks, alongside the second 6-in-1 and rotavirus.

n.0: This omits the third dose of the 6-in-1 vaccine due at 16 weeks.
n.2: MenB is not due at 16 weeks, and the PCV dose would be missed.
n.3: MenB is given at 8 and 12 weeks with a booster at 1 year, not at 16 weeks.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Jacob has his first birthday next week. His father asks which vaccines are due at his 1-year appointment. Which answer is correct?
o: Hib/MenC, PCV booster and MMR
PCV booster, MenACWY and MMR
PCV booster, MenB booster and MMRV
MenB booster, Hib/MenC and MMRV
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: UKHSA routine schedule (from 1 September 2026): on or after the first birthday, PCV booster, MenB booster and MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella and varicella). The Hib/MenC vaccine is no longer part of the 1-year appointment.

n.0: Hib/MenC has been removed and MMR has been replaced by MMRV at 1 year.
n.1: MenACWY is given at 14 years (Year 9), and MMRV has replaced MMR.
n.3: Hib/MenC is no longer given at 1 year, and the PCV booster would be missed.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: A nurse is giving Hana, aged 12 weeks, her routine injections. Which site should be used for the intramuscular vaccines?
o: The ventrogluteal site of the hip
The deltoid muscle of the upper arm
The anterolateral aspect of the thigh
The dorsogluteal muscle of the buttock
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: The UKHSA schedule lists the thigh as the usual site for the 8, 12 and 16 week injections; intramuscular vaccines go into the anterolateral thigh in infants, with the deltoid or thigh used from 1 year.

n.0: The ventrogluteal site is not a recommended site for routine infant vaccines.
n.1: The deltoid is too small in young infants; the upper arm is used from around 1 year.
n.3: The buttock is not recommended for vaccines because of fat depth and sciatic nerve risk.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ellie, aged 8 weeks, is due her first immunisations. The nurse notices that the record of her newborn screening for severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is not available. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the injections and check the SCID result before rotavirus
Give all three vaccines today because SCID is very rare
Delay all three vaccines until the screening result is found
Give the oral rotavirus vaccine and delay the two injections
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Rotavirus vaccine is live, and the UKHSA schedule states it should only be given after checking the SCID screening result (the same applies to BCG). The inactivated injected vaccines can still be given on time. Two steps: identify which vaccine is live, then act.

n.1: The schedule requires the SCID result to be checked before the live rotavirus vaccine, however rare the condition.
n.2: The inactivated injections are safe and should not be delayed.
n.3: Oral administration does not make it safe; rotavirus is the live vaccine that needs the SCID check, and the injections should not be delayed.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ava, aged 4, is receiving chemotherapy for leukaemia and is severely immunosuppressed. Her parents ask about her annual flu vaccine. What is the correct advice?
o: Give inactivated flu vaccine by injection, because the nasal vaccine is live
Give the nasal vaccine but delay it until her blood counts recover
Avoid any flu vaccine until chemotherapy has finished
Give the nasal live vaccine as usual, as it is the routine childhood product
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: The childhood flu programme uses live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV, nasal). The UKHSA schedule states that if LAIV is contraindicated or otherwise unsuitable, inactivated flu vaccine is used; live vaccines are contraindicated in severe immunosuppression (P2.11; T2 pathogenesis and immunology).

n.1: LAIV remains contraindicated while she is severely immunosuppressed on treatment.
n.2: Children in clinical risk groups need flu protection; the inactivated vaccine can be given.
n.3: A live vaccine can cause disease in a severely immunosuppressed child.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Grace, aged 18 months, was born in September 2024. Her mother asks why her older son, born in March 2024, did not have an appointment at this age. What is the correct explanation?
o: It is a catch-up appointment for children who missed the 1-year vaccines
Children born from 1 July 2024 are given a BCG vaccine at the 18-month visit
Children born from 1 July 2024 get a 4th 6-in-1 and 2nd MMRV at 18 months
It is an appointment to give the HPV vaccine early to girls born after July 2024
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: UKHSA routine schedule (from 1 September 2026): children born on or after 1 July 2024 are offered a fourth 6-in-1 (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB) and a second MMRV at 18 months; those born on or before 30 June 2024 have no 18-month appointment.

n.0: It is a routine appointment for a whole birth cohort, not a catch-up for missed vaccines.
n.1: BCG is a selective vaccine given within 28 days of birth to at-risk infants.
n.3: HPV is given at 12 to 13 years to boys and girls, not at 18 months.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Oliver, aged 14 and in Year 9, attends the school immunisation session. The school nurse checks his record and finds he has had only one dose of MMR. Which vaccines should he receive?
o: Td/IPV now, with MenACWY delayed until he reaches 17
HPV and a MenB booster, with no change to his MMR plan
Td/IPV and MenACWY, and arrange his second MMR dose
Td/IPV and MenACWY, and restart the MMR course from the beginning
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: UKHSA schedule: at 14 years (Year 9), Td/IPV and MenACWY are given and MMR status is checked. Two steps: give the due vaccines, then catch up the missing second MMR dose; doses already given do not need repeating.

n.0: MenACWY is due in Year 9 at around 14, so delaying it to 17 is wrong; his MMR also needs completing.
n.1: HPV is due at 12 to 13 years and MenB is not given in Year 9; the incomplete MMR also needs action.
n.3: A documented first MMR dose counts; only the missing second dose is needed.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Ayesha brings her son Zain, aged 9 months, to a health visitor review. She is worried because Zain picks up small pieces of food with his whole hand in a raking movement and cannot yet pick up a raisin between his thumb and index finger. He sits without support and babbles. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer Zain to a paediatrician for assessment of delayed fine motor development
Arrange a hearing test because fine motor delay often accompanies hearing loss
Explain that a raking grasp is expected now and a pincer grip follows
Advise Ayesha to stop finger foods until Zain develops a pincer grip
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Fine motor skills develop in sequence: a palmar or raking grasp comes first and a fine pincer grip (thumb and index finger) typically appears around 12 months (CDC 2022 milestones list a raking grasp at 9 months and the pincer grip at 1 year). Zain is following the expected sequence, so reassurance and explanation is appropriate (P3.1: applying knowledge of human development).

n.0: Referral is not indicated: a raking grasp at 9 months is within the expected sequence, so there is no delay to assess.
n.1: There is no hearing concern: Zain babbles, and fine motor skills are not used to screen hearing.
n.3: Finger foods help develop grasp and self-feeding; stopping them would remove practice and is not advised.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: A student nurse on a children's ward asks about the order in which gross motor skills usually develop in the first 18 months. Which sequence is correct?
o: Holds head up, sits without support, pulls to stand, walks independently
Sits without support, holds head up, cruises around furniture, walks independently
Rolls over, cruises around furniture, sits without support, walks independently
Holds head up, pulls to stand, sits without support, walks independently
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: Gross motor development proceeds head to toe (cephalocaudal): head control (around 2 months), sitting without support (around 9 months), pulling to stand and cruising (around 12 months), then walking independently (by 18 months) (CDC 2022 milestones; T2 child development).

n.1: Head control is the first gross motor milestone and comes before sitting.
n.2: Cruising needs trunk control from sitting, so it comes after, not before, independent sitting.
n.3: Pulling to stand requires the trunk control gained from sitting, so sitting comes first.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Grace was born at 30 weeks' gestation and is now 6 months old by her date of birth. Her mother is upset that Grace cannot sit yet when her friend's baby of the same age can. How should the nurse assess Grace's development?
o: Use her corrected age, about 3.5 months, until she is 2 years old
Use her corrected age until she is 6 months old, then use her actual age
Use her age from birth until she starts school, then switch to corrected age
Use her actual age of 6 months because prematurity has no effect on milestones
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: For babies born prematurely, developmental age is calculated from the original due date (corrected age) until the child is 2 years old (NHS, baby health and development reviews). Grace was born 10 weeks early, so at 6 months she has a corrected age of about 3.5 months, when independent sitting is not yet expected.

n.1: Correction does not stop at 6 months; it continues until 2 years of age.
n.2: Corrected age is used up to 2 years, not until school entry, and should be used now rather than later.
n.3: Prematurity does affect expected milestones, which is why correction is used for the first 2 years.

Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.q: Tom, aged 18 months, attends clinic with his father. He walks independently, scribbles with a crayon, points to show things he wants and uses about five single words. His father asks whether Tom should be joining words together yet. What is the best reply?
o: He should be speaking in short sentences of three or four words by now
Two-word phrases usually appear around 2 years, so his speech is on track
Single words are expected by 2 years, so he is ahead of his age
Two-word phrases usually appear by 12 months, so he needs a speech referral
Growth, Development and Family-Centred C.w: At 18 months children typically use several single words and follow simple instructions; combining two words ('more milk') is expected around 2 years (CDC 2022 milestones). Tom's language and other skills fit his age, so the nurse can reassure his father and explain what to expect next.

n.0: Three- to four-word sentences belong to around 3 years, not 18 months.
n.2: Single words are expected well before 2 years (around 12 to 18 months), so Tom is on track rather than ahead.
n.3: Two-word phrases are not expected at 12 months, when a child typically says 'mama' or 'dada'.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ruby, aged 4, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days. She is quiet. Heart rate is 165 beats/min, capillary refill time 4 seconds, and blood pressure 100/60 mmHg. A student says the normal blood pressure is reassuring. What is the best response?
o: Disagree, because low blood pressure is a late sign in children
Agree, because a normal blood pressure shows her circulation is coping
Disagree, because her breathing rate is a better guide than her pulse
Agree, but ask for the blood pressure to be rechecked in an hour
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Children compensate for circulatory failure with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, so blood pressure stays normal until late; hypotension signals decompensation and risk of arrest (RCUK 2025 Table 2). Tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill already indicate compensated shock needing urgent escalation.

n.1: Blood pressure is maintained in compensated shock, so a normal reading does not rule it out.
n.2: Breathing rate matters, but here her heart rate and capillary refill show compensated shock; no single sign outranks the others.
n.3: Waiting an hour delays treatment of compensated shock.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ali, 7 months, has bronchiolitis and is on oxygen. His saturations have been 91 to 92%. He becomes quiet and floppy; his heart rate falls from 170 to 55 beats/min and he has poor perfusion despite effective bag-mask ventilation by the team. What should happen next?
o: Start chest compressions
Recheck the heart rate in 5 minutes
Give a fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg
Increase the oxygen and observe
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Two steps: recognise that bradycardia in a hypoxic infant is pre-terminal, then act. RCUK 2025: start chest compressions if the heart rate is below 60 beats/min with poor perfusion despite adequate ventilation.

n.1: Waiting 5 minutes in a pre-arrest state risks cardiac arrest.
n.2: Fluids do not treat hypoxic bradycardia; compressions are needed when HR is below 60 with poor perfusion despite ventilation.
n.3: Oxygen and ventilation are already being given; the criteria for compressions are met.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ella, aged 1 month, is admitted with poor feeding. Her respiratory rate is 72 breaths/min and heart rate 150 beats/min. She is not crying. Which interpretation is correct?
o: Her heart rate is within range and her breathing is rapid
Her heart rate is raised and her breathing is normal
Both values are within normal limits for a 1-month-old
Both values are raised and she needs immediate review
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: RCUK 2025 (Table 1): at 1 month, the approximate normal respiratory rate is 25 to 60 breaths/min and heart rate 110 to 180 beats/min. A respiratory rate of 72 is above range (tachypnoea), while a heart rate of 150 is within range and below the NICE NG143 amber threshold of 160 for infants under 12 months.

n.1: A heart rate of 150 is within the 110 to 180 range at 1 month, and it is the breathing rate that is raised.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 72 is above the upper limit of 60 at 1 month.
n.3: A heart rate of 150 is within range at 1 month; the abnormal value is the respiratory rate.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Tia, aged 3, is critically unwell with pneumonia and receiving oxygen through a face mask. Her saturations are 100%. What saturation target should the nurse aim for?
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: RCUK 2025 paediatric guidance: target SpO2 of 94 to 98% in critical illness and after return of spontaneous circulation, avoiding both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia. Oxygen should be titrated down to keep within this range.

n.0: Aiming for 100% risks hyperoxaemia; oxygen should be titrated to 94 to 98%.
n.1: 92 to 96% is not the RCUK paediatric target and allows lower saturations than advised.
n.2: 88 to 92% is a target for adults at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, not for a critically ill child.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Freddie, aged 4 months, is found unresponsive in his cot and breathing noisily. The nurse calls for help and opens his airway. How should his head be positioned?
o: Turned to one side, with the neck extended over a pillow
In the neutral position, with the head level and face parallel to the bed
Flexed forward slightly, with the chin resting down towards the chest
Fully extended, with the head tilted back as far as it will go
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Infants have a large occiput and a short neck, and the soft trachea is easily compressed by over-extension. RCUK paediatric life support: open an infant's airway with the head in the neutral position and chin lift; children need a slightly more extended 'sniffing' position (T2 physiological differences; AnnexB.2.7).

n.0: Turning and extending over a pillow does not open the airway and over-extends the neck.
n.2: Flexion pushes the chin to the chest and obstructs the airway, which the large occiput already tends to do.
n.3: Over-extension kinks the soft infant trachea and can obstruct the airway.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Sami, aged 18 months, is carried into the children's assessment unit by his mother. Before touching him, the nurse looks at him from the doorway. Which features make up this rapid first look?
o: Pupils, posture and capillary refill
Behaviour, breathing and body colour
Weight, hydration and urine output
Temperature, heart rate and blood glucose
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: RCUK 2025 recommends a quick look using BBB (Behaviour, Breathing, Body colour) or the Paediatric Assessment Triangle to judge whether a child is seriously ill before hands-on ABCDE assessment. It can be done without upsetting the child (T2 ABCDE).

n.0: Pupils and capillary refill require examination, which follows the quick look.
n.2: Weight and urine output are not part of the immediate visual assessment.
n.3: These need hands-on measurement and come during the ABCDE assessment, not the doorway look.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Isla, aged 6 weeks, has a cold. Her parents say she becomes distressed and pulls away during feeds, and her nose is blocked. Her saturations are 97% and she is alert. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Clear her nose gently with saline drops before feeds
Advise the parents to lie her flat during feeds
Suggest the parents stop feeds until her nose clears
Offer feeds by spoon until her cold has fully resolved
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Young infants breathe preferentially through the nose, so nasal blockage makes feeding difficult as they cannot breathe while sucking. Gentle nasal clearing (for example saline drops) before feeds helps, while monitoring intake and signs of increasing respiratory distress (T2 physiological differences; NICE NG9 for bronchiolitis feeding support).

n.1: Lying her flat worsens nasal congestion and feeding difficulty.
n.2: Stopping feeds risks dehydration and is not needed in an alert baby with good saturations.
n.3: Spoon feeding a 6-week-old is inappropriate and does not address nasal obstruction.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: A nurse is assessing the circulation of Ava, aged 3, during an ABCDE assessment. How should central capillary refill time be measured and interpreted?
o: Press on the forehead for 10 seconds; normal is under 4 seconds
Press on the sternum for 5 seconds; normal is 2 seconds or less
Press on the sole of the foot for 5 seconds; normal is 3 seconds or less
Press on a fingertip for 2 seconds; normal is under 5 seconds
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Central capillary refill is measured by pressing on the sternum for 5 seconds and timing the return of colour; 2 seconds or less is normal, and 3 seconds or more is an amber sign in NICE NG143 (AnnexB.2.8: circulatory assessment).

n.0: The forehead is not the recommended site, and 4 seconds would be abnormal.
n.2: A peripheral site is affected by temperature; 3 seconds or more is abnormal (NG143 amber).
n.3: Two seconds of pressure is too short, and under 5 seconds is far too long a normal limit.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Daniel, aged 7, has acute asthma. An hour ago he had marked recession and a respiratory rate of 40. Now his recession is less obvious, his respiratory rate is 18, he is drowsy and SpO2 is 87% in oxygen. What is the most likely explanation?
o: His asthma is improving, as his work of breathing has reduced
He has a normal rate for his age, so treatment can be reduced
He is falling asleep, which shows his anxiety has settled
He is tiring and decompensating, so an emergency call is needed
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Decreasing work of breathing with bradypnoea, falling consciousness and SpO2 below 90% are signs of decompensated respiratory failure (RCUK 2025 Table 2). Exhaustion can look like improvement; this child is at risk of arrest and needs an emergency response.

n.0: Less recession here reflects exhaustion, not improvement, given his drowsiness and falling saturations.
n.1: A rate of 18 after 40, with drowsiness and SpO2 of 87%, is bradypnoea from exhaustion, not a normal finding.
n.2: Drowsiness with hypoxaemia is a sign of hypercapnia and exhaustion, not relaxation.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Leah, aged 2, has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days and is now drowsy, responding only to voice. Airway and breathing are satisfactory, and fluids are being started for poor perfusion. What should the nurse check next under D?
o: Her temperature
Her weight
Her blood glucose
Her serum sodium
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Under D (disability), assess conscious level (AVPU), pupils and posture, and check blood glucose: young children have limited glycogen stores and become hypoglycaemic quickly when unwell (RCUK 2025; T2 physiological differences). Hypoglycaemia is a treatable cause of reduced consciousness.

n.0: Temperature belongs to E (exposure), after D.
n.1: Weight is needed for dosing but does not assess her reduced consciousness.
n.3: Sodium matters with fluid therapy, but a bedside glucose is the immediate D check for drowsiness.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: During the E (exposure) part of an ABCDE assessment of Kai, a 5-month-old with suspected sepsis, what should the nurse do?
o: Leave him uncovered so that the rash can be monitored
Bathe him in tepid water to cool him
Delay exposure until his temperature has been measured
Examine him in stages and keep him covered and warm
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Infants have a large surface area to weight ratio and lose heat quickly, so the whole body (including skin for rashes and injuries) should be examined while preventing heat loss, uncovering in stages and covering again (T2 physiological differences; RCUK ABCDE).

n.0: Leaving an infant uncovered risks hypothermia, which worsens outcomes in sepsis.
n.1: Tepid sponging is not recommended (NICE NG143) and risks cooling a sick infant.
n.2: Exposure is needed to find rashes or injuries; measuring temperature does not replace examining the skin.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ellie, aged 3 months, is admitted with bronchiolitis. The nurse hears a short noise at the end of each breath out and sees her nostrils flaring. What does the noise most likely indicate?
o: Normal breathing sounds in a young infant
Wheeze, a sign that the illness is improving
Grunting, a sign of severe respiratory distress
Stridor from narrowing of the upper airway
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Grunting is a noise on expiration as the infant breathes out against a partly closed glottis to keep alveoli open; it signals severe respiratory distress (NICE NG9 and NG143 list grunting as a red feature; RCUK 2025 Table 2). Escalate urgently.

n.0: Grunting is not a normal infant sound and indicates significant distress.
n.1: Wheeze is a musical sound on expiration and does not mean improvement.
n.3: Stridor is a harsh sound mainly on breathing in, from upper airway narrowing.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Jacob, aged 13, is admitted to a general children's ward in England that uses the national PEWS charts. Which chart should the nurse use for his observations?
o: The 5 to 12 years chart, because he is on a children's ward
The 13 years and over chart
The chart chosen by the nurse in charge for his size
The adult NEWS2 chart, because he is over 12
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: The national PEWS (NHS England, RCPCH and RCN, November 2023) has four age-band charts: 0 to 11 months, 1 to 4 years, 5 to 12 years, and 13 years and over. A 13-year-old on a children's ward uses the 13 years and over chart.

n.0: The 5 to 12 years chart ends at 12; Jacob is 13.
n.2: Chart choice is set by age band, not by individual judgement of size.
n.3: NEWS2 is for adults; children's wards use PEWS, which has a chart for 13 and over.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Mia, aged 3, has a temperature of 39.2°C, heart rate 120, respiratory rate 28 and SpO2 97% in air. A student asks how the temperature affects her national PEWS score. What is correct?
o: Temperature adds 2 points because it is above 39°C
Temperature doubles the score for heart rate
Temperature adds 1 point because it is above 38°C
Temperature is recorded but does not add to the score
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: On the national PEWS charts, heart rate, respiratory rate, respiratory distress, systolic blood pressure, SpO2, oxygen delivery and capillary refill time are scored. Temperature, AVPU and pain are recorded but not scored, although fever with other signs should prompt the nurse to think about sepsis (FACTS 4.2).

n.0: Temperature does not score points on the national PEWS.
n.1: No parameter multiplies another on PEWS; temperature is unscored.
n.2: There is no point for fever on the national PEWS score.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Noah, aged 2, has a PEWS of 2. When the nurse asks the carer question, his father says, 'He's worse; he's not himself and won't look at me.' How should the nurse respond?
o: Recheck the observations in 4 hours as set out in his current care plan
Reassure his father, as the PEWS score of 2 is reassuringly low
Escalate for medical review, as carer concern is a separate trigger
Document the father's comment and continue with routine care
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: The national PEWS escalation uses the highest level reached by any one criterion: the score, AVPU, clinical intuition or the carer question. Carer words suggesting the child needs a clinical review trigger escalation for medical review irrespective of the PEWS (national PEWS charts; Martha's Rule principle that families notice change first).

n.0: Waiting 4 hours ignores a trigger that calls for review now.
n.1: A low score does not override parental concern, which is a separate trigger on the chart.
n.3: Recording the comment without acting fails to respond to an escalation trigger.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Harvey, aged 6, scores a PEWS of 6 on the national chart. There are no other triggers. What response does the chart require?
o: Call for a Rapid Review within 15 minutes with observations every 30 minutes
Make an immediate 2222 call stating a Paediatric Medical Emergency
NIC review, ST3+ medical review within 30 minutes, reassess within 30 minutes
Inform the nurse in charge, consider medical review, and reassess within 60 minutes
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: National PEWS: a score of 5 to 8 is the Medium escalation level, requiring review by the nurse in charge, a request for ST3+ (or equivalent) medical review within 30 minutes and reassessment within 30 minutes (FACTS 4.2; national PEWS charts, all age bands).

n.0: A Rapid Review within 15 minutes is the High response for a score of 9 to 12.
n.1: A 2222 call is the Emergency response for a score of 13 or more or a collapse.
n.3: This is the Low response for a score of 1 to 4.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Lily, aged 8 months, with pneumonia has a PEWS of 10. She is responsive to voice. Her mother is worried. What is the required escalation?
o: Ask her mother to use the Martha's Rule number before escalating
Inform the nurse in charge and reassess within 60 minutes
Request ST3+ medical review within 30 minutes
Immediate nurse in charge review and a Rapid Review within 15 minutes
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: National PEWS: a score of 9 to 12, or a change in AVPU to V, is the High level, requiring immediate nurse in charge review and a call for a Rapid Review (airway-skilled ST3+ and outreach) within 15 minutes, with observations every 30 minutes and continuous monitoring.

n.0: Staff must escalate themselves; Martha's Rule is an extra route for families, not a step before staff escalation.
n.1: This is the Low response for a score of 1 to 4.
n.2: Review within 30 minutes is the Medium response; a score of 10 is High.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Sophie, aged 4, is on high-flow nasal oxygen for bronchiolitis. A newly qualified nurse is unsure how to score oxygen delivery on the national PEWS. What is correct?
o: High flow scores 2 because it is given by nasal cannula
High flow scores the maximum of 4 for oxygen delivery
High flow is recorded but not scored, like temperature
High flow scores 0 because the saturations are normal
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: The national PEWS charts state that high flow, BiPAP and CPAP score the maximum of 4 on oxygen delivery, reflecting the level of respiratory support needed.

n.0: The method of delivery does not reduce the score; high flow scores the maximum.
n.2: Oxygen delivery is a scored parameter, unlike temperature.
n.3: Normal saturations on support do not cancel the oxygen delivery score.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ethan, aged 5, with suspected meningitis, now responds only to pain. His PEWS is 7. What should the nurse do?
o: Call for a Rapid Review within 15 minutes
Request ST3+ review within 30 minutes, as the PEWS is 7
Make an immediate 2222 Paediatric Medical Emergency call
Recheck his AVPU in 15 minutes before escalating
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Two steps: identify the highest trigger, then act on it. A change in AVPU to P or U (or abnormal pupils) is an Emergency trigger on the national PEWS whatever the score, requiring an immediate 2222 call stating 'Paediatric Medical Emergency'. The chart says respond to the highest level reached by any one criterion.

n.0: A Rapid Review is the High response; responding only to pain is an Emergency trigger.
n.1: This responds to the score alone and misses the higher-level AVPU trigger.
n.3: Delaying escalation in a child responding only to pain risks airway compromise and arrest.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Amira, aged 9, has been reviewed twice for abdominal pain after an operation. Her father remains very worried that she is getting worse and feels his concerns have not been acted on. What should the nurse tell him?
o: He can call the Martha's Rule number for a rapid review by another team
He should wait for the consultant ward round the following morning
He can ask for a second opinion at her next outpatient appointment
He should make a formal complaint to the Patient Advice and Liaison Service
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Martha's Rule gives patients, families and carers the right to request a rapid review from a different team if they remain worried that the patient is deteriorating and feel their concerns are not being addressed. Each hospital has its own number; it is not a second opinion (NHS England, Martha's Rule). The nurse should also escalate herself.

n.1: Waiting until the morning ignores a family's concern about deterioration.
n.2: Martha's Rule is distinct from a second opinion and is for possible deterioration now, not at a later appointment.
n.3: PALS handles complaints and concerns about services, not urgent clinical deterioration.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Amelia, aged 2 weeks, is brought to the children's emergency department because she feels hot. Which method should the nurse use to measure her temperature?
o: An electronic thermometer in the axilla
A forehead chemical strip thermometer
A chemical dot thermometer under the tongue
An infra-red tympanic thermometer
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG143: in infants under 4 weeks, measure body temperature with an electronic thermometer in the axilla. From 4 weeks to 5 years, an electronic or chemical dot thermometer in the axilla or an infra-red tympanic thermometer can be used (AnnexB.4.8).

n.1: NG143 says forehead chemical thermometers are unreliable and should not be used by healthcare professionals.
n.2: The oral route is not used routinely in children aged 0 to 5 years.
n.3: Tympanic thermometers are an option from 4 weeks of age, not in a 2-week-old.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Oliver, aged 6 weeks, has a temperature of 38.2°C measured in the axilla. He is feeding a little less than usual but is pink and alert. Using the NICE traffic light system, how should he be categorised?
o: Amber, because his temperature is still below 39°C
Red, as he is under 3 months with a fever of 38°C or more
Green, because he is alert and pink and still feeding well
Amber, because his feeding has reduced from his usual
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG143: a child aged under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher is in the red (high risk) group, whatever other features are present, and needs urgent assessment. Infants this young cannot be judged reliably on appearance.

n.0: The 39°C threshold applies to babies aged 3 to 6 months; under 3 months, 38°C or more is red.
n.2: Appearing well does not lower the risk category for an infant under 3 months with fever.
n.3: Reduced feeding is an amber feature, but his age and temperature already place him in red.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Poppy, aged 2, has a fever of 38.7°C and is playing happily. Her mother asks whether she should give paracetamol and ibuprofen together to bring the temperature down. What is the best advice?
o: Give both alternately every 2 hours until her temperature is normal
Give one medicine if Poppy becomes distressed, not both together
Give paracetamol now to prevent a febrile seizure, even if she is happy
Give both together, as this brings the temperature down fastest
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG143: consider paracetamol or ibuprofen if the child appears distressed, not solely to reduce body temperature. Do not give both at the same time; consider alternating only if distress persists or recurs before the next dose is due. Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures.

n.0: Alternating is considered only for persistent distress, and the aim is comfort, not a normal temperature.
n.2: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures and are not given for temperature in a happy child.
n.3: NG143 advises against giving both agents simultaneously.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ravi, aged 3, has a fever. His father has been sponging him with lukewarm water and has wrapped him in extra blankets to stop him shivering. What advice should the nurse give?
o: Stop the sponging but keep the extra blankets on him
Continue the sponging but take off the extra blankets
Continue both, as this is a safe way to manage a fever at home
Stop sponging and use light clothing, not under- or over-wrapped
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG143: tepid sponging is not recommended for treating fever, and children with fever should not be underdressed or over-wrapped. Offer regular fluids and check on the child, including at night.

n.0: Over-wrapping a feverish child is not advised and can raise the temperature further.
n.1: Tepid sponging is not recommended, so continuing it is wrong.
n.2: Both sponging and over-wrapping are against NICE advice.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Zara, aged 4 months, has a temperature of 39.3°C. She is alert, pink and feeding normally, with a respiratory rate of 42. How should she be categorised under NICE NG143?
o: Red, because any infant under 6 months with a fever is red
Green, because she has no other abnormal features
At least amber, as she is 3 to 6 months old with 39°C or more
Green, because her temperature came down after paracetamol
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG143: in children aged 3 to 6 months, a temperature of 39°C or higher is at least an intermediate-risk (amber) feature, so she needs assessment and a safety net or referral. The red temperature criterion (38°C or more) applies under 3 months.

n.0: The automatic red criterion for fever applies to infants under 3 months, not up to 6 months.
n.1: Her temperature of 39.3°C at 4 months is itself an amber feature.
n.3: NG143 says not to use response to antipyretics to judge severity of illness.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Leo, aged 2, has had a fever for 6 days. He has red eyes without discharge, cracked red lips and a rash. His mother says the GP thought it was a virus. What should the nurse consider?
o: Kawasaki disease, because fever has lasted 5 days or more
Scarlet fever, needing oral antibiotics at home
A viral illness that will resolve without assessment
Measles, needing isolation and no further assessment
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG143: fever lasting 5 days or longer is an amber feature, and the clinician should assess for Kawasaki disease (fever with conjunctival injection without discharge, red cracked lips or strawberry tongue, rash, changes in hands and feet, neck lymph nodes). Early treatment reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysm (NHS, Kawasaki disease).

n.1: Scarlet fever is possible in children with fever and rash, but 6 days of fever with non-purulent red eyes and cracked lips points to Kawasaki disease, which needs specialist assessment.
n.2: Fever for 5 days or more is amber and should not be assumed viral.
n.3: Measles needs isolation, but this pattern does not fit as well, and any prolonged fever still needs assessment.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Kian, aged 2, has a temperature of 38.9°C. He responds normally to his parents but is not smiling. Respiratory rate is 46, SpO2 96% in air, heart rate 135 and capillary refill 2 seconds. Which NICE traffic light feature is present?
o: An SpO2 of 96% in air, which is an amber feature
A respiratory rate above 40, amber when over 12 months
No amber features, so he is in the green category
A heart rate above the amber threshold for his age
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Two steps: compare each value with the NG143 table, then classify. A respiratory rate above 40 breaths/min in a child over 12 months is amber; not smiling is also amber (reduced response to social cues). His heart rate (amber threshold above 140 at 2 to 5 years), SpO2 (amber at 95% or less) and capillary refill are not amber.

n.0: The amber SpO2 threshold is 95% or less in air; 96% is not amber.
n.2: He has amber features (respiratory rate and not smiling), so he is not green.
n.3: The NG143 amber heart rate threshold at 2 to 5 years is above 140; his is 135.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ellie, aged 18 months, has a fever with some amber features but no diagnosis has been reached. The doctor decides she can go home. What must the nurse ensure before discharge?
o: A plan for her parents to measure her temperature hourly overnight
A safety net, with written warning signs and how to get help
A clinic appointment in 2 weeks to recheck her temperature
A prescription for regular paracetamol and ibuprofen for 5 days
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG143: if any amber features are present and no diagnosis has been reached, provide a safety net (verbal and/or written information on warning symptoms and how to access further care, arranged follow-up, or liaison with other professionals) or refer to specialist care. Parents should check the child during the night and seek help if concerned.

n.0: Hourly temperatures are not required and do not tell parents what to do if their child worsens.
n.2: A 2-week follow-up is too late to act as a safety net for an acute febrile illness.
n.3: Regular combined antipyretics are not recommended; they are given for distress, one at a time.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Isaac, aged 7, is admitted with a high temperature and vomiting. His mother says he is 'not himself'. Observations: heart rate 124, capillary refill 3 seconds, and he complains of leg pain. Using NICE NG254, which finding is a high risk criterion for sepsis?
o: His complaint of leg pain
His capillary refill time of 3 seconds
His heart rate of 124 beats/min
His mother's concern about his behaviour
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG254 Table 2 (children aged 5 to 11): for ages 6 to 7, a heart rate of 120 or more is a high risk criterion (110 to 119 is moderate to high). Capillary refill of 3 seconds or more, leg pain and parental concern about behaviour are moderate to high risk criteria.

n.0: Leg pain is a moderate to high risk criterion.
n.1: Capillary refill of 3 seconds or more is a moderate to high risk criterion in NG254.
n.3: Parent or carer concern about behaviour is a moderate to high risk criterion.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Grace, aged 3, on a children's ward, has suspected sepsis with a non-blanching rash and mottled skin. The senior clinician has reviewed her and taken blood cultures. By when should she receive a broad-spectrum antimicrobial?
o: Once the blood culture result is available
Within 3 hours of meeting a high risk criterion
Within 1 hour of meeting a high risk criterion
Within 6 hours, after the lactate result is known
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG254 rec 1.7.2: for people under 16 with suspected sepsis and 1 or more high risk criteria, give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial without delay, within 1 hour of identifying that they meet any high risk criterion. A non-blanching rash and mottled skin are high risk criteria.

n.0: Culture results take days; waiting would dangerously delay treatment.
n.1: The 3-hour window applies to the antibiotic decision for moderate to high risk, not high risk.
n.3: Lactate guides fluids and escalation; it does not delay antibiotics in high risk sepsis.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Mason, aged 4, weighs 18 kg and has suspected sepsis with high risk criteria and a lactate of 3.2 mmol/L. An IV fluid bolus is prescribed in line with NICE NG254. What should the nurse expect to give?
o: 180 mL of glucose-free crystalloid over less than 10 minutes
180 mL of glucose-free crystalloid over 1 hour
360 mL of glucose-free crystalloid over less than 10 minutes
180 mL of 5% glucose over 30 minutes
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Two steps: calculate, then select the fluid. NG254 rec 1.9.2: glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 130 to 154 mmol/L, 10 mL/kg over less than 10 minutes (maximum 250 mL). 10 mL x 18 kg = 180 mL. Rec 1.7.7: with high risk criteria and lactate 2 to 4 mmol/L, give the bolus within 1 hour.

n.1: A resuscitation bolus is given over less than 10 minutes, not 1 hour.
n.2: 360 mL is 20 mL/kg, the upper neonatal bolus, and exceeds the 250 mL maximum.
n.3: Glucose-containing fluids are not used for resuscitation boluses.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Chloe, aged 11, weighs 38 kg and has suspected sepsis needing an IV fluid bolus. What is the correct bolus volume according to NICE NG254?
o: 380 mL over less than 10 minutes
250 mL over less than 10 minutes
500 mL over 15 minutes
760 mL over 30 minutes
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG254 rec 1.9.2: for people under 16, give 10 mL/kg of glucose-free crystalloid over less than 10 minutes, up to a maximum bolus of 250 mL. 10 mL x 38 kg = 380 mL, which is capped at 250 mL.

n.0: 380 mL is the calculated 10 mL/kg volume, but it exceeds the 250 mL maximum.
n.2: 500 mL is the adult bolus volume and exceeds the paediatric maximum.
n.3: 760 mL is 20 mL/kg and far above the maximum bolus.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Arlo, aged 3 weeks, is brought to the emergency department with a temperature of 38.4°C. He is feeding reasonably and is pink. What does NICE advise about antibiotics?
o: Give parenteral antibiotics, as he is under 1 month with fever
Give antibiotics if his fever is still present after 48 hours
Wait for a urine result before deciding whether to start antibiotics
Give oral antibiotics now and review him again in 24 hours
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG254 rec 1.7.4 (from NG143): give parenteral antibiotics to children younger than 1 month with fever, to all children aged 1 to 3 months with fever who appear unwell, and to those aged 1 to 3 months with a white cell count below 5 or above 15 x 10^9/L.

n.1: Waiting 48 hours is dangerous; fever in a baby under 1 month needs immediate treatment.
n.2: Investigations should not delay parenteral antibiotics in a febrile baby under 1 month.
n.3: Oral antibiotics are not appropriate for a febrile neonate, who needs parenteral treatment.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ruby, aged 6, has suspected sepsis with high risk criteria. Her venous lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. She has had antibiotics. What else does NICE NG254 recommend?
o: Consider a fluid bolus and recheck her lactate in 4 hours
Give oral fluids and repeat her observations every hour
Start maintenance fluids and review on the next ward round
Give a fluid bolus within 1 hour and refer to critical care
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG254 rec 1.7.5: for children under 12 with suspected sepsis, any high risk criteria and lactate over 4 mmol/L, give an IV fluid bolus without delay (within 1 hour) and refer to a critical care specialist or team to review management, including central access and inotropes.

n.0: 'Consider a bolus' applies when lactate is below 2 mmol/L; above 4, a bolus is given and critical care involved.
n.1: Oral fluids are not adequate resuscitation for a child with high risk sepsis and a raised lactate.
n.2: Maintenance fluids do not treat shock, and waiting for a ward round delays critical care.
