Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Leo, aged 9, is on a children's ward. He has two moderate to high risk criteria for sepsis and no high risk criteria. Blood tests including lactate have been taken. What does NICE NG254 advise about review and antibiotics?
o: Review on the next ward round, with antibiotics if fever persists
Antibiotics within 1 hour and an urgent critical care referral
Review results within 1 hour; antibiotic decision within 3 hours
Discharge home with safety-netting advice if his lactate is normal
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG254 (recs 1.7.12 to 1.7.14): with 2 or more moderate to high risk criteria, carry out blood tests and arrange clinician review of the condition and venous lactate results within 1 hour; if lactate is 2 mmol/L or lower and no definitive condition is found, reassess and decide on antibiotics within 3 hours. Lactate over 2 means treating as high risk.

n.0: Waiting for a ward round misses the 1-hour review and 3-hour decision times.
n.1: Antibiotics within 1 hour and critical care referral are for high risk criteria with a raised lactate.
n.3: A normal lactate does not end assessment; the child still needs review and an antibiotic decision.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Amira, aged 5, has high risk sepsis and has received antibiotics and a fluid bolus. How should the nurse monitor her, according to NICE NG254?
o: Continuous, or at least every 30 minutes, using track and trigger
Hourly observations, including a pain score each time
Observations every 2 hours, with continuous oximetry overnight
Four-hourly observations recorded on a NEWS2 chart
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG254: monitor people with suspected sepsis who meet any high risk criteria continuously, or a minimum of once every 30 minutes depending on setting, and use physiological track and trigger systems (in children's wards, PEWS).

n.1: Hourly observations are less frequent than the 30-minute minimum for high risk sepsis.
n.2: Two-hourly observations are too infrequent for a child with high risk sepsis.
n.3: NEWS2 is not validated for children, and 4-hourly observations are far too infrequent.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Alfie, aged 2, weighs 12 kg and has gastroenteritis. He is still breastfed and his mother asks what he can drink. He has no red flag signs. Which advice follows NICE CG84?
o: Continue breastfeeding and avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks
Give plain water in place of milk until vomiting has stopped for 24 hours
Stop breastfeeding and give diluted fruit juice until the diarrhoea settles
Give flat cola and stop all milk feeds for 48 hours
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE CG84: in children with gastroenteritis without red flags, continue breastfeeding and other milk feeds, encourage fluid intake, discourage fruit juices and carbonated drinks, and offer oral rehydration solution (ORS) as supplemental fluid to those at increased risk of dehydration.

n.1: Water lacks electrolytes, and CG84 advises continuing breastfeeding and milk feeds rather than replacing them.
n.2: Breastfeeding should continue, and fruit juice can worsen diarrhoea.
n.3: Fizzy drinks are discouraged and milk feeds should continue.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Sophie, aged 18 months, has gastroenteritis. Which finding is a red flag sign that she is at increased risk of progressing to shock (NICE CG84)?
o: She has had three loose stools today
Her eyes appear sunken
She is thirsty and drinking eagerly
Her temperature is 37.9°C
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE CG84 Table 1: red flag symptoms and signs of clinical dehydration include appearing unwell or deteriorating, altered responsiveness, sunken eyes, tachycardia, tachypnoea and reduced skin turgor. Children with red flags need ORS only (no other oral fluids) and closer monitoring.

n.0: Loose stools are expected in gastroenteritis; their number alone is not a red flag sign.
n.2: Thirst is a feature of dehydration but not one of the red flag signs.
n.3: A mild fever is common in gastroenteritis and is not a dehydration red flag.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ellie, aged 3, has gastroenteritis. Her mother asks when she can go back to nursery. What advice is correct?
o: When her stools have become fully formed again
Once she has gone 24 hours without any vomiting
48 hours after her last diarrhoea or vomiting
After she finishes a 5-day course of ORS at home
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE CG84: children should not attend school or other childcare facilities while they have diarrhoea or vomiting caused by gastroenteritis, and should not go back until at least 48 hours after the last episode. Handwashing with soap and water is the most important measure to prevent spread.

n.0: Stool consistency is not the measure; the rule is 48 hours after the last episode.
n.1: 24 hours is too short; the exclusion period is 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting.
n.3: ORS is used for rehydration as needed, not as a fixed course linked to return.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Harry, aged 10 months, has clinical dehydration from gastroenteritis but no red flags. He keeps refusing oral rehydration solution from a cup. Which approach does NICE CG84 support?
o: Give ORS often in small amounts, by syringe or spoon if needed
Start IV fluids as soon as he refuses ORS on one occasion
Stop ORS and give him diluted apple juice, which he prefers
Give the full volume of ORS as one large drink every 4 hours
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE CG84: give ORS frequently and in small amounts; consider supplementing with usual fluids (milk feeds or water, not fruit juice or fizzy drinks) if the child refuses enough ORS and has no red flags; consider a nasogastric tube if they cannot drink it or vomit persistently. IV fluids are for shock, red flags with deterioration or persistent vomiting of ORS.

n.1: A single refusal is not an indication for IV fluids; other ways of giving ORS come first.
n.2: Fruit juice is discouraged in gastroenteritis.
n.3: Large volumes at once are more likely to be vomited.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Lily, aged 2, weighs 14 kg and has clinical dehydration without shock. Oral rehydration is prescribed in line with NICE CG84. How much ORS is needed for her fluid deficit, and over what time?
o: 700 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance fluid
700 mL over 24 hours, in place of maintenance fluid
1,400 mL over 4 hours, including maintenance
280 mL over 1 hour, then reassess
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE CG84: for oral rehydration therapy give 50 mL/kg for fluid deficit replacement over 4 hours as well as maintenance fluid. 50 mL x 14 kg = 700 mL over 4 hours, given frequently in small amounts, plus maintenance.

n.1: The deficit is replaced over 4 hours, and maintenance must also be given.
n.2: 1,400 mL is 100 mL/kg, the IV deficit used after shock, not the oral deficit.
n.3: 280 mL is 20 mL/kg and not the CG84 regimen.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Zak weighs 16 kg and needs IV maintenance fluids after surgery. Using the Holliday-Segar formula in NICE NG29, what is his maintenance requirement?
o: 1,000 mL per 24 hours, about 42 mL/h
1,120 mL per 24 hours, about 47 mL/h
1,300 mL per 24 hours, about 54 mL/h
1,600 mL per 24 hours, about 67 mL/h
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG29 rec 1.4.1: 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg/day for the next 10 kg and 20 mL/kg/day above 20 kg. Working: (10 x 100) + (6 x 50) = 1,000 + 300 = 1,300 mL per 24 hours, which is 1,300 / 24 = about 54 mL/h.

n.0: 1,000 mL counts only the first 10 kg and omits the remaining 6 kg.
n.1: 1,120 mL applies 20 mL/kg to the 6 kg above 10 kg; 20 mL/kg/day is the rate for weight above 20 kg, and the second 10 kg takes 50 mL/kg/day.
n.3: 1,600 mL applies 100 mL/kg to all 16 kg instead of 50 mL/kg above 10 kg.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Mia, aged 6, starts IV maintenance fluids on the ward. Which fluid and monitoring plan follows NICE NG29?
o: 5% glucose; capillary glucose checked every 4 hours
0.18% saline with 4% glucose; electrolytes and glucose checked weekly
Isotonic crystalloid; electrolytes and glucose at start and at least daily
Isotonic crystalloid; electrolytes checked if she becomes unwell
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG29 recs 1.4.3 and 1.4.4: for routine maintenance, initially use isotonic crystalloids containing sodium 131 to 154 mmol/L, and measure plasma electrolytes and blood glucose when starting IV fluids and at least every 24 hours thereafter. Hypotonic fluids risk hyponatraemia.

n.0: 5% glucose is hypotonic once glucose is metabolised and risks dangerous hyponatraemia.
n.1: Hypotonic 0.18% saline risks hyponatraemia, and weekly checks are too infrequent.
n.3: Electrolytes and glucose must be checked at least every 24 hours, not when she becomes unwell.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Noah, aged 18 months, weighs 11 kg. He has gastroenteritis and is now pale, mottled and cold, with a capillary refill of 5 seconds and weak pulses. What is the immediate fluid management under NICE CG84?
o: IV maintenance fluid at 44 mL/h and recheck in 4 hours
ORS 550 mL over 4 hours given down a nasogastric tube
Rapid IV infusion of 110 mL 0.9% sodium chloride, reassess
Rapid IV infusion of 220 mL of 5% glucose, then reassess
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Two steps: recognise clinical shock, then treat. NICE CG84: treat suspected or confirmed shock with a rapid IV infusion of 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride (10 x 11 = 110 mL); if still shocked, give another 10 mL/kg and consider other causes, and consult paediatric intensive care if shock persists after the second.

n.0: Maintenance fluid does not treat shock, and waiting 4 hours is dangerous.
n.1: Oral or nasogastric rehydration is not appropriate for a child in shock.
n.3: Glucose solutions are not used for shock, and 220 mL is 20 mL/kg.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Rosie, aged 18 months, has returned from theatre after repair of a forearm fracture. She is crying and drawing her legs up. Which pain assessment tool is most appropriate for her?
o: A visual analogue line marked by Rosie
The Wong-Baker FACES scale
A 0 to 10 numerical rating scale
The FLACC behavioural scale
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: FLACC (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) is a behavioural observation scale validated in children aged 2 months to 7 years after surgery (Merkel et al. 1997), suited to a child who cannot self-report (AnnexB.3.1).

n.0: A visual analogue line needs abstract understanding beyond a toddler.
n.1: Wong-Baker FACES is a self-report scale for people aged 3 and over.
n.2: A numerical scale needs number concepts that an 18-month-old does not have.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: A student nurse asks how the FLACC pain scale is scored. Which description is correct?
o: Five categories each scored 0 to 3, giving a total of 0 to 15
Five categories each scored 0 to 2, giving a total of 0 to 10
Six faces scored 0 to 10, chosen by the child
Four categories each scored 0 to 2, giving a total of 0 to 8
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: FLACC scores five behaviours (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability), each from 0 to 2, giving a total from 0 to 10 (Merkel et al. 1997).

n.0: Each FLACC item is scored 0 to 2, not 0 to 3.
n.2: Six faces chosen by the child describes the Wong-Baker FACES self-report scale.
n.3: FLACC has five categories, not four.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Jamal, aged 4, has had an appendicectomy. He can talk about how he feels and points to pictures. Which pain tool is most suitable?
o: The Wong-Baker FACES scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale
A score based on his heart rate
A 0 to 10 numerical rating scale
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Self-report is preferred when a child can give it. The Wong-Baker FACES scale is a self-report tool for people aged 3 and over, using faces from no hurt to hurts worst (Wong-Baker FACES Foundation; AnnexB.3.1).

n.1: The Glasgow Coma Scale assesses conscious level, not pain.
n.2: Heart rate changes with many factors and is not a validated pain score on its own.
n.3: Numerical scales are generally used from about 7 to 8 years, when children understand number ranges.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ella, aged 10, has abdominal pain after surgery. She says her pain is '7 out of 10', but her mother thinks she is exaggerating because she is chatting with friends. What should the nurse do?
o: Wait until Ella looks distressed before giving analgesia
Score Ella's pain on the FLACC scale instead
Use the mother's estimate, because she knows Ella best
Accept Ella's self-report and act on it, then reassess
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Self-report is the preferred measure of pain when a child can give it; children may use distraction or socialising to cope, so behaviour can underestimate pain. The nurse should believe and act on Ella's score, give prescribed analgesia and reassess (P4.8; AnnexB.3.5).

n.0: Waiting for visible distress leaves pain untreated and ignores her report.
n.1: FLACC is for children who cannot self-report and is validated up to 7 years.
n.2: Parents' views help, but a capable child's own report takes priority.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Tom, aged 8, is due to go home after a tonsillectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea. The discharge prescription includes codeine. What should the nurse do?
o: Give half the dose of codeine to reduce the risk
Give the codeine, as it is effective for post-tonsillectomy pain
Withhold the codeine and query the prescription with the prescriber
Give the codeine at night, when the pain is usually worst
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: MHRA (Drug Safety Update, July 2013): codeine is contraindicated in all children under 18 who undergo tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea, and should be used for acute pain only in children over 12 when other analgesics have not worked, because ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolisers can develop morphine toxicity. The prescription must be queried.

n.0: Reducing the dose does not remove the risk of morphine toxicity in rapid metabolisers.
n.1: Codeine is contraindicated after tonsillectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea in under-18s.
n.3: Night-time doses carry the same risk and are not permitted in this situation.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Lucy, aged 11, has a sprained ankle. Her father asks whether he can give her aspirin at home, as that is what he takes. What should the nurse advise?
o: Aspirin is safe for sprains when it is taken with food
Aspirin can be given for up to 3 days and then stopped
Aspirin is safe at half the adult dose for children over 10
Do not give aspirin under 16 unless prescribed; use paracetamol
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Aspirin should not be given to children under 16 unless prescribed by a doctor (for example in Kawasaki disease), because of the risk of Reye's syndrome (NHS). Paracetamol or ibuprofen are suitable for a sprain.

n.0: Taking aspirin with food reduces stomach upset but does not remove the risk of Reye's syndrome.
n.1: Short courses still carry the risk; aspirin is avoided in under-16s unless prescribed.
n.2: There is no half-dose exception; aspirin is avoided in under-16s unless prescribed.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Kai, aged 2, is 4 hours after hernia repair. He is grimacing, kicking, arching, crying steadily and hard to console. His FLACC score is 8. Analgesia is prescribed. What should the nurse do?
o: Recheck the FLACC score in 4 hours before taking action
Give the prescribed analgesia and reassess once it has had time to work
Use distraction and comfort measures and avoid medicines at his age
Ask his parents to settle him and record the score as behaviour
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Two steps: interpret, then act. A FLACC score of 7 to 10 indicates severe pain. The nurse should give the prescribed analgesia promptly, use comfort and distraction alongside, and reassess pain after the medicine has had time to work to judge whether it is effective (AnnexB.3.5; P4.8).

n.0: Waiting 4 hours leaves severe pain untreated.
n.2: Distraction helps, but severe post-operative pain needs analgesia; age 2 is no reason to withhold prescribed medicines.
n.3: Labelling the score as behaviour ignores severe pain that needs treatment.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Maya, aged 9, has severe cerebral palsy and does not use speech. After hip surgery, her mother says Maya's 'pain face' is a fixed smile and she goes very still when hurting. How should the nurse assess her pain?
o: Use a numerical scale, with her mother choosing the number for her
Use a behavioural tool based on her own pain cues and her mother's input
Use the Wong-Baker FACES scale and read her smile as no pain
Rely on her heart rate and blood pressure as the main pain measure
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Children with cognitive or communication impairments may show pain in individual ways. A behavioural observation tool adapted to the child's known pain behaviours (for example individualised FLACC), with parents' knowledge of their cues, gives the most accurate assessment (P4.8; AnnexB.3.1).

n.0: A parent choosing a number is a proxy guess, not a structured assessment of Maya's behaviour.
n.2: FACES needs self-report, and her smile is her pain cue, so this would underestimate pain.
n.3: Vital signs are not reliable pain measures on their own.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Toby, aged 14 months, is admitted for observation after falling from a sofa. He babbles but has no words yet. How should the nurse assess his conscious level?
o: Asking his parents whether he seems his normal self
Pupil size and reaction, without a GCS score
A paediatric GCS with a modified verbal score or grimace alternative
The adult GCS, scoring verbal response as 1 because he cannot talk
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG232 rec 1.3.4: the paediatric version of the GCS includes a 'grimace' alternative to the verbal score so that preverbal children can be scored, and staff should be trained in the paediatric version (AnnexB.2.12 neurological observations).

n.0: Parental views are valuable, but a structured paediatric GCS is needed for monitoring.
n.1: Pupils are part of neurological observations but do not replace a conscious level score.
n.3: Scoring a preverbal child's verbal response as 1 falsely lowers the score and misrepresents his conscious level.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ava, aged 7, is admitted after a head injury. Her GCS has been 15 since she arrived in the emergency department. How often should her neurological observations be recorded, following NICE NG232?
o: Hourly for 4 hours, then 4-hourly until she is discharged
Every 15 minutes for 1 hour, then hourly until the morning
Four-hourly from admission, as her GCS has been normal
Half-hourly for 2 hours, then hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG232 rec 1.9.11: for people with a GCS of 15, the minimum frequency after initial assessment is half-hourly for 2 hours, then 1-hourly for 4 hours, then 2-hourly. If she deteriorates after the first 2 hours, revert to half-hourly (rec 1.9.12).

n.0: Hourly then 4-hourly is less frequent than the NICE minimum schedule.
n.1: This does not follow the NICE schedule and stops intensive monitoring too soon.
n.2: A normal GCS still needs the structured schedule, as deterioration can occur later.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Leo, aged 6, has a cardiac monitor on the ward. The nurse notices his heart rate rises to 110 when he breathes in and falls to 85 when he breathes out. He is well and playing. What is the most likely explanation?
o: An atrial arrhythmia that needs an urgent 12-lead ECG
A faulty monitor lead that needs replacing
Early heart block that needs medical review
Sinus arrhythmia, a normal finding in children
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Sinus arrhythmia, in which heart rate increases on inspiration and slows on expiration, is a normal physiological finding in children and young people and needs no treatment (T2 cardiac monitoring; AnnexB.2.5). The nurse should document it and continue routine monitoring.

n.0: Rate variation with breathing in a well child is physiological, not a pathological arrhythmia.
n.1: The variation follows his breathing pattern, which points to physiology rather than a lead fault.
n.2: Heart block causes slow rates or dropped beats, not a regular rise and fall with breathing.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: A nurse is attaching a three-lead cardiac monitor to Isla, aged 5, using the UK colour code. Where should the electrodes be placed?
o: Yellow on the right shoulder, green on the left shoulder, red on the left lower chest
Red on the right shoulder, yellow on the left shoulder, green on the left lower chest
Red on the left shoulder, yellow on the right shoulder, green on the right lower chest
Green on the right shoulder, red on the left shoulder, yellow on the left lower chest
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: In the UK (IEC) colour code for three-lead monitoring, red goes on the right shoulder (right arm), yellow on the left shoulder (left arm) and green on the left lower chest or abdomen (left leg). Placing electrodes on bony areas away from muscle helps reduce interference (AnnexB.2.5).

n.0: This places all three colours in the wrong positions.
n.2: This reverses red and yellow and places green on the wrong side.
n.3: Green belongs on the left lower chest, not the right shoulder.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ruby, aged 3, has a head injury. Her GCS has been 14. On her next observations, her right pupil is larger than her left and slow to react. Her GCS is still 14. What should the nurse do?
o: Document it as stable because her GCS has not fallen
Arrange urgent reappraisal by the supervising doctor
Repeat the pupil check in 30 minutes to confirm the change
Dim the lights and recheck her pupils after she has slept
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: NICE NG232 rec 1.9.13: new or evolving neurological signs such as pupil inequality need urgent reappraisal by the supervising doctor, even if the GCS has not changed. Unequal pupils may indicate rising intracranial pressure.

n.0: A new pupil inequality is a significant change, regardless of an unchanged GCS.
n.2: Waiting 30 minutes delays urgent review of a new focal sign.
n.3: Letting her sleep without review risks missing deterioration.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Noah, aged 4 months, is feeding poorly. His monitor shows a narrow complex tachycardia at 270 beats/min with no visible P waves and no beat-to-beat variation. He is pink, alert and capillary refill is 2 seconds. Help has been called. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
o: Chest compressions at a ratio of 15:2
A vagal manoeuvre, an ice pack to the face
A fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline
Synchronised DC cardioversion at 1 J/kg
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Two steps: recognise SVT, then judge whether he is compensated. RCUK 2025: in narrow complex SVT without decompensated circulatory failure, consider vagal manoeuvres (for example an ice pack to the face), then IV adenosine 0.1 to 0.2 mg/kg as a rapid flush with a 12-lead ECG running; seek paediatric cardiology advice early.

n.0: Compressions are for cardiac arrest or HR below 60 with poor perfusion, not a perfusing tachycardia.
n.2: A fluid bolus does not terminate SVT, and he has no signs of shock.
n.3: Immediate synchronised cardioversion is for decompensated circulatory failure; Noah is well perfused.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Jess, aged 8, has acute asthma. Earlier, wheeze was heard throughout her chest. Now she is too breathless to talk, her SpO2 is 90%, and on auscultation the nurse hears very little air entry and almost no wheeze. What does this finding mean?
o: A silent chest, a life-threatening sign that needs an emergency call
Normal breath sounds now her wheeze has stopped
Her bronchospasm is resolving, so nebulisers can be spaced out
Mucus plugging that will clear with chest physiotherapy
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Reduced air entry with little or no wheeze in a breathless child (silent chest) shows very poor air movement and is listed as a life-threatening feature of acute asthma in children in the BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244); RCUK 2025 also lists diminished air entry as decompensated respiratory failure. It needs immediate senior help.

n.1: Breath sounds are not normal; air entry is greatly reduced.
n.2: Loss of wheeze here reflects too little air movement, not improvement; she cannot talk and is hypoxic.
n.3: Physiotherapy is not the treatment for life-threatening asthma.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: A nurse needs to auscultate the chest of Aiden, aged 2, who is crying and clinging to his mother. What is the best approach?
o: Listen on his mother's lap, with a warmed stethoscope and distraction
Listen while he is crying, as his deep breaths make sounds clearer
Wait until he falls asleep, which may take several more hours
Lie him flat on the bed and ask his mother to hold his arms down
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Auscultation is most accurate when a young child is calm. Examining on a parent's lap, warming the stethoscope, using distraction and comparing both sides systematically helps get reliable findings; crying adds noise and alters breathing (AnnexB.2.8; T2 chest auscultation).

n.1: Crying produces noise and irregular breathing that masks added sounds.
n.2: Waiting several hours delays assessment of a possibly unwell child.
n.3: Lying him down and holding his arms increases distress and noise, making auscultation less accurate.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Maisie, 2 years old, is admitted for observation after a minor head injury. She is playing calmly. Her respiratory rate is 30 breaths/min and heart rate 120 beats/min. How should the nurse interpret these values?
o: The breathing rate is raised but the heart rate is normal
Both are within the normal range for her age
The heart rate is raised but the breathing rate is normal
Both are raised and need escalation for review
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: RCUK 2025 (Table 1, approximate normal ranges): at 2 years, respiratory rate 18 to 40 breaths/min and heart rate 90 to 160 beats/min. A rate of 30 and heart rate of 120 in a calm toddler are normal (T2 vital signs by age).

n.0: A respiratory rate of 30 is within the 18 to 40 range at 2 years.
n.2: A heart rate of 120 is well within the 90 to 160 range at 2 years.
n.3: Neither value is above the upper limit for a 2-year-old, so escalation for these values is not needed.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Ben, aged 10, is resting in bed with a chest infection. His heart rate is 150 beats/min and respiratory rate 32 breaths/min. He is afebrile. What does this indicate?
o: Normal values, because children have faster rates than adults
A raised heart rate but normal breathing for a 10-year-old
Both values are above the normal range for his age
A normal heart rate but rapid breathing for a 10-year-old
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: RCUK 2025 (Table 1): at 10 years, the approximate normal respiratory rate is 14 to 25 breaths/min and heart rate 60 to 120 beats/min. Both values are well above the upper limit at rest without fever, so the nurse should assess further and escalate.

n.0: Rates are faster in children, but a resting heart rate of 150 and breathing rate of 32 exceed the range at 10 years.
n.1: A respiratory rate of 32 is above the upper limit of about 25 at 10 years.
n.3: A heart rate of 150 is above the upper limit of about 120 at 10 years.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: A nurse needs to record the respiratory rate of Leo, a 4-month-old baby who is asleep in his cot. Which technique is most accurate?
o: Count for 15 seconds and multiply the number by four
Count while he is asleep, watching the abdomen for 60 seconds
Wake him gently first so his chest movements are clearer
Use the reading displayed on the pulse oximeter instead
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: Infants breathe mainly with the diaphragm and often irregularly, so the respiratory rate should be counted for a full 60 seconds by watching the abdomen, ideally before disturbing the baby, as crying and handling raise the rate (AnnexB.2.1: observations; P3.12).

n.0: Irregular infant breathing makes short counts inaccurate.
n.2: Waking him causes crying and raises the rate, giving a falsely high reading.
n.3: A pulse oximeter measures saturation and pulse, not respiratory rate.

Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.t: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.q: Jayden, aged 6, has a blood pressure reading of 135/85 mmHg on the ward. The nurse notices the cuff covers only half the length of his upper arm. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the reading and inform the doctor of hypertension
Record the reading and repeat it in 4 hours
Repeat the reading with the same cuff on the other arm
Repeat the reading with a correctly sized cuff
Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Chi.w: A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high blood pressure reading. The cuff must be the correct size for the child's arm before a reading is interpreted, so the reading should be repeated with an appropriately sized cuff (AnnexB.2.1: taking blood pressure manually and via electronic devices).

n.0: The reading is unreliable because of the cuff size, so it should not yet be reported as hypertension.
n.1: Recording a reading taken with the wrong cuff puts inaccurate data on the chart.
n.2: Using the same small cuff on the other arm repeats the same error.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Leo, 5, is choking on a sweet at a school health clinic. He is conscious but cannot speak or cough effectively. The nurse has given 5 back blows with Leo leaning forward, but the sweet has not come out. What is the next action?
o: Give up to 5 chest thrusts with two thumbs
Lie Leo down and start 15:2 chest compressions
Give a further 5 back blows before any thrusts
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: for a conscious child over 1 year with an ineffective cough, give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, and keep alternating while checking the child's condition.

n.0: Two-thumb chest thrusts are the infant technique; a child over 1 year receives abdominal thrusts after back blows.
n.1: CPR begins when the child becomes unconscious; Leo is still conscious.
n.2: The algorithm alternates 5 back blows with 5 thrusts; repeating back blows first delays the more forceful manoeuvre.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Isla, 10 months, has been choking on a grape. After two rounds of back blows and chest thrusts she becomes limp and unresponsive. The nurse lays her on a firm surface and opens her airway, but cannot see the grape. What should the nurse do next?
o: Continue cycles of back blows and chest thrusts
Give 5 rescue breaths and start CPR at 15:2
Give 5 abdominal thrusts with Isla lying on her back
Perform a single finger sweep to feel for the grape
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: if a choking child becomes unconscious, open the airway, remove the object only if clearly visible, give 5 rescue breaths and continue with CPR (15:2 if trained). Compressions help dislodge the object.

n.0: Back blows and thrusts are for the conscious child; once unconscious the algorithm moves to rescue breaths and CPR.
n.2: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants, and an unconscious child needs rescue breaths and CPR.
n.3: A finger is used to remove an object only when it is clearly visible; blind sweeping can impact it further.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Mason, 6, weighs 21 kg and is in cardiac arrest in a hospital outpatient area. CPR is in progress and an AED arrives. It has a paediatric mode and child pads are available. How should the AED be used?
o: Paediatric mode, with pads front and back of the chest
Adult mode, with pads on the front and back of the chest
Paediatric mode, with pads attached once the arrest team arrives
Adult mode, with pads below the right clavicle and left side
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: use the paediatric (attenuated) mode under 25 kg (about 8 years), with pads anteroposterior in smaller children (one left of the sternum, one between the scapulae). Adult mode is used above 25 kg.

n.1: Mason is under 25 kg and paediatric mode is available, so the attenuated energy should be used.
n.2: The AED should be attached as soon as it arrives so the rhythm can be analysed; waiting for the team delays any shock.
n.3: Adult mode and sternal-apical pads are for children over 25 kg or adults; Mason weighs 21 kg.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: A children's nurse is alone in a park when Amir, 7, collapses. He is unresponsive and not breathing normally. The nurse has a mobile phone. A public AED is in a cafe about 2 minutes' walk away. What should the nurse do?
o: Give 1 minute of CPR and then leave Amir to call 999
Call 999 on speaker phone and start CPR with 5 rescue breaths
Give 5 rescue breaths, then go to the cafe to fetch the AED
Run to fetch the AED, then call 999 on the way back to Amir
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: a single rescuer calls the ambulance (using the speaker function) and starts CPR immediately; calling and starting CPR take priority over fetching an AED, because paediatric arrest is usually hypoxic.

n.0: One minute of CPR before going for help applies when no phone is available; this nurse can call on speaker without leaving.
n.2: Leaving after rescue breaths interrupts CPR; the AED is fetched if someone else is available.
n.3: Leaving to fetch the AED delays both the call and CPR; RCUK prioritises calling and starting CPR for a lone rescuer.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Toby, 4, develops stridor, wheeze and widespread hives 10 minutes after eating a cashew at a children's day unit. His respiratory rate is 44 and his lips are swelling. The nurse has 1 mg/mL (1:1000) adrenaline. What IM dose should be given?
o: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL)
150 micrograms (0.15 mL)
50 micrograms (0.05 mL)
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL into the anterolateral thigh: 6 months to 6 years 150 micrograms (0.15 mL); 6-12 years 300 micrograms; over 12 years 500 micrograms; under 6 months 100-150 micrograms.

n.0: 500 micrograms is the dose for over 12s and adults.
n.1: 300 micrograms is the dose for children aged 6-12 years; Toby is 4.
n.3: 50 micrograms is below every RCUK age band; under-dosing delays reversal of airway swelling.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ruby, 5 months, develops facial swelling, a hoarse cry and pallor shortly after her first taste of egg on the children's ward. Her heart rate is 190. The nurse recognises anaphylaxis. Which IM adrenaline dose (1 mg/mL) is recommended for an infant of Ruby's age?
o: 500 micrograms (0.5 mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL)
100 to 150 micrograms (0.1 to 0.15 mL)
10 micrograms/kg given intravenously
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current) added a specific dose for infants under 6 months: 100-150 micrograms (0.1-0.15 mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if ABC problems persist.

n.0: 500 micrograms is the dose for over 12s and adults.
n.1: 300 micrograms is the 6-12 year dose and is excessive for a 5-month-old.
n.3: 10 micrograms/kg IV is the cardiac arrest dose; IV adrenaline in anaphylaxis is for specialists, and first-line treatment is IM.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Sami, 9, has anaphylaxis after a bee sting during a hospital open day. The nurse has drawn up 300 micrograms of adrenaline 1 mg/mL. Where should it be injected?
o: Intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh
Intramuscularly into the deltoid muscle
Intramuscularly into the dorsogluteal muscle
Subcutaneously into the abdomen
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): give IM adrenaline early into the anterolateral thigh, which gives reliable absorption in children and adults.

n.1: The deltoid is a smaller muscle with less reliable absorption; RCUK specifies the anterolateral thigh.
n.2: The buttock carries a risk of sciatic nerve injury and slower absorption; RCUK specifies the thigh.
n.3: Subcutaneous absorption is slower and less predictable than IM in a shocked child.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Maya, 14, weighs 58 kg and has reached puberty. She has anaphylaxis with wheeze and a blood pressure of 78/40 mmHg after an IV antibiotic on the adolescent ward. Which IM adrenaline dose (1 mg/mL) is appropriate?
o: 150 micrograms (0.15 mL)
500 micrograms (0.5 mL)
1 mg (1 mL)
300 micrograms (0.3 mL)
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): over 12 years the IM dose is 500 micrograms (0.5 mL), with 300 micrograms reserved for a child who is small or prepubertal. Maya is 58 kg and pubertal.

n.0: 150 micrograms is the dose for children aged 6 months to 6 years.
n.2: 1 mg IM is double the recommended maximum single IM dose.
n.3: 300 micrograms suits a 6-12 year old or a small, prepubertal over-12; Maya is neither.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Five minutes after IM adrenaline 300 micrograms for anaphylaxis, Leo, 8, remains wheezy with a respiratory rate of 36 and a heart rate of 150. He is on high-flow oxygen, the paediatric team is on the way and IV access is being attempted. What should the nurse do next?
o: Give IV chlorphenamine and reassess in 15 minutes
Wait a further 10 minutes for the first dose to work
Give a second IM dose of adrenaline 300 micrograms
Give IV hydrocortisone before any further adrenaline
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist, and give an IV fluid bolus if circulation problems continue.

n.0: Antihistamines are third-line and must not be used to treat ABC problems in the emergency phase.
n.1: RCUK sets the repeat at 5 minutes; waiting longer allows airway and circulatory compromise to progress.
n.3: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for the routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Olivia, 7, weighs 24 kg and has anaphylaxis. After a second IM adrenaline dose her blood pressure is still low and her capillary refill time is 4 seconds. IV access is in place and the paediatric team requests a crystalloid bolus. What volume is appropriate?
o: 240 mL
500 mL
120 mL
480 mL
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): give a crystalloid bolus of 10 mL/kg in a child (adults 500-1000 mL) and reassess. 10 mL/kg x 24 kg = 240 mL.

n.1: 500 mL is the lower adult bolus volume and is over 20 mL/kg for Olivia.
n.2: 120 mL is 5 mL/kg, half the recommended bolus for a shocked child.
n.3: 480 mL is 20 mL/kg, double the RCUK paediatric bolus.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ethan, 11, has anaphylaxis after eating sesame. Despite two correctly given IM adrenaline doses 5 minutes apart and a fluid bolus, he remains hypotensive and wheezy. The paediatric registrar is present. What does RCUK guidance advise now?
o: Get critical care help early for IV adrenaline infusion
Give a third IM dose and observe for 30 minutes
Give IV hydrocortisone as the main next treatment
Give oral cetirizine and continue close observations
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): refractory anaphylaxis is no improvement in respiratory or cardiovascular symptoms despite 2 appropriate IM doses; IV adrenaline infusion is the basis of treatment, with expert (critical care) help sought early.

n.1: IM doses may continue every 5 minutes while help arrives, but observing for 30 minutes delays the infusion that refractory anaphylaxis needs.
n.2: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment and do not act fast enough here.
n.3: Non-sedating oral antihistamines are for persisting skin symptoms after stabilisation, not for hypotension and wheeze.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Amira, 10, had anaphylaxis with hypotension and has received IM adrenaline. Her breathing is now quiet and unlaboured, but her blood pressure is still low and she feels faint. She asks to stand up and walk to the toilet. How should the nurse position her?
o: Keep her lying flat with her legs raised
Place her in the recovery position on her side
Help her to walk slowly to the toilet
Sit her upright in a chair beside the bed
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis (2021, current): avoid sudden changes in posture. A patient with cardiovascular instability is kept flat, with or without legs raised, to maximise venous return; standing or sitting up has been linked to cardiovascular collapse and death.

n.1: The recovery position is for an unconscious patient who is breathing; Amira is conscious and needs maximal venous return.
n.2: Standing and walking reduce venous return and have been associated with fatal collapse in anaphylaxis.
n.3: A semi-recumbent or sitting position suits predominantly respiratory symptoms; Amira's problem is hypotension.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Leo, 4, attends the children's emergency department with an asthma attack. He can say only two or three words per breath. His SpO2 is 91% in air, heart rate 150 and respiratory rate 46. He is alert, pink and has audible wheeze throughout. How should the nurse classify this attack?
o: Moderate asthma exacerbation
Acute severe asthma
Near-fatal asthma
Life-threatening asthma
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244, acute asthma in children from SIGN 158): acute severe in a child aged 1-5 = cannot complete sentences, SpO2 < 92%, HR > 140, RR > 40. Life-threatening needs SpO2 < 92% plus a feature such as silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, exhaustion or confusion, none of which Leo has.

n.0: Moderate asthma means talking in sentences with SpO2 of 92% or more; Leo cannot finish sentences and his SpO2 is 91%.
n.2: Near-fatal asthma is defined by raised PaCO2 or the need for ventilation, which is not described.
n.3: Leo is alert, pink and wheezy with good air entry; life-threatening features such as silent chest or exhaustion are absent.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Grace, 8, has an asthma attack on the children's ward. She is drowsy, her chest is silent on auscultation and her SpO2 is 88% in air. Which action is the immediate priority?
o: Call for senior help; give high-flow oxygen and nebulised salbutamol
Give oral prednisolone and recheck her observations within the hour
Record a peak flow reading to grade the severity of the attack
Give 10 puffs of salbutamol via spacer and reassess in 20 minutes
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244, acute asthma in children from SIGN 158): silent chest, drowsiness and SpO2 < 92% mean life-threatening asthma; summon senior help immediately and give oxygen (target 94-98%) with oxygen-driven nebulised bronchodilators.

n.1: Steroids are given early but take hours to act; they do not address immediate hypoxia and airflow obstruction.
n.2: Peak flow is not attempted in a drowsy child in a life-threatening attack; it delays treatment.
n.3: A spacer is first-line in mild to moderate attacks; a drowsy child with a silent chest cannot inhale effectively from it.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Zara, 2, has a mild wheezy episode and is prescribed salbutamol via a pressurised metered dose inhaler (pMDI). Her father asks how to give it at home. Which technique should the nurse teach?
o: Through a spacer with a face mask, one puff at a time with 5 breaths
Through a spacer with a mouthpiece, holding her breath for 10 seconds
Through a dry powder inhaler with a fast, deep breath
Directly from the pMDI, timed with a deep breath in
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244, acute asthma in children from SIGN 158): salbutamol via pMDI and spacer is first line; children under 3 use a face mask attached to the spacer; give one puff at a time with about 5 tidal breaths per puff.

n.1: A mouthpiece and breath-hold need cooperation a 2-year-old cannot give; a face mask is used under 3.
n.2: Dry powder devices need a fast, forceful inhalation that toddlers cannot generate.
n.3: A young child cannot coordinate actuation with inhalation, so most of the dose would be lost without a spacer.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ayaan, 4, is treated for an acute asthma attack in the emergency department. The doctor asks the nurse to give oral prednisolone early as recommended in the asthma pathway. What dose is appropriate for Ayaan's age?
o: 20 mg
40 mg
10 mg
60 mg
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244, acute asthma in children from SIGN 158): oral prednisolone given early: 10 mg under 2 years, 20 mg for 2-5 years, 30-40 mg over 5 years, usually for up to 3 days.

n.1: 30-40 mg is for children over 5; Ayaan is 4.
n.2: 10 mg is the dose for children under 2.
n.3: 60 mg exceeds the recommended paediatric dose for any age band.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ben, 7, has a moderate asthma attack. He is talking in sentences, his SpO2 is 95% in air, heart rate 118 and respiratory rate 28. He has not yet had any treatment today. What is the first-line bronchodilator treatment?
o: Oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium 250 micrograms
Ipratropium bromide via spacer as the initial bronchodilator
Salbutamol via pMDI and spacer, up to 10 puffs, titrated to response
IV salbutamol bolus followed by an infusion
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244, acute asthma in children from SIGN 158): in mild to moderate attacks a pMDI plus spacer is the preferred delivery (2-4 puffs, up to 10, one at a time). Nebulisers are used when SpO2 is below 92%.

n.0: Oxygen-driven nebulisers are for acute severe or life-threatening attacks with SpO2 < 92%; Ben's SpO2 is 95%.
n.1: Ipratropium is added to salbutamol when the response is poor; it is not the first bronchodilator.
n.3: IV bronchodilators are for attacks that fail to respond to inhaled therapy.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ivy, 6, has had 10 puffs of salbutamol via spacer for an asthma attack. Twenty minutes later her SpO2 is 90% in air, respiratory rate 34 and she can manage only short phrases. She has no silent chest and is alert. What should the nurse do?
o: Give oxygen to SpO2 94-98% and oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol
Give oxygen to SpO2 88-92% and air-driven nebulised salbutamol
Repeat 10 puffs of salbutamol via spacer in air and review in an hour
Give IV magnesium sulfate before further inhaled bronchodilator
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma pathway (SIGN 244, acute asthma in children from SIGN 158): Ivy now has acute severe asthma (SpO2 < 92%, too breathless to talk). Give oxygen to maintain 94-98% and switch to oxygen-driven nebulised salbutamol (2.5-5 mg), adding ipratropium if the response is poor.

n.1: 88-92% is the target for adults at risk of hypercapnic failure; children with asthma are given oxygen to 94-98%.
n.2: Repeating a spacer dose in air leaves her hypoxic; SpO2 below 92% calls for oxygen and nebulised bronchodilator.
n.3: IV magnesium is considered after first-line inhaled therapy fails, not before nebulised bronchodilators.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Finley, 8, has a confirmed diagnosis of asthma. He has symptoms three nights a week and uses his reliever most days. He takes no other asthma treatment. According to NICE NG245, what should be offered first as maintenance therapy?
o: Paediatric high-dose inhaled corticosteroid with SABA as needed
Regular montelukast with SABA as needed
Paediatric low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with SABA as needed
SABA as needed with no regular preventer medicine
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG245 Asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN, November 2024): for children aged 5-11 with newly diagnosed asthma, offer a twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS with SABA as needed; MART is the next step if control is not achieved.

n.0: High-dose ICS is reserved for specialist-led care after lower steps fail; it is not the starting dose.
n.1: A leukotriene receptor antagonist is a later add-on option, not initial maintenance for a 5-11 year old.
n.3: Reliever-only treatment leaves airway inflammation untreated and SABA over-use is linked to severe attacks (MHRA 2025).

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Sofia, 9, has a two-month history of night cough and wheeze. Her GP suspects asthma and refers her to the practice nurse for objective testing under NICE NG245. Which test should be done first?
o: Peak flow variability recorded over 2 weeks
Bronchial challenge testing with methacholine
Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO)
Skin prick testing to house dust mite
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG245 Asthma (BTS/NICE/SIGN, November 2024): in children aged 5-11, measure FeNO first (35 ppb or more supports asthma); if not confirmed, do spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, then peak flow variability.

n.0: Peak flow variability is a later step in the NG245 diagnostic sequence for 5-11 year olds.
n.1: Bronchial challenge is a specialist test used when earlier tests are inconclusive.
n.3: Skin prick testing identifies sensitisation but does not diagnose asthma.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Alfie, 4 months, has had a runny nose for two days. He now has a cough, a respiratory rate of 58, mild subcostal recession and fine crackles throughout both lungs. His temperature is 37.9°C. Which condition is most likely?
o: Bronchiolitis
Lobar pneumonia
Acute asthma
Croup
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): bronchiolitis affects children under 2 (peak 3-6 months): a 1-3 day coryzal prodrome, then persistent cough plus tachypnoea or chest recession, plus wheeze or crackles. Fever is usually below 39°C.

n.1: Pneumonia is suggested by fever of 39°C or more and focal crackles; Alfie's crackles are widespread with a low fever.
n.2: Asthma is rarely diagnosed in a 4-month-old; a coryzal start with widespread crackles fits bronchiolitis.
n.3: Croup presents with a barking cough and inspiratory stridor, usually from 6 months to 3 years, rather than widespread crackles.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Harper, 3 months, was born at term and has no underlying conditions. She is admitted with bronchiolitis. She is feeding about 80% of her usual amount and her SpO2 has been 91% in air for the last hour, with mild recession. What should the nurse do about oxygen?
o: Keep monitoring her in air; oxygen is not yet indicated
Start oxygen to keep her saturations at 94-98%
Start oxygen because her saturations are below 92%
Start nasal high-flow oxygen to reduce her work of breathing
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): give supplemental oxygen if SpO2 is persistently below 90% in children aged 6 weeks and over (below 92% under 6 weeks or with underlying conditions). Harper is 3 months, otherwise well, at 91%.

n.1: A 94-98% target is used in other acute illness; NG9 sets a lower threshold of 90% for bronchiolitis from 6 weeks.
n.2: 92% is the threshold for babies under 6 weeks or with underlying conditions; Harper is 3 months and otherwise well.
n.3: High-flow or CPAP is for impending respiratory failure; Harper has mild recession and acceptable saturations.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Jacob, 5 months, has bronchiolitis. He is becoming tired with feeds and is now taking about half his usual milk. His parents ask what will help. According to NICE NG9, which intervention is recommended?
o: A short course of oral prednisolone
Nebulised salbutamol via face mask
Nasogastric or orogastric fluids
Nebulised 3% hypertonic saline
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): give fluids by nasogastric or orogastric tube if a child cannot take enough fluid by mouth; consider IV isotonic fluids if NG/OG is not tolerated or respiratory failure is impending.

n.0: NG9 says do not use corticosteroids in bronchiolitis.
n.1: NG9 says do not use salbutamol in bronchiolitis.
n.3: NG9 says do not use hypertonic saline in bronchiolitis.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ruby, 2, wakes at night with a barking cough and noisy breathing when she is upset. At rest in the emergency department she has no stridor, no recession and is alert and playing. Which treatment does NICE CKS recommend?
o: Steam inhalation at home before bedtime
A five-day course of oral amoxicillin
A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg
Nebulised adrenaline before discharge home
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE CKS Croup (last revised May 2022): prescribe a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg to be taken immediately for mild croup, and advise that symptoms usually resolve within 48 hours.

n.0: Steam is not recommended for croup; it is ineffective and risks scalds.
n.1: Croup is viral, so antibiotics are not indicated.
n.3: Nebulised adrenaline is for moderate to severe croup needing admission; Ruby has mild croup.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ava, 3 weeks, born at 39 weeks, is brought to the children's emergency department with a two-day cold. While on the observation trolley she stops breathing for 20 seconds and becomes dusky, then recovers with stimulation. What does this presentation most suggest?
o: Bronchiolitis with apnoea, needing urgent medical review
Normal periodic breathing of a term newborn during sleep
Reflux episode needing smaller, more frequent feeds
Croup, needing a single dose of oral dexamethasone
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): young infants (particularly under 6 weeks) may present with apnoea without other clinical signs. Apnoea is a red flag for immediate referral and urgent medical review.

n.1: Periodic breathing involves brief pauses of a few seconds without colour change; a dusky 20-second apnoea is not normal.
n.2: Reflux does not explain apnoea with colour change alongside a viral illness; the risk of bronchiolitis apnoea must be assumed.
n.3: Croup causes barking cough and stridor in older infants and toddlers, not apnoea at 3 weeks.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Leon, 9 months, has bronchiolitis on day 4 of illness. His respiratory rate rises to 74 and he is grunting with marked recession and SpO2 87% despite oxygen. Thick secretions are not a problem. Which action is the priority?
o: Escalate urgently for senior review and consider CPAP
Give a trial of nebulised salbutamol and reassess
Perform routine upper airway suction before each feed
Request a chest X-ray to look for consolidation
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): grunting, marked recession and RR above 70 are signs of severe illness; consider CPAP for impending respiratory failure, with urgent senior escalation (national PEWS high or emergency response).

n.1: NG9 says do not use salbutamol in bronchiolitis.
n.2: Routine suction is not recommended; suction is for secretions causing distress, feeding difficulty or apnoea, which Leon does not have.
n.3: NG9 advises against routine chest X-ray; it does not change management and delays escalation.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Theo, 18 months, has croup. He now has stridor at rest, moderate sternal recession and is agitated. His mother asks the nurse to look in his throat to see what is causing the noise. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Take a throat swab now to check for a bacterial infection
Avoid examining his throat; keep him calm on his mother's lap
Use a tongue depressor quickly while his mother holds him still
Lie him flat on the trolley to examine his throat more easily
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE CKS Croup (last revised May 2022) and NHS croup advice: keep the child calm and upright; do not examine the throat, which can precipitate complete obstruction (and epiglottitis must be considered). Stridor at rest with recession is moderate croup needing admission.

n.0: Throat swabbing distresses the child and risks obstruction; croup is viral and needs no swab.
n.2: A tongue depressor can trigger laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction in a child with stridor.
n.3: Lying flat and distress worsen airway obstruction; the child should stay upright and calm.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Maisie, 7 months, was admitted with bronchiolitis. For the last 4 hours, including a sleep, her SpO2 has stayed at 93-95% in air. She is feeding adequately and her breathing is settling. Her parents ask about going home. What does NICE NG9 advise?
o: She should complete a course of antibiotics before discharge
She can go home with safety-netting advice for her parents
She should stay for 24 hours with saturations of 95% or more
She should stay until her cough has fully resolved
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG9 Bronchiolitis in children (updated 2021): discharge when clinically stable, taking adequate oral fluids and maintaining SpO2 above 90% in air (6 weeks and over) for 4 hours including a period of sleep, with safety-netting (cough may last up to 3 weeks).

n.0: NG9 says do not use antibiotics in bronchiolitis.
n.2: NG9 requires 4 hours above 90% including sleep, not 24 hours at 95%.
n.3: The cough resolves within 3 weeks in 90%; waiting for it to stop is not a discharge criterion.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Lily, 3, has had a fever since this morning and is now drowsy. Her father noticed a few dark red spots on her legs which do not fade when pressed with a glass. Her heart rate is 170 and capillary refill time is 4 seconds. What does this presentation most suggest?
o: Viral rash that can be reviewed by the GP tomorrow
Immune thrombocytopenia needing a routine blood count
Meningococcal disease needing emergency treatment
Chickenpox that is entering the crusting stage
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024): fever with a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash suggests meningococcal disease; with tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill there are signs of shock. Transfer or escalate as an emergency.

n.0: A non-blanching rash with fever and drowsiness is a red flag; deferring review risks death from meningococcal sepsis.
n.1: ITP causes petechiae in a well child; Lily is febrile, drowsy and shocked.
n.3: Chickenpox lesions are vesicles that crust, not non-blanching petechiae with shock.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: A practice nurse is assessing Sami, 18 months, who has a fever and is irritable. His skin is dark brown and the nurse cannot see any rash on his limbs or trunk. According to NICE NG240, where else should she check for petechiae?
o: The conjunctivae
The scalp hairline
The tongue
The soles of the feet
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024) rec 1.1.12: check all over the body including nappy areas, and look for petechiae in the conjunctivae because rashes can be hard to detect on brown, black or tanned skin.

n.1: The scalp is not a site NG240 highlights; dense hair makes petechiae harder to see.
n.2: NG240 does not name the tongue; the conjunctivae are specified.
n.3: The soles are checked as part of the whole body, but NG240 names the conjunctivae as the site to check on darker skin.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ellie, 6, has fever, a spreading purpuric rash and cold hands. The GP strongly suspects meningococcal disease and has called 999. The ambulance will arrive in 8 minutes. Ceftriaxone is available. What does NICE NG240 advise?
o: Give oral amoxicillin before the ambulance arrives
Give IV or IM ceftriaxone without delaying transfer
Delay transfer until a lumbar puncture has been arranged
Wait for the hospital to give antibiotics after blood cultures
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024): in suspected meningococcal disease give IV or IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin as soon as possible outside hospital, unless this would delay transfer. Do not delay transfer to give antibiotics.

n.0: Oral antibiotics are not used; NG240 specifies IV or IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin.
n.2: Lumbar puncture is a hospital investigation and must not delay emergency transfer.
n.3: Meningococcal disease can kill within hours; NG240 advises pre-hospital parenteral antibiotics as soon as possible.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Noor, 9 months, is reviewed at home by a community children's nurse for fever. A single small spot on her chest blanches under a glass and she is alert and feeding. She is being managed at home. What advice should the nurse give her parents about the rash?
o: Recheck the rash once her fever has lasted 5 days
Expect the rash to fade once paracetamol is given
Use the glass test hourly through the night
Seek help urgently if the rash stops blanching
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024) rec 1.1.12: tell families to look out for changes in the rash, because it can change from blanching to non-blanching, and to return if it does or if symptoms worsen.

n.0: Five days of fever prompts assessment for Kawasaki disease; a rash becoming non-blanching needs immediate help at any time.
n.1: Antipyretics do not affect a meningococcal rash and may mask fever and ill appearance.
n.2: Waking an alert, feeding baby hourly is not advised; families watch for change and return if worried.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ishaan, 4, is admitted with suspected bacterial meningitis. He has a purpuric rash, heart rate 165, CRT 5 seconds and is responsive to voice. The doctor wants to do a lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics. What is the most appropriate response from the nurse?
o: Position him for the LP after a CT head scan is completed
Suggest antibiotics are held until the CSF results return
Prepare him for the LP so that antibiotics can follow the sample
Ask for antibiotics now, as LP is unsafe while he is shocked
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024): LP before antibiotics only if safe and not causing a clinically significant delay; shock must be treated and stabilised first. In shock with a purpuric rash, antibiotics and fluid resuscitation come first.

n.0: NG240 says not to routinely perform neuroimaging before LP, and it delays treatment.
n.1: Antibiotics must never wait for CSF results in a shocked child.
n.2: Shock is a reason to defer LP; delaying antibiotics for the sample risks rapid deterioration.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Freya, 2, is on a children's ward with confirmed bacterial meningitis. She is now haemodynamically stable and drinking. A junior doctor suggests restricting her fluids to two-thirds of maintenance. According to NICE NG240, what is the best response?
o: Restrict to two-thirds maintenance for the first 48 hours
Restrict to half maintenance and give mannitol
Give her normal maintenance fluids by mouth, unrestricted
Give maintenance as IV fluids and stop oral intake
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024) recs 1.9.1-1.9.2: do not routinely restrict fluid intake below maintenance in bacterial meningitis; give maintenance fluids orally or enterally if tolerated. Osmotic agents are not routine.

n.0: Routine fluid restriction is not recommended; it risks under-perfusion.
n.1: Mannitol is considered only for raised intracranial pressure with herniation concerns, and fluid restriction is not routine.
n.3: NG240 prefers oral or enteral maintenance when tolerated, and Freya is drinking.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Jamal, 7, is recovering from pneumococcal meningitis and is due for discharge next week. His mother asks what follow-up he will need. Which follow-up does NICE NG240 specify for every child after bacterial meningitis?
o: An MRI brain scan around 6 months after he is discharged
Annual pneumococcal vaccine boosters until he is 16
Audiological assessment within 4 weeks of being well enough
A repeat lumbar puncture before he goes back to school
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024) rec 1.12.7: offer an audiological assessment within 4 weeks of being well enough for testing (preferably before discharge), because hearing loss is a common complication; rec 1.13.1 adds a paediatrician review 4 to 6 weeks after discharge.

n.0: Routine MRI is not part of NG240 follow-up.
n.1: Annual pneumococcal boosters are not recommended; vaccination follows the UK schedule and specialist advice.
n.3: Repeat LP is not routine follow-up after recovery.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Mia, 14 months, has fever and irritability. Her rash blanches, but she has a bulging fontanelle and a weak high-pitched cry. On the ward, which observation finding should the nurse escalate as an emergency, and to whom?
o: Bulging fontanelle and weak cry: immediate medical review
Temperature of 38.4°C: routine review at the next ward round
Blanching rash: phone the GP with an update after discharge
Irritability: offer antipyretics and recheck in 4 hours
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG240 Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease (March 2024): bulging fontanelle, weak high-pitched or continuous cry and altered behaviour are signs of bacterial meningitis that may occur without a rash; this needs immediate escalation (PEWS emergency or high response).

n.1: Fever alone is not the key finding; deferring review misses the meningitis signs.
n.2: A blanching rash does not exclude meningitis; NG240 lists bulging fontanelle and abnormal cry as signs.
n.3: Antipyretics may mask fever and ill appearance (NG240) and delay review.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Maya, 18 months, has a cold and a temperature of 39.2°C. Her mother phones the children's assessment unit: Maya has just had her first ever fit, which lasted about 2 minutes and has stopped. Maya is now sleepy but breathing normally. What should the nurse advise?
o: Keep Maya at home as febrile seizures are harmless
Sponge Maya with cool water and call back if it happens again
Bring Maya to hospital now to be checked, by ambulance if needed
Give ibuprofen and book a GP appointment for tomorrow
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NHS febrile seizures guidance: call 999 or go to A&E if a child has a seizure for the first time; a child needs checking in hospital after a first febrile seizure. Do not drive while the child is fitting or unconscious.

n.0: Most febrile seizures are not serious, but a first seizure must be assessed to exclude other causes such as meningitis.
n.1: NHS advice is not to cool a child by sponging or undressing; it does not prevent seizures.
n.3: A first febrile seizure needs same-day hospital assessment, not a routine GP review.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Leo, 2, is being discharged after his first febrile seizure. His father asks whether giving paracetamol and ibuprofen every few hours when Leo has a fever will stop it happening again. What should the nurse explain?
o: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizures; use them if Leo is distressed
Giving paracetamol at the first sign of fever will prevent a seizure
Alternating both medicines regularly will prevent most further seizures
Keeping Leo undressed when feverish will prevent another seizure
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG143 and NHS febrile seizures guidance: antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions and should not be used specifically for this; they are given if the child is distressed. Febrile seizures cannot be prevented.

n.1: Early paracetamol does not prevent febrile seizures.
n.2: Regular alternating antipyretics do not reduce recurrence and NG143 advises against routine alternation.
n.3: Undressing or cooling is not recommended and does not prevent seizures.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ben, 7, starts having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the playroom of the children's ward. He is on the floor next to a toy box. What should the nurse do first?
o: Note the time, move the toy box away and cushion his head
Hold his arms and legs firmly to stop him injuring himself
Lift him on to the nearest bed to examine him
Place a padded tongue depressor between his teeth
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: Seizure first aid (NHS febrile seizures guidance, NG217): note the start time, protect the child from injury by moving hard objects and cushioning the head, do not restrain or put anything in the mouth, and place in the recovery position when the jerking stops.

n.1: Restraining limbs can cause injury and does not shorten the seizure.
n.2: Lifting a convulsing child risks injury to both; protect him where he is.
n.3: Nothing should be put in the mouth; it can break teeth or obstruct the airway.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Aisha, 9, has epilepsy. At school, she starts a tonic-clonic seizure. Her individualised emergency management plan, available in the school office, says to give buccal midazolam if a seizure lasts 5 minutes. After 5 minutes she is still fitting. What should the school nurse do?
o: Give rectal paracetamol to treat a possible fever
Wait until 10 minutes before giving any medicine
Give buccal midazolam as set out in her plan
Wait for the ambulance crew to give IV lorazepam
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG217 Epilepsies (chapter 7, status epilepticus) 7.1.1-7.1.2: convulsive status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more; if an individualised emergency management plan is immediately available, give the medication as detailed in the plan.

n.0: Paracetamol does not stop a seizure.
n.1: Treatment is due at 5 minutes; waiting longer makes the seizure harder to stop.
n.3: IV lorazepam is used where IV access and resuscitation are immediately available; in school the plan's buccal midazolam is given now.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Oscar, 6, is having a convulsive seizure on the children's ward that has lasted 5 minutes. He has a working IV cannula, the resuscitation trolley is at the bedside and he has no individual emergency plan. Which first-line treatment does NICE NG217 recommend?
o: IV levetiracetam
IV lorazepam
Rectal diazepam
Buccal midazolam
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG217 Epilepsies (chapter 7, status epilepticus) 7.1.3: without an individualised plan, give buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community, or IV lorazepam if IV access and resuscitation facilities are immediately available, as they are here.

n.0: Levetiracetam is the second-line treatment after two benzodiazepine doses.
n.2: Rectal diazepam is a community alternative and is slower than IV lorazepam when IV access exists.
n.3: Buccal midazolam is the first-line community option; with IV access and resuscitation facilities NG217 advises IV lorazepam.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Zara, 4, has been fitting for 12 minutes at nursery. The nursery nurse gave buccal midazolam from Zara's plan 8 minutes ago and called 999 straight afterwards. Zara is still convulsing and the ambulance is 5 minutes away. Her plan allows a second dose. What should happen now?
o: Give a second dose once the ambulance crew arrive
Give oral levetiracetam from her daily medicines
Wait, as one benzodiazepine dose is the limit outside hospital
Give the second dose of benzodiazepine set out in her plan
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG217 Epilepsies (chapter 7, status epilepticus) 7.1.7-7.1.8: if status does not respond to the first dose, call emergency services, and continue to follow the individualised plan or give a second benzodiazepine dose if the seizure has not stopped 5 to 10 minutes after the first.

n.0: Waiting for the crew adds further delay when the plan already allows a second dose now.
n.1: Nothing should be given by mouth to a convulsing child, and oral maintenance doses do not stop status epilepticus.
n.2: NG217 allows a second benzodiazepine dose 5-10 minutes after the first when the plan says so.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ethan, 10, with type 1 diabetes, has a generalised seizure that stops after 3 minutes. He is now in the recovery position, breathing with SpO2 97% on oxygen, and responds only to voice. What should the nurse check next?
o: Serum calcium
Blood pressure in both arms
Temperature by tympanic probe
Capillary blood glucose
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG217 Epilepsies (chapter 7, status epilepticus) 7.1.4 and RCUK 2025 (D of ABCDE): consider underlying causes such as hypoglycaemia; check glucose in any child with a seizure or reduced consciousness, especially with diabetes, and treat if low.

n.0: Calcium is checked in some settings, but hypoglycaemia is the urgent, readily reversible cause for a child with diabetes.
n.1: Blood pressure is recorded, but bilateral readings do not address the likely cause.
n.2: Temperature is part of the assessment, but glucose is the priority after a seizure in a child with diabetes.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Jamie, 11, had a seizure 30 minutes ago and is now drowsy on the children's ward. The nurse is doing neurological observations. Which finding should be escalated immediately as a new concern?
o: Complains of a headache and wants to sleep
Unequal pupils, with the left pupil slower to react
Sleepy but rouses to voice and knows his own name
Heart rate 92 and respiratory rate 20
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: Neurological observations after a seizure: post-ictal drowsiness and headache are expected, but new pupil inequality or a sluggish pupil suggests raised intracranial pressure or a structural cause and is an emergency trigger on the national PEWS chart (abnormal pupils).

n.0: Headache and sleepiness are common after a seizure and are monitored rather than escalated alone.
n.2: Rousing to voice and knowing his name fits expected post-ictal recovery.
n.3: HR 92 and RR 20 are within normal ranges for an 11-year-old (RCUK 2025).

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ruby, 6, has lost weight over three weeks, is drinking constantly and has started wetting the bed again. At a GP practice her capillary glucose is 19 mmol/L. She is alert and not vomiting. What should happen next?
o: Same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team
Routine paediatric outpatient referral within 2 weeks
Repeat capillary glucose at the practice in 48 hours
Fasting glucose test booked for next week
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.1.2: refer children and young people with suspected type 1 diabetes immediately (on the same day) to a multidisciplinary paediatric diabetes team, because DKA can develop quickly.

n.1: A routine referral is too slow for suspected type 1 diabetes.
n.2: Delaying 48 hours risks progression to DKA.
n.3: Waiting a week for a fasting test risks DKA; NG18 requires same-day referral.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Jake, 10, has type 1 diabetes. In the school nurse's office he is shaky and sweaty and his capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. He is alert and able to swallow. What should the nurse give first?
o: A slice of wholemeal toast and a glass of milk
A chocolate bar and a biscuit
