15 g of fast-acting glucose, such as juice
IM glucagon 1 mg into the thigh
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.2.89: treat mild to moderate hypoglycaemia immediately with oral fast-acting glucose (10-20 g; liquid may be easier), recheck within 15 minutes, then give complex carbohydrate.

n.0: Toast and milk are complex carbohydrate, given after glucose has been restored, not first.
n.1: Fat in chocolate slows glucose absorption; fast-acting glucose works within 5-15 minutes.
n.3: Glucagon is for severe hypoglycaemia when oral treatment is unsafe; Jake can swallow.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: After treating Kiran, 12, for hypoglycaemia with 15 g of glucose tablets, the nurse plans the next step. Kiran has type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections, and his next meal is 2 hours away. When should his capillary glucose be rechecked?
o: After 1 hour
After 30 minutes
Within 15 minutes
At his next meal
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.2.89: recheck blood glucose within 15 minutes (fast-acting glucose should act within 5-15 minutes) and give more if still low; then complex carbohydrate as his meal is not imminent.

n.0: One hour is far too long to leave a possible ongoing hypo.
n.1: Thirty minutes leaves a persistent hypo untreated for too long.
n.3: Waiting 2 hours risks recurrent or worsening hypoglycaemia.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Lola, 6, weighs 21 kg and has type 1 diabetes. At home she is drowsy and cannot swallow safely; her glucose meter reads 2.2 mmol/L. Her mother has a glucagon kit and phones the community children's nurse. What dose of IM glucagon should be given?
o: 2 mg
500 micrograms
250 micrograms
1 mg
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people rec 1.2.91: IM glucagon 500 micrograms for children under 8 years or under 25 kg; 1 mg if over 8 years or 25 kg or more. Seek medical help if no response within 10 minutes.

n.0: 2 mg exceeds every NG18 dose.
n.2: 250 micrograms is below the NG18 dose.
n.3: 1 mg is for children over 8 years or weighing 25 kg or more; Lola is 6 and 21 kg.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Amir, 13, presents with vomiting, abdominal pain and deep sighing breathing. His glucose is 28 mmol/L, venous pH 7.15, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L and blood ketones 5.2 mmol/L. He has a heart rate of 120, warm hands and CRT 2 seconds. How is his DKA classified under BSPED 2021?
o: Severe DKA
Hyperglycaemia without DKA
Moderate DKA
Mild DKA
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BSPED DKA guideline (2021): DKA = acidosis (pH < 7.3 or bicarbonate < 15) with ketones > 3.0 mmol/L. Severity by pH: mild 7.2-7.29, moderate 7.1-7.19 (or bicarbonate < 10), severe < 7.1 (or bicarbonate < 5). pH 7.15 = moderate.

n.0: Severe DKA is pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 5.
n.1: Acidosis with ketones above 3.0 mmol/L meets the DKA definition.
n.3: Mild DKA is pH 7.2-7.29; Amir's pH is 7.15.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ella, 9, has moderate DKA and is not shocked. She received a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 minutes and her IV deficit and maintenance fluids started 40 minutes ago. The registrar asks when the insulin infusion should begin. What does BSPED advise?
o: Start the infusion 1-2 hours after IV fluids began, with no bolus
Start the infusion at the same time as the first fluid bolus
Give an insulin bolus now, then start the infusion
Wait until her pH is above 7.3 before starting any insulin
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BSPED DKA guideline (2021): start IV insulin infusion 1-2 hours after beginning IV fluids, at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour, and do not give an insulin bolus, because early insulin and boluses may increase the risk of cerebral oedema.

n.1: Insulin started with the first fluids is linked to higher cerebral oedema risk; BSPED delays it 1-2 hours.
n.2: BSPED says do not give bolus doses of insulin.
n.3: Insulin is needed to switch off ketone production; waiting for pH to normalise would prolong DKA.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Noah, 7, is 6 hours into treatment for severe DKA. He was alert on admission. He now complains of a headache, is irritable and his heart rate has fallen from 130 to 78 while his blood pressure has risen. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Call the doctor urgently for suspected cerebral oedema
Increase the IV fluid rate to treat dehydration
Give oral paracetamol and recheck observations in 1 hour
Reduce the insulin infusion and recheck glucose in 2 hours
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: BSPED DKA guideline (2021): headache, irritability, slowing pulse, rising blood pressure and reduced consciousness are warning signs of cerebral oedema; report immediately (even at night). Treatment is hypertonic saline or mannitol and senior help.

n.1: Extra fluid may worsen cerebral oedema; fluids are restricted, not increased.
n.2: Treating the headache as minor delays emergency treatment of cerebral oedema.
n.3: Adjusting insulin does not treat cerebral oedema and delays urgent review.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Sophie, 11, has type 1 diabetes and a vomiting illness at home. Her glucose is 16 mmol/L. Her mother asks the diabetes nurse what to check, following the sick-day rules. Which check is most important now?
o: Urine for protein, using a reagent dipstick
Her HbA1c, using a home finger-prick test kit
Her blood pressure, using a home monitor
Blood ketones, using her ketone meter and strips
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people: offer blood ketone strips and a meter, and advise testing for ketonaemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate) during illness or hyperglycaemia, as part of sick-day rules, to detect early DKA.

n.0: Proteinuria does not detect impending DKA; ketones do.
n.1: HbA1c reflects 2-3 months of control and is measured 4 times a year in clinic, not during acute illness.
n.2: Blood pressure does not show developing ketoacidosis.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Freddie, 2, weighs 12 kg and has had gastroenteritis for two days. He has dry mucous membranes and is passing less urine, but he is alert with normal skin turgor and capillary refill. The plan is oral rehydration solution (ORS) for clinical dehydration. What volume should be given for rehydration?
o: 1200 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance
600 mL over 24 hours, including maintenance
120 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance
600 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s: for clinical dehydration without red flags give low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, in small frequent amounts. 50 mL/kg x 12 kg = 600 mL.

n.0: 1200 mL is 100 mL/kg, the IV deficit used for a child who was shocked at presentation.
n.1: Spreading 600 mL over 24 hours as total intake ignores maintenance and corrects the deficit too slowly.
n.2: 120 mL is 10 mL/kg, far below the CG84 rehydration volume.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Poppy, 3, attends nursery and has gastroenteritis. Her last episode of vomiting and diarrhoea was on Monday at 18:00. Her mother asks when Poppy can go back to nursery. What should the nurse advise?
o: From Thursday at 18:00
Once she has passed a formed stool
From Wednesday at 18:00
From Tuesday at 18:00
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s rec 1.8.2.1: children should not return to school or childcare until at least 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting. Monday 18:00 + 48 hours = Wednesday 18:00.

n.0: Thursday at 18:00 is 72 hours, longer than required.
n.1: Exclusion is timed from the last episode, not from a formed stool.
n.3: Tuesday at 18:00 is only 24 hours after the last episode.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ayla, 8 months, is breastfed and has diarrhoea for a day. She is alert, feeding and has no signs of dehydration. Her mother wants to stop breastfeeding and give diluted apple juice instead. What should the nurse advise?
o: Give flat cola between breastfeeds to replace sugar and salt
Continue breastfeeding and offer extra fluids such as ORS
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and give diluted apple juice
Change to diluted formula until the diarrhoea has stopped
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s: continue breastfeeding and other milk feeds, encourage fluid intake, and discourage fruit juices and carbonated drinks; offer ORS as supplemental fluid if at increased risk of dehydration.

n.0: Carbonated drinks are discouraged because their sugar and low sodium can worsen diarrhoea.
n.2: CG84 says continue breastfeeding and discourage fruit juice, which can worsen diarrhoea.
n.3: Diluting milk feeds is not recommended; full-strength milk is given.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Daisy, 10 months, has a fever and is being assessed for a urinary tract infection on the children's assessment unit. Her mother suggests putting a cotton wool ball inside Daisy's nappy to collect urine. Which method should the nurse use first?
o: A gauze pad in the nappy
A suprapubic aspirate
A cotton wool ball in the nappy
A clean catch urine sample
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022): use a clean catch wherever possible; if not possible use urine collection pads per manufacturer's instructions. Do not use cotton wool balls, gauze or sanitary towels. Catheter or suprapubic aspiration only if non-invasive methods are not possible.

n.0: NG224 says do not use gauze to collect urine.
n.1: Suprapubic aspiration is invasive and used when non-invasive methods are not possible.
n.2: NG224 says do not use cotton wool balls to collect urine; fibres contaminate the sample.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Josh, 5, has had dysuria and frequency for a day. He is well, with a temperature of 37.6°C. A dipstick test on a fresh clean catch sample is positive for both leukocyte esterase and nitrite. He has had no previous UTIs. What does NICE NG224 advise?
o: Treat as a UTI and start antibiotics
Send for culture and wait for the result
Request an urgent renal ultrasound scan
Repeat the dipstick on a second sample
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022) Table 2 (3 years or older): leukocyte esterase and nitrite both positive = assume UTI and give antibiotics; send for culture only if high or intermediate risk of serious illness or previous UTI.

n.1: With both markers positive NG224 says assume UTI and start antibiotics, rather than waiting for culture.
n.2: Ultrasound is not needed in the acute phase for a typical first UTI responding to treatment.
n.3: Dipstick testing in a child aged 3 or over is as useful as microscopy and culture; a repeat adds nothing.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Leah, 7 weeks, has a temperature of 38.3°C and is feeding less. The practice nurse obtains a clean catch urine sample, which is cloudy and smells offensive. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start oral amoxicillin and review in 24 hours
Refer her immediately to a paediatric specialist
Send the sample for culture and review in 48 hours
Dipstick the urine and start oral trimethoprim
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022) and NICE NG143: babies under 3 months with suspected UTI are referred immediately to paediatric specialist care; a temperature of 38°C or more under 3 months is red (high risk), and parenteral antibiotics are given.

n.0: Oral antibiotics in the community are not appropriate for a febrile baby under 3 months.
n.2: Waiting 48 hours for culture is unsafe for a febrile baby under 3 months.
n.3: Oral treatment in primary care is for children over 3 months; Leah needs specialist care.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Rania, 6, has a fever and vomiting but no urinary symptoms. A dipstick on her clean catch urine is positive for leukocyte esterase and negative for nitrite. According to NICE NG224, what should happen?
o: Repeat the dipstick test on a fresh sample in 1 week
Treat as asymptomatic bacteriuria with no further action
Start antibiotics for a UTI straight away
Send urine for culture and look for another cause of fever
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG224 Urinary tract infection in under 16s (2022) Table 2: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative = send for microscopy and culture; do not give antibiotics unless there is good clinical evidence of UTI. A positive leukocyte result may reflect infection elsewhere.

n.0: A one-week delay leaves a febrile child without a diagnosis.
n.1: Rania is febrile and unwell, so this is not asymptomatic, and culture is needed.
n.2: Antibiotics are withheld unless there is good clinical evidence of UTI, which Rania lacks.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: A children's ward has three children with norovirus gastroenteritis. A parent of one child asks whether using the alcohol hand gel by the bed is enough after changing nappies. What should the nurse advise?
o: Use the alcohol hand gel after each nappy change
Wash hands with soap and warm running water, then dry well
Wear gloves for nappy changes so hand washing is not needed
Use antibacterial hand wipes after every nappy change instead
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s rec 1.8.2.1: washing hands with soap (liquid if possible) in warm running water and careful drying are the most important factors in preventing spread. Alcohol gel is less effective against norovirus.

n.0: Alcohol gel does not reliably inactivate norovirus and does not remove soiling.
n.2: Gloves reduce contamination, but hands still need washing after removing them.
n.3: Wipes do not replace washing with soap and running water.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Sarah and Tom have a son, Jack, 3, who has cystic fibrosis. Neither parent has the condition. They are planning another baby and ask the nurse what the chance is that their next child will have cystic fibrosis. What is the correct answer?
o: 1 in 2 for each pregnancy
1 in 4 across all future pregnancies
1 in 4 for each pregnancy
2 in 3 for each pregnancy
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive. Two unaffected carrier parents have a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of an affected child in EACH pregnancy, a 1 in 2 chance of a carrier and 1 in 4 of a non-carrier. Chance does not change with previous outcomes.

n.0: 1 in 2 is the chance in each pregnancy for an autosomal dominant condition with one affected parent, or of a carrier child here.
n.1: The risk applies independently to each pregnancy; it is not shared out across them.
n.3: 2 in 3 is the chance that an UNAFFECTED sibling is a carrier, not the chance of an affected child.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Baby Amelia's newborn blood spot test shows a raised immunoreactive trypsin result, and the screening laboratory reports a likely cystic fibrosis result. She is feeding well and gaining weight. Her parents ask how the diagnosis will be confirmed. Which test is used?
o: A repeat blood spot test at 6 weeks
A sweat test, with gene testing
A chest X-ray and sputum culture
A faecal elastase stool test
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG78 Cystic fibrosis: diagnosis and management rec 1.1.1: CF can be diagnosed from positive infant screening (blood spot immunoreactive trypsin) followed by sweat and gene tests for confirmation; refer to a specialist CF centre.

n.0: A repeat blood spot does not confirm CF; NG78 specifies sweat and gene tests.
n.2: A chest X-ray and sputum culture assess lung involvement but do not confirm the diagnosis.
n.3: Faecal elastase tests for pancreatic insufficiency once CF is known; it does not diagnose CF.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Two children with cystic fibrosis are admitted to the same children's ward. Ollie, 9, has chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection; Ava, 8, does not. They know each other and ask to spend the afternoon together in the playroom. What should the nurse do?
o: Let them play together if they sit at least 1 metre apart
Let them play together as they already know each other
Arrange separate play and explain the cross-infection risk
Let them share the playroom if both wear surgical masks
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG78 Cystic fibrosis: diagnosis and management recs 1.8.2-1.8.6: prevent cross-infection by cohorting and keeping people with CF separate; keep people with chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Burkholderia cepacia complex separate from those without, including in communal and recreation areas.

n.0: One metre does not prevent transmission of Pseudomonas between people with CF; NG78 advises separation.
n.1: Friendship does not reduce cross-infection risk; Ava could acquire chronic Pseudomonas.
n.3: Masks do not make shared communal space safe; NG78 separates people with CF from each other.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Maddie, 6, has cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency. Her mother says Maddie has greasy, foul-smelling stools and is not gaining weight. Maddie takes her pancreatic enzyme capsules only with breakfast. What advice should the nurse give, with the dietitian?
o: Stop the enzymes for a week to see if her stools change
Give a double dose of enzymes with breakfast only
Give enzymes with every fat-containing meal and snack
Reduce the fat in her diet so that she needs fewer enzymes
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE NG78 Cystic fibrosis: diagnosis and management recs 1.7.2 and 1.7.6: offer oral pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and adjust the dose to minimise malabsorption; enzymes are taken with all fat-containing meals, snacks and milk drinks. Calorie intake is increased, not reduced.

n.0: Stopping enzymes would worsen malabsorption and weight loss.
n.1: Enzymes act on the food eaten at that time; a large breakfast dose does not cover later meals.
n.3: Children with CF need high-energy diets; reducing fat worsens faltering growth.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Noah, 5 months, has unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot and is awaiting surgery. While crying during a blood test he becomes deeply blue, breathes fast and then becomes limp. What should the nurse do first?
o: Sit him upright and encourage him to keep crying
Lie him flat and raise his legs on a pillow
Calm him and hold him with his knees drawn up to his chest
Give a rapid bolus of IV fluid before calling for help
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: A hypercyanotic (tet) spell: crying increases right-to-left shunting. First aid is to calm the infant and place him in the knee-chest position, which raises systemic vascular resistance and pulmonary blood flow; then give oxygen and call for urgent medical help.

n.0: Continued crying worsens the shunt and cyanosis.
n.1: Lying flat with legs raised does not increase systemic resistance in the way the knee-chest position does.
n.3: Fluids may be prescribed by the medical team, but positioning and calling for help come first.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Kai, 10, had surgical repair of tetralogy of Fallot as a baby and is at increased risk of infective endocarditis. His mother asks how to reduce the risk at his routine dental check-ups. What should the nurse advise, in line with NICE CG64?
o: Take amoxicillin before every routine check-up
Use chlorhexidine mouthwash before each dental visit
Delay check-ups until he moves to adult services
Keep up good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: NICE CG64 recs 1.1.2-1.1.4: give people at increased risk clear information on maintaining good oral health, symptoms of endocarditis and the risks of piercing or tattooing. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routine, and chlorhexidine mouthwash should not be offered.

n.0: A routine check-up is not an invasive procedure, and antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely recommended.
n.1: CG64 rec 1.1.4 says chlorhexidine mouthwash should not be offered as prophylaxis for dental procedures.
n.2: Poor dental health increases endocarditis risk; regular check-ups are encouraged.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Leila, 3, has a palliated cyanotic congenital heart condition. Her usual SpO2 is 78-82% in air, and her cardiology plan records this. She is admitted with a cough. On the national PEWS chart, how should the nurse handle her saturations?
o: Score SpO2 as charted and record her usual baseline on the chart
Leave SpO2 unscored because low readings are normal for her
Add a correction so that her baseline counts as a zero score
Stop measuring SpO2 and rely on her colour and work of breathing
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: National PEWS (NHS England/RCPCH, 2023): children with 'normally abnormal' saturations still score, because low baseline saturations mean less reserve; there is no derogation. Baseline values are recorded in the chart's box for context and clinical judgement.

n.1: The national PEWS has no derogation; leaving SpO2 unscored hides reduced reserve.
n.2: PEWS does not allow local corrections to the score for cardiac patients.
n.3: SpO2 is a scored parameter; stopping it removes a key trend in a child with less reserve.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ben, 4, has just been diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive condition. Genetic testing shows his mother is a carrier and his father is unaffected. His parents ask about the risk for a future son. What is the chance that a future son will be affected?
o: 1 in 2
1 in 4
Nil, as his father is unaffected
1 in 8
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: X-linked recessive inheritance: a carrier mother passes her affected X to half of her children. Each son has a 1 in 2 chance of being affected; each daughter a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier.

n.1: 1 in 4 is the chance across ALL children (sons and daughters) of an affected son, not the chance for a son.
n.2: Sons inherit their X chromosome from the mother, so the father's status does not protect a son.
n.3: 1 in 8 does not apply to any child of a carrier mother.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: During a home visit, a community children's nurse trained in paediatric basic life support finds Ivy, 4 months, unresponsive in her cot and not breathing normally. Her mother has called 999 on speaker phone. The nurse has opened Ivy's airway in a neutral position. What should the nurse do next?
o: Feel for a brachial pulse for up to 30 seconds before acting
Start chest compressions at a ratio of 15 compressions to 2 breaths
Give 5 initial rescue breaths covering Ivy's mouth and nose
Give 2 rescue breaths and then 30 chest compressions
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: after opening the airway and confirming absent or abnormal breathing (no more than 10 seconds), give 5 initial rescue breaths, mouth-to-mouth-and-nose in an infant, before starting compressions at 15:2.

n.0: Pulse palpation is unreliable and delays CPR; RCUK limits the check for breathing or signs of life to no more than 10 seconds.
n.1: Compressions at 15:2 follow the 5 initial rescue breaths; children usually arrest from hypoxia, so oxygenation comes first.
n.3: Two breaths then 30 compressions is the adult sequence; RCUK 2025 starts paediatric CPR with 5 rescue breaths.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Kai, 7 weeks, is in cardiac arrest on a children's ward. Two nurses trained in paediatric life support are giving CPR while the arrest team is on the way. According to RCUK 2025, which chest compression technique should be used for Kai?
o: Two thumbs side by side on the upper third of the sternum
Two fingertips placed on the lower half of the sternum
The heel of one hand placed on the lower half of the sternum
Two thumbs on the lower sternum with hands encircling the chest
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support recommends the two-thumb encircling technique for ALL infant compressions (single or two rescuers), on the lower half of the sternum, depth at least one third of the chest, 100-120 per minute.

n.0: Compressions are delivered over the lower half of the sternum; the upper sternum does not compress the heart effectively.
n.1: The two-finger technique was used for lone rescuers in earlier guidance; RCUK 2025 uses two-thumb encircling for every infant.
n.2: One hand (or two) is the technique for a child over 1 year, not for a 7-week-old infant.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Noah, 6, collapses on a children's ward and is not breathing. Two registered nurses trained in paediatric basic life support start resuscitation after the initial rescue breaths. What ratio of compressions to ventilations should they use?
o: 5 compressions to 1 breath
15 compressions to 2 breaths
30 compressions to 2 breaths
3 compressions to 1 breath
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support: rescuers trained in paediatric BLS use 15:2 for infants and children, in and out of hospital. 30:2 is for untrained or adult-trained bystanders.

n.0: 5:1 is an outdated ratio that is not part of current RCUK paediatric guidance.
n.2: 30:2 is advised for rescuers not trained in paediatric BLS; trained ward nurses use 15:2.
n.3: 3:1 is the newborn life support ratio at birth, not the ratio for a 6-year-old.

Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.q: Ella, 9 months, is choking on a piece of apple in a clinic waiting room. She is conscious, but her cough is now silent and she cannot cry. Help has been called. What should the nurse do first?
o: Give up to 5 back blows with Ella head-down along the forearm
Give up to 5 abdominal thrusts with Ella held upright
Sweep a finger through Ella's mouth to hook out the food
Give 5 rescue breaths with Ella lying flat on her back
Paediatric Emergencies and Common Condit.w: RCUK 2025 Paediatric Basic Life Support choking algorithm: if the cough becomes ineffective in a conscious infant, give up to 5 back blows with the infant face down along the forearm and head lower than the chest, then up to 5 chest thrusts.

n.1: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants because of the risk of abdominal organ injury; infants receive chest thrusts after back blows.
n.2: Blind finger sweeps can push the object further down; remove it only if clearly visible.
n.3: Rescue breaths start when a choking child becomes unconscious; Ella is still conscious.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Baby Isaac was born at 38 weeks. His mother takes labetalol for hypertension in pregnancy. Isaac breastfed at 40 minutes old. At 3 hours, before the second feed, his blood glucose is 1.6 mmol/L. He is alert, warm and showing feeding cues. Which action does the BAPM framework support?
o: Give 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg with a supported breastfeed
Give formula at 150 mL/kg/day and recheck glucose in 6 hours
Continue feeding with no further glucose checks
Start IV 10% glucose before the next feed
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice points 16 and 18: if the first pre-feed glucose is 1.0-1.9 mmol/L with no abnormal signs (Flowchart B), buccal 40% glucose gel 200 mg/kg may be given alongside feeding support, with repeat measurement.

n.1: Formula volumes in the first 24 hours are 40-60 mL/kg/day, and a 6-hour wait is too long.
n.2: A baby at risk with glucose of 1.6 mmol/L needs treatment and repeat measurement.
n.3: IV glucose is for severe (below 1.0 mmol/L) or persistent hypoglycaemia, or abnormal signs, after medical review.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Baby Ruby, born at term to a mother with type 1 diabetes, is 4 hours old. She has been jittery and her pre-feed blood glucose on the ward blood gas analyser is 0.8 mmol/L. What is the priority?
o: Repeat the measurement on a handheld meter to confirm it
Urgent medical review for IV access and glucose treatment
Give 40% glucose gel and recheck glucose in 4 hours
Give a breastfeed and recheck glucose before the next feed
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice points 19-21: blood glucose below 1.0 mmol/L at any time is severe hypoglycaemia; arrange urgent medical review including IV access and glucose. Gel may be used only as an interim measure while IV access is obtained.

n.0: Ward blood gas analysers are accurate; many handheld meters are inaccurate below 2.0 mmol/L, so repeating delays treatment.
n.2: Gel is an interim measure while IV access is obtained, and a 4-hour recheck is far too late.
n.3: Feeding alone is not enough for glucose below 1.0 mmol/L at any time; BAPM requires urgent medical review and IV glucose.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Four babies were born at term on the same day. Which baby has a recognised risk factor that means blood glucose monitoring should start before the second feed?
o: Dev, who was born after a labour of 14 hours
Cara, whose mother had an epidural in labour
Ava, whose mother took labetalol in the third trimester
Ben, born by planned caesarean section under spinal
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024): risk factors for impaired metabolic adaptation include fetal growth restriction (birth weight below the 2nd centile), maternal diabetes and maternal beta-blockers in the third trimester or at birth. At-risk babies have glucose measured before the second feed (2-4 hours after birth).

n.0: A 14-hour labour is not a BAPM risk factor.
n.1: Maternal epidural is not a BAPM risk factor.
n.3: Caesarean birth is not a BAPM risk factor for neonatal hypoglycaemia.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Baby Mia, born at 39 weeks to a mother with gestational diabetes, fed well at 30 minutes old and is now 2 hours old. She is asleep, warm and pink. When should her first blood glucose be measured, according to BAPM?
o: Immediately at birth, before her first feed
At 1 hour of age, whether or not she has fed
At 24 hours, if she shows any signs of illness
Before her second feed, 2 to 4 hours after birth
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice point 15: measure blood glucose before the second feed (2 to 4 hours after birth), or immediately if there are clinical signs suggestive of hypoglycaemia.

n.0: A glucose at birth reflects normal transitional lows and prompts unnecessary intervention.
n.1: A 1-hour check falls within the normal postnatal glucose dip and is not the BAPM timing.
n.2: Waiting 24 hours misses early hypoglycaemia in an at-risk baby.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Baby Oscar was born on Monday morning at 39 weeks and went home on Tuesday. His mother asks the community children's nurse when the heel prick (newborn blood spot) test will be done. What should the nurse tell her?
o: Before he leaves hospital at 24 hours
When he is 14 days old
At the 6 to 8 week check with the GP
Usually when Oscar is 5 days old
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NHS newborn blood spot test guidance: the test is normally done when the baby is 5 days old (sometimes a little earlier or later), usually at home by the community midwife or health visitor.

n.0: Testing at 24 hours is too early for reliable results for some conditions, such as PKU, which need feeding to be established.
n.1: Fourteen days is too late; treatment for conditions such as MCADD may need to start in the first weeks.
n.2: The 6-8 week check is the second NIPE examination, not the blood spot test.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Amara's parents ask what the newborn blood spot test will look for. Which condition is included in the routine NHS newborn blood spot screen?
o: Sickle cell disease
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Coeliac disease
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NHS newborn blood spot test guidance: the screen covers sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism and inherited metabolic diseases (PKU, MCADD, MSUD, IVA, GA1, HCU, HT1); SMA in some areas only.

n.1: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is not part of the UK newborn blood spot screen.
n.2: Hip dysplasia is checked by physical examination (NIPE), not by the blood spot.
n.3: Coeliac disease is not part of the newborn blood spot screen.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Baby Ellie is 30 hours old and ready for discharge. Her mother asks what the newborn physical examination (NIPE) checks and when it is done. What should the nurse explain?
o: A hearing test using a soft earpiece before 4 weeks
Eyes, heart, hips and testes, checked within 72 hours
A heel prick blood test done on day 5 at home
A check of growth and development at 2 years
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NHS newborn screening: the newborn and infant physical examination (NIPE) is done within 72 hours of birth (and again at 6-8 weeks) and checks the eyes, heart, hips and, in boys, testes.

n.0: That is the newborn hearing screen, a separate programme.
n.2: That describes the blood spot test, not the physical examination.
n.3: That is the 2 to 2.5 year health visitor review, not NIPE.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Jade has brought her 3-week-old son to a children's clinic. She says he settles better on his tummy and asks whether she can put him to sleep that way. What should the nurse advise?
o: Place him on his back for every sleep, day and night
Place him on his side, propped with a rolled towel
Let him sleep on his tummy if she checks him often
Place him on his tummy for daytime naps
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Lullaby Trust safer sleep advice: the safest sleep position is on the back for every sleep, day or night, in a clear, flat cot. Front and side sleeping increase the risk of SIDS.

n.1: Side sleeping is unsafe because babies can roll on to their front, and rolled towels are a suffocation risk.
n.2: Frequent checking does not remove the increased SIDS risk of front sleeping.
n.3: The back position is advised for daytime naps as well as at night.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: During a home visit to 6-week-old Theo, the community children's nurse notes the nursery thermometer reads 24°C. Theo is in a cot with a duvet and a hat on. What advice should the nurse give?
o: Keep the room at 16-20°C and take off his hat and duvet
Keep the room at 24°C but replace the duvet with a quilt
Keep the room at 24°C, as young babies need extra warmth
Keep the hat on at night and turn the room down to 22°C
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Lullaby Trust safer sleep advice: the recommended room temperature is 16-20°C; babies should not wear hats indoors for sleep and should sleep in a clear cot without duvets or pillows. Overheating increases SIDS risk.

n.1: 24°C is above the recommended range, and quilts are as risky as duvets.
n.2: Overheating increases SIDS risk; 16-20°C is advised.
n.3: 22°C is still above the recommended range, and hats for sleep cause overheating.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Priya's daughter is 10 weeks old and sleeps in a cot beside her parents' bed. Priya says friends have told her to move the baby into her own room now. What does the Lullaby Trust advise?
o: Move her into her own room once she reaches 3 months
Keep her in the same room with you until she is 2 years old
Keep her in the same room for at least the first 6 months
Move her to her own room once she sleeps through
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Lullaby Trust safer sleep advice: sleep the baby in a cot in the same room as the parents for at least the first 6 months; safer sleep advice applies until 12 months (corrected for prematurity).

n.0: Three months is earlier than the advised minimum of 6 months.
n.1: Two years is not the safer sleep recommendation; the advice is at least 6 months.
n.3: Sleeping through the night is not a safe sleep milestone.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: A health visitor is reviewing four situations described by parents of young babies. Which situation carries the greatest risk of sudden infant death?
o: Baby breastfed in bed, then returned to her cot
Baby asleep on her back in a pram in the garden in a sleeping bag
Baby asleep on his back in a cot in the parents' room
Falling asleep holding the baby on a sofa after a night feed
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Lullaby Trust safer sleep advice: sleeping with a baby on a sofa or armchair greatly increases the risk of SIDS and accidental suffocation; parents should put the baby down in a clear cot if they may fall asleep.

n.0: Feeding in bed and returning the baby to her own cot follows safer sleep advice.
n.1: A pram with a correctly fitted sleeping bag and the baby on her back is a lower-risk arrangement.
n.2: Back sleeping in a cot in the parents' room is the recommended safe arrangement.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Lucy is formula feeding her 2-week-old son and shows the nurse how she makes up feeds: she fills the bottle with cooled boiled water from a jug left out overnight, then adds the powder. What should the nurse advise?
o: Add the powder first, then fill with cold tap water
Use bottled mineral water at room temperature for each feed
Use cooled boiled water from the jug if it was boiled within 24 hours
Use freshly boiled water left no more than 30 minutes, at 70°C or above
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NHS formula preparation guidance: make up each feed with freshly boiled water left to cool for no more than 30 minutes so it is at least 70°C, which kills bacteria such as Cronobacter in the powder. Water first, then powder.

n.0: Cold tap water does not make the powder safe, and adding powder first gives an inaccurate concentration.
n.1: Bottled mineral water can contain high sodium and is not hot enough to make the powder safe.
n.2: Water that has stood overnight is below 70°C and will not kill bacteria in the powder.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Jamie, 3, weighs 14 kg and is prescribed IV gentamicin 7 mg/kg once daily. The nurse is checking the prescription before preparing the dose. What dose should be given?
o: 49 mg
980 mg
9.8 mg
98 mg
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Weight-based dosing: 7 mg/kg x 14 kg = 98 mg. Children's doses are calculated from a current weight in kilograms and checked against the BNF for Children.

n.0: 49 mg is half the dose (3.5 mg/kg) and would under-treat infection.
n.1: 980 mg is a ten-fold overdose, the characteristic paediatric error.
n.2: 9.8 mg is a ten-fold under-dose from a misplaced decimal point.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ava, 2, weighs 12 kg and is prescribed oral morphine for post-operative pain. The ward guideline gives 200 micrograms/kg per dose. The prescription reads 'morphine oral 24 mg'. What should the nurse do?
o: Withhold it and ask the prescriber to review the dose
Give half the dose now and the remainder in 1 hour
Give the dose, as morphine needs vary between children
Give 2.4 mg, then ask the prescriber to amend the chart
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: 200 micrograms/kg x 12 kg = 2400 micrograms = 2.4 mg, so 24 mg is ten times the expected dose. The nurse must not give it, should contact the prescriber to amend it and report the near miss (NMC Code standard 18 on administering medicines and 19.1 on near misses; local incident reporting).

n.1: Splitting a ten-fold overdose still gives five times the safe dose within the hour.
n.2: A ten-fold opioid overdose risks respiratory arrest; variation in need does not justify it.
n.3: The nurse cannot give a dose that differs from the prescription; the prescriber must rewrite it first.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Leo, 4, is admitted to the children's ward for IV antibiotics. His father says Leo weighed 'about two and a half stone' at the GP a few months ago. What should the nurse do before medicines are prescribed?
o: Weigh Leo now and record his weight in kilograms
Convert two and a half stone to kilograms and record it
Estimate his weight using an age-based formula
Use the weight in his GP record from a few months ago
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Children's doses are weight-based, so the child should be weighed on admission and the weight recorded in kilograms. Estimated, converted or old weights are a recognised source of dosing error.

n.1: Converting an old, approximate weight in stones adds conversion error to an out-of-date figure.
n.2: Age-based estimates are for emergencies when weighing is not possible; Leo can be weighed.
n.3: A weight from months ago may be inaccurate in a growing or unwell child.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Maya, 18 months, is prescribed oral paracetamol suspension. The nurse finds that the only syringes in the clean utility room are IV (Luer) syringes. What should the nurse use to measure and give the dose?
o: A Luer syringe with the tip removed after drawing up
A Luer IV syringe, labelled clearly as 'for oral use'
A 5 mL medicine spoon instead of any syringe
An oral or enteral syringe from another ward or pharmacy
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: National patient safety guidance requires oral liquids to be measured and given with oral or enteral (ENFit) syringes, which cannot connect to IV devices, to prevent wrong-route administration. Spoons are inaccurate for small paediatric volumes.

n.0: Altering a syringe does not remove the wrong-route risk and is unsafe practice.
n.1: A labelled Luer syringe can still be connected to an IV line, causing a wrong-route error.
n.2: A spoon is inaccurate for a measured paediatric dose and spills easily.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Sami, 2, is prescribed paracetamol oral suspension 180 mg. The stock suspension is 120 mg in 5 mL. What volume should the nurse give?
o: 3.3 mL
10 mL
5 mL
7.5 mL
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Volume = (dose required / stock strength) x stock volume = (180 / 120) x 5 mL = 7.5 mL.

n.0: 3.3 mL comes from inverting the calculation (120/180 x 5).
n.1: 10 mL contains 240 mg, an overdose of 60 mg.
n.2: 5 mL contains 120 mg, an under-dose.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Grace, 6, weighs 20 kg. Her chart shows a medicine prescribed at 15 mg/kg every 4 hours, six doses a day. The children's formulary states a maximum of 60 mg/kg in 24 hours for this medicine. What should the nurse do?
o: Query the prescription, as the daily total exceeds the maximum
Give four of the six doses so the daily total is correct
Give the doses 6-hourly, without contacting the prescriber
Give it as prescribed, as each single dose is within range
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Two steps: single dose 15 mg/kg x 20 kg = 300 mg; daily total 300 mg x 6 = 1800 mg = 90 mg/kg/day, above the 60 mg/kg/day maximum (1200 mg). The prescription must be queried with the prescriber before giving further doses.

n.1: Nurses cannot change the prescribed frequency themselves; the prescriber must amend it.
n.2: Changing the frequency without the prescriber is giving a medicine not as prescribed.
n.3: Each dose may be within range, but the 24-hour total of 90 mg/kg exceeds the maximum.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Finn, 8 months, is prescribed digoxin 62.5 micrograms orally. The stock is digoxin elixir 50 micrograms per mL. What volume should be given?
o: 0.8 mL
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Volume = 62.5 micrograms / 50 micrograms per mL = 1.25 mL. Keep dose and stock in the same unit (micrograms) to avoid ten-fold and thousand-fold errors.

n.0: 0.125 mL is a ten-fold under-dose.
n.2: 0.8 mL comes from inverting the calculation (50 / 62.5).
n.3: 12.5 mL is a ten-fold overdose from a decimal slip.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Kai, 16, weighs 92 kg. A medicine is prescribed at 10 mg/kg per dose, giving 920 mg. The usual adult dose is 500 mg. What should the nurse do?
o: Query it, as the dose is above the usual adult dose
Give 920 mg, as Kai is still under 18 years old
Give 500 mg and inform the prescriber after the dose
Give 920 mg, as his dose is calculated from his weight
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BNF for Children principle: a weight-calculated dose should not normally exceed the adult dose. A large adolescent's weight-based dose of 920 mg is almost double the adult dose, so the prescriber must review it before administration.

n.1: Being under 18 does not justify exceeding the adult dose in a 92 kg adolescent.
n.2: The nurse cannot give a dose other than that prescribed; the prescription must be amended first.
n.3: Weight-based calculation is capped at the adult dose in larger children; 920 mg exceeds it.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ruby, 7, has epilepsy and is prescribed a medicine at a dose outside its licence for her age. Her mother has read the leaflet in the box, which says the medicine is not recommended for children under 12, and she is worried. What is the best response from the nurse?
o: Explain that off-label use is common and evidence based in children
Explain that the nurse giving the medicine takes legal responsibility
Explain that the leaflet applies to adults and can be disregarded
Advise her to stop the medicine until a licensed product is found
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Off-label and unlicensed use is common and legitimate in paediatrics because few medicines are tested in children; it should be explained to parents and young people (NMC proficiency 4.16; NICE guidelines flag off-label use). Child-specific leaflets such as Medicines for Children can help.

n.1: The prescriber carries the responsibility for an off-label prescribing decision, though the nurse must understand the medicine.
n.2: The leaflet is accurate about the licence; dismissing it undermines trust instead of explaining off-label use.
n.3: Stopping an antiseizure medicine abruptly risks seizures; the prescriber has chosen it deliberately.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: A student nurse on a children's ward asks for an example of an UNLICENSED medicine, as opposed to an off-label one. Which example should the nurse give?
o: A licensed adult tablet prescribed for a child aged 8
An oral liquid 'special' made because no licensed liquid exists
A licensed IV antibiotic given at a higher dose than the licence
A licensed medicine used for a different indication
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: An unlicensed medicine has no UK marketing authorisation, such as a 'special' made by a manufacturing unit or an imported product. Off-label use is a licensed medicine used outside its licence (age, dose, route or indication).

n.0: A licensed tablet used outside its licensed age range is off-label, not unlicensed.
n.2: A licensed product given at an unlicensed dose is off-label use.
n.3: Using a licensed medicine for a different indication is off-label use.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Oliver, 10, has a fractured wrist. He has had paracetamol and ibuprofen and still has moderate pain. The new prescription is oral codeine phosphate. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the codeine, as the restriction applies to tonsillectomy
Give the codeine with a reduced first dose and monitor closely
Query the prescription, as codeine is restricted to children over 12
Give the codeine, as paracetamol and ibuprofen have not worked
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2013): codeine for analgesia restricted in children: codeine should be used for acute moderate pain only in children over 12 years and only when paracetamol or ibuprofen alone have not worked; younger children are excluded because of the risk of morphine toxicity, so the prescription must be queried.

n.0: The tonsillectomy contraindication is an additional restriction; under-12s are excluded as well.
n.1: The MHRA restricts codeine for pain to children over 12; a reduced first dose does not change that.
n.3: Failure of first-line analgesia allows codeine in children over 12; Oliver is 10.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: A parent asks why codeine is no longer given to young children for pain. Which explanation is correct?
o: Codeine is poorly absorbed from the gut in children under 12 years
Codeine is converted to an inactive drug in young children
Codeine causes Reye's syndrome in children under the age of 16
Some children convert it to morphine too quickly, causing toxicity
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2013): codeine for analgesia restricted in children: codeine is converted to morphine by the liver enzyme CYP2D6. Ultra-rapid metabolisers produce high morphine levels quickly, causing respiratory depression; deaths have occurred in children.

n.0: Codeine is absorbed in children; the danger is its variable conversion to morphine.
n.1: Codeine is a prodrug converted to active morphine; the problem is excess conversion.
n.2: Reye's syndrome is linked to aspirin, not codeine.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ella, 15, had a tonsillectomy this morning for obstructive sleep apnoea. Her pain is not controlled by paracetamol and ibuprofen and a junior doctor suggests oral codeine. What should the nurse say?
o: Codeine is contraindicated under 18 after tonsillectomy for sleep apnoea
Codeine is suitable at a reduced dose with continuous SpO2 monitoring
Codeine is suitable for her because she is now over 12 years of age
Codeine is suitable once she is eating and drinking after surgery
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2013): codeine for analgesia restricted in children: codeine is contraindicated in all children and young people under 18 who undergo tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea, because of the risk of fatal respiratory depression.

n.1: Monitoring and dose reduction do not remove a contraindication.
n.2: Being over 12 is not enough; the post-tonsillectomy OSA contraindication applies until 18.
n.3: Eating does not alter the contraindication.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Isla, 9, has a fever and a sore throat. At an urgent treatment centre her father says he gave her one of his aspirin tablets last night and asks if he can continue. What should the nurse advise?
o: Stop the aspirin and use paracetamol or ibuprofen if she is distressed
Continue the aspirin, as the restriction applies under 5s
Give the aspirin with food to protect her stomach
Continue the aspirin at half the adult dose until the fever settles
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Aspirin should not be given to children under 16 unless prescribed by a doctor (for example for Kawasaki disease) because of the risk of Reye's syndrome. NICE NG143: use paracetamol or ibuprofen if a febrile child is distressed.

n.1: The aspirin restriction applies to all children under 16, not only under 5s.
n.2: Food protects the stomach but does not address the Reye's syndrome risk.
n.3: A reduced dose does not remove the Reye's syndrome risk in under 16s.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Noah, 3, has Kawasaki disease after 6 days of fever, red palms and a strawberry tongue. He is prescribed IV immunoglobulin and oral aspirin. His mother says she was told children should not have aspirin. What should the nurse explain?
o: Aspirin is safe for him because he is over 2 years old
Kawasaki disease is a recognised reason to prescribe aspirin
The aspirin is a prescribing error and she should refuse it
Aspirin is used to bring down his fever more quickly
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Aspirin is not given to under 16s unless prescribed, with Kawasaki disease a recognised exception: it is prescribed with IV immunoglobulin to reduce inflammation and the risk of coronary artery complications (NHS Kawasaki disease guidance).

n.0: The under-16 restriction is not about being over 2; it applies to all children unless prescribed for a specific reason.
n.2: Aspirin is deliberately prescribed in Kawasaki disease; it is not an error.
n.3: Aspirin in Kawasaki disease reduces inflammation and clot risk in the coronary arteries; it is not used as an antipyretic.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Harry, 8, has a cough and cold. His mother asks a practice nurse whether she can give him a codeine-containing cough medicine left over from his older brother. What should the nurse advise?
o: Do not give it, as codeine is not used for cough under 12
Give it at night to help him sleep through the cough
Give half the amount given to his older brother
Give it, as codeine is effective for cough in children
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2015): codeine-containing medicines must not be used for cough and cold in children under 12, because of the risk of opioid toxicity and limited evidence of benefit.

n.1: Night-time use still exposes him to the opioid toxicity risk under 12.
n.2: A reduced amount does not make codeine appropriate under 12.
n.3: The MHRA found limited evidence that codeine is effective for cough in children.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ayesha, 5, weighs 18 kg and needs a red cell transfusion. The junior doctor writes the prescription as '1 unit red cells'. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the unit and record the volume given afterwards
Ask for it to be rewritten as a volume in millilitres
Give half the unit and return the rest to the laboratory
Give the whole unit, as one unit is the smallest available
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline) section 6.1.2: to prevent over-transfusion, paediatric blood components are prescribed in millilitres rather than units (unless a local risk-assessed protocol allows units for larger, older children), with the volume calculated from weight.

n.0: Recording afterwards does not prevent over-transfusion; the volume must be prescribed first.
n.2: The nurse cannot decide the volume; the prescriber must calculate and prescribe it in mL.
n.3: A whole adult unit (about 270 mL) may be about 15 mL/kg or more for an 18 kg child without any calculation; the prescription must state a volume.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Leo, 4, weighs 15 kg and is not bleeding. His Hb is 62 g/L. The team aims for a post-transfusion Hb of 90 g/L and uses the BSH formula with a factor of 4: volume (mL) = (desired Hb - actual Hb) x weight x 4 / 10. What volume of red cells should be prescribed?
o: 420 mL
168 mL
112 mL
300 mL
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline): (90 - 62) = 28 g/L; 28 x 15 x 4 = 1680; 1680 / 10 = 168 mL (about 11 mL/kg), below the 20 mL/kg top-up check.

n.0: 420 mL uses a factor of 10 instead of 4; it is 28 mL/kg and an over-transfusion.
n.2: 112 mL uses an Hb rise of about 19 g/L instead of 28 g/L.
n.3: 300 mL is a flat 20 mL/kg, the upper check limit, not the calculated volume.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Grace, 6, weighs 18 kg and is prescribed a top-up red cell transfusion of 450 mL. She is not bleeding. Before collecting the blood, what should the nurse do?
o: Give it, as larger volumes reduce donor exposure
Give it over 6 hours to reduce the risk of overload
Query the volume, as it is over 20 mL/kg for a top-up
Give it, as it is less than two adult units of red cells
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline): because Hb units changed to g/L, clinicians are asked to double-check that a calculated top-up volume is not more than 20 mL/kg. 450 mL / 18 kg = 25 mL/kg, so the prescription must be queried.

n.0: Reducing donor exposure does not justify transfusing above 20 mL/kg.
n.1: Slowing the rate does not correct an over-prescribed volume, and units must finish within 4 hours of removal from storage.
n.3: Comparison with adult units is not the paediatric check; 25 mL/kg exceeds the 20 mL/kg limit.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Sami, 8, weighs 24 kg and is prescribed 240 mL of red cells for a top-up transfusion. According to BSH paediatric guidance, what is the usual infusion rate?
o: 120 mL/h (5 mL/kg/h)
60 mL/h (2.5 mL/kg/h)
240 mL/h (10 mL/kg/h)
480 mL/h (20 mL/kg/h)
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline) Table I: red cell transfusion rate 5 mL/kg/h (usual maximum 150 mL/h). 5 x 24 = 120 mL/h, so 240 mL takes 2 hours, within the 4-hour limit.

n.1: 2.5 mL/kg/h is half the usual rate and prolongs the transfusion unnecessarily.
n.2: 10 mL/kg/h is double the usual red cell rate; 10-20 mL/kg/h is the rate for platelets and plasma.
n.3: 20 mL/kg/h is the upper rate for platelets or FFP, not red cells.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Mia, 10, is on the paediatric intensive care unit after an infection. She is stable, not bleeding and has no cyanotic heart disease. Her Hb is 76 g/L. The team asks whether she meets the BSH threshold for a red cell transfusion. What is the answer?
o: Yes, the usual threshold in stable children is 80 g/L
No, the usual threshold in stable children is 70 g/L
No, the usual threshold in stable children is 60 g/L
Yes, the usual threshold in stable children is 90 g/L
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline) section 3.2.1: use an Hb threshold of 70 g/L pre-transfusion in stable non-cyanotic children (1B); a higher threshold may be considered if unstable or symptomatic.

n.0: 80 g/L is not the BSH threshold for stable non-cyanotic children.
n.2: Mia does not need transfusion, but the BSH threshold is 70 g/L, not 60 g/L.
n.3: 90 g/L is a liberal threshold not supported for stable children.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Tom, 3, is about to start a red cell transfusion. At the bedside check, the nurse finds that he pulled off his identification wristband during the night. His mother is present and states his full name and date of birth. What should the nurse do?
o: Have a new wristband applied before completing the check
Proceed, as his mother has confirmed his identity verbally
Proceed, using the name label on the end of his cot
Tape the old wristband to his arm and proceed
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline) section 6.1.1 notes wristbands removed by children or parents as a cause of paediatric identification errors. The bedside check matches the wristband to the component and prescription; with no attached band the transfusion must not start until a new one is applied using verified details.

n.1: Verbal confirmation by a parent supplements but does not replace the attached wristband check.
n.2: Cot labels are not attached to the child and are not a valid identifier.
n.3: Reattaching a removed band breaks the secure identification chain; a new band should be generated.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Amir, 9 months, is 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion. He has become irritable and flushed. His temperature has risen from 36.9°C to 38.5°C and his heart rate from 130 to 175. What should the nurse do first?
o: Stop the transfusion, assess ABCDE and call the doctor urgently
Continue, as infants often become irritable during transfusions
Slow the transfusion and recheck observations in 30 minutes
Give paracetamol and continue the transfusion
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline) key practice point: monitoring is essential because infants cannot report symptoms. A temperature rise of this size with tachycardia early in a transfusion may signal a serious reaction; stop the transfusion, keep the line open, assess ABCDE and get urgent medical review (SHOT/BSH reaction guidance).

n.1: Irritability with fever and tachycardia must be treated as a possible reaction in an infant who cannot describe symptoms.
n.2: Slowing the rate does not stop exposure to a possibly incompatible component.
n.3: Paracetamol may mask fever and does not address a possible serious reaction.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ruby, 7 months, has anaemia and needs her first red cell transfusion. A newly qualified nurse asks which type of component the laboratory will issue for a child of her age. What does BSH recommend?
o: Red cells with neonatal or infant specification
A standard adult unit with half removed on the ward
Platelets with neonatal or infant specification
A standard adult unit, as she is older than 4 months
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (New et al, 2016; still the current BSH paediatric guideline): recipients under 1 year should be transfused with components of neonatal or infant specification (1C), such as paediatric 'paedipacks' or infant large-volume red cells.

n.1: Components are not split on the ward; the laboratory supplies suitable paediatric packs.
n.2: Platelets do not treat anaemia; red cells are needed.
n.3: The neonatal or infant specification applies to all recipients under 1 year, not just under 4 months.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Chloe, 14, is admitted to a general paediatric ward overnight after taking an overdose of paracetamol. She is medically stable on treatment. According to NICE NG225, which arrangement should be in place while she is on the ward?
o: Joint daily review by paediatric and children's mental health teams
A mental health review once she is medically fit for discharge
A weekly multidisciplinary meeting led by her GP and school nurse
Transfer to an adult mental health ward for assessment
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022) rec 1.7.24: children and young people admitted to a paediatric ward after self-harm should have 24-hour access to CAMHS/CYPMHS or age-appropriate liaison psychiatry, a joint daily review by paediatric and mental health teams, daily family access and regular MDT meetings.

n.1: Mental health input starts during the admission, with joint daily review, not at discharge.
n.2: NG225 specifies regular MDT meetings between the paediatric team and mental health services, not weekly GP-led meetings.
n.3: An adult ward is not age-appropriate; NG225 keeps her on the paediatric ward with CYPMHS input.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ryan, 15, attends the children's emergency department after cutting his arms. His wounds have been dressed. Who should carry out his psychosocial assessment, according to NICE NG225?
o: The GP, at a routine appointment within 2 weeks
A CYP mental health professional experienced in self-harm
The emergency department nurse, using a suicide risk scale
The school nurse, once he returns to school
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022): for children and young people, a mental health professional experienced in assessing children and young people who self-harm carries out the psychosocial assessment, offered as soon as possible after arrival via a crisis or liaison service. Risk scales must not be used to predict suicide or decide care.

n.0: Waiting for a routine GP appointment delays a specialist assessment that should be offered on arrival.
n.2: NG225 says do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict suicide or decide treatment.
n.3: School nurses support young people but do not replace a specialist psychosocial assessment after self-harm.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Amira, 13, is going home after an overdose of her mother's sertraline tablets. She has a safety plan agreed with the CAMHS team. Her mother asks what she can do at home to help keep Amira safe. What should the nurse advise?
o: Lock away or remove medicines and other means Amira could use
Check Amira's bedroom every 15 minutes through the night
Keep Amira off school until her CAMHS follow-up
Avoid talking with Amira about her self-harm to prevent ideas
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG225 Self-harm (2022): the safety plan should establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing them with the person and family; families are given information on reducing access to means and on getting help in a crisis.

n.1: Fifteen-minute night checks are not practical home advice and do not remove access to means.
n.2: Keeping her off school is not part of NG225 safety planning and can increase isolation.
n.3: Talking openly about self-harm does not plant ideas; avoiding it can increase isolation.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ella, 15, was diagnosed with mild depression 2 weeks ago and was offered watchful waiting. At review her low mood is unchanged. She has no suicidal ideas and no other mental health problems. What does NICE NG134 recommend now?
o: A further 6 weeks of watchful waiting before any treatment
A choice of psychological therapy, such as digital or group CBT
Referral for inpatient admission to a CAMHS unit
Fluoxetine started by the GP with review in 4 weeks
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG134 Depression in children and young people: for 12 to 18 year olds with mild depression continuing after 2 weeks of watchful waiting, without significant comorbidity or active suicidal ideas, offer a choice of psychological therapies (digital CBT, group CBT, group IPT or group NDST) for about 2 to 3 months.

n.0: Watchful waiting is for about 2 weeks; prolonging it delays effective treatment.
n.2: Inpatient care is for severe depression with high risk, not mild depression.
n.3: NG134 says antidepressant medication should not be used for the initial treatment of mild depression in children and young people.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Josh, 16, has moderate to severe depression and has not responded to 6 sessions of CBT. After multidisciplinary review he starts fluoxetine alongside continuing therapy. His mother asks how closely he will be monitored. What does NICE NG134 suggest?
o: A review at 6 weeks, when the medicine will be fully effective
Weekly contact with Josh and his parents for the first 4 weeks
Monthly contact for 3 months, then 3-monthly reviews
A review when he next attends his CBT session
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG134 Depression in children and young people: antidepressants for moderate to severe depression are offered in combination with a concurrent psychological therapy, and specific arrangements are made for careful monitoring of adverse reactions and mental state, for example weekly contact with the young person and parents for the first 4 weeks.

n.0: Six weeks is too long to wait, because suicidal thoughts and agitation can emerge early in treatment.
n.2: Monthly contact is less frequent than NG134 suggests for the first 4 weeks.
n.3: Therapy sessions alone do not provide the specific monitoring for adverse drug reactions.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Mia, 14, has lost 6 kg in 3 months by restricting food and exercising heavily. Her BMI centile is still within the normal range. Her mother asks the school nurse whether Mia is ill enough to be referred. What is the best response?
o: Monitor her weight monthly at school for 6 months
Refer her now; a normal BMI does not rule out an eating disorder
Refer her once she has missed three menstrual periods
Wait until her BMI centile has fallen below the 2nd centile
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG69 Eating disorders: do not use single measures such as BMI or duration of illness to determine whether to offer treatment; rapid weight loss with restriction and over-exercise warrants referral to a community eating disorder service.

n.0: Months of monitoring delays assessment of a rapidly progressing eating disorder.
n.2: Amenorrhoea is not required for diagnosis or referral, and waiting delays treatment.
n.3: Waiting for a low BMI ignores NG69 and allows dangerous weight loss to continue.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Leah, 13, has been diagnosed with anorexia nervosa and will be treated in the community. Her parents ask which treatment is usually considered first for young people with anorexia. What does NICE NG69 recommend?
o: Admission to an inpatient unit for weight restoration
Individual psychodynamic therapy without family involvement
Anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-AN)
An SSRI antidepressant as the main treatment
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG69 Eating disorders rec 1.3.10: consider anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-AN) for children and young people, delivered as single-family therapy or single- and multi-family therapy, with the option of some single-family sessions.

n.0: Inpatient admission is for severe physical compromise that cannot be managed in outpatients, not routine first-line care.
n.1: Individual therapy is an alternative if FT-AN is unsuitable or ineffective; family therapy is the first consideration.
n.3: Medication is not the main treatment for anorexia nervosa.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Sophie, 15, has severe anorexia nervosa and has been admitted to a paediatric ward for medical stabilisation and refeeding. Which blood result is the priority to monitor closely in the first days of refeeding?
o: Serum cholesterol
HbA1c
Serum phosphate
Serum amylase
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG69 Eating disorders and RCPsych MEED guidance (2022): staff must recognise and manage refeeding syndrome, in which phosphate (with potassium and magnesium) falls as feeding restarts, risking cardiac and respiratory failure; electrolytes are monitored closely in the first days.

n.0: Cholesterol may be abnormal in anorexia but does not signal refeeding syndrome.
n.1: HbA1c reflects glucose control over months and does not detect refeeding syndrome.
n.3: Amylase does not reflect the electrolyte shifts of refeeding syndrome.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ethan, 7, is autistic and is admitted for elective surgery tomorrow. His father says Ethan becomes very distressed by noise, bright lights and unexpected changes. Which plan best reflects reasonable adjustments for Ethan?
o: A bay near the nurses' station so staff can observe him closely
A quiet side room, visual timetable and his father's routines
Admission to the general paediatric bay with other children
Sedation on arrival so that he does not become distressed
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: The Equality Act 2010 (s20) requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people, including autistic children. Adjustments include a quiet environment, preparation with visual supports, predictable routines and using the family's knowledge of the child (NG213 person-centred care; NHS reasonable adjustment guidance).

n.0: A busy area near the nurses' station increases noise, light and interruptions that distress Ethan.
n.2: A busy general bay increases sensory overload and unpredictability.
n.3: Routine sedation is a restrictive intervention that does not address his needs and needs a clinical indication.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ava, 9, is autistic and does not use speech. She uses a picture symbol book. Before a blood test, the nurse wants to prepare her. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Do the test quickly without explanation to avoid anxiety
Use her symbol book to show each step, at her own pace
Give her a written leaflet about blood tests to read
Explain the procedure verbally to her parents only
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Communication should be adapted to the child's preferred format (NG213 rec 1.1.17; Annexe A communication skills), using augmentative and alternative communication such as symbols, with preparation and time to process each step.

n.0: Proceeding without explanation increases fear and distress for an autistic child.
n.2: A written leaflet does not match Ava's preferred communication format.
n.3: Talking only to parents excludes Ava from information about her own care.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: A parent asks the children's community nurse what an education, health and care (EHC) plan is. Which explanation is correct?
o: An NHS continuing care plan funded by the integrated care board
A legal plan from the local authority setting out needs and support up to 25
A hospital care plan written by the consultant for a child's admissions
A school behaviour plan agreed between teachers and parents
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: SEND Code of Practice: 0 to 25 years (2015) and Children and Families Act 2014: an EHC plan is a legal document issued by the local authority describing a child or young person's special educational needs and the education, health and social care provision to meet them, from birth to 25.

n.0: Continuing care is a separate NHS assessment, although it can inform the EHC plan.
n.2: EHC plans are issued by the local authority, not written by hospital consultants.
n.3: A school behaviour plan has no statutory status and does not cover health and social care.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Liam, 6, has cerebral palsy and complex health needs. His parents requested an EHC needs assessment and the local authority agreed to assess. They ask how long the whole process should take. What should the nurse tell them?
o: No more than 6 weeks from request to final plan
No more than 20 weeks from request to final plan
No more than 40 weeks from request to final plan
No more than 12 months from request to final plan
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: SEND Code of Practice: 0 to 25 years (2015), para 9.40, issued under the Children and Families Act 2014: the whole process, from the request for an EHC needs assessment to issuing the final plan, must take no more than 20 weeks, subject to limited exceptions. The local authority decides whether to assess within 6 weeks.

n.0: Six weeks is the deadline for deciding whether to carry out an assessment, not for issuing the plan.
n.2: Forty weeks is double the statutory limit.
n.3: Twelve months is far longer than the statutory limit.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Noah, 12, is autistic and has a learning disability. He has been banging his head and is more distressed than usual for two days. Staff at his school say it is 'just his autism'. What should the community children's nurse do first?
o: Increase his behaviour support plan and review in a month
Assess for a physical cause such as toothache or constipation
Advise the school to use a helmet and continue as usual
Refer him to CAMHS for a medication review
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Diagnostic overshadowing (attributing new behaviour to a person's autism or learning disability) leads to missed physical illness. A change in behaviour may communicate pain or illness, so a physical assessment comes first (P3.7: recognise complex needs; NHS reasonable adjustments).

n.0: Changing the behaviour plan without assessment risks missing a treatable physical cause.
n.2: A helmet protects him but does not find the cause of a new change in behaviour.
n.3: Medication review comes after physical causes have been excluded.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Practitioners are writing the section of Maya's EHC plan that records her views. Maya, 14, has cerebral palsy and communicates with an eye-gaze device. How should her views be recorded, according to NICE NG213?
o: In professional language so the plan is clear to services
As a summary by her teacher, who knows her well
In her own words through her device, without rewriting them
As a summary of her views written by her parents
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG213 Disabled children and young people up to 25 with severe complex needs (2022, updated 2023) rec 1.4.13: preserve the child or young person's voice: use their preferred communication format, use their own words (or the equivalent if they do not communicate verbally) and do not rewrite what they have said; rec 1.4.8 makes clear which parts are their contributions.

n.0: Rewriting Maya's views in professional language loses her voice, which NG213 says not to do.
n.1: A teacher's summary replaces Maya's own words with another person's interpretation.
n.3: Parents' views are recorded too, but they do not replace Maya's own contribution.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Freya, 10, has complex needs and a gastrostomy. Her school wants teaching assistants to give her feeds. According to NICE NG213, what should be in place before staff carry out this delegated clinical task?
o: Written consent from Freya's parents for each feed given
A registered nurse present in school for every feed
Parents attending school to give every feed themselves
Training and assessed competence for the staff giving feeds
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG213 Disabled children and young people up to 25 with severe complex needs (2022, updated 2023): people carrying out delegated clinical tasks should be trained and assessed as competent, and the EHC plan should state who is responsible for providing support and the level of expertise needed (recs 1.4.11 and 1.15.24-1.15.25).

n.0: Per-feed written consent is not required; the agreed plan and competence of staff are what matter.
n.1: Delegated tasks are designed so trained, competent non-registered staff can carry them out.
n.2: Requiring parents to attend for every feed would restrict Freya's education and family life.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Oscar, 8, is autistic and is distressed in the outpatient waiting area, covering his ears and rocking. His appointment is in 40 minutes. What reasonable adjustment should the nurse offer?
o: A quiet room to wait in until the clinician is ready
Move him to the front of the queue ahead of urgent cases
Rebook the appointment for another day
Ask his parents to calm him so he does not upset others
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Reasonable adjustments (Equality Act 2010 s20) for autistic children include reducing sensory overload and waiting, such as a quiet waiting space or a call when the clinician is ready, so the child can attend the appointment.

n.1: Clinical priority is still based on need; pushing ahead of urgent cases is not a reasonable adjustment.
