n.2: Rebooking delays his care when a simple adjustment would allow the appointment.
n.3: Leaving his family to manage his distress places the burden on them and ignores the duty to adjust.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Jordan, 12, has cystic fibrosis and is in Year 7. His mother asks the children's CF nurse when they should start planning his move to adult services. What does NICE NG43 recommend?
o: From his 16th birthday
From Year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest
Once the adult team accepts the referral
In the 6 months before his 18th birthday
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.2.1: start planning for adulthood from Year 9 (age 13 or 14) at the latest, or immediately if a young person enters children's services close to the point of transfer.

n.0: Sixteen is later than NG43 advises; planning starts by Year 9.
n.2: Planning starts long before referral; it prepares the young person for the move.
n.3: Six months before 18 is far too late for gradual, developmentally appropriate planning.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Aisha, 17, has type 1 diabetes and is due to move to the adult diabetes clinic next month. She has just had two admissions with DKA and her parents have separated. Her children's diabetes nurse is reviewing the transfer date. What does NICE NG43 advise?
o: Transfer her now so adult services manage the DKA
Transfer her on her 18th birthday as planned
Time the transfer for a period of relative stability
Delay transfer until she is 25 years old
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.2.3: transition planning is developmentally appropriate; the point of transfer should not be based on a rigid age threshold and should take place at a time of relative stability for the young person.

n.0: Transferring during a crisis increases the risk of disengagement and further DKA.
n.1: A rigid age threshold is not the basis for transfer; Aisha is currently unstable.
n.3: There is no NG43 rule to wait until 25; the timing depends on readiness and stability.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ben, 15, has epilepsy and is preparing to move to adult services. He sees a different nurse at almost every clinic and says he never knows who to ask for help. Which NG43 recommendation addresses this?
o: Give him a named worker to coordinate his care
Ask his GP to take over his care until transfer
Give his parents a phone number for the adult ward
Ask him to attend adult A&E if he has any concerns
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016): a named worker coordinates care and transition support, links the young person with the practitioners involved (including the GP) and hands over to someone in adults' services.

n.1: The GP is involved, but NG43 gives coordination to a named worker, not a handover of all care.
n.2: An adult ward number does not coordinate care before transfer or support Ben himself.
n.3: Using A&E for queries is not transition support.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Leah, 16, has juvenile idiopathic arthritis. At her clinic appointment her mother always answers for her. Leah says she wants to manage her own condition. What should the nurse do to support her transition?
o: Offer Leah time with the team without her parents present
Ask her mother to stay away from future appointments
Continue directing questions to her mother until Leah is 18
Arrange for Leah to start attending the adult clinic now
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) recs 1.2.19-1.2.21: ask the young person how they want parents involved and help them develop confidence by giving them the chance to raise concerns separately from parents, while respecting the parents' role.

n.1: Excluding her mother entirely ignores Leah's own preferences and the family's role.
n.2: Waiting until 18 ignores Leah's wishes and her developing independence.
n.3: Transfer timing is planned, not triggered by one consultation; this skips preparation.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ravi, 17, has a rare metabolic condition and is moving to adult services. The children's team want to reduce his anxiety about meeting new staff. Which action does NICE NG43 recommend before transfer?
o: His parents visit the adult clinic on his behalf
He is discharged to his GP until the adult clinic writes
A practitioner from adult services meets him before transfer
He is sent the adult clinic address with his first appointment
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.3.1: service managers ensure a practitioner from the relevant adult service meets the young person before transfer, for example through joint appointments or joint clinics.

n.0: Parents visiting does not let Ravi meet the team or make his own informed choices.
n.1: Discharge to the GP creates a gap in specialist care rather than a managed transfer.
n.3: Sending an address does not introduce him to the adult team as NG43 recommends.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ellie, 18, moved to the adult cystic fibrosis service three months ago and has not attended her last two appointments. The adult team cannot reach her by phone. What does NICE NG43 advise?
o: Discharge her back to the GP as she has not engaged
Try to contact Ellie and family, follow up and involve the GP
Refer her back to children's services as she is not ready
Send her a letter and wait for her to rebook
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.4.1: if a young person does not attend or engage after transfer, adult health and social care, working within safeguarding protocols, should try to contact the young person and family, follow them up and involve other professionals including the GP.

n.0: Discharging after non-attendance leaves a young person with a serious condition without specialist care.
n.2: NG43 rec 1.4.2 refers a young person who does not engage back to the named worker, not to children's services.
n.3: A letter and passive wait does not meet the active follow-up NG43 requires.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Tom, 17, has complex needs and does not meet the criteria for any specialist adult health service. His children's team is planning his transition. Whose involvement does NICE NG43 describe as critical?
o: The local pharmacy
His GP
The adult A&E department
His school SENCO
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.3.9: if a young person does not meet the criteria for specialist adult health services, involving the GP in transition planning is absolutely critical.

n.0: The pharmacy supplies medicines but does not take on ongoing care coordination.
n.2: A&E provides emergency care, not ongoing coordination.
n.3: The SENCO supports education, but NG43 names the GP as critical where no adult specialist service exists.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Sara, 16, has congenital heart disease and will move to adult services in about a year. Her named worker suggests preparing something to share with the adult team. What does NICE NG43 suggest?
o: A copy of her full paediatric medical notes for her to carry
A letter from her parents describing her condition and needs
A list of her medicines printed by the pharmacy
A personal folder in her own format, such as a one-page profile
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG43 Transition from children's to adults' services (2016) rec 1.3.3: consider creating with the young person a personal folder in their preferred format to share with adults' services, for example with a one-page profile, condition information, preferences about parent involvement, emergency plans and goals.

n.0: Full notes are transferred between services; NG43's folder is a personal summary she owns and shapes.
n.1: A parental letter replaces Sara's own voice and preferences.
n.2: A medicines list is useful but does not cover the personal information NG43 describes.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Lily, 6, has a life-limiting neurodegenerative condition. A newly qualified nurse sees 'Advance Care Plan' in her notes and assumes this means Lily is not for resuscitation. What should the nurse in charge explain?
o: An Advance Care Plan is the same document as a DNACPR order
An Advance Care Plan is a legal order made by the family court
An Advance Care Plan applies once Lily is in the last days of life
An Advance Care Plan covers wishes and care; it is not a DNACPR order
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.2.14: all children with life-limiting conditions should have an Advance Care Plan in their record (wishes, place of care, management of life-threatening events) and it should not be confused with a do-not-attempt-resuscitation order. Resuscitate unless a DNACPR order is in place.

n.0: NG61 says the Advance Care Plan should not be confused with a DNACPR order.
n.1: An Advance Care Plan is agreed with the child and family and the team, not made by a court.
n.2: Advance Care Planning starts early and is reviewed regularly, not only in the last days.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Sophie is 22 weeks pregnant. A scan has shown that her baby has a life-limiting condition and she plans to continue the pregnancy. When does NICE NG61 advise that discussions about an Advance Care Plan should begin?
o: After the baby reaches 28 days old and leaves neonatal care
During the pregnancy, with the right professionals involved
Once the baby has been born and assessed by a neonatologist
When the baby is first admitted to hospital after birth
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions: begin discussing an Advance Care Plan with parents during the pregnancy if there is an antenatal diagnosis of a life-limiting condition, considering who should take part (for example obstetric, neonatal and palliative care teams).

n.0: Waiting four weeks after birth misses planning for birth and the neonatal period.
n.2: Waiting until birth leaves no plan in place for decisions at delivery.
n.3: A first admission may be an emergency, which is too late for planning.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ahmed, 9, has a life-limiting condition and is seen by neurology, respiratory, gastroenterology and the community team. His parents say they do not know who is in charge of his care. What does NICE NG61 recommend?
o: A named medical specialist who leads on and coordinates his care
His GP coordinates his care, as he is seen by several teams
His parents choose which consultant to contact for each problem
The specialist who saw him most recently leads his care
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.2.2: every child with a life-limiting condition should have a named medical specialist who leads on and coordinates their care; explain that this person may change if the care needed or setting changes.

n.1: The GP is involved, but NG61 names a medical specialist as care lead.
n.2: Leaving parents to coordinate between consultants is what NG61 seeks to avoid.
n.3: Leadership by whoever saw him last gives no consistent coordination.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ruby, 11, is approaching the end of life with cancer and weighs 22 kg, much less than average for her age. The team is starting oral morphine. How should the dose be calculated, according to NICE NG61?
o: By the adult dose, as she is over 10 years old
By weight, as she is underweight for her age
By age, using the 11-year-old dose band
By her weight before she became unwell
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.3.32: calculate opioid dosages for children and young people approaching the end of life using weight rather than age, because they may be underweight for their age.

n.0: Adult doses are not appropriate for a 22 kg child.
n.2: An age-band dose may overdose a child who is underweight for her age.
n.3: Her previous weight no longer reflects her current body mass and would overdose her.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Leo, 8, has background oral morphine for end of life pain. He also has 2 anticipatory doses before daily dressing changes and needed 2 breakthrough doses yesterday. The team is reviewing his daily background dose. Which doses should be left out of that calculation?
o: Both the anticipatory and breakthrough doses
The anticipatory doses before dressing changes
The regular background doses
The breakthrough doses given yesterday
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.3.31: consider anticipatory doses for predictable pain (dressings, moving and handling), and do not include anticipatory doses when calculating the required daily background dose. Breakthrough use informs titration of background analgesia (1.3.30).

n.0: Breakthrough doses should be considered; only anticipatory doses are excluded.
n.2: The regular background doses are the basis of the calculation.
n.3: Breakthrough doses show uncontrolled pain and inform titration of the background dose.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Grace, 7, is dying at a children's hospice. She takes small sips of water but can no longer drink much. Her parents ask whether she needs a drip. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Start IV fluids now, as dying children need full hydration to be comfortable
Support sips and mouth care; discuss if a drip is in her best interests
Stop offering drinks, as sipping fluids may cause her more discomfort
Pass a nasogastric tube so she can have full maintenance fluids
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions recs 1.3.48-1.3.51: encourage and support the child to drink if she wants to and is able, continue lip and mouth care, and discuss with the family whether enteral or IV fluids are in her best interests, as they may be a burden and may change the place of care.

n.0: NG61 says IV fluids may be a burden for a dying child; starting them is a best interests decision, not routine.
n.2: NG61 says encourage and support drinking if she wants to and is able.
n.3: A nasogastric tube is a best interests decision discussed with the family, not routine.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Noah, 4, is in the last days of life on a children's ward. His breathing has become irregular and noisy, his hands and feet are cold and mottled and he has stopped feeding. His parents ask why the nurse is not taking blood pressure every hour. What should the nurse explain?
o: He may die within days; gentle, non-invasive checks keep him comfortable
Observations are stopped because Noah no longer needs nursing care
Hourly blood pressure will now restart so that any change is detected
These signs are a reaction to his medicines, which will be stopped
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions rec 1.3.57: changes in breathing pattern, impaired peripheral perfusion and loss of interest in food or drink are common in the last hours or days of life; monitor these non-invasively as far as possible while continuing comfort care.

n.1: Nursing care continues; it is focused on comfort rather than routine observations.
n.2: Hourly blood pressure disturbs a dying child and does not change his care; NG61 advises monitoring the signs of dying non-invasively as far as possible.
n.3: These are recognised signs of approaching death, not a medicine reaction.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Ella, 13, is on a children's ward and may die within the next day or two. Her Advance Care Plan records that she wants to die at home, and her parents ask whether this is still possible. What should the team do?
o: Transfer her to a hospice, as homes are unsuitable
Consider a rapid transfer home, updating the plan with her family
Keep her on the ward, as the plan cannot change now
Explain that transfer is not possible once a child is this unwell
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE NG61 End of life care for infants, children and young people with life-limiting conditions recs 1.3.15-1.3.19: if a child may die soon and is not in their preferred place of death, think about whether rapid transfer is possible and in their best interests, discuss it with them and their family, and update the Advance Care Plan.

n.0: Ella's preferred place is home; a hospice is not a substitute unless she and her family choose it.
n.2: The Advance Care Plan is updated as wishes and circumstances change.
n.3: NG61 supports rapid transfer to the preferred place of death where possible and in her best interests.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Baby Zainab was born at 39 weeks and is 18 hours old on the postnatal ward. During a feed her mother notices her skin and eyes look yellow. The nurse confirms visible jaundice. What should happen next?
o: Serum bilirubin measured within 6 hours if still yellow
Reassurance that this is normal physiological jaundice
Transcutaneous bilirubin measured at the 24-hour check
Serum bilirubin measured within 2 hours and medical review
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days (updated 2023) recs 1.2.10-1.2.12: jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proved otherwise; measure serum bilirubin urgently (within 2 hours) and arrange urgent medical review (within 6 hours). Serum, not transcutaneous, measurement is used in the first 24 hours.

n.0: Within 6 hours is the timeframe for babies more than 24 hours old; Zainab is 18 hours old.
n.1: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is not physiological; it may signal haemolysis or infection.
n.2: Transcutaneous measurement is not used in the first 24 hours (rec 1.2.15), and waiting delays an urgent test.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Leo was born at 40 weeks and is now 16 days old. He is breastfed and still looks jaundiced. His mother says his stools have become pale and chalky and his urine darkens the nappy. What should the health visitor do?
o: Arrange same-day medical assessment, including conjugated bilirubin
Reassure her that breast milk jaundice can last up to 12 weeks
Advise stopping breastfeeding for 48 hours to see if it fades
Advise placing Leo near a sunny window for short periods
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days (updated 2023) rec 1.7.1: jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby (21 days if preterm) needs assessment for pale chalky stools and dark urine, and measurement of conjugated bilirubin. Pale stools and dark urine suggest conjugated jaundice such as biliary atresia, which needs urgent specialist referral.

n.1: Breast milk jaundice does not cause pale stools and dark urine; these suggest liver disease.
n.2: CG98 advises that breastfeeding can usually continue; stopping it does not investigate the cause.
n.3: CG98 says do not use sunlight as treatment for jaundice.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: A children's nurse is checking Kofi, 3 days old, for jaundice. Kofi has dark brown skin and the ward lighting is dim. Which approach does NICE CG98 recommend?
o: Check the colour of his palms and soles under the ward lights
Rely on his mother's report, as jaundice is hard to see on his skin
Use an icterometer held against his nose to grade the jaundice
Look at sclerae, gums and blanched skin in bright natural light
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: NICE CG98 Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days (updated 2023): check the naked baby in bright and preferably natural light, examine the sclerae and gums and press lightly on the skin to look for jaundice in blanched skin. Do not use an icterometer.

n.0: Dim ward light and palms and soles alone miss jaundice; CG98 specifies bright natural light, sclerae, gums and blanched skin.
n.1: Jaundice can be detected on darker skin using sclerae, gums and blanched skin; parental report alone is unsafe.
n.2: CG98 says do not use an icterometer to measure bilirubin.

Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.q: Baby Grace, born at term, is admitted to a children's ward at 2 days old for observation. Her axillary temperature is 36.0°C. She is alert, pink and feeding well, and her mother is with her. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Undress her under a fan heater directed at the cot
Place a hot water bottle in the cot beside her
Bath her in warm water to raise her temperature quickly
Skin-to-skin with her mother in a warm, draught-free room
Neonates, Medicines and Specialist Care.w: Thermoregulation in newborns (BAPM framework: neonatal hypoglycaemia in the full-term infant (January 2024, corrected September 2024) practice point 8; neonatal care principles): newborns lose heat quickly by evaporation, conduction, convection and radiation. Dry the baby, use a hat, place skin-to-skin with the parent and keep the room warm and draught-free, then recheck temperature.

n.0: Undressing increases heat loss, and a directed fan heater risks burns and convective loss.
n.1: Hot water bottles risk burns and are not used to warm newborns.
n.2: Bathing increases evaporative heat loss once the baby is out of the water.
